### paperscope:gap:28 — 首轮并行覆盖后结束；不能把省轮全归于社区

**问题：** I’m building a multi-modal product: a real-time detector that links hands/face to the correct person in crowded scenes (COCO-like), a text-to-image module that uses a diffusion prior but must respect user prompts via posterior sampling, and an online safety layer that keeps the miscoverage rate under control while labeling only a small MNIST/CIFAR-100-sized stream. I also need my time-series controller to train stably (considering E/I-style constraints and spectral regularization) and I plan to fine-tune large backbones with End-to-end LoRA. Gold 1：

> {'answer': '- PBADet (one-stage anchor-free part–body association)\n  - Requires accurate detection of both body and part boxes; the association step (“choose the unassigned body that encloses the part and is nearest to the predicted body center”) fails if the body is missed or heavily occluded. This dependence on NMS-filtered detections and enclosure constraints is explicit in their decoding procedure.\n  - Benefit over body-to-part methods is limited when there is only a single part to associate per body (e.g., face–body on CrowdHuman); the paper notes its advantage is “not as pronounced” in such single-part settings.\n  - Multiple dataset-specific knobs must be tuned (e.g., distinct NMS IoU/conf thresholds per dataset; scaling factor λ for center offsets; top‑K anchor selection, α/β task-alignment exponents, loss weights), as detailed in the implementation and ablation sections. This introduces hyperparameter sensitivity.\n  - Gains rely on TOOD-style task-alignment and multi-scale supervision; removing either component degrades performance in ablations, indicating sensitivity to these design choices.\n\n- Relative Trajectory Balance (RTB) for amortized posterior sampling under diffusion priors\n  - Training is simulation-based on full denoising trajectories; the authors explicitly state it can be slow and memory‑intensive. They introduce stochastic subsampling and batched gradient tricks to cope with memory, which implies practical training burdens.\n  - The loss provides no local (per‑step) credit assignment; gradients are taken from a trajectory-level residual, leading to high-variance updates acknowledged by the authors.\n  - Asymptotic unbiasedness assumes idealized conditions; the paper notes there are “no guarantees” yet on errors from imperfect prior fit, amortization, and time discretization—important gaps for practical deployments.\n  - Stability depends on the quality of the prior and on heuristics (e.g., loss clipping, VarGrad-style normalization, inductive biases). These are introduced to mitigate sensitivity to imperfect priors but may themselves become tuning points.\n\n- Active, anytime-valid risk-controlling prediction sets (RCPS)\n  - The anytime-valid guarantees are developed under an i.i.d. streaming setting; the authors highlight extension to distribution shift as future work. Current results do not cover common shift patterns without additional assumptions.\n  - The active-labeling theory relies on a lower bound on the label probability (Assumption 2) and the existence of an optimal policy of a prescribed form (Proposition 5). The paper explicitly calls these out as limitations and notes removing them would need more analysis.\n  - Utility hinges on quality of the predictor r̂(x,β); the authors show poor predictors inflate variance and slow wealth growth, reducing label efficiency and delaying convergence to safe β.\n  - Performance/regret guarantees require tuning and maintaining a betting schedule (λ) within bounds and often an online learner (e.g., ONS) to control regret—additional moving parts that affect practical robustness.\n\n- JEPA (deep linear self-distillation) implicit-bias analysis\n  - The main theoretical results depend on restrictive assumptions: deep linear encoders, special orthogonal initializations, and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances (Σxx and Σyx). The paper clearly states these constraints and that generalization to nonlinear/realistic regimes remains open.\n  - The beneficial bias (prioritizing “influential” features with large regression coefficients) depends strongly on encoder depth; with shallow encoders the effect largely disappears, limiting robustness across architectures.\n  - The same bias can make JEPA gravitate toward low-variance or “slow” features, which the authors note may render JEPA vulnerable to spurious/slow signals in some settings.\n\n- EI RNNs under Dale’s Law: ColEI vs. DANN (spectral perspective)\n  - Column EI (ColEI) RNNs exhibit “spectral pathology”: multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra with large singular values, causing unstable learning (exploding/vanishing gradients), high variance across seeds, and heavy reliance on gradient clipping. The paper documents these instabilities and sensitivity.\n  - ColEI performance degrades markedly in small networks and when the inhibitory fraction is small (biologically plausible E/I ratios). The authors show worse spectra and learning in these regimes.\n  - Even when the spectral radius is constrained, ColEI can retain large singular values; performance depends on careful radius choice and remains fragile.\n  - DANN RNNs alleviate many issues (spectra closer to standard RNNs) but still rely on sign-constrained parameterizations and special initializations; the study is largely empirical on benchmark tasks and does not provide guarantees for broader architectures or data regimes.\n\nCross-cutting practical constraints noted across papers\n  - Heavy reliance on dataset/task-specific hyperparameters (e.g., NMS thresholds, scaling factors, loss weights in PBADet; temperature/reward weights or LoRA configs and step counts in RTB/T2I; labeling budgets, λ schedules in RCPS) implies nontrivial tuning burdens.\n  - Many results depend on pretraining/backbone quality (YOLO-family backbones for PBADet; Stable Diffusion or diffusion LMs for RTB; behavior priors in offline RL), making end performance sensitive to the base model rather than only the proposed algorithm.'}

**naive 最终答案**

> Yes — the collection covers every requested area, though one topic ("End-to-end LoRA") only appears as LoRA fine-tuning studied indirectly. Papers and their development defects:
> 
> **1. Anchor-free part–body association — PBADet (ICLR 2024)**
> One-stage, anchor-free hand/face–body association via a single part-to-body center offset; evaluated on COCO-like datasets (COCO-WholeBody, COCO-HumanParts, CrowdHuman, WiderFace).
> Defects: advantage over BPJDet shrinks on the single-part (face–body) CrowdHuman task; ablation shows performance drops without multi-scale center offsets and task-alignment learning; qualitative results show unreliable part predictions for limbs (legs/arms), especially under occlusion, which clouds body–part association.
> 
> **2. Amortized inference for diffusion models — RTB (NeurIPS 2024), plus Universal Guidance & AdjointDEIS**
> RTB (Reward Trajectory Balance) trains diffusion models to sample posteriors under diffusion priors, including fine-tuning Stable Diffusion for text-to-image.
> Defects: simulation-based training is slow and memory-intensive; the objective is computed on complete trajectories without local credit assignment, causing high gradient variance; no guarantees on error from imperfect prior fit, amortization, or time discretization; reward-vs-diversity tradeoff; discrete-diffusion infilling was limited by a weak prior and reward models favoring repetitions (~3000 GPU-hours total). Universal Guidance defects: slower generation, per-network hyperparameter tuning, requires differentiable guidance. AdjointDEIS: face-morphing-only evaluation, limited hyperparameter search, SDE step-size sensitivity.
> 
> **3. Active anytime-valid risk control — "Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets" (NeurIPS 2024)**
> Extends RCPS to sequential, actively-labeled streams with e-processes/betting; guarantees miscoverage risk ≤ θ at all times with prob ≥ 1−α under a label budget.
> Defects: relies on an i.i.d. assumption, a bounded label-policy assumption, and an existence assumption in Proposition 5; authors note stronger guarantees would need covariate/label-shift modeling; violation-rate control is finite-sample but bounded by the betting wealth process.
> 
> **4. Self-supervised training prioritizing useful features over noise — LDReg & "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"**
> LDReg regularizes local intrinsic dimensionality to counter dimensional collapse. The JEPA paper shows JEPA self-distillation is biased toward high-influence features and suppresses noise vs MAE.
> Defects (LDReg): LID estimation degrades in high dimensions and relies on minibatch nearest neighbors; forcing very low LID triggers complete collapse. Defects (JEPA): analysis assumes deep linear MLPs, special initialization, and simultaneous diagonalizability; generalization is only qualitative.
> 
> **5. Time-series/controller stability with E/I constraints and spectral regularization — "Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly" (NeurIPS 2023)**
> Shows E/I (ColEI) RNNs train poorly due to multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra, not sign constraints; normalised SVD entropy predicts performance; gradient clipping stabilizes.
> Defects: ColEI networks show high training variance and are highly unstable without gradient clipping; small networks with skewed E:I ratios learn less effectively; open questions remain on the origin of the multimodal spectra and why large ColEI networks learn well despite a large maximum singular value.
> 
> **6. End-to-end LoRA fine-tuning of large backbones**
> No paper proposes exactly this; LoRA appears only as a technique: "Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure" fine-tunes TinyLlama with LoRA and finds the power-law Hessian structure does **not** emerge with LoRA-only fine-tuning as with full fine-tuning, suggesting different (weaker) generalization dynamics; Themis fine-tunes Vicuna-7B with LoRA; NFTS searches adapter placement per layer.
> Defects noted: LoRA has minimal impact on the Hessian structure of the pretrained model; Hessian-based analysis excludes SOTA LLMs due to cost; NFTS's per-layer adapter decisions are complex and its N=3 ensemble is best only empirically.
> 
> **7. Practical guidance: SGD/Adam, cosine similarity, F1/AUROC**
> - SGD/Adam: Hessian paper compares SGD, Adam, AMSGrad, RAdam, etc. (all produce the power-law spectrum; large-batch training destroys it); 4-bit AdamW matches 32-bit on LLaMA fine-tuning (quantization may be task-dependent); the contrastive-learning paper gives concrete SGD recipes (cosine decay, linear warmup, momentum 0.9, weight decay); the coarse-graining paper discusses Adam/AdaGrad for slow-mode disparity.
> - Cosine similarity: used in contrastive embedding analysis (negative-pair similarity bounds; variance-reduction loss), NFTS prototypical loss via cosine distance, and cosine LR schedules.
> - F1/AUROC: PBADet reports precision/recall/F1 vs ED-Pose; DiffusionFake uses AUC and EER (AUC = probability a positive ranks above a negative); TuCo uses AUC for jailbreak discrimination; graph-FM and Synthcity benchmarks use ROC-AUC. HASSOD provides a caution: AP can mislead class-agnostic detectors, advocating AR instead.
> 
> **Overarching development-defect pattern across these methods:** most are validated only on narrow benchmarks (MNIST/CIFAR-10 for RTB; CIFAR-10/ImageNet for SSL; small synthetic/real RL tasks), rely on restrictive assumptions (i.i.d. data for risk control, linear models for SSL theory, special initialization for EI analysis), and their practical components (association heads, task alignment, gradient clipping, betting wealth, LID estimation, LoRA rank/placement) each introduce sensitive hyperparameters whose failure modes are documented only via ablations, not formal guarantees.

**community 最终答案**

> Below is the mapping of your requirements to papers actually present in the collection, followed by each method's development defects as reported in those papers.
> 
> ## Papers found in the collection
> 
> **1. Anchor-free part–body association → PBADet (ICLR 2024)**
> One-stage anchor-free detector linking hands/face to their parent person via a single part-to-body center offset; validated on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman (face–body).
> 
> **2. Amortized inference for diffusion priors (respecting prompts via posterior sampling) → RTB / Reward Trajectory Balance (NeurIPS 2024)**
> Amortizes posterior sampling p(x)·r(x) under a diffusion prior, incl. fine-tuning Stable Diffusion v1-5 for text-to-image while respecting a reward/prompt constraint. (Related: AdjointDEIS training-free guidance, Universal Guidance.)
> 
> **3. Active anytime-valid risk control → "Anytime-Valid Risk-Controlling Active Labeling"**
> Extends RCPS to streaming data with active labeling and a label budget; guarantees miscoverage ≤ θ simultaneously at all times via e-processes/betting (valid even for MNIST/CIFAR-scale streams).
> 
> **4. Self-supervised learning prioritizing useful features over noise → "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"**, plus **LDReg** and **HASSOD**
> JEPA provably prioritizes high-influence features and suppresses noisy ones vs MAE; LDReg counters local dimensional collapse; HASSOD does self-supervised object detection.
> 
> **5. Stable training of time-series/RNN controllers with E/I constraints + spectral regularization → "Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"**
> Shows E/I (Dale's-law) RNNs train poorly mainly due to their initial recurrent-weight spectrum, and that DANN reparameterization + gradient clipping stabilizes training.
> 
> **6. End-to-end LoRA fine-tuning of large backbones → NOT a dedicated paper in the collection**
> Only indirect coverage: the Hessian-spectrum paper studies LoRA fine-tuning of TinyLlama (and notes LoRA-only fine-tuning does not produce the power-law Hessian that full fine-tuning does); the 4-bit-optimizer paper fine-tunes LLaMA with AdamW/Adam. No paper literally covers "End-to-end LoRA."
> 
> **7. SGD/Adam, cosine similarity, F1/AUROC guidance → scattered, no single guide**
> Hessian-spectrum paper (SGD/Adam/AMSGrad/RAdam/Yogi comparisons, batch-size phases, power-law ↔ generalization); "On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning" (cosine similarity/temperature); F1/AUROC appear only as evaluation metrics inside specific papers (e.g., PBADet's precision/recall/F1, DiffusionFake's AUC, RLCD's F1) — no paper offers general practical guidance tying them together.
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods
> 
> **PBADet**
> - On the single-part CrowdHuman face–body task, its advantage over BPJDet is only marginal (its strength is multi-part scalability).
> - Prior anchor-based approaches it replaces degrade as part count grows and fail when parts are occluded; PBADet's own part-to-body offsets depend on anchor points inside part boxes and on task-alignment supervision (removing it hurts all metrics).
> 
> **RTB / amortized diffusion**
> - Simulation-based training is slow and memory-intensive; objective is computed on complete trajectories (no local-in-time objectives).
> - Under a weak discrete-diffusion prior, infilling was limited (reward model favored repetitions).
> - Stable Diffusion fine-tuning shows a reward-vs-diversity tradeoff; KL-regularized RL baselines are biased/mode-collapse; off-policy RTB helped only 2 of 3 D4RL tasks.
> 
> **Active anytime-valid risk control**
> - Assumes i.i.d. stream; bounded label-policy assumption (Assumption 2) and an existence assumption (Prop. 5) are required but not justified; no guarantees for covariate/label shift or average-risk control.
> 
> **JEPA/self-supervised (noise-prioritizing)**
> - JEPA analysis limited to deep linear networks, special initialization, simultaneous diagonalizability; only qualitative generalization.
> - LDReg: LID estimation degrades in high dimensions and uses minibatch nearest neighbors; forcing very low LID triggers total collapse.
> - HASSOD: hierarchy misaligns with human perception; fails on overlapping similar objects, heterogeneous wholes, and text.
> 
> **E/I (Dale's-law) controller**
> - Simple ColEI sign-partitioning trains worse with higher variance and is unstable without gradient clipping; sign constraints alone impair learning and don't fully explain the gap; performance worsens for small networks and few inhibitory units (spectral pathology, measured by NSE).
> 
> **LoRA fine-tuning (as covered)**
> - LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the power-law Hessian that full fine-tuning does (different spectral regime, Hessian trace is a more reliable indicator there); power-law itself breaks with small width/depth, limited data, noisy labels, and large batches. 4-bit optimizers' optimal quantization is task-dependent and only tested on language/vision.
> 
> **Optimizer/cosine/F1–AUROC guidance**
> - Hessian paper: large-batch training destroys power-law structure and sharpness correlation with test error.
> - Contrastive-similarity paper: the proposed variance-reduction loss adds a tuning hyperparameter and may suppress meaningful semantic variance; smaller batches increase negative-pair similarity variance.
> 
> **Bottom line:** Five of your six component areas have direct papers (PBADet, RTB, active anytime-valid RCPS, JEPA/LDReg, Dale's-law spectral). "End-to-end LoRA" and a unified SGD/Adam + cosine + F1/AUROC practical guide are **not** covered as such; the closest available material is the Hessian-spectrum paper (LoRA dynamics + optimizer comparison) and the contrastive-embeddings paper (cosine similarity).

</details>

<a id="case-paperscope-gap-34"></a>

### paperscope:gap:34 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building a resource‑constrained perception‑to‑control stack for robots: the vision front‑end must robustly link hands/face to the right person in crowded, COCO‑style scenes; the control side will use diffusion‑driven planners/policies with transformer‑conditioned guidance; and model updates must rely on low‑memory optimizers while I LoRA‑fine‑tune large SFT backbones. I also want self‑supervised pretraining that avoids latching onto noisy pixels for better interpretability, and my time‑series modules should respect excitatory/inhibitory neuron separation yet still train stably. What set of papers covers these components end‑to‑end?Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Development defects and limitations, organized by method:
> 
> 1) PBADet (one-stage anchor‑free part–body association detection)
> - Limited advantage on single‑part association: On the CrowdHuman face–body association (a single‑part setting), the authors report PBADet is only comparable to BPJDet and its advantages are “not as pronounced” as in multi‑part cases because the task is singular in nature.
> - Sensitivity to key components and hyperparameters: Ablations show removing multi‑scale supervision or task‑alignment learning degrades association performance, and the design depends on numerous tuned hyperparameters (e.g., λiou, λdfl, λcls, λassoc, scaling λ, top‑K, α, β, and NMS thresholds). This implies non‑trivial sensitivity to these choices for best results.
> - Inference specifics still required: Decoding relies on NMS and a nearest‑body‑center heuristic constrained to bodies that enclose the part; thresholds must be set per dataset, which introduces operational tuning.
> - Dataset/task coverage: Reported strongest wins are on BodyHands and COCOHumanParts; on CrowdHuman (face‑body only), improvements are limited, indicating task‑dependent gains.
> 
> 2) Dale’s-law‑respecting EI RNNs (ColEI vs DANN)
> - ColEI network learning pathologies: The paper demonstrates ColEI RNNs learn poorly due to multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra (including large singular value modes), causing instability, high variance across seeds, and frequent need for gradient clipping. Small networks and realistic E/I ratios (fewer inhibitory units) exacerbate poor learning.
> - Sensitivity to size and EI ratio: Performance and spectra noticeably worsen in smaller ColEI networks and as the inhibitory proportion decreases; robust learning emerges only in larger networks with more balanced EI ratios.
> - Reliance on spectral properties/initialization: Good learning depends more on spectral properties than just sign constraints; ColEI often requires careful spectral radius setting and specific initializations to function well.
> - Theoretical scope limits: Analyses and positive results rely on special assumptions (orthogonal/“balanced” initialization; diagonal, simultaneously‑diagonalizable covariances); generalization beyond these settings or to more biologically faithful models remains open.
> - Biological fidelity trade‑offs: DANNs model fast PV+ inhibition well but are not a universal model of inhibitory subtypes; ColEI is more general biologically but suffers the learning defects above.
> 
> 3) JEPA‑style self‑distillation (implicit bias in deep linear models)
> - Feature selection bias and depth dependence: In deep linear encoders, JEPA prioritizes “influential” (high regression‑coefficient) features over merely high‑variance/covarying features learned by MAE; this can invert the order of learned features compared to MAE. The bias weakens in shallow encoders, so benefits hinge on sufficient depth.
> - Potential vulnerability to spurious/slow features: The bias toward high regression coefficients may emphasize slowly varying or spurious “predictive” features over high‑variance but possibly relevant ones, depending on data.
> - Theory limitations: Results are derived for deep linear networks under simultaneously‑diagonalizable covariances and special initializations; extension to non‑linear encoders, non‑diagonal covariances, and fully practical regimes is not established.
> 
> 4) 4‑bit memory‑efficient optimizers (4‑bit Adam/AdamW and factorized variants)
> - Zero‑point failure in second‑moment quantization: Mapping zero in low‑bit quantization causes severe errors because updates scale with 1/sqrt(v); quantizing non‑zeros to zero leads to catastrophic deviations. The paper must exclude zero or change mappings (e.g., linear, DE‑0) and introduces rank‑1 normalization to mitigate this.
> - Outlier‑pattern mismatch with coarse blocks: Large block sizes (e.g., 2048) miss complicated row/column outlier patterns in moments, causing poor approximation; smaller blocks or rank‑1 normalization are required, increasing design complexity.
> - Task‑specific tuning and scope: Authors note optimal quantization settings likely depend on the task/data/training details; evaluations focus on language and vision—applicability to RL, audio, or graphs remains unvalidated.
> - Speed and memory trade‑offs: While 4‑bit states cut optimizer memory, total training memory may saturate due to activations/other buffers, and unfused implementations can be slower than 8‑bit until operator fusion is applied. Factorization helps only for second moments.
> 
> 5) CleanDiffuser (diffusion models for decision making: planners, policies, data synthesizers)
> - Sampling inefficiency: Diffusion sampling is slow due to iterative denoising; the authors highlight the need for acceleration (e.g., warm‑starting, rectified flows) for real‑time control.
> - Sensitivity and open issues in guided generation: Diffusion planners are sensitive to guided sampling and can generate out‑of‑distribution trajectories; conservative/safety mechanisms are needed to ensure dynamic legitimacy.
> - Sampling degradation: Empirically, more sampling steps can sometimes reduce performance (“sampling degradation”), making the step–performance trade‑off non‑trivial and still an open question.
> - Unclear SDE vs ODE impacts: The performance differences and guidance sensitivity between SDE‑ and ODE‑based solvers in decision‑making remain unexplained; solver choice can affect both results and robustness.
> - Architecture speed–quality trade‑offs: Stronger policy backbones (e.g., 1D‑UNet variants) improve success but increase model size and inference time; transformer or CNN choices present practical latency trade‑offs.
> - Coverage limitations: Current library does not directly support discrete or hybrid action spaces; users may need additional techniques (e.g., action representation or categorical diffusion) and tailored engineering.
> - Practical complexity: Despite modularity, effectively applying DMs in decision‑making still demands substantial understanding of modules, hyperparameters, and compute resources, as evidenced by large‑scale benchmarks run by the authors.
> 
> These limitations come directly from the respective papers’ empirical findings, ablations, and stated constraints, and they pinpoint where each method may require careful tuning, extra mechanisms, or further research to meet robust, resource‑constrained perception‑to‑control deployment requirements.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Paper Set (end-to-end)
> 
> 1. **Vision front-end (hand/face → person, crowded COCO-style):** **PBADet** (Gao et al., ICLR 2024) — one-stage anchor-free part-body association using a single part-to-body center offset; outperforms BPJDet/HierR-CNN on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman.
> 2. **Diffusion control + transformer-conditioned guidance:** **RTB: Reward Trajectory Balance** (NeurIPS 2024) for reward-guided diffusion policies/planners with arbitrary guidance; **Universal Guidance** (ICLR 2024) for training-free transformer/classifier-conditioned guidance; **CleanDiffuser** as the modular diffusion planner/policy library (Diffuser, Diffusion Policy, DQL, etc.).
> 3. **Low-memory optimizer + LoRA on SFT backbones:** **4-bit Optimizers** (NeurIPS 2023) for memory-efficient optimizer states; **LoRA-related fine-tuning analyses** (Hessian-spectrum paper; **NEFTune** for instruction fine-tuning; **OctoPack** as an SFT/instruction-tuned LLM backbone).
> 4. **Self-supervised pretraining that avoids noisy pixels:** **"Why JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024) — JEPA's implicit bias to high-influence features vs. MAE's pixel-space reconstruction; plus **HASSOD** (hierarchical self-supervised detection with interpretable part-whole structure).
> 5. **E/I-separated, stable time-series modules:** **"Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly"** (NeurIPS 2023) — spectral analysis of excitatory/inhibitory RNNs; **BSO/T-BSO** — memory-efficient stable online training for spiking (binary) networks.
> 
> ## Development Defects
> 
> **PBADet:** Advantage over BPJDet shrinks on the single-part face-body task (CrowdHuman body-face mMR⁻² 50.8 vs. 50.1); still needs post-processing; part detection degrades with occlusion; anchor-free per-pixel training is dense and computationally heavy; qualitative results show speculative pose-based baselines (ED-Pose) are more reliable for limbs.
> 
> **RTB:** Simulation-based training is slow and memory-intensive; objective computed on complete trajectories (no local-in-time formulation); RL-based alternatives are biased and mode-collapse prone; fine-tuning requires careful timestep subsampling and batched gradient computation.
> 
> **Universal Guidance:** Slower generation; per-network hyperparameter tuning (guidance coefficients, refinement steps); requires differentiable guidance functions — object-detection/segmentation guidance needs a hand-built loss, and forward-only guidance produces wrong objects/locations (mAP 0.18–0.39) unless backward guidance is added.
> 
> **CleanDiffuser:** No direct support for discrete/hybrid action spaces; 5 sampling steps often suffice and more steps can degrade quality; solver/architecture choices matter and algorithm choice dominates model size — i.e., no universal recipe.
> 
> **4-bit Optimizers:** Optimal quantization appears task-dependent; only language/vision tasks validated; memory savings saturate at low bitwidths; quantization of second moment risks zero-point errors; sublinear optimizers (Adafactor/SM3) still degrade on classification.
> 
> **LoRA fine-tuning (Hessian paper/NEFTune/OctoPack):** LoRA-only fine-tuning fails to induce the power-law Hessian structure of full fine-tuning (generalization signal unreliable); NEFTune's gains rely on GPT-4 judging and lack a conclusive mechanism; OctoPack models still fail on length constraints, small fixes, and code/text switching, and HumanEval is near saturation/contamination-prone.
> 
> **JEPA analysis:** Theoretic result is limited to deep linear MLPs with special initialization and simultaneous diagonalizability; the noise-avoidance conclusion is only qualitatively generalized from linear to nonlinear settings.
> 
> **Dale's-Law RNNs:** ColEI networks learn worse with higher variance across all tasks; they need gradient clipping and show pathological (multimodal, dispersed) singular-value spectra; no spectral radius value closes the gap with standard RNNs; DANN is more stable but models only fast PV+ interneurons (less general biology). **BSO:** binary weights and surrogate-gradient BPTT still restrict precision; regret bounds are sublinear but performance lags full-precision SNNs; temporal processing adds overhead.

**community 最终答案**

> ## Paper set (end-to-end coverage)
> 
> 1. **Vision front‑end (hand/face→person association in crowded COCO‑style scenes):** *PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association Detection* (doc `08b70bc3…`) — one‑stage anchor‑free detector linking hands/face/feet to a parent body on COCO‑HumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman.
> 2. **Diffusion planners/policies with transformer‑conditioned guidance:** *CleanDiffuser* (doc `c122328b4…`) — modular library covering diffusion planners (Diffuser), policies (Diffusion Policy incl. transformer/DiT‑based variants), plus *Universal Guidance* (doc `9134ed60…`, training‑free arbitrary‑modality guidance) and/or *RTB* (doc `756d1e62…`, reward‑guided diffusion posterior sampling for control).
> 3. **Low‑memory optimizers + LoRA fine‑tuning of large SFT backbones:** *4-bit Optimizers* (doc `8d5e1455…`) — 4‑bit Adam/AdamW optimizer states; validated on LLaMA‑7B/13B/33B Alpaca (SFT) fine‑tuning, where LoRA is the cited parameter‑efficient baseline.
> 4. **Self‑supervised pretraining avoiding noisy pixels for interpretability:** *How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features* (doc `40fde037…`) — shows JEPA self‑distillation suppresses noise and prioritizes high‑influence (perceptual) features vs. MAE; optionally *HASSOD* (doc `ef986d59…`) for interpretable hierarchical self‑supervised object detection.
> 5. **Time‑series modules with E/I neuron separation but stable training:** *Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly* (doc `e63a94c4…`) — analyzes excitatory/inhibitory (Dale's‑law) RNNs and how to make them train stably.
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods
> 
> - **PBADet:** on the single‑part CrowdHuman face‑body task its advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced; its part‑to‑body representation still contains unused placeholder positions, and association fails when parts are occluded/not visible (a limitation it inherits from part detection); head/face parts were excluded from pose comparisons due to inconsistent keypoints. Prior two‑stage methods (BodyHands, heuristic matching) are flagged as complex and efficiency‑compromising.
> - **CleanDiffuser:** does not directly support discrete/hybrid action spaces; requires tailored adjustments for specific problems; more sampling steps can degrade results (5 often enough); SDE vs ODE solvers differ; diffusion policies are slower than ACT; algorithm choice matters more than model size.
> - **Universal Guidance:** slower generation, per‑network hyperparameter tuning, and requires differentiable guidance functions. **RTB:** discrete‑diffusion infilling was limited by a weak prior and reward models favoring repetitions; offline‑RL gains appeared on only two of three D4RL medium‑replay tasks; reward‑vs‑diversity tradeoff persists.
> - **4‑bit optimizers:** optimal quantization may be task‑dependent; tested only on language/vision tasks; total‑memory savings saturate as bitwidth drops because data, activations, and memory fragments remain.
> - **JEPA analysis:** theory is restricted to deep linear networks, special initialization, and simultaneous diagonalizability; generalization to real networks is only qualitative; noise suppression involves a noise/temporal‑correlation tradeoff. **HASSOD:** hierarchy can misalign with human perception; fails on overlapping similar objects, heterogeneous wholes, and text.
> - **Dale's‑law RNNs:** sign‑constrained ColEI networks learn worse and with higher variance (gradient clipping is needed); the cause is a multimodal, dispersed singular‑value spectrum with a large mode rather than sign constraints alone; small networks with realistic (few inhibitory) E:I ratios degrade further; normalized SVD entropy predicts failure. DANN variants fix this but only model fast PV+ interneurons and omit I→I connections and cell‑type‑specific time constants.

</details>

### paperscope:gap:37 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively tackle efficient and robust training for deep networks under practical constraints: memory-light optimizer states (e.g., 4-bit for Adam/AdamW and SGD), offline learning for combinatorial decision spaces with bandit-style formulations and evaluation by F1/Precision, biologically informed recurrent models that respect excitatory/inhibitory structure via spectral regularization, anchor-free vision detectors validated on COCO for part–body association, and self-supervised learning (JEPA) that avoids noisy latent features. I’m interested in approaches compatible with Transformers and ResNet-50, using cross-entropy/MSE losses, cosine similarity, and fine-tuning workflows including End-to-end LoRA.Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> - PBADet (one-stage anchor-free part–body association)
>   - Advantage not pronounced on single-part association: On CrowdHuman (face–body association is a single-part task), the authors note the benefit over BPJDet is not as pronounced because the task is “singular in nature.”
>   - Sensitivity to design choices: Ablations show that removing task-alignment learning or multi-scale formulation degrades conditional accuracy and joint AP, indicating reliance on these components.
>   - Heavy resolution/threshold dependence: Training and inference use large fixed input sizes (e.g., 1024–1536) and multiple NMS/confidence/IoU thresholds; performance is reported under those settings and degrades when components (e.g., multi-scale, task-align) are ablated.
> 
> - Recurrent EI networks with Dale’s Law (DANN RNNs vs. Column EI)
>   - ColEI networks (column-sign constrained RNNs):
>     - Poor learning and instability: Learn worse than standard RNNs/DANNs, show high variance across seeds, and are highly unstable without gradient clipping due to pathological, multimodal and dispersed singular value spectra.
>     - Sensitive to EI ratio and size: Performance and spectra worsen when networks are small or have few inhibitory units; require larger networks and more balanced E/I ratios to learn well.
>     - Initialization dependence: Require constrained initialization (balanced, spectral-radius tuning); spectra/pathology tied to initialization and sign constraints.
>   - DANN RNNs:
>     - Biological fidelity limits: Current recurrent DANNs omit features like inhibitory-to-inhibitory connections and cell-type–specific time constants; authors frame them as modeling fast PV+ interneurons only and suggest future hybridization for realism.
> 
> - JEPA (self-distillation joint-embedding predictive architectures)
>   - Collapse risk without architectural bias: Non-contrastive JEPAs require StopGrad or similar tricks to avoid trivial collapse.
>   - Depth-dependent benefit: The influential-feature bias that helps avoid noisy features emerges with deep encoders and “diminishes substantially” for shallow encoders.
>   - Potential vulnerability to spurious/slow features: The same bias toward high-regression-coefficient (often slow/low-variance) features can make JEPAs focus on slowly varying or spurious features.
>   - Theory scope limits: Results are for deep linear models with simultaneously diagonalizable covariances and special initializations; generalization to nonlinear/realistic settings is not established.
> 
> - 4-bit Optimizers (Adam/AdamW; quantized first/second moments)
>   - Zero-point failure in second-moment quantization: Standard dynamic exponent mapping with a zero point collapses many entries to zero, causing catastrophic errors in 1/sqrt(v) and training instability; requires zero-free mapping (DE-0) or linear mapping plus rank-1 normalization to stabilize.
>   - Task/setting sensitivity: Authors note optimal quantization settings likely depend on task/dataset/training details; evaluation is limited to language/vision tasks (RL, audio, graphs not studied).
>   - Performance/efficiency caveats: Without fused kernels, 4-bit implementations can be slower than 8-bit on smaller models; memory savings can appear to “saturate” at the system level since activations/data/fragmentation dominate total memory.
>   - Method scope constraints: Factorization reduces only the second moment (and only for tensors with dimension >1); small tensors (≤4096 elements) are deliberately not quantized, and practical baselines often exclude embedding states from quantization.
> 
> - Off-CMAB (offline CMAB with CLCB)
>   - Coverage and smoothness prerequisites: Guarantees require monotonic rewards and 1-norm TPM bounded smoothness, and dataset coverage conditions (∞-norm or 1-norm TPM). If coverage coefficients (C*∞ or C*1) are large or conditions fail, sample complexity and suboptimality bounds deteriorate or may not apply.
>   - Oracle dependence: Requires an α-approximate combinatorial solver; computational quality hinges on the availability/quality of such oracles for non-linear rewards.
>   - Assumption-heavy application instantiations:
>     - LLM cache: Strongest improved bounds rely on full feedback for arrivals and, for the cleanest case, an empty-cache sampling strategy during data collection.
>     - Influence maximization (node-level feedback): Analysis assumes a product-form seed sampling distribution and lower bounds on seed sampling probability (γ) and activation probability (η); bounds scale with network size (V, d_max) and σ(S*; G).
>   - Pessimism conservatism: The CLCB’s arm-level LCB penalization can be overly conservative when data coverage is thin, inflating gaps until sufficient samples accrue for triggered arms.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based only on the provided collection, here are the matching papers and their development defects (limitations) as reported in the documents.
> 
> ## 1. 4-bit Optimizer States — "4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States" (doc 8d5e1455…)
> Matches: 4-bit Adam/AdamW states; SGDM is covered by the compression framework with a convergence theorem for quantized SGDM (AdamW convergence is only inferred, not proven).
> Defects:
> - Optimal quantization setting likely depends on task/dataset/training details; task-specific settings might be better but are out of scope.
> - Only language and vision tasks tested; applicability to RL, audio, graph learning not verified.
> - Zero-point exclusion wastes one of 16 quantization levels; smaller models are slower than 8-bit AdamW because fused operators are not yet implemented.
> - Quantizing both moments yields a marginal accuracy drop; memory savings saturate at lower bitwidth.
> - Convergence guarantee is proven only for quantized SGDM, not AdamW.
> 
> ## 2. Offline combinatorial bandits — "Offline Learning for Combinatorial Multi-armed Bandits (Off-CMAB/CLCB)" (doc d8faaa7f…)
> Matches: offline learning, combinatorial action space, bandit formulation.
> Defects / mismatch:
> - Evaluation is by **suboptimality gap**, not F1/Precision; no F1/Precision evaluation exists in this paper. The collection contains no bandit paper evaluated by F1/Precision (F1/Precision appears only in detection/entity-alignment/causal-discovery contexts).
> - Requires data-coverage conditions; datasets may exclude optimal/feasible actions (OOD samples).
> - Validated only on cascading bandits and LLM cache; extension to offline RL with combinatorial actions left for future work.
> - Not a deep-network training paper: no Transformers/ResNet-50, cross-entropy/MSE, or LoRA.
> 
> ## 3. Biologically informed E/I recurrent models — "Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly: A Spectral Perspective" (doc e63a94c4…)
> Matches: excitatory/inhibitory structure respected via spectral analysis (normalised SVD entropy as spectral diagnostic; spectrum shown more important than sign constraints).
> Defects:
> - It is a **diagnostic/analysis** work, not a spectral-regularization training method; it proposes better initialization/hybridization as future work.
> - ColEI networks train poorly: higher variance, unstable without gradient clipping, multimodal dispersed singular-value spectrum; smaller networks or fewer inhibitory units worsen both spectrum and performance.
> - Sign constraints themselves still impair learning (~1% for ColEI).
> - Only feedforward/recurrent nets on adding, sMNIST, PTB, object recognition — no Transformer/ResNet-50, no LoRA; I→I connections and cell-type time constants not modeled.
> 
> ## 4. Anchor-free part–body detection — "PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association" (doc 08b70bc3…)
> Matches: one-stage anchor-free detector; validated on COCO (COCO-HumanParts, COCO val) for part–body (hand/feet/face–body) association with Precision/Recall/F1 evaluation.
> Defects:
> - Advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced for the single-part face–body task (CrowdHuman).
> - Facial/head parts excluded from the ED-Pose comparison due to inconsistent keypoint counts; animal (AP-10K) results are qualitative only.
> - Uses YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones, not ResNet-50 or Transformer; anchor-free YOLOv7 variant needed because the base models are anchor-based.
> 
> ## 5. JEPA avoiding noisy latent features — "Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features" (doc 40fde037…)
> Matches: JEPA self-distillation, latent-space prediction, shows bias toward high-influence features and suppression of noisy features (vs MAE).
> Defects:
> - Analysis limited to deep **linear** networks, balanced orthogonal initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable data; extension to nonlinear models is only qualitative.
> - JEPA can still learn noisy features (converging to lower-amplitude weights) and is vulnerable to spurious or slow features.
> - Findings may not generalize to joint-embedding architectures that don't rely on self-distillation.
> 
> ## Relevant supporting papers (partial matches)
> - **LDReg** (doc 51526068…): SSL local-dimensionality regularization on **ResNet-50 and ViT-B** (ImageNet, COCO detection/segmentation). Defect: LID estimation accuracy degrades in high dimensions and uses minibatch nearest neighbors.
> - **Hessian power-law study** (doc 582d138d…): LoRA fine-tuning on TinyLlama/Transformers. Defect: LoRA-only fine-tuning does **not** induce the power-law Hessian structure that full fine-tuning does, suggesting different generalization behavior; SOTA LLMs excluded due to Hessian cost.
> - **NEFTune** (doc fad0fb20…): noisy embeddings for instruction fine-tuning incl. QLoRA; defects: relies on GPT-4 judging, limited 30B/70B validation, no conclusive mechanism/safety evaluation.
> 
> ## What the collection does NOT support
> - **"End-to-end LoRA"**: no paper with that exact method exists in the collection; only standard LoRA/QLoRA fine-tuning analyses appear.
> - **F1/Precision evaluation for the bandit paper**: not present (the bandit work uses suboptimality gap; F1/Precision appears only in detection/other tasks).
> - **Spectral regularization as an explicit training objective** for E/I RNNs: the RNN paper analyzes spectra and proposes initialization guidance but doesn't train with a spectral-regularization loss.
> - **Cosine similarity / cross-entropy / MSE specifics**: mentioned in related contexts (e.g., cross-entropy in fine-tuning proofs, contrastive embedding similarity) but not as a unifying design criterion across these papers.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the five matched papers and the development defects of each method, based only on the collection.
> 
> ## Matched papers
> 
> 1. **Memory-light optimizer states** — *4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States* (NeurIPS 2023). 4-bit Adam/AdamW (+ quantized/factorized second moment; 4-bitFactor), covering Adam/AdamW/SGDM-style optimizers; evaluated on RoBERTa-L, Swin-T, GPT-2, Transformer, LLaMA fine-tuning (Transformers; cross-entropy/CLS/QA/NLG losses). Not ResNet-50.
> 2. **Offline combinatorial bandits** — *Offline Learning for Combinatorial Multi-armed Bandits* (Off-CMAB / CLCB). Bandit-style offline decision making over combinatorial actions (cascading bandits, LLM cache). Note: it is **not** a deep-network training method, and its evaluation uses suboptimality gap / LLM inference cost, **not F1/Precision** — that part of your criterion is not met by any paper found.
> 3. **Biologically informed recurrent models** — *Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective* (NeurIPS 2023). E/I (Dale's-law) RNNs (ColEI vs DANN) analyzed via spectral properties/NSE; spectral analysis rather than a proposed spectral regularizer. RNNs only, not Transformers/ResNet-50.
> 4. **Anchor-free part-body detection** — *PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association* (ICLR 2024). Validated on COCOHumanParts (COCO), BodyHands, CrowdHuman; YOLOv5/v7 backbones, not ResNet-50/Transformers.
> 5. **JEPA avoiding noisy features** — *How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks* (NeurIPS 2024). Explains why JEPA suppresses noisy latent features; ImageNet I-JEPA/MAE experiments (Transformers). Related: *LDReg* (ResNet-50/ViT-B) and contrastive-embedding-similarity work (ResNet-50, cosine similarity).
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods
> 
> **1. 4-bit optimizers**
> - Optimal quantization settings are task/dataset-dependent; lossless performance is not guaranteed, and quantizing both moments causes a marginal accuracy drop.
> - Speed: on small models (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2) 4-bit is slower than 8-bit because fused operators are not implemented (fusion is claimed to fix this).
> - Rank-1 normalization only matches B128 at moderate scale (hidden_size≈1024); falls back to B128 for 1-D tensors; combining block-wise and rank-1 is left to future work.
> - Evaluated only on language and vision; RL, audio, and graph applications unstudied; convergence proof covers quantized SGD(M) only.
> 
> **2. Offline CMAB (CLCB)**
> - Guarantees rely on data-coverage conditions (infinity/1-norm TPM); quality of the offline dataset directly determines performance, and optimal action may have zero sampling probability (needs miss-estimation tricks).
> - Requires an offline α-approximation oracle because exact optimum is NP-hard even with known means.
> - Validation is limited: synthetic + Yelp cascading data and LLM cache cost with GPT-4-o/GPT-4-turbo only; no F1/Precision-based evaluation.
> 
> **3. Dale's-law RNNs**
> - ColEI networks learn worse with much higher variance and are unstable without gradient clipping; sign constraints alone impair learning (RNNs −0.7±0.3%, ColEI −1±1%) but do not explain the full gap.
> - Small networks with biologically realistic (few inhibitory) units degrade in both spectrum and performance; NSE is only a predictive diagnostic — the paper does not deliver the spectral-regularization fix itself (alternative initialization is left as future work).
> - Biologically incomplete: no I→I connections in DANNs, no cell-type time constants; ColEI and DANN model different inhibitory populations, with hybridization unexplored.
> 
> **4. PBADet**
> - On CrowdHuman (single-part face-body), its advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced.
> - Ablations show dependence on all components: removing the association loss, multi-scale center offsets, or task alignment each degrade hand AP/conditional accuracy/joint AP.
> - Limited backbone scope (YOLO-family anchor-free heads); no ResNet-50 or Transformer validation; COCO results are restricted to COCOHumanParts-style metrics.
> 
> **5. JEPA noise-avoidance analysis**
> - Theory holds only for deep linear MLPs with restricted (balanced orthogonal) initialization and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances; real data deviate from these assumptions, and non-linear generalization is unproven.
> - The implicit bias is a double-edged sword: JEPA can be vulnerable to spurious/slow features, and the bias weakens substantially for shallow encoders.
> - JEPA objectives remain collapse-prone and rely on architectural tricks (StopGrad); experimental support is qualitative (CCA on ImageNet).
> 
> **Cross-cutting compatibility gaps**: no single paper satisfies all of your constraints — none of the five combines Transformers + ResNet-50 + cross-entropy/MSE + cosine similarity + End-to-end LoRA. LoRA appears only as related work in the 4-bit optimizer paper (and LoRA fine-tuning is analyzed in the Hessian-spectrum paper, not among the five); cosine similarity losses appear in the contrastive/JEPA-side papers (LDReg, embedding-similarity work), not in the bandit, detector, or RNN papers.

### paperscope:gap:40 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building a production system with three needs: (1) a medical vision module that reliably links hands/faces to the right person in crowded rooms (COCO-style benchmarks, anchor-free detection, evaluate with F1/Precision); (2) an LLM service that decides cache contents and ranked lists using only offline logs (bandit-style offline learning, no online exploration); and (3) a training stack for Transformers/ResNet-50 that must fine-tune with self-supervised objectives while keeping optimizer state tiny (prefer 4-bit AdamW/SGD) and steering representations away from noisy features. We also have an RNN component that should obey excitatory/inhibitory constraints but remain trainable via spectral guidance. Are there papers that bring together anchor-free part–body detection, offline combinatorial bandits, JEPA-style self-supervised learning, memory-efficient optimizers, and spectral perspectives on biologically constrained RNNs—using CE/MSE, cosine similarity, and LoRA fine-tuning?Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below are method-specific development defects distilled strictly from the cited papers.
> 
> 1) PBADet (one-stage, anchor-free part–body association)
> - Limited advantage for single-part association: The authors note that on face–body association (a single part), PBADet’s gains over BPJDet are “not as pronounced” as in multi-part scenarios (CrowdHuman results). This reduces its benefit in deployments that only track one part class.
> - Anchor-based variants underperform: Their own ablation shows an anchor-based part-to-body implementation and BPJDet (anchor-based body-to-part) both trail the anchor-free head; if a production stack is tied to anchor-based heads, expect accuracy loss unless refactoring to anchor-free.
> - Sensitivity to training components: Removing task alignment or multi-scale supervision reduces conditional accuracy and joint AP; PBADet’s best numbers rely on these ingredients (and the extra association loss), implying performance drop if training constraints force simpler heads/losses.
> - Compute/training cost: Reported runs use 1024–1536 px inputs, 4×V100 GPUs, and 100 epochs with AMP and SGD; this footprint may be heavy for quick iteration or on modest hardware. 
> - Metric alignment: Main reports use AP, MR, and mMR; F1/Precision are only provided in an auxiliary comparison to ED-Pose, so an F1/Precision-first evaluation workflow may need extra adaptation.
> 
> 2) Off-CMAB/CLCB (offline learning for combinatorial bandits)
> - Requires data coverage conditions on the optimal action’s arms: Both C*_∞ (∞-norm TPM coverage) and C*_1 (1-norm TPM coverage) drive sample complexity; poor coverage on the optimal action’s triggered arms directly degrades the suboptimality gap and can make learning ineffective.
> - Structural assumptions on reward: The guarantees need monotonicity and 1-norm TPM bounded smoothness (with coefficient B1). Practical reward models that violate these (e.g., non-monotone or non-smooth) lose the stated bounds.
> - Dependence on combinatorial oracles: The algorithm assumes access to an α-approximation solver; for hard objectives this adds engineering overhead and any weakening of α directly worsens the bound.
> - Application-specific extra assumptions: For influence maximization with node-level feedback, results depend on lower bounds for seed-sampling probability γ and activation probability η; if these are small or unknown in logs, the bound deteriorates. For LLM caching, the strongest improvement exploits full-feedback over arrival probabilities; without that, the tighter result does not apply.
> 
> 3) 4-bit optimizer states (4-bit AdamW/SGD)
> - Instability from zero-point quantization of second moments: Quantizing v to formats that include zero produces severe errors in 1/√v and destabilizes training; the paper must exclude zero (DE-0) or switch to a linear map, and stochastic rounding alone did not fix it.
> - Extra quantization machinery is required: Good results depended on rank-1 normalization (row/column statistics) and careful block sizing; simpler block-only schemes (e.g., large blocks) underperform, and task-agnostic settings can fail.
> - Incomplete quantization coverage and task dependency: Small tensors are excluded by a size threshold; 8-bit baselines skip embeddings. The authors caution that optimal quantization settings are task-dependent and were validated only on language/vision; RL, audio, and graphs remain untested.
> - Throughput limitations without kernel fusion: Their 4-bit implementation can be slower than 8-bit without fused operators; they show speed recovery only after fusion.
> 
> 4) JEPA implicit bias (deep linear self-distillation analysis)
> - Restricted theoretical setting: Results are proven only for deep linear encoders with simultaneously diagonalizable covariance/correlation; real neural nets and general data distributions may not satisfy these assumptions.
> - Depth-dependent benefit: The advantageous JEPA bias (toward high regression-coefficient “influential” features) diminishes with shallow encoders; for L=1 it matches MAE, undercutting gains if production uses shallow backbones or light heads.
> - Possible vulnerability to slow/spurious features: The authors explicitly caution that JEPA’s bias may favor slowly varying or spurious low-variance features; this is a potential failure mode in noisy environments.
> 
> 5) Dale’s Law RNNs (spectral perspective)
> - Column EI (naïve Dale’s Law) trains poorly: ColEI networks exhibit dispersed, multi-modal singular spectra with large modes that harm learning; they show worse final performance and much higher seed variance than standard RNNs or DANNs.
> - High sensitivity to EI ratio and network size: ColEI performance degrades in small networks and with realistic E/I ratios (few inhibitory units). Large max singular values persist even as width grows, and small models often need gradient clipping to avoid instability.
> - Initialization/spectral radius fragility: ColEI’s performance differs from standard/DANN across spectral radii; gradient clipping benefits ColEI “substantially more,” indicating greater instability and hyperparameter sensitivity.
> - Biological mapping constraints: While DANN RNNs learn well, they specifically model fast PV+ inhibitory circuits; modeling other interneuron classes (e.g., SOM+, CCK+) may require different architectures that re-introduce spectral issues.
> 
> All statements above are drawn from the respective papers’ results, ablations, assumptions, or limitations sections and reflect conditions under which performance drops, added engineering burden appears, or guarantees no longer hold.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Direct answer
> 
> **No.** There is no single paper in the collection that brings together all five components (anchor-free part–body detection, offline combinatorial bandits, JEPA SSL, memory-efficient optimizers, and spectral/EI-constrained RNNs) with CE/MSE, cosine similarity, and LoRA fine-tuning. The collection contains **separate, disconnected papers**, each covering one piece:
> 
> 1. **PBADet** (ICLR 2024) – one-stage anchor-free part–body association; evaluated with Precision/Recall/F1 on COCO-HumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman.
> 2. **Off-CMAB / CLCB** – first offline framework for combinatorial multi-armed bandits; applied to cascading bandits (ranked lists) and LLM cache optimization from logged data only, no online exploration.
> 3. **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** – JEPA self-distillation analysis showing it learns high-influence features and suppresses noisy ones (with LDReg as a related, separate SSL regularizer).
> 4. **4-bit Optimizers** (NeurIPS 2023) – 4-bit AdamW/4-bit Factor optimizer states, up to 57.7% memory savings, LoRA mentioned only as related work.
> 5. **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** – EI (excitatory/inhibitory) RNNs analyzed via singular-value spectra and normalised SVD entropy.
> 
> Elements like CE/MSE, cosine similarity, and LoRA appear only scattered across unrelated papers (e.g., cosine similarity in a contrastive-learning theory paper, LoRA in the 4-bit optimizer's related work and a Hessian-spectrum paper). No work integrates them into one production stack.
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods (from the context)
> 
> **PBADet**
> - Its advantage over prior BPJDet is much less pronounced on the single-part CrowdHuman face–body task; gains come mainly from multi-part settings.
> - Comparison vs ED-Pose had to exclude face/head parts due to inconsistent keypoint counts, so part evaluation is limited to 4 parts (hands/feet).
> - As a one-stage anchor-free detector it depends on the backbone (YOLOv5l6/YOLOv7) and on visible parts; association quality rides on detection accuracy, and body-part offsets in rival methods degrade when parts are occluded.
> - Two-stage baselines remain complex and the method's robustness in heavy occlusion is not fully resolved.
> 
> **Off-CMAB / CLCB (offline combinatorial bandits)**
> - Correctness depends on data-coverage conditions (1-norm/infinity-norm transition-matrix coverage); with partial-coverage logs, only gap bounds under those conditions are proven, and a matching lower bound shows the gap is unavoidable.
> - Purely offline (no exploration) means it cannot adapt to distribution shift; the pessimistic (LCB) estimation may be overly conservative and relies on log quality for the LLM-cache/ranking applications.
> 
> **JEPA "Avoids Noisy Features"**
> - Theory is restricted to deep *linear* networks, special balanced orthogonal initialization, and a simultaneous-diagonalizability assumption; generalization to real nonlinear encoders is only qualitative/experimental.
> - JEPA does not eliminate noisy features—it learns them more slowly and with lower weight amplitude, so under limited training it may under-use informative features too.
> 
> **LDReg (related SSL regularizer)**
> - LID estimation degrades in high dimensions and uses minibatch nearest neighbors; overly forcing low LID can cause complete collapse.
> 
> **4-bit optimizers**
> - Optimal quantization is likely task/dataset-dependent (not covered by the study); only language and vision tasks were tested.
> - Quantizing both first and second moments causes a marginal accuracy drop; without fused operators, 4-bit variants are slower than 8-bit on smaller models (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2 Medium).
> 
> **Spectral EI RNNs (Dale's Law)**
> - Column-constrained EI (ColEI) networks learn poorly and with high variance; sign constraints themselves impair learning; the rank-one column-mean structure yields multimodal, dispersed singular spectra that cause instability (heavy reliance on gradient clipping).
> - Smaller networks and fewer inhibitory units worsen spectra and performance; the paper is largely a diagnosis (NSE as predictor) rather than a complete trainable solution—only a suggested "alternative initialization" is offered.
> 
> **Cross-cutting gaps**
> - No paper addresses combining these: e.g., no work shows 4-bit AdamW/SGD being used for JEPA fine-tuning of Transformers/ResNet-50 with LoRA under CE/MSE plus cosine-similarity regularization while also serving PBADet and offline bandits; nor any unified evaluation of F1/Precision, suboptimality gap, and spectral health in one system.

**community 最终答案**

> ## Are there matching papers?
> 
> No single paper unifies all five needs, but each component maps to a distinct paper in this collection:
> 
> 1. **Anchor-free part–body detection (F1/Precision, crowded rooms, COCO)** → **PBADet** (doc `08b70bc3…`): one-stage anchor-free detector linking hands/feet/face to bodies via a single part-to-body center offset; evaluated on COCO-WholeBody/HumanParts, CrowdHuman, BodyHands; reports Precision/Recall/F1 vs. ED-Pose.
> 2. **Offline combinatorial bandits for cache/ranked lists (offline logs, no exploration)** → **Off-CMAB/CLCB** (doc `d8faaa7f…`): the first offline CMAB framework; applies to **cascading bandits (ranked lists)** and **LLM cache optimization**, cutting LLM inference cost 36% vs. LFU.
> 3. **JEPA-style SSL that avoids noisy features + memory-efficient optimizers** → **"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features"** (doc `40fde037…`, JEPA/MAE feature dynamics, cosine-similarity CCA analysis) and **4-bit Optimizers** (doc `8d5e1455…`, 4-bit AdamW states; LoRA fine-tuning included among benchmarks).
> 4. **Spectral perspective on Dale's-law (E/I constrained) RNNs** → **"Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly"** (doc `e63a94c4…`): shows spectrum, not sign constraints, dominates learning.
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods
> 
> **PBADet**
> - On the single-part face-body task (CrowdHuman) its advantage over BPJDet is **less pronounced**; the framework shines mainly with many parts.
> - Gains depend on auxiliary design choices (association loss, multi-scale center offsets, task-alignment); removing any degrades accuracy/association.
> - Association relies on the part being detected and the one-to-one offset being valid in dense occlusions.
> 
> **Off-CMAB (CLCB)**
> - Requires **data-coverage conditions** (partial 1-norm coverage); quality of decisions is bounded by how well offline logs cover arms/positions.
> - It is a pessimistic estimator—near-optimal only up to a logarithmic factor vs. the lower bound; unexplored actions are inherently under-served (no exploration to fill gaps).
> - Coverage coefficient depends on the logging distribution, so poor/biased logs directly degrade regret guarantees.
> 
> **4-bit optimizers**
> - Optimal quantization (block size, rank-1 vs. linear, factorization) is **task/dataset-dependent**; settings outside the study may outperform them.
> - Quantizing both moments still causes a small accuracy drop; unfused implementation is **slower** than 8-bit on smaller models (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2), needing operator fusion to be competitive.
> - Only language/vision tasks were validated.
> 
> **JEPA noisy-feature analysis**
> - The theoretical result holds only for **deep linear MLPs** under special balanced-orthogonal initialization and simultaneous diagonalizability; generalization to real nonlinear transformers/ResNets is qualitative, not proven.
> - The "avoid noisy features" property is established via critical-time/feature-ordering analysis, not a complete practical training recipe.
> 
> **Dale's-law RNNs (spectral view)**
> - ColEI networks are **unstable without gradient clipping** and show high variance across seeds/initializations; the multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectrum at initialization is the root defect.
> - The work is diagnostic (NSE predicts poor performance) rather than a training fix—small networks and low I-unit ratios remain fundamentally impaired; DANN helps but only by mimicking standard-RNN spectra.
> 
> In short: the collection covers all requested components, each with notable limitations—detection robustness under occlusion, coverage-dependence of offline bandits, task-sensitivity and speed of 4-bit optimizers, linear-only theory for JEPA, and an inherent initialization spectrum pathology for E/I-constrained RNNs.

</details>

<a id="case-paperscope-gap-46"></a>

### paperscope:gap:46 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** We’re building an edge AI system that must: (a) detect and associate body parts (e.g., hands→person) from video streams with high precision, (b) dynamically choose between chain-of-thought and a direct answer to save tokens, and (c) fine-tune large attention-based Transformers under very tight VRAM; we also have a small EI-constrained RNN handling time-series signals. Are there works showing how to use token-probability trends to trigger or skip CoT, quantize optimizer states to ~4-bit for memory-efficient fine-tuning, design anchor-free part–body association models, and analyze spectral properties to stabilize EI RNNs while guiding self-distillation to ignore noisy features? Ideally they report CE/MSE objectives, discuss feedforward heads and Transformer-based conditional guidance (ResNet-50–class backbones are fine), and provide implementation diagrams we can follow.Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

**score：3→2（Δ-1）；rounds：5→3（Δ-2）。**
