Gold 1：

> Below are the key development defects and limitations, grouped by method, as stated or implied in the cited papers.
> 
> 1) PBADet (ICLR 2024; one-stage, anchor-free part–body association on COCO-style datasets)
> - Benefits depend on multi-part settings: On single-part association (e.g., face–body in CrowdHuman), authors explicitly note their advantage over BPJDet is “not as pronounced,” so gains are task-dependent rather than universal.
> - Post-processing sensitivity: Decoding uses NMS plus nearest-center (ℓ2) matching. Performance depends on confidence/IoU thresholds and can be brittle in crowded scenes where many centers are close; this is acknowledged via fixed threshold choices and the need for NMS.
> - Many tunable hyperparameters: Training and assignment rely on numerous knobs (loss weights λiou, λdfl, λcls, λassoc; scaling factor λ; top‑K, α, β; NMS thresholds), making the approach potentially sensitive and increasing engineering overhead.
> - Resource-heavy training: Experiments require multiple V100 GPUs, long schedules (100 epochs), high-resolution inputs (1024–1536), and large batches; these demands can hinder adoption in constrained settings.
> - Small-object reporting gap: COCO-HumanParts small-object APs are not provided (authors note other works also omit APS, but this limits comparability and visibility into small-part behavior).
> 
> 2) EI RNNs under Dale’s Law (NeurIPS 2023; “Learning better with Dale’s Law: A Spectral Perspective”)
> - Restricted theoretical scope: Core claims and proofs are derived in deep linear networks under strong assumptions (balanced orthogonal initialization, diagonal Σxx/Σxy, small initialization). Authors explicitly state generalization to non-simultaneously-diagonalizable data and non-linear models remains open.
> - Stability contingent on gradient clipping: ColEI RNNs are “highly unstable” without gradient clipping and show larger variance across runs, indicating practical fragility of strict EI partitions.
> - Pathology in small/realistic EI ratios: ColEI networks degrade with few inhibitory units and smaller widths due to multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra; performance is vulnerable to EI ratio and size.
> - Open, unresolved issues: Authors highlight unresolved origins of the ColEI spectrum pathology and why large ColEI networks can learn despite a large maximum singular value—important open questions that limit prescriptive design guidance.
> 
> 3) JEPA vs MAE (NeurIPS 2024; “How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features”) 
> - Linear/deep-only theory: Results assume deep linear encoders with specific initializations; the analysis relies on simultaneous diagonalizability of Σxx and Σxy. Authors explicitly note generalization to non-linear encoders and realistic data distributions is not established.
> - Depth-dependent bias: JEPA’s beneficial “influential-feature” bias diminishes substantially for shallow encoders; gains depend on having deep encoders.
> - Potential vulnerability to slow/spurious features: The paper notes JEPA’s focus on “slow features” can be advantageous for semantics but may make it vulnerable to spurious/overly slow signals in certain regimes.
> 
> 4) Memory-Efficient 4‑bit Optimizers (NeurIPS 2023; “Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States”) 
> - Zero-point failure mode for second moment: Authors identify a critical instability when second moments are quantized to zero; the method must explicitly exclude zero (DE-0) or switch to linear mapping to avoid catastrophic update deviations.
> - Speed regressions without fused kernels: For smaller models (e.g., RoBERTa-L, GPT-2), 4‑bit optimizers are slower than 8‑bit baselines unless custom fused operators are used; this is reported directly in timing results.
> - Task-specific tuning burden: Optimal block sizes and normalization/mapping (e.g., rank‑1 normalization, B128, linear vs DE-0) are task-sensitive; authors note performance depends on dataset and training details.
> - Accuracy trade-offs do occur: In pretraining (e.g., Swin-T on ImageNet-1k), accuracy is “comparable” rather than strictly lossless (e.g., 80.8 vs 81.2), indicating a small but real performance gap in some setups.
> - Evaluation scope limits: Authors explicitly state their evaluation is limited to vision and language; applicability to RL, audio, or graph learning is not assessed.
> 
> 5) Combinatorial RL with Preference Feedback (ICML 2025; “MNL‑VQL”)
> - Strong modeling assumptions: Results hinge on a contextual MNL preference model with linear utilities (known feature map), and on the assumption that rewards/transitions depend only on the chosen item (independence from the rest of the slate). These assumptions can be restrictive in real recommender systems.
> - Realizability/completeness requirements: The method assumes the function class F contains the true optimal item‑level Q and the outputs of Bellman (and second-moment) operators. Authors acknowledge this is stronger than in prior RL work and is essential for their point‑wise bonus analysis, but it is a heavy assumption in practice.
> - Algorithmic complexity and sensitivity: The approach alternates optimistic/pessimistic utilities because naïve optimism can fail when the outside option’s estimated value is largest; correctness depends on carefully chosen thresholds (uk), confidence sets, and a consistent bonus oracle, increasing sensitivity and implementation burden.
> - κ and horizon dependencies remain: Although the leading term avoids κ, the regret still contains terms that scale with 1/κ and high powers of H (e.g., O(1/κ·d²·H²) polylog factors), implying performance can deteriorate in difficult preference landscapes (small κ) and with long horizons.
> - Practical evaluation scope: Experiments are limited to a synthetic budget environment and a MovieLens subset with engineered “junk items.” Real-world dynamics (e.g., inter-item externalities in slates) and broader domains are not yet covered.
> 
> These defects are taken directly from statements, assumptions, empirical findings, and limitations described in the cited papers. They reflect sensitivity to hyperparameters and spectra (vision and EI-RNNs), theoretical scope constraints (JEPA and EI-RNNs), quantization-specific failure modes and speed regressions (4-bit optimizers), and strong model/realizability assumptions with κ/H-dependent regret terms (MNL‑VQL).

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved context, I can identify papers matching each category. Note: I found no document in the collection that explicitly compares regression-like vs. classification-style objectives in joint-embedding SSL (c), and no paper explicitly analyzing development defects of these methods collectively—I can only report defects/limitations stated in each paper's own text.
> 
> **Five papers:**
> 
> **(a) PBADet** (One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association; ICLR 2024)
> - One-stage, anchor-free part-to-body association via a single part-to-body center offset; evaluated on COCOHumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman, AnimalPose/AP-10K. Outperforms BPJDet/HierR-CNN; on COCOHumanParts all-categories AP 42.7–43.0, AP.5 69.5–70.0.
> - Development defects (from its own analysis): two-stage/anchor-based predecessors (BodyHands, BPJDet) suffer complexity, redundant extended representations, invalid body-to-part offsets when parts are occluded, and degradation as part count grows; anchor-based methods face anchor hyper-parameter tuning, positive/negative imbalance, and offsets falling outside anchor boxes. PBADet's own ablations show removing association loss, multi-scale offsets, or task alignment each degrades performance.
> 
> **(b) "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Recurrent networks with strict E/I separation (ColEI and recurrent DANN), analyzed via singular-value spectrum, trained on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and naturalistic object recognition with SGD-style training.
> - Development defects: sign-constrained ColEI RNNs learn worse and more variably than standard RNNs/DANNs; gradient clipping mitigates but does not fix; spectral pathology (multimodal, dispersed singular values, large unconstrained singular values) impairs learning, worse for small networks/fewer inhibitory units; sign constraints also impair learning though less than spectrum.
> 
> **(c)** No document in the retrieved collection explicitly compares regression (MSE) vs. classification (cross-entropy) objectives within a joint-embedding SSL method. Closest related works: "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (JEPA vs MAE, latent-space regression bias, with limitations: deep linear MLPs, special initialization, simultaneous diagonalizability) and LDReg (dimensional-collapse regularization for SSL). Neither directly tests classification-style targets, so this exact paper could not be identified.
> 
> **(d) "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - 4-bit AdamW (quantized first/second moments, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer, factorization) supporting Transformers (Swin-T, Transformer-Base, RoBERTa-L, GPT-2, LLaMA-7B/13B/33B) and LoRA-style parameter-efficient tuning (explicitly references LoRA; instruction-following on Alpaca/MMLU).
> - Development defects (stated): optimal quantization setting likely task-dependent; only language/vision tasks tested (RL/audio/graphs untested); small-model speed slower than 8-bit without fused operators; quantization of both moments causes marginal accuracy drop; sublinear-memory baselines (Adafactor β1=0, SM3) suffer performance degradation on classification.
> 
> **(e) "Combinatorial Reinforcement Learning with Preference Feedback" (MNL-VQL)** (ICML 2025)
> - Combinatorial RL for slate/assortment selection under MNL preference feedback, item values via general function approximation, optimism via alternating optimistic/pessimistic utilities, nearly minimax-optimal regret (lower bound Ω(d√(HK)+d_lin√(HK)) in linear MDPs).
> - Development defects/challenges (stated): unknown item values and long-term values, maintaining optimism with tractable assortment selection in exponentially large action space, tighter regret than summing MNL-bandit regrets; myopic MNL-bandit baselines converge to suboptimal solutions, and LSVI-UCB becomes impractical as assortment count grows.
> 
> **Summary of development defects across the set:** the methods are constrained by architectural complexity and anchor/representation redundancy (a), spectral pathologies and training instability from biological constraints (b), incomplete/limited empirical validation of loss-objective design choices in SSL (c, per available evidence), task-dependent quantization settings and limited domain coverage plus implementation overhead (d), and exponential action spaces, optimism-tractability tension, and myopic baselines in combinatorial RL (e). The user's request for a collective "development defects" analysis is only partially supported: the corpus contains each paper's individual limitations, but no cross-paper synthesis.

> Here is my answer:
> 
> ## Papers matching each requested topic
> 
> **(a) One-stage no-anchor human part–person association** — **PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association** (Gao et al., ICLR 2024, doc `08b70bc3…`). One-stage, anchor-free detector extending YOLOv5/YOLOv7; introduces a single part-to-body center offset, evaluated on BodyHands, COCO-HumanParts, CrowdHuman (face–body), and COCO-style benchmarks; also tested on AnimalPose/AP-10K quadruped extension.
> 
> **(b) Recurrent networks with strict E/I separation via spectral analysis for stable training** — **Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective** (Li, Cornford, Ghosh & Richards, NeurIPS 2023, doc `e63a94c4…`). Analyzes RNNs with Dale's-Law E/I constraints (ColEI) and recurrent DANNs; shows the pathological multimodal singular-value spectrum (not sign constraints) impairs SGD-style training, and that normalised SVD entropy predicts performance. Tasks: adding problem, sequential MNIST (digit stream), Penn Tree Bank (natural language), naturalistic object recognition.
> 
> **(c) Joint-embedding self-supervised methods preferring predictive latent targets** — **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks** (Littwin et al., NeurIPS 2024, doc `40fde037…`). Formalizes JEPA (predict latent target) vs MAE (pixel reconstruction); proves JEPA's regression objective prioritizes high-influence features and suppresses noisy ones, with ImageNet-1K CCA confirmation. Note: no paper in the collection directly compares regression-like vs classification-style SSL objectives; this paper compares regression-in-latent-space (JEPA) vs regression-in-pixel-space (MAE).
> 
> **(d) Memory-lean quantized Adam/AdamW** — **Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States** (Li, Chen & Zhu, NeurIPS 2023, doc `8d5e1455…`). Quantizes first/second moments of Adam/AdamW to 4-bit (B128 blockwise + rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer, factorization). Evaluated on RoBERTa-L (GLUE/SQuAD), Swin-T (ImageNet), GPT-2 (E2E-NLG), Transformer (WMT14 MT), and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning (Alpaca→MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA), up to 57.7% memory savings; LoRA cited as the delta-tuning baseline it compares against.
> 
> **(e) Combinatorial RL with MNL preference feedback** — **Combinatorial Reinforcement Learning with Preference Feedback** (Lee & Oh, ICML 2025, doc `90d499d9…`). Agent sequentially offers assortments under a multinomial-logit choice model; algorithm MNL-VQL provides the first regret upper bound plus a matching Ω(d√(HK)+d_lin√(HK)) lower bound (nearly minimax-optimal) in linear MDPs, reformulating assortment selection as an LP to avoid combinatorial enumeration.
> 
> ---
> 
> ## Development defects (limitations) of these methods
> 
> **(a) PBADet**
> - Heavily relies on the base detector (YOLOv5/v7); it extends rather than replaces the anchor-free object representation, so its gains are tied to the chosen backbone.
> - The single part-to-body offset is designed for parts, but the CrowdHuman face-body single-part task shows a weaker advantage over BPJDet; association benefit shrinks when few parts exist.
> - Requires multi-scale feature maps, task-alignment learning, and an explicit association loss — performance degrades if any of these components (multi-scale offsets, task alignment, association head) is removed.
> - Benchmarks emphasize hand/face/body; occlusion handling is only addressed indirectly via the one-to-one part-to-body guarantee (it avoids the invalidity of body-to-part offsets when parts are invisible, but doesn't explicitly solve occlusion).
> 
> **(b) E/I RNN spectral analysis**
> - The analysis is empirical and partly theoretical on simple linear/recurrent setups; the mechanism (column-mean rank-one nilpotent structure) is derived from initialization, and open theoretical questions remain (origin of multi-modal spectra; why large ColEI networks learn well despite large max singular value).
> - ColEI networks show more variance across seeds/initializations and are highly unstable without gradient clipping — practical stability still requires clipping; small networks with few I units train poorly.
> - Findings are demonstrated on sequential MNIST/adding/PTB; scaling to larger, more complex architectures is not established.
> 
> **(c) JEPA analysis**
> - Formal results rely on deep linear networks with special (balanced orthogonal) initialization and simultaneously-diagonalizable data — non-linear models and general distributions are not covered (the authors note this as a limitation).
> - The regression-style latent prediction is susceptible to representation collapse (mitigated only via StopGrad/self-distillation), and the implicit bias may make JEPA vulnerable to spurious or slow features.
> - The comparison is JEPA-vs-MAE; there is no direct head-to-head of regression-like vs classification-style (cross-entropy) SSL objectives in this work.
> 
> **(d) 4-bit optimizer**
> - Accuracy is matched on the tested tasks, but the optimal quantization mapping appears task-dependent; only language and vision tasks were tested (no claim of universal transferability).
> - 4-bitFactor (sublinear-memory second-moment factorization) is only applicable to the second moment and mainly to tensor-shaped parameters; 1-D tensors fall back to B128 quantization.
> - Implementation speed was slower than 8-bit for smaller models due to lack of fused operators (corrected only via fusing); the quantization scheme adds design complexity (block size, zero-point exclusion, rank-1 normalization choices).
> - Convergence guarantees are provided for quantized SGD(M), not directly for the full Adam/AdamW 4-bit pipeline.
> 
> **(e) Combinatorial RL / MNL-VQL**
> - Assumes the MNL choice model with linear utilities for the theoretical guarantees; deviation from MNL choice behavior is not covered.
> - The minimax-optimal lower bound is established only for the linear-MDP special case (d≥2, d_lin≥6); general-function-approximation setting lacks a matching lower bound.
> - Optimism is maintained by alternating optimistic/pessimistic utility estimates, a delicate procedure; experiments show a myopic baseline converges to a suboptimal solution, and LSVI-UCB becomes impractical as assortments grow — indicating sensitivity to the problem structure and scalability concerns.
> - Evaluation is on an online-shopping style environment; the theory is tailored to long-term user-engagement settings, so applicability to other combinatorial RL domains is untested.
> 
> **Cross-cutting note:** The collection does not contain a single paper directly comparing regression vs classification-style SSL objectives (item c is matched only by the JEPA-vs-MAE analysis), and no one paper spans all five areas — these are five independent contributions.

</details>

### paperscope:gap:64 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building a production system that: detects and links body parts to the right person on common object datasets; pretrains encoders with joint-embedding SSL to avoid overfitting to pixel noise; trains under tight GPU memory by using low-precision moment states while still fine-tuning attention models end-to-end (e.g., with LoRA); enforces an excitatory/inhibitory split in recurrent modules for time-series stability via spectral control; and deploys a slate recommendation policy trained from user choice signals (discrete-choice style) with provable efficiency. Can you point me to research covering these pieces—covering optimization (SGD/AdamW), reconstruction vs predictive losses (MSE vs CE), and transformer-based pipelines—that has results on COCO-like, MNIST/CIFAR-100, and modern NLU/MT benchmarks?Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

Gold 1：

> Development defects and limitations by method
> 
> PBADet (ICLR 2024; one-stage anchor-free part–body association)
> - Diminished advantage in single-part settings: On CrowdHuman’s face–body association (single part), the paper explicitly notes the advantage over BPJDet is “not as pronounced” (Appendix A.1), indicating reduced benefit when only one part type is present.
> - Sensitivity to thresholds and alignment hyperparameters: Inference requires dataset-specific NMS/confidence thresholds (BodyHands vs COCOHumanParts) and relies on task-alignment hyperparameters (K, α, β). Ablations show removing task alignment or multi-scale handling degrades results, implying sensitivity to these choices.
> - Post-hoc Euclidean assignment can be brittle: Decoding assigns each part to the nearest predicted body center that encloses it. This simple rule can be sensitive to localization noise and close-proximity bodies in crowded scenes.
> - High input resolution and compute: Training/evaluation often use 1024–1536 px inputs and multi-GPU setups (4×V100, 100 epochs), which may be costly for production-scale deployments.
> - Limited empirical scope for generalization: The “universal framework” claim (e.g., wheel–car) is not validated beyond human parts; performance on small objects (APS) is not consistently reported for baselines, and gains vary by category.
> 
> Dale’s-law RNNs (NeurIPS 2023; ColEI vs recurrent DANNs)
> - Instability and high variance for ColEI: Column-sign-constrained (ColEI) networks learn poorly without gradient clipping and show high variance across seeds and training (Fig. 2; App. Fig. 10), indicating unstable optimization.
> - Strong dependence on spectral initialization: Performance hinges on spectral properties at initialization; ColEI often yields multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra that impede learning, especially for small networks or low inhibitory ratios (Fig. 3, 5, 6).
> - Hyperparameter fragility: ColEI requires tuning spectral radius (ρ) and benefits from larger ρ than standard/DANN RNNs; performance degrades at smaller ρ (App. Fig. 9).
> - Open theoretical gaps remain: The origin of pathological multi-modal spectra and why large ColEI networks can learn despite large max singular values are unresolved; NSE is diagnostic but does not prescribe a construction for robust ColEI training.
> - Biological fidelity trade-offs: Recurrent DANNs improve learning but do not capture all inhibitory subtypes; practical modeling may require hybrid approaches and added biological details (e.g., I–I connections, time constants).
> 
> JEPA implicit bias (NeurIPS 2024; deep linear analysis of self-distillation)
> - Theory restricted to simplified regimes: Results rely on deep linear networks, special initializations, and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances; generalization to nonlinear encoders and realistic data is not established (Limitations section).
> - Depth-dependent bias: The beneficial bias toward “influential” (high regression coefficient) features emerges only with deep encoders; with shallow encoders the effect diminishes, limiting robustness across architectures.
> - Potential vulnerability to spurious/slow features: The analysis acknowledges that JEPA’s bias toward low-variance, predictive subspaces may make it vulnerable to spurious or excessively slow-varying features, depending on data/task composition.
> - Learning order inversion risk: When variance (λ) and regression strength (ρ) disagree across features, JEPA can prioritize features differently than MAE (Fig. 1), which could hurt tasks where high-variance cues matter early in training.
> 
> 4-bit optimizers (NeurIPS 2023; memory-efficient AdamW)
> - Configuration sensitivity, instability modes: Ablations show many 4-bit second-moment settings are unstable (high Unstable%) unless the zero-point issue is addressed and rank-1/linear quantization is used (Table 1). Performance hinges on block size, mapping (DE vs linear), and normalization (rank-1 vs blockwise), requiring careful tuning.
> - Zero-point pitfall in v: Standard mappings that include zero severely distort updates (inverse-sqrt amplification), necessitating special mappings (DE-0 or linear without zero). This adds implementation complexity and risk if misconfigured.
> - Throughput penalty without fused kernels: 4-bit versions can be slower than 8-bit baselines absent fused ops; the paper reports slower runs for RoBERTa/GPT-2 unless fused kernels are used (Table 4).
> - Minor accuracy regressions in pretraining: On Swin-T pretraining, 4-bit variants are “comparable” but not strictly equal to full-precision (e.g., 80.8 vs 81.2 top-1), indicating small but real trade-offs.
> - Factorization compatibility gaps: The factorized second-moment variant (more memory efficient) can’t be applied when tensors are packed to 1-D (e.g., FSDP-packed LLaMA-7B), limiting deployment in certain parallelization schemes.
> - Scope limits: Experiments cover vision and language; suitability for RL, audio, and graphs remains untested (Limitations).
> 
> Combinatorial RL with preference feedback (ICML 2025; MNL-VQL)
> - Modeling assumptions may be restrictive:
>   - MNL choice with linear utilities and the “chosen item’s reward/transition independent of other items” (footnote 2). These structural assumptions may not hold in richer user/item interactions.
>   - Completeness/realizability for general function approximation (Assumption 3.3) is strong and can be hard to meet in practice.
> - κ-sensitivity remains: Although the leading regret drops the 1/κ factor, lower-order terms still include 1/κ·d^2·H^2 and related factors, so small κ can degrade guarantees.
> - Algorithmic complexity: Each step solves an LP reformulation of assortment optimization and maintains dual Q-estimate sequences (optimistic and overly optimistic/pessimistic), online mirror-descent MNL fits, and a consistent bonus oracle with online sub-sampling—computationally heavier than standard Q-learning.
> - Many moving parts and thresholds: The switch threshold u_k, multiple bonus radii, cover sizes, and sub-sampling schedules add tuning burden; correctness depends on consistent bonus oracles and covering arguments.
> - Evaluation scope: Experiments use a synthetic budgeted-shopping task and a MovieLens subset; baselines are limited (myopic and holistic LSVI-UCB), and performance/scalability for very large slates or long horizons in production are not fully characterized.
> 
> Cross-cutting observations relevant to production integration
> - Hyperparameter and threshold sensitivity (PBADet, 4-bit optimizers, MNL-VQL) suggests additional tuning/load testing may be required per domain/dataset (e.g., NMS thresholds; block size/mapping for 4-bit v; u_k and oracle settings for MNL-VQL).
> - Compute trade-offs: PBADet benefits from high-resolution inputs and multi-scale heads; MNL-VQL adds LPs and sub-sampled regression per step; 4-bit optimizers save memory but can cost throughput without fused kernels.
> - Assumption gaps: MNL utilities and independence assumptions (RL slate), deep-linear assumptions (JEPA analysis), and spectral constraints (Dale’s-law RNNs) may limit plug-and-play transfer; validate these assumptions on your distributions before adoption.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Research coverage
> 
> **1. Body-part detection/linking (COCO-like):** *PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association* (ICLR 2024). Detects parts (hands, feet, head, face) and links each to its parent body via a single part-to-body center offset, on COCO-HumanParts, COCO, CrowdHuman, BodyHands, and animal datasets (AnimalPose, AP-10K). Also reviews alternatives (BPJDet, HierR-CNN, BodyHands, ED-Pose).
> 
> **2. Joint-embedding SSL vs. pixel reconstruction:** *Why JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks* (NeurIPS 2024). Formally compares JEPA (predict in latent space) vs MAE (MSE reconstruction in input space): MAE prioritizes high-variance/noisy subspaces, JEPA learns high-influence (high-regression-coefficient) features, verified on ImageNet-1K with I-JEPA vs MAE. *LDReg* (ICLR 2024) addresses SSL dimensional collapse and reports transfer to COCO detection/segmentation. The *Video-Based Representation Learning for RL in Exogenous Block MDPs* paper also compares forward (reconstruction) modeling vs temporal contrastive (predictive) learning under pixel noise.
> 
> **3. Low-precision optimizer states + LoRA fine-tuning:** *Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States* (NeurIPS 2023). 4-bit AdamW/Adam quantizes first/second moments (B128/DE, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluding linear quantizer, optional factorization). Results on GLUE (RoBERTa-L, NLU), SQuAD (QA), E2E-NLG (GPT-2), WMT14 en-de (Transformer, MT), ImageNet (Swin-T), and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning; explicitly compatible with LoRA. The *Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure* (ICML 2025) paper studies SGD/AdamW-trained models and LoRA adapters (GPT-2, TinyLlama on MathQA/Shakespeare).
> 
> **4. Excitatory/inhibitory recurrent modules with spectral control:** *Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly* (NeurIPS 2023). Shows ColEI (column E/I partition) RNNs underperform due to pathological (multimodal, dispersed) singular-value spectra, not sign constraints; proposes normalised SVD entropy (NSE) as a pre-training diagnostic and spectral-transplant experiments. Benchmarks: adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition.
> 
> **5. Slate recommendation from discrete-choice signals with efficiency guarantees:** *Combinatorial Reinforcement Learning with Preference Feedback* (MNL-VQL). Models user choice via multinomial logit (MNL); optimistic value iteration over assortments with provable regret bounds and matching lower bound (minimax-optimal in linear MDPs). *Offline Learning for Combinatorial Multi-armed Bandits* (CLCB) covers offline/slate-style cascading recommendations with regret guarantees under partial coverage.
> 
> **Cross-cutting (SGD/AdamW, MSE vs CE, transformers):** the 4-bit optimizer paper covers SGDM/Adam/AdamW compression with a convergence proof for quantized SGD(M) and CE-based NLU/MT; the Hessian paper covers SGD and AdamW dynamics on MNIST/CIFAR-10/100/ImageNet and LLMs; PCP/TAPT covers RoBERTa AdamW fine-tuning with MLM cross-entropy; the contrastive-learning analysis paper covers InfoNCE (CE-style) losses on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet.
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods
> 
> **PBADet:** On the single-part CrowdHuman face-body task its advantage over BPJDet is marginal (better body MR-2, competitive AP only); small-part AP is still low (hands ≈40, feet ≈30 AP); the ED-Pose comparison uses ground-truth part boxes, an idealized setup; extension beyond humans/quadrupeds untested; ablation shows all three components (association loss, multi-scale offsets, task alignment) are needed — removing any degrades conditional accuracy/joint AP.
> 
> **JEPA noise-avoidance analysis:** Theory is restricted to deep *linear* networks with balanced orthogonal initialization and simultaneous-diagonalizability assumptions (the authors acknowledge these are "somewhat unrealistic"); the high-influence-feature bias appears only with deep encoders and vanishes when shallow; JEPA is inherently collapse-prone (needs stop-grad/non-contrastive tricks); the bias can invert feature-learning order so JEPA may neglect high-variance features that matter; ImageNet evidence is qualitative (CCA alignment) rather than end-to-end task gains.
> 
> **4-bit optimizers:** Optimal quantization settings are task-dependent (no one-size-fits-all); evaluated only on language/vision — RL, audio, graph tasks unvalidated; small models run slower without fused operators; quantizing both moments yields a marginal accuracy drop; memory savings saturate as bitwidth decreases; the convergence proof covers quantized SGD(M), not the full Adam/AdamW update.
> 
> **Dale's-Law/spectral RNNs:** ColEI networks train worse and with much higher seed variance; gradient clipping is needed for stability (unstable without it); sign constraints themselves still cost ~0.7–1% error; small networks with few inhibitory units are particularly bad; the spectrum pathology is explained heuristically (rank-one nilpotent column-mean component) without a complete theory; NSE is only a diagnostic — no improved initialization/algorithm is delivered; tests are small-scale (sMNIST, PTB, adding problem).
> 
> **MNL-VQL / slate RL:** Assumes an MNL preference model with *linear* utilities, a known feature map, completeness/realizability plus second-moment completeness (stronger than prior work); the chosen item's reward/transition is assumed independent of other items in the assortment; experiments are synthetic with a simulated user (no production deployment); guarantees depend on generalized Eluder dimension, and regret lower bounds hold only for the linear-MDP special case.
> 
> **Hessian power-law analysis:** The power-law structure only holds for well-trained networks and is lost with small width/depth, limited data, noisy labels, or large-batch training; SOTA LLMs are excluded due to Hessian computation cost; findings (including LoRA behavior) are correlation-based on a few models/datasets; notably, LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the power-law Hessian structure that full fine-tuning does — a caveat for your end-to-end LoRA plan.
> 
> **LDReg:** LID estimation degrades in high dimensions and relies on minibatch nearest neighbors; forcing very low LID can trigger complete collapse; global covariance/variance regularizers barely help, so the method hinges on the local estimator.
> 
> **Exogenous-noise video RL:** Both forward modeling and temporal contrastive learning fail when exogenous noise is too large, and a lower-bound construction shows video-only data cannot identify the endogenous state in a hard family (exponential identifiability barrier) — a fundamental limit for pixel-based pretraining.
> 
> **Offline CMAB (CLCB):** Requires partial-coverage assumptions and offline logged data; gains are demonstrated on synthetic/Yelp data and an LLM-cache proxy task, not a real slate recommender.
> 
> **PCP/TAPT:** Task-adaptive pre-training (TAPT) often *hurts* sentence-pair performance; results are grid-searched over a narrow hyperparameter range and limited to sentence-pair tasks.
> 
> In short, each component has a matching paper with benchmarks in the requested families (COCO-like for detection, MNIST/CIFAR-100 for SSL/optimization analysis, GLUE/WMT/MMLU for NLU/MT), but the guarantees are mostly for simplified or synthetic settings, and the papers' own limitations sections flag assumptions (linear models, idealized initialization, structural choice models, partial coverage, small scale) that you should treat as risks when building the production system.

**community 最终答案**

> Here is the research coverage for each piece, with the development defects (limitations) noted from the papers themselves.
> 
> **1. Part–body detection/association on COCO-like data** — *PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association* (ICLR 2024; evaluated on COCO-HumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman, AnimalPose/AP-10K).
> - Development defects: single part-to-body center offset, so association is only valid for visible parts; on single-part face–body CrowdHuman its advantage over BPJDet is small; comparisons to ED-Pose are favorable (ground-truth part boxes used for the pose baseline); performance still depends on the anchor-free detector backbone; one-to-many body-to-part cases are avoided by design rather than solved.
> 
> **2. Joint-embedding SSL pretraining to avoid pixel noise** — *How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks* (NeurIPS 2024; ImageNet-1K I-JEPA vs MAE with ViT encoders).
> - Development defects: theory holds only for deep *linear* networks with special initialization and simultaneous diagonalizability; qualitative generalization is supported empirically but not proven; the predictive (latent) loss trades pixel fidelity for abstractness, so reconstruction (MSE/MAE) still overfits pixel noise when the model is small; the analysis is limited to two paradigms (JEPA vs MAE) and does not cover all SSL losses.
> 
> **3. Low-precision optimizer moments + end-to-end attention/LoRA fine-tuning** — *Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States* (NeurIPS 2023; Adam/AdamW/SGD(M); GLUE/NLU, SQuAD/QA, E2E-NLG, MT with Transformer, Swin-T ImageNet, LLaMA fine-tuning; LoRA discussed as complementary). Also *BSO: Binary Spiking Online Optimization* covers low-memory moment states on CIFAR-10/100/ImageNet but for spiking (not attention) models.
> - Development defects: optimal quantization is task/data-dependent; memory savings saturate as bitwidth drops (total memory reported); smaller models are slower without fused kernels; quantizing both moments yields a marginal accuracy drop; second-moment zero-point problem requires special linear/rank-1 quantizers; evaluation is restricted to language/vision tasks.
> 
> **4. Excitatory/inhibitory recurrent modules with spectral control** — *Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective* (NeurIPS 2023; adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition).
> - Development defects: naive E/I partitioning (ColEI) learns worse and with higher variance, is highly unstable without gradient clipping, and has pathological (multimodal/dispersed) singular-value spectra at initialization; small networks or few inhibitory units degrade both spectra and performance; spectral design (e.g., DANN-style, high NSE) matters more than sign constraints; no established recipe for guaranteed stable time-series training.
> 
> **5. Slate recommendation from discrete-choice signals with provable efficiency** — *Combinatorial Reinforcement Learning with Preference Feedback (MNL-VQL)* (assortment/slate recommendation under a multinomial-logit choice model; regret upper/lower bounds, minimax optimality in linear MDPs; synthetic online-shopping experiments).
> - Development defects: assumes MNL choice with linear utilities and general function approximation measured by (generalized) Eluder dimension; guarantees proven for linear MDPs (matching lower bounds) but experiments are on synthetic budget environments, not real large-scale deployments; myopic baselines converge to suboptimal policies; item values are unknown and must be estimated online.
> 
> **Cross-cutting coverage of your requirements:** optimization (SGD/AdamW) and modern NLU/MT are covered by the 4-bit optimizer paper (GLUE, SQuAD, SacreBLEU); reconstruction (MSE/CE) vs predictive losses by the JEPA paper (and GEEA's BCE/MSE reconstruction vs prediction-matching analysis); transformer pipelines by the 4-bit optimizer (Transformer MT, Swin-T, LLaMA) and JEPA (ViT); COCO-like results by PBADet; MNIST by the Dale's-Law RNN paper (sequential MNIST); CIFAR-100 by the BSO spiking-optimizer paper. No single paper covers all benchmarks; the strongest defects across the set are task-dependent quantization, linear-only SSL theory, E/I spectral instability, and MNL/linear-model assumptions in the recommender.

</details>

<a id="case-paperscope-gap-67"></a>

### paperscope:gap:67 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively cover: (a) single-pass, anchor-free human part-to-body association on COCO-style datasets and report standard losses (MSE, cross-entropy) and metrics (Precision, F1); (b) the learning dynamics of recurrent nets with biologically inspired excitatory/inhibitory separation, analyzed via spectral properties (e.g., singular-value distributions, entropy) under SGD/AdamW; (c) self-supervised joint-embedding predictive training that biases latent features toward high-influence signals (beyond raw pixel variance), with demonstrations on MNIST/CIFAR-100 and Transformer/ResNet-50 backbones; (d) memory-efficient optimization using sub-byte (≈4-bit) states for Adam/AdamW with block/group quantization and handling zero-point issues; and (e) uncertainty-aware reinforcement learning using ensembles of value distributions where disagreement (e.g., 1-Wasserstein) drives exploration. Prefer works discussing interpretability, attention, and common evaluation protocols.Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

**score：4→3（Δ-1）；rounds：6→6（Δ+0）。**

工具安排：naive 为第1轮5次、第2轮3次、第3轮3次、第4轮2次、第5轮2次；community 为第1轮5次、第2轮3次、第3轮2次、第4轮3次、第5轮3次。最终回答另占一轮。

两边均为 6 轮，但工具总数 15→16，同轮并发安排及工具工作量仍可能不同。

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below are the development defects/limitations explicitly stated or directly evidenced in the provided papers. Each item stays within the claims, experiments, or formal statements made by the authors.
> 
> 1) PBADet (one-stage, anchor-free part–body association)
> - Advantage diminishes in single-part settings: On CrowdHuman (face–body only), the paper notes “the advantages of our method over BPJDet are not as pronounced” (A.1), i.e., PBADet’s gains rely on multi-part association and are smaller when only one part is present.
> - Not consistently superior in COCO-style detection metrics: On COCOHumanParts, the authors state “our method achieves APs that are on par with BPJDet,” with gains mainly for specific sizes/categories (Tables 2–3). Thus, detection performance is comparable rather than universally better.
> - Dataset-specific tuning required: Inference thresholds (τconf, τiou) are set differently for BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, and CrowdHuman; training also depends on several hyperparameters (λiou, λdfl, λcls, λassoc, scaling λ, K, α, β) that are chosen per setup (Section 4.1 and A.1). This indicates sensitivity to dataset/task hyperparameters.
> 
> 2) Learning better with Dale’s Law (recurrent EI networks; ColEI vs. DANN)
> - ColEI RNNs learn poorly and unstably: The paper repeatedly shows ColEI networks underperform DANNs/standard RNNs and are “highly unstable without gradient clipping,” with higher variance across runs (Figures 2, 4; discussion section). This instability reflects a problematic multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectrum.
> - Strong dependence on size and E/I ratio: Small networks and/or few inhibitory units degrade both spectrum and learning (“worse for small networks with fewer I units”), while larger networks and balanced ratios improve performance; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) is predictive (Figures 5–7).
> - Theoretical results rely on restrictive assumptions: Key derivations assume special initializations and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances (Assumption 3.1; Section 3; “ODE Equivalence”). This limits the direct generality of the proofs to broader, practical settings.
> - Open issues remain: The origin of ColEI’s multi‑modal spectra and why large ColEI networks learn well despite large max singular values are unresolved (Discussion), highlighting incomplete theoretical closure.
> 
> 3) How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features (deep linear self-distillation)
> - Scope limited to deep linear models and special data assumptions: The authors explicitly state the theory assumes deep linear encoders, specific orthogonal/“balanced” initializations, and simultaneously diagonalizable Σxx and Σyx; generalization to nonlinear nets and real data is “currently unexplored” (Limitations, Sections 3–6).
> - Depth dependence: The key JEPA bias (toward high‑influence features) “takes hold only when the encoder is deep and diminishes substantially when the encoder is shallow” (Abstract, Sections 2–3). Shallow encoders may not exhibit the desired bias.
> - Potential vulnerability to slow/spurious signals: The Discussion cautions that JEPA’s bias toward predictive low-variance/slow features “may shed light on JEPAs vulnerability to spurious or slow features.” This is an acknowledged risk in practical use.
> 
> 4) Memory-Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States
> - Fragility if the second moment is quantized naively (zero‑point problem): Including zero in the quantization mapping for v causes severe error/instability (“quantizing non-zero quantities to zero will cause significant deviation”; Fig. 3; Table 1 shows many unstable runs). Robust training requires a mapping that excludes 0 (DE‑0) or a linear map and often rank‑1 normalization.
> - Quantizer design and block size are critical: Large blocks (e.g., B2048) harm approximation at 4‑bit; the paper needs smaller blocks (B128), rank‑1 normalization, or factorization to maintain accuracy (Sections 3–4; C.3).
> - Speed overhead without kernel fusion: On RoBERTa-L and GPT‑2, 4‑bit optimizers “appear to be slower than 8‑bit” until a fused implementation is used (Table 4), i.e., real-world speed benefits require extra engineering.
> - Small accuracy gaps in some pretraining tasks: While finetuning is “lossless,” pretraining tasks can be slightly lower vs. FP32 (e.g., ImageNet CLS 80.8 vs. 81.2; WMT14 MT 26.28 vs. 26.61 in Table 2).
> - Applicability not yet shown beyond language/vision: The authors note evaluations are “currently limited to language and vision,” with applicability to RL, audio, graphs “still needs further study” (Limitations).
> - Task-dependent quantization choices: They acknowledge “optimal quantization setting probably depends on task/datasets/training details,” indicating extra tuning burden (Limitations).
> 
> 5) Diverse Projection Ensembles for Distributional RL (PE‑DQN)
> - Residual epistemic error at convergence: Because each member uses a projection, the ensemble’s fixed point need not match the true return distribution; “undesired properties are twofold: (1) bias; (2) ensemble disagreement does not vanish in the fixed point” (Appendix A.4, Propositions 8–9). This can complicate disentangling aleatoric vs. epistemic uncertainty.
> - Shared TD targets bias disagreement toward TD-target error, not true-value error: The paper stresses that with joint bootstrapping, raw ensemble disagreement measures error w.r.t. projected targets rather than the true return (Section 4.2); they introduce an uncertainty propagation scheme to compensate—but the method’s optimism bonus then depends on this extra estimator and its hyperparameters.
> - Uniform mixture only: The authors explicitly “only considered the use of uniform mixtures,” noting that more selective weighting across state–action regions is left for future work (Conclusion), limiting flexibility.
> - Computation/training cost: On the full bsuite, PE‑DQN (and IDS) required substantially more wall-clock time than DLTV and BDQN+P (Appendix B.2). Although PE‑DQN uses fewer models than some baselines, the approach still carries nontrivial compute overhead.
> - Sensitivity of optimism/UCB scaling: The implementation required schedules that decay the bonus β to ensure convergence (Appendix B.2), indicating sensitivity to the exploration-bonus scale and the need for careful scheduling.
> 
> These defects are taken from the papers’ own experimental findings, formal analyses, discussion/limitations sections, or explicit hyperparameter/procedure notes. They reflect constraints, sensitivities, or unresolved issues that would affect further development or deployment of each method.

**naive 最终答案**

> I have enough evidence to compile the answer with identified papers and their development defects.
> 
> ---
> 
> ## Papers collectively covering the five topics
> 
> **Topic (a) — PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association** (ICLR 2024)
> - **Match:** One-stage, anchor-free detector for human part-to-body association using a single part-to-body center offset; evaluated on COCO-HumanParts, COCO-WholeBody, BodyHands, CrowdHuman. Losses include classification loss (cross-entropy-style), localization (IoU/DFL), and an ℓ1-based association loss; reports AP, Precision/Recall/F1 vs. ED-Pose, conditional accuracy, joint AP.
> - **Partial match:** It uses IoU/DFL + classification + ℓ1 association losses rather than explicitly MSE; Precision/F1 are reported mainly in the comparison vs. ED-Pose.
> 
> **Topic (b) — Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly: A Spectral Perspective** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - **Match:** RNNs with biologically inspired E/I separation (ColEI and DANN), analyzed via singular-value distributions, eigenvalues (circle law, Marchenko-Pastur), and normalized SVD entropy (NSE); trained with gradient descent / projected gradient descent with gradient clipping. Benchmarks: adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, object recognition.
> - **Partial match:** Optimization is gradient descent/projected gradient descent; SGD/AdamW are not explicitly named as the studied optimizers.
> 
> **Topic (c) — How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks** (NeurIPS 2024)
> - **Match:** Self-supervised JEPA/self-distillation predictive training whose implicit bias favors high-influence features (high regression coefficients ρ) beyond raw pixel variance, in contrast to MAE; demonstrated with deep linear networks trained by (stochastic) gradient descent and on ImageNet-1K with ViT encoders (I-JEPA vs MAE).
> - **Partial match:** Demonstrations are on synthetic data + ImageNet (ViT), not MNIST/CIFAR-100 with ResNet-50 backbones; backbones are ViT, not ResNet-50.
> 
> **Topic (d) — Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - **Match:** Sub-byte ≈4-bit optimizer states for Adam/AdamW with smaller block size (B128) for the first moment, rank-1 normalization, block/group-wise quantization, and explicit handling of the zero-point problem for the second moment (DE-0/linear mapping excluding zero); validated on RoBERTa-L, Swin-T, GPT-2, Transformer, LLaMA-7B/13B/33B.
> - **Partial match:** It is 4-bit states, not block/group quantization per se (though block-wise B128 and rank-1 normalization are used); zero-point handling is for the second moment.
> 
> **Topic (e) — Diverse Projection Ensembles for Distributional RL** (ICLR 2024, PE-DQN)
> - **Match:** Uncertainty-aware RL using ensembles of value distributions (quantile + categorical projections) where ensemble disagreement measured by average 1-Wasserstein distance drives deep exploration; theory for propagation of epistemic uncertainty via distributional TD errors; evaluated on bsuite and VizDoom.
> 
> ---
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods
> 
> **PBADet (a)**
> - **Loss mismatch with common protocols:** Uses task-alignment learning with IoU/DFL/classification + ℓ1 association loss rather than standard MSE/cross-entropy losses, making it less aligned with the requested "standard losses" protocol.
> - **Association decoding is heuristic:** At inference, part-body association is resolved by Euclidean distance to enclosing unassigned body centers, which can fail with occlusions or ambiguous enclosures.
> - **Anchor-point dependency:** Only the top-K task-aligned anchor points supervise association; misalignment or K choice can degrade association accuracy.
> - **Evaluation inconsistency:** Precision/F1 are reported mainly against ED-Pose on COCO-HumanParts, not on standard COCO-WholeBody protocols; comparison is less favorable on single-part CrowdHuman face-body task.
> 
> **Dale's Law spectral RNN (b)**
> - **Spectral pathology at initialization:** ColEI networks have multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure), causing exploding/vanishing gradients; performance degrades sharply for small networks or few inhibitory units.
> - **Optimizer mismatch:** Analysis relies on (projected) gradient descent with gradient clipping; the effect under SGD/AdamW with adaptive learning rates is not studied, so findings may not transfer to the requested optimizer setup.
> - **NSE as a proxy:** Normalized SVD entropy is a heuristic metric; the paper itself notes eigenvalue analysis is insufficient due to non-orthogonal eigenvectors (non-normality).
> - **Limited generality:** Conclusions based on initialization spectra and specific E/I initializations; no proof of generalizability to other E/I architectures (I-to-I connections, cell-type time constants not modeled).
> 
> **JEPA deep linear self-distillation (c)**
> - **Idealized model:** Analysis assumes deep linear networks, simultaneous diagonalizability, balanced orthogonal initialization, and small-initialization regime — deviations from real nonlinear Transformers/ResNets.
> - **Data/backbone mismatch:** Demonstrations are on synthetic data and ImageNet with ViT encoders, not MNIST/CIFAR-100 with ResNet-50, so the requested evaluation protocol is not covered.
> - **Bias vs. vulnerability trade-off:** Implicit bias toward high-ρ (high-influence) features can make JEPA vulnerable to spurious or slow features; noise suppression increases with depth but depends on ρ-λ relationships, which can reverse feature-learning order vs. MAE.
> 
> **4-bit optimizer states (d)**
> - **Zero-point problem:** Quantizing the second moment to zero causes catastrophic deviation of update directions (inverse-square-root blow-up); solved only by excluding zero from the quantization map (DE-0/linear), wasting a quantization point.
> - **Outlier-pattern sensitivity:** Moments have heterogeneous outlier patterns across tensors; fixed small block size (B128) and rank-1 normalization do not always beat task-specific settings; optimal quantization likely task/dataset-dependent.
> - **Computational overhead:** Not fused; slower than 8-bit AdamW on small models; convergence proof only for quantized SGD(M), not directly Adam/AdamW.
> - **Scope limitation:** Only validated on language/vision tasks; applicability to RL, audio, graph learning untested.
> 
> **Projection ensembles for distributional RL (e)**
> - **Uncertainty estimation is indirect:** Ensemble disagreement estimates error w.r.t. bootstrapped distributional TD targets, not the true return distribution; TD backups prohibit consistent uncertainty quantification, requiring the proposed propagation scheme.
> - **Projection inductive bias:** The projection step (categorical vs. quantile) strongly shapes generalization; different projections give different exploration behaviors for higher moments, making design choices brittle.
> - **Bonus heuristic:** The 1-Wasserstein disagreement bonus is a heuristic epistemic-uncertainty measure that should vanish at convergence but can be misestimated in practice.
> - **Sample/ensemble cost:** Gains depend on diversity of projections and ensemble size; performance improvements vary by task, with most pronounced gains only in directed-exploration problems.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the papers matching each topic, followed by a defect analysis.
> 
> ## Matching papers
> 
> **(a) Part-to-body association** — **PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association** (ICLR 2024). Single-pass, anchor-free detector on COCO-style datasets (BodyHands, COCO-HumanParts, CrowdHuman, COCO val). Losses: classification (TOOD-style, incl. IoU/DFL) plus an L1 part-to-body association loss; reports AP, conditional accuracy, joint AP, and Precision/Recall/F1 (vs ED-Pose). *(Note: it does not use MSE; the association loss is L1.)*
> 
> **(b) EI recurrent nets via spectral analysis** — **Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly** (NeurIPS 2023). Compares ColEI/DANN/standard RNNs; finds initial singular-value spectra (multimodal/dispersed for ColEI), normalised SVD entropy (NSE) predict performance. *(Note: the paper uses projected gradient descent + gradient clipping; I found no explicit SGD/AdamW comparison in the retrieved content.)*
> 
> **(c) JEPA bias toward influential features** — **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks** (NeurIPS 2024). Shows JEPA/self-distillation biases latent features toward high-regression-coefficient ("high-influence") features rather than high pixel-variance ones; validated on deep linear models, temporal/static generative models, and I-JEPA vs MAE on ImageNet (ViT). *(Note: it does not demonstrate on MNIST/CIFAR-100 or ResNet-50 — those specifics are not covered.)*
> 
> **(d) Sub-byte optimizer states** — **Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States** (NeurIPS 2023). 4-bit Adam/AdamW states using block-wise (B128) quantization, rank-1 normalization, and zero-point-excluding linear/DE-0 mapping for the second moment (plus optional factorization).
> 
> **(e) Uncertainty-aware distributional RL** — **Diverse Projection Ensembles for Distributional RL (PE-DQN)** (ICLR 2024). Ensembles of categorical (C51) and quantile (QR-DQN) value distributions; exploration bonus = average 1-Wasserstein disagreement, propagated through distributional TD errors.
> 
> ## Development defects
> 
> **(a) PBADet**: Detection and association are tightly coupled — association quality inherits detector errors (part misdetection kills association). The single 2D part-to-body offset relies on task-alignment/top-K anchor selection and multi-scale normalization; ablations show each is fragile (removing them degrades all metrics). It needs anchor-based YOLO backbones retrofitted with anchor-free heads. Evaluation is inconsistent across protocols (IoU>0.5 true positives vs ED-Pose's keypoint-in-box), and its CrowdHuman advantage over BPJDet is marginal for the single-part face-body case.
> 
> **(b) Dale's Law RNNs**: ColEI networks train poorly and with high seed variance; their multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra with a large σmax cause exploding-gradient instability, requiring gradient clipping (which helps ColEI far more). Performance collapses for small networks/few inhibitory units. The spectral pathology originates from a rank-one nilpotent column-mean component that spectral-radius constraint cannot control. Sign constraints still cost ~0.7–1% error; the analysis is initialization-centric and limited to specific RNN formulations, with no clear fix for ColEI beyond architectural redesign (DANN).
> 
> **(c) JEPA implicit bias**: The theory is restricted to deep linear MLPs with balanced orthogonal initialization and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances; generalization to nonlinear, realistic architectures is explicitly left open. The bias toward high-influence/low-variance features can make JEPA susceptible to spurious/slow features and slower to learn noisy features; at large depths the encoder becomes low-rank (a single dominating eigenvalue), and MAE's fixed points become unreachable by JEPA (and vice versa) — a design constraint, not just a benefit.
> 
> **(d) 4-bit optimizers**: The zero-point problem is severe — quantizing near-zero second moments to zero flips the update direction (1/√v blows up to ~10⁶); excluding zero wastes quantization points and the linear mapping's smallest value (0.0625) still limits resolution. Outlier patterns are heterogeneous, so no single block size fits all tensors; optimal settings are task-dependent, and the non-fused implementation is slower than 8-bit AdamW in some settings. Factorization applies only to the second moment, and the convergence proof covers quantized SGD(M), not Adam/AdamW directly.
> 
> **(e) PE-DQN**: Projection ensembles inherit irreducible per-projection approximation errors, so the "epistemic" bonus never vanishes at convergence (only controllable via atom count K). Ensemble disagreement actually measures error w.r.t. the bootstrapped TD target, not the true return distribution, so optimism can be misdirected. Both diverse projections and TD-error propagation are necessary (ablations show each alone fails); only uniform mixtures were tested, and evaluation is limited to bsuite and VizDoom.

</details>

### paperscope:gap:70 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building an interactive vision and robotics system with tight GPU memory: we need robust per-person hand/face detection in crowded scenes (one-stage, anchor-free on COCO-like data) and an exploration-heavy control module where an RL agent uses distributional value ensembles to guide behavior via disagreement; our representation learning stack favors latent-space prediction to avoid noisy pixels for a feedforward classifier; training must fit in memory by using low-bit optimizer states for AdamW; and our time-series module should keep biologically plausible E/I separation in RNNs while remaining trainable. Are there papers that address these needs and discuss standard losses (MSE, CE), optimizers (SGD/Adam/AdamW), attention/Transformers, interpretability, and benchmarks like MNIST/CIFAR-100?Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

Gold 1：

> {'answer': 'Here are the development defects/limitations explicitly evidenced in the provided papers, grouped by method:\n\nPBADet (one-stage, anchor-free part-body association)\n- Gains are not pronounced on single-part association tasks: On CrowdHuman (face-body is a single part), the authors note “the advantages of our method over BPJDet are not as pronounced” (Appendix A.1). Quantitatively, mMR−2 is still around ~50 for body-face pairs (Table 5), showing considerable mismatches remain.\n- Mixed detection/association trade-offs across categories: On COCOHumanParts, PBADet’s AP improvements are not universal; performance is “on par” with BPJDet on all categories (Table 2) and average mMR−2 varies by part (Table 3), indicating parts (e.g., hands, feet) remain challenging.\n- Strong training compute/memory demands: Experiments require large input resolutions (1024×1024 or 1536×1536), batch sizes up to 24, and 4× Tesla V100 GPUs (Section 4.1), which is an obstacle under tight GPU memory.\n- Hyperparameter sensitivity and complex decoding assumptions: Association depends on top‑K task‑alignment anchors (K=13, α=1.0, β=6.0) and NMS thresholds; inference assumes bodies enclosing parts to find nearest centers (Section 3.4). Errors in detection boxes or occlusions can break the “enclose-and-closest-center” assumption.\n- Reduced benefits vs. anchor-based baselines in some settings: The authors highlight that advantages shrink when only one part is present; and small-object metrics (APS) are not centrally improved (Appendix A.5); indicating limits in crowded tiny-part scenarios.\n\nLearning better with Dale’s Law (ColEI vs. DANN RNNs)\n- Poor learning and instability with simple column EI (ColEI) partitioning: ColEI networks “learn poorly,” show higher variance across seeds, and are “highly unstable” without gradient clipping (Sections 3.1, 4; Appendix Figure 10). They require stronger gradient clipping and exhibit training instability due to large singular values.\n- Spectral pathology tied to EI ratio and network size: Small networks and fewer inhibitory units degrade learning; maximum singular values increase as inhibitory ratio drops; normalized SVD entropy correlates tightly with performance (Section 3.4–3.5, Figures 5–7).\n- Heavy dependence on initial spectral properties: Performance depends more on singular value spectra than sign constraints; spectrum transplant experiments show sign constraints alone don’t explain the gap (Section 3.3, Figure 4).\n- Theoretical scope limitations: Analysis relies on deep linear models, orthogonal/“balanced” initializations, and simultaneously diagonalizable Σxx and Σyx; generalization to non-linear networks and non-diagonalizable data is not proven (Section 6 Limitations).\n- Biological fidelity gaps: DANN RNNs specifically model fast PV+ interneurons and omit certain biological details (e.g., I-to-I connections), while ColEI is a coarse model of inhibitory cells; the paper calls for hybridization but doesn’t provide it (Section 4 Discussion).\n\nJEPA implicit bias (deep linear self-distillation)\n- Narrow theoretical setting: Results are restricted to deep linear encoders, special orthogonal initializations, and simultaneously diagonalizable covariance/correlation matrices; generalization to realistic non-linear networks and broader data distributions remains unaddressed (Section 6 Limitations).\n- Bias depends on encoder depth and data properties: The “influential-feature” bias (toward high regression coefficients ρ) emerges strongly only with deep encoders; shallow encoders behave differently and may not yield the JEPA advantage (Section 3.2–3.4).\n- Applicability limits: Claims are derived under simplified generative processes (random masking and temporal models) and toy settings; practical generalization is explicitly “yet remains unexplored” (Section 6).\n\n4-bit optimizers (Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States)\n- Zero-point quantization problem for the second moment: Quantizing v to include zero leads to catastrophic deviations in update directions (1/√v), causing instability; many settings are “unstable” (e.g., B128/DE shows 33–66% instability rates on GPT‑2 Medium E2E‑NLG, Table 1). The fix (DE‑0 or linear mapping excluding zero) is necessary but reduces representable resolution and wastes a code in DE‑0.\n- Task-dependent sensitivity and limited coverage: Authors state optimal quantization settings “probably depend on task,” and evaluation is limited to language and vision; applicability to RL, audio, or graphs “needs further study” (Section 7 Limitations).\n- Residual accuracy gaps and instability in naïve configurations: Some 4‑bit configurations underperform (e.g., Swin‑T ImageNet 80.8% vs. 81.2% full‑precision; MT 26.28 vs. 26.61, Table 2), and stochastic rounding or smaller blocks alone do not solve instability (Table 1).\n- Overhead/trade-offs and implementation constraints: Rank‑1 normalization outperforms B128 in many cases but not all (Appendix C.2), introducing memory/compute trade‑offs; tensors ≤4096 elements are not quantized (Appendix D.1), limiting savings; 4‑bit training can be slower unless fused operators are used (Table 4).\n\nDiverse Projection Ensembles for Distributional RL (PE‑DQN)\n- Residual approximation error that does not vanish: Due to finite projections (categorical/quantile), the ensemble’s fixed point differs from the true return distribution and disagreement may persist (Section 4.2, Appendix A.4 Propositions 8–9; Corollary 12), potentially biasing epistemic estimates.\n- Requires uncertainty propagation beyond raw disagreement: Shared TD targets make disagreements reflect TD target errors—not the true return—so an extra propagation scheme and a learned bonus are needed; ablations show independent training or removing propagation degrades exploration (Section 4.2; Figure 4b).\n- Limited ensemble diversity and mixture design: Only uniform mixtures of categorical and quantile projections are explored; authors note they “only considered uniform mixtures,” leaving performance on other projection sets or weighting schemes unknown (Section 7 Conclusion).\n- Hyperparameter sensitivity and decay scheduling: Exploration bonus β must be decayed; authors use fixed schedules to avoid non-convergence (Appendix B.2 Bonus decay), indicating sensitivity to tuning.\n- Computational cost: Bsuite runs are longer than some baselines (Appendix B.2; e.g., ~72h for PE‑DQN vs. ~38–80h for others), reflecting extra complexity from ensembles and bonus learner.\n\nThese defects/limitations are drawn directly from the respective papers’ results, ablations, discussions, and limitations sections.'}

**naive 最终答案**

> Yes — five papers in the collection map directly to your five needs, and the collection also covers the requested standard losses, optimizers, Transformers/attention, interpretability, and MNIST/CIFAR-100 benchmarks.
> 
> **1. Detection (one-stage, anchor-free, crowded, COCO-like)** — *PBADet* (one-stage anchor-free part-body association for hands/face). Benchmarks: COCO-WholeBody, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman, WiderFace, BodyHands; losses: classification, box regression (DFL), task-aligned association loss.
> Development defects: on CrowdHuman face-body association its gain over BPJDet is small (single-part case); ablation shows removing the association loss, task-alignment, or multi-scale center offsets degrades accuracy; it depends on YOLO-style backbones and adds an association branch.
> 
> **2. Exploration via distributional value-ensemble disagreement** — *PE-DQN* (diverse projection ensembles of categorical/quantile value distributions, bonus = average 1-Wasserstein disagreement). Benchmarks: bsuite, VizDoom.
> Defects: uses only a uniform mixture over ensemble members (conservative); each projection member carries irreducible approximation error, so epistemic uncertainty does not vanish at convergence; best gains are concentrated in directed-exploration tasks and only ~4 models were used.
> 
> **3. Latent-space prediction to avoid noisy pixels** — *JEPA/self-distillation analysis* (predicting in latent space avoids noisy features) and the *video representation-learning paper* (forward modeling, temporal contrastive, autoencoder; explicit noise analysis).
> Defects: the JEPA analysis is restricted to deep *linear* MLPs, special initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable weights (generalization qualitative); in video learning, temporal contrastive fails entirely under exogenous noise, forward modeling degrades as exogenous noise grows, and autoencoder performance is unpredictable — action-labeled trajectory data (ACRO) is required for robustness.
> 
> **4. Low-bit AdamW optimizer states for tight memory** — *4-bit Optimizers* (4-bit first moment, rank-1/linear quantized second moment, optional factorization).
> Defects: optimal quantization is task/dataset dependent; tested only on language/vision tasks; non-fused implementation is slower than 8-bit on small models; quantizing both moments gives a marginal accuracy drop, and only up to ~57.7% total memory saving (activations/fragments dominate the rest).
> 
> **5. Trainable biologically plausible E/I RNNs** — *Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly* (ColEI vs DANN).
> Defects: simple E/I partitioning (ColEI) learns worse and with higher variance across all four tasks; sign constraints themselves impair learning; performance is worse for small networks with fewer inhibitory units; gradient clipping is needed substantially. DANN is robust but models a different inhibitory-cell population.
> 
> **Coverage of the extra requested topics:** MSE/CE — squared loss (forward modeling), quantile-regression loss, and cross-entropy (contrastive-learning paper, RZ-NAS). Optimizers — SGD/Adam/AdamW (4-bit optimizer paper; Hessian paper trains LeNet with SGD on MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 and ViT-Base with Adam on CIFAR-100). Attention/Transformers — ViT-Base on CIFAR-100, RZ-NAS, Neural Comprehension (CoNN), TuCo. Interpretability — TuCo (per-prompt fine-tuning attribution) and Neural Comprehension (compiled, interpretable transformer modules). Benchmarks — sequential MNIST and Penn Tree Bank (RNN paper), MNIST label noise and CIFAR-100 (Hessian paper), plus CIFAR-10/100 (contrastive learning).

**community 最终答案**

> Yes — each of your needs maps to a paper in this collection, and each paper also states clear development defects/limitations.
> 
> **1. Hand/face detection in crowds (one-stage, anchor-free, COCO-like)** — *PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association* (ICLR 2024). Evaluated on COCO-HumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman; uses IoU/DFL/classification losses and task-alignment; compares against Transformer (DETR-based) detectors.
> - Defects: on the single-part face-body task (CrowdHuman) its advantage over BPJDet is much smaller; body AP is only "comparable" to DETR-based detectors, not clearly better; performance relies on YOLO backbones and NMS post-processing; occlusion handling remains a challenge for multi-part associations.
> 
> **2. RL exploration via distributional value ensembles / disagreement** — *Projection Ensembles for Deep Q-Learning (PE-DQN)* (ICLR 2024). Uses categorical (KL) and quantile (QR) projection losses, ensemble disagreement as an exploration bonus on bsuite and VizDoom.
> - Defects: each member inherits irreducible projection approximation errors, so epistemic uncertainty does not vanish at convergence (only bounded via atom count K); theory assumes idealized settings before deep RL; only uniform mixtures were studied; residual approximation error bounds are loose in practice.
> 
> **3. Latent-space prediction avoiding noisy pixels for a feedforward classifier** — *How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features* (NeurIPS 2024) and *Towards Principled Representation Learning from Videos for RL*. JEPA's MSE-style latent prediction prioritizes high-influence, low-noise features; ImageNet linear-probing experiments confirm this.
> - Defects: JEPA theory is restricted to deep linear networks, special initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances; generalization to nonlinear/practical settings unproven; JEPA is susceptible to collapse without stop-grad. The video-representation paper shows that with temporally correlated exogenous noise, video-only latent learning (forward modeling/temporal contrastive) can be exponentially worse than trajectory-based learning — temporal contrastive can even overfit to noise.
> 
> **4. Low-bit AdamW optimizer states for GPU memory** — *Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States* (NeurIPS 2023). Covers SGD/Adam/AdamW framework, quantization (B128, rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion, factorization); evaluated on ImageNet (Swin-T transformer), GLUE, SQuAD, MT, LLaMA (transformers).
> - Defects: optimal quantization is task/dataset-dependent; only language/vision tasks were validated (RL, audio, graph learning untested); without fused operators 4-bit is slower than 8-bit; memory savings saturate because activations/data dominate; zero-point problem for the second moment still needs special handling.
> 
> **5. Biologically plausible E/I-separated RNNs that remain trainable** — *Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly* (NeurIPS 2023). Benchmarks: sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, adding problem, object recognition; trained with SGD/gradient descent; interpretability via spectral (SVD/NSE) analysis.
> - Defects: naive column-wise E/I (ColEI) networks learn worse and with much higher variance across all tasks; the cause is a multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectrum, not just sign constraints; small networks or low I-unit ratios degrade both spectrum and performance; gradient clipping is required; only DANN-style recurrent nets escape these problems.
> 
> **6. Common tooling benchmarks (MNIST/CIFAR-100, optimizers, Transformers, interpretability)** — *Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure* (ICML 2025) is the best fit: LeNet on MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/CIFAR-10/100, ResNet18, ViT fine-tuned on CIFAR-100, GPT-2/TinyLlama with AdamW, and many SGD/Adam-family optimizers; interpretability via power-law Hessian spectra as a generalization predictor. Also relevant: *What Does Automatic Differentiation Compute for Neural Networks?* (ICLR 2024), which analyzes training (MSE-style losses) on MNIST MLPs and CIFAR-10 VGG/ResNet.
> - Defects (Hessian paper): power-law structure is lost with small width/depth, limited data, noisy labels, and large-batch training; only an indicator, not a causal explanation; SOTA LLMs excluded due to Hessian cost. Defects (AD paper): guarantees that AD returns a Clarke subdifferential fail for minibatches or shared biases (general maxpool networks may fail); an LP-checkable condition is needed and verification is only sufficient, not necessary.
> 
> Overall, the collection addresses all five needs plus the common tooling (losses, optimizers, Transformers, interpretability, MNIST/CIFAR-100), but every method has noted limitations — chiefly narrow theoretical assumptions (linear models), single-domain validation, residual/spectral pathologies, and task-specific hyperparameter sensitivity.

### paperscope:gap:73 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively address: (1) avoiding local and global dimensional collapse in self-supervised learning via local intrinsic dimensionality regularization and analysis of feature embeddings; (2) the implicit bias of joint-embedding predictive approaches compared to reconstruction (e.g., how cosine-similarity vs. MSE objectives shape learned features); (3) memory-efficient fine-tuning with 4-bit optimizer states for Adam/AdamW and SGD on Transformers and ResNet-50; (4) spectral perspectives on recurrent networks under excitatory/inhibitory constraints for interpretability; and (5) a one-stage anchor-free method for associating detected human parts to the correct body, evaluated on COCO. I’m looking for works reporting results on datasets like ImageNet, COCO, CIFAR-100, and MNIST, using losses such as cosine similarity and cross-entropy (CE), and discussing regularization strategies, fine-tuning, and practical metrics.Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

**score：2→4（Δ+2）；rounds：2→4（Δ+2）。**
