**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below are the development defects and limitations explicitly stated or directly implied by the provided papers, organized by method/family. Each point is grounded in the cited text and evidence.
> 
> 1) One-stage anchor-free part–body association (PBADet)
> - Benefit depends on multi-part settings; limited advantage with single-part association: On CrowdHuman (face–body only), the authors note “the face-body association task is singular… Consequently, the advantages of our method over BPJDet are not as pronounced as seen in scenarios with multiple parts-to-body associations.”
> - Does not uniformly outperform anchor-based baselines across all metrics/datasets: On COCOHumanParts, PBADet’s per-category head and face AP are slightly below BPJDet (e.g., Table 2 shows head AP 54.5 vs 56.6; face AP 44.7 vs 46.3 for YOLOv5l6 backbones), indicating no universal dominance across categories.
> - Comparable, not superior, to strong box detectors on crowded pedestrian tasks: On CrowdHuman, PBADet is “comparable” to DETR-based detectors for body AP and MR, not clearly surpassing them across all metrics.
> 
> 2) EI-constrained RNNs: Column EI (ColEI) vs Dale’s ANNs (DANNs)
> - ColEI (sign-constrained columns) – key defects:
>   - Spectral pathology degrades learning: ColEI initial recurrent spectra are multimodal and dispersed with a “notable mode of large singular values,” unlike the unimodal clustered spectra of standard RNNs/DANNs. This causes heavily deformed activations/gradients and poor learning.
>   - Poor learning stability and high variance: ColEI networks exhibit greater variability across seeds and training instability, benefiting disproportionately from gradient clipping; without clipping they are “highly unstable,” consistent with pathological singular value distributions.
>   - Sensitivity to EI ratio and size: Performance worsens with fewer inhibitory units and small networks; normalized SVD entropy decreases and test error increases as EI ratio becomes more skewed. Small ColEI with realistic I counts (e.g., 10%) learn less effectively.
>   - Unfavorable relationship with spectral radius: ColEI require different radius settings than standard/DANN RNNs, learning better only at larger radii and worse at smaller ones; no single radius matches standard/DANN performance across tasks.
> - DANN RNNs – stated limitations:
>   - Biological fidelity is limited: Authors note DANNs could be made “more biologically faithful” (e.g., add I→I connections, cell-type-specific time constants). The current architecture specifically models fast PV+ interneurons and may not capture other interneuron subtypes.
>   - Open theoretical gaps: The origin of ColEI’s unusual multimodal spectra and why large ColEI networks can learn despite large maximum singular values remain unresolved.
> 
> 3) Latent prediction vs reconstruction (JEPA vs MAE) in deep linear self-distillation
> - MAE (reconstruction) – defects:
>   - Prefers highly covarying (high-variance) features irrespective of predictiveness: In the analyzed linear setting, MAE prioritizes features by covariance λ, even when such features are noisy and less informative for downstream prediction/perception, echoing empirical observations that reconstruction can yield uninformative features for perception.
> - JEPA (latent prediction/self-distillation) – defects:
>   - Depth-sensitive bias and potential to overfocus on “slow/spurious” features: JEPA’s preferential learning of high-regression-coefficient features (ρ) strengthens only with deep encoders; the authors caution this can make JEPA “vulnerable to spurious or slow features.” With depth, solutions become increasingly low-rank and suppress other directions.
>   - Theory limited to linear, simultaneously diagonalizable settings and special inits: Theoretical claims rely on deep linear models, a special balanced initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable Σxx and Σxy. Generalization to non-linear networks and realistic data assumptions is explicitly unproven.
> 
> 4) Low-precision optimizers with 4-bit states
> - Second-moment “zero-point” failure mode at 4-bit: Using DE mapping with zero (e.g., B128/DE) quantizes many second-moment entries to zero, which catastrophically distorts update directions (since updates scale by 1/sqrt(v)). Smaller blocks or stochastic rounding do not fix this; zero must be excluded (DE-0) or replaced with linear mapping.
> - Block-wise only scaling cannot capture complex outliers: Moments exhibit heterogeneous outlier patterns (row/column fixed), and large block sizes (e.g., 2048) lead to poor approximation; even smaller blocks aren’t universally adequate without improved normalization.
> - Need for specialized normalization and mappings: Robust training requires rank-1 normalization (row/column statistics) and zero-excluding/linear mappings for v; vanilla 8-bit-style block quantization is insufficient at 4-bit.
> - Practical performance/maturity gaps:
>   - Speed overhead without fused kernels: 4-bit can be slower than 8-bit on smaller models unless fused ops are used (authors report slower times before fusion for RoBERTa-L and GPT-2 M).
>   - Memory gains saturate in end-to-end pipelines: Reported total memory savings are bounded by other components (activations, fragments), so optimizer-state compression alone does not scale linearly in end-to-end savings.
>   - Factorization applies only to second moments and to tensors with dim ≥ 2 (1D moments still need quantization), limiting where the most aggressive memory savings can be realized.
>   - Task-dependent tuning and limited domains: Authors caution the “optimal quantization setting probably depends on task” and evaluations were limited to language/vision; applicability to RL, audio, graph tasks is untested.
> 
> 5) Video-based pretraining for RL (forward modeling, temporal contrastive, autoencoding)
> - Fundamental statistical limitation with exogenous noise:
>   - Lower bound: With temporally dependent exogenous noise, any compact, frozen video-pretrained representation can make downstream RL exponentially harder than pretraining from action-labeled trajectories; sample complexity can be exponentially worse regardless of video dataset size.
> - Temporal Contrastive Learning – defects:
>   - Especially prone to latch onto exogenous noise: Empirically and theoretically, TCL can minimize its loss by relying on predictive nuisance dynamics (e.g., moving background “diamonds”), failing to capture the agent’s latent state. In experiments (GridWorld and ViZDoom), TCL performs well without exogenous noise but “completely fails” when such noise is present.
>   - Requires margin/realizability and time-encoding assumptions: Guarantees require realizability, positive temporal margin βtemp, and observations encoding time; these assumptions may not hold in practice.
> - Forward Modeling – defects:
>   - Still degrades with exogenous noise: Although more robust than TCL, performance “quickly degrades” as exogenous noise increases; success provably hinges on positive forward-margin βfor and realizability.
>   - Requires time-encoding and sufficient state coverage: Theory assumes observations encode timestep and the video mix provides good state coverage; both can be restrictive in real data.
> - Autoencoding – defects:
>   - No finite-sample guarantees; unpredictable empirically: The authors find autoencoder performance “unpredictable” and note finite-sample guarantees remain an open problem.
> - Dependence on video data assumptions:
>   - Noise-free data-collection policies and coverage: Guarantees assume data policies that do not act on noise and that videos provide good coverage of the state space—plausible in some domains (e.g., abundant gameplay videos) but not guaranteed.
>   - Disjoint emission/decodability required: Analyses rely on latent states being decodable (disjoint emission), which may not hold in real video streams.
> 
> Cross-method takeaways tied to your pipeline
> - Latent prediction vs reconstruction: In the linear regime, MAE prioritizes high-variance (possibly noisy) content; JEPA prioritizes high-regression (predictive) content but can over-index slow/spurious features and needs depth to exhibit its bias. With exogenous noise in videos, both forward strategies (JEPA/TCL flavors) require care; theory shows fundamental limits for video-only pretraining under exogenous distractors.
> - Contrastive vs forward in videos: Without exogenous noise, both can learn usable latent states and enable efficient RL; with exogenous noise, TCL is especially brittle (can solve its loss via nuisance dynamics), and forward modeling still degrades as noise grows.
> - EI-constrained RNNs: ColEI suffers from inherent spectral pathologies—expect unstable training, high variance, and poor learning unless network is large and E/I balanced; DANN mitigates this but is not yet fully biologically faithful.
> - 4-bit optimizers: Deployment requires addressing the second-moment zero-point problem and using rank-1 normalization; otherwise, catastrophic update distortion occurs. Speed can trail 8-bit without fused ops, and task/domain retuning is expected.
> - Anchor-free part–whole detection: PBADet is simple and strong, but gains depend on task structure; on single-part association benchmarks and some COCO categories it is only comparable (or slightly worse) than strong anchor-based baselines.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Recommended reading (per your pipeline need)
> 
> **1. Latent prediction vs reconstruction / contrastive vs forward (video pretraining before RL)**
> - *Towards Principled Representation Learning from Videos for Reinforcement Learning* (Misra et al., ICLR 2024): analyzes exactly your three options — autoencoding (reconstruction), temporal contrastive, and forward modeling — on unlabeled video from GridWorld/ViZDoom (game-like videos) before downstream RL. It gives sample-complexity bounds for forward modeling and temporal contrastive, and a lower bound showing video-only learning can be exponentially worse than action-labeled trajectory data under exogenous noise.
> - *How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks* (Littwin et al., NeurIPS 2024): contrasts latent-space prediction (JEPA/self-distillation) against reconstruction (MAE) with squared-error losses, explaining why latent prediction prioritizes high-influence perceptual features while reconstruction chases high-variance pixel subspaces.
> 
> **2. Spectral issues in EI-constrained RNNs**
> - *Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective* (Li et al., NeurIPS 2023): the key read. It shows simple column-partitioned E/I RNNs (ColEI) have multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra (vs. quarter-circle Marchenko–Pastur spectra of standard/DANN RNNs), that spectra matter more than sign constraints, that normalised SVD entropy (NSE) predicts performance, and that gradient clipping is needed. Benchmarks: adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, object recognition.
> - (Optional) *Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure* (ICML 2025): power-law Hessian spectra under SGD/Adam on MNIST/CIFAR — useful if you want spectral diagnostics for the optimizer side of training.
> 
> **3. Low-precision (≈4-bit) optimizers**
> - *Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States* (Li et al., NeurIPS 2023): 4-bit AdamW/Adam (framework also covers SGDM) with B128 block quantization for the first moment, zero-point-excluding linear/rank-1 quantization and factorization for the second moment. Memory savings up to 57.7%, lossless fine-tuning on RoBERTa/Swin-T/GPT-2/LLaMA.
> 
> **4. Anchor-free part–whole detection**
> - *PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association* (ICLR 2024): single part-to-body center offset on multi-scale anchor-free heads (YOLOv5/v7); evaluated on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman (face-body), WiderFace-style face/left-hand/right-hand classes; real-time capable.
> - (Optional, for unlabeled/self-supervised part-whole) *HASSOD* (NeurIPS 2023): self-supervised hierarchical whole/part/subpart detection from DINO features (fits your "unlabeled" constraint), though not human-part-specific.
> 
> **Benchmark coverage found in context:** MNIST (Dale's Law, Hessian papers), CIFAR-10/100 (Hessian, contrastive-learning papers), COCOHumanParts/BodyHands/CrowdHuman (PBADet). **SVHN does not appear in any retrieved document — no SVHN evidence is available in this collection.**
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods (from the context)
> 
> **Video pretraining paper:** Video-only methods have an inherent identifiability barrier — sample complexity can be *exponentially* worse than trajectory-based methods when exogenous noise exists. Temporal contrastive learning can fail completely (it can win by modeling predictable noise), forward modeling degrades as exogenous noise grows, and autoencoding works empirically only in some domains with no theoretical guarantees. Trajectory-based ACRO always outperforms all video-based approaches.
> 
> **JEPA paper:** Latent prediction is susceptible to representation collapse without stop-gradient/negative-pair mechanisms; the analysis is restricted to deep linear networks with special initializations and simultaneous diagonalizability, so conclusions are qualitative for real Transformers; reconstruction losses are sub-optimal for perception because perceptual features explain little input variance.
> 
> **Dale's Law RNN paper:** Naive E/I partitioning (ColEI) trains poorly and with high variance, is unstable without gradient clipping, and its spectra worsen for small networks with few inhibitory units. The paper explicitly leaves open the origin of the multimodal spectra, only compares two EI architectures, and does not explore hybridizations (e.g., I→I connections, cell-type time constants). Its NSE diagnostic works at initialization but is only a heuristic predictor.
> 
> **4-bit optimizer paper:** The optimal quantization scheme is task/dataset-dependent (no single setting is universally best); experiments cover only language/vision (not RL or embodied tasks); 4-bit AdamW is slower than 8-bit without fused operators; memory savings saturate because total memory includes activations, data, and fragments; compression-based methods reduce memory only by a fixed fraction and are less memory-efficient than sublinear-memory methods (Adafactor/SM3), which however lose accuracy.
> 
> **PBADet:** Anchor-free dense prediction inherits positive/negative sample imbalance issues; YOLOv1-style near-center points give lower recall; dropping multi-scale offsets or task-alignment hurts all metrics; the part-to-body offset requires visible parts with well-defined boxes (poses like ED-Pose are unreliable on limbs); on CrowdHuman's single-part (face-body) task its advantage over BPJDet is much smaller; on COCOHumanParts the subordinate (part) APs are consistently lower than the original-category APs.
> 
> **HASSOD:** Its part-whole hierarchy can misalign with human perception; it fails on overlapping similar objects, heterogeneous wholes, and text; it is class-agnostic and evaluated with AR rather than AP (the paper argues COCO AP is misleading), so it is not directly a human-parts detector.
> 
> **Hessian spectrum paper:** The power-law structure disappears with small width/depth, limited data, noisy labels, or large-batch training; LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce it; generalization prediction for LLMs is still open; very large models are excluded by Hessian computation cost.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, here is what can be established (with development defects noted):
> 
> **1. Latent prediction vs reconstruction, contrastive vs forward (for video pretraining → RL)** — Read **"Towards Principled Representation Learning from Videos for RL"** (doc 631d23bf). It studies autoencoding (reconstruction), forward modeling, and temporal contrastive learning on unlabeled gameplay-like video for downstream RL.
> - Defects: no theoretical guarantee for autoencoders (empirically good in ViZDoom but fails in GridWorld); forward modeling and temporal contrastive both provably work only with no exogenous noise. With temporally-correlated exogenous noise (e.g., background people/cars), temporal contrastive fails entirely (it can cheat by focusing on predictable noise), forward modeling degrades but stays more robust. Lower bound: compact frozen video-pretrained representations can be exponentially worse than action-labeled trajectory pretraining. No guarantee that latent-space (JEPA) vs reconstruction prediction transfers to RL.
> 
> **2. Latent prediction (JEPA) vs reconstruction (MAE) implicit bias** — Read **"Why JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (doc 40fde037).
> - Defects: analysis is limited to deep linear networks, balanced orthogonal initialization, and simultaneous diagonalizability. JEPA is biased to high-influence (predictive) features and suppresses noise, whereas MAE prioritizes variance-explaining (possibly noisy) features. But JEPA objectives are susceptible to collapse (trivially minimized by constant encoders); avoiding collapse requires contrastive negatives or StopGrad-style bias. Notably, this paper was NOT validated on MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR; its images are ImageNet-based.
> 
> **3. EI (excitatory-inhibitory) RNN spectral issues** — Read **"Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly"** (doc e63a94c4, NeurIPS 2023).
> - Defects: Dale's-law column-constrained (ColEI) RNNs learn worse and with higher variance on adding/sequential-MNIST/PTB/object-recognition tasks. Root cause is spectral: multimodal, dispersed singular values (rank-one column-mean nilpotent plus random part) instead of Marchenko–Pastur quarter-circle; large singular values deform activations/gradients → exploding/vanishing gradients. Sign constraints alone explain little of the gap; spectrum matters more. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) predicts performance (anti-correlates with test error). DANN (separate E/I units) avoids the pathology and learns as well as standard RNNs, so it is the better architecture for your interpretable RNN. Gradient clipping helps ColEI substantially. Limitations: only ColEI column-constraint form analyzed; DANN interpretation models only fast PV+ interneurons.
> 
> **4. 4-bit optimizer states** — Read **"4-bit Optimizers"** (doc 8d5e1455, NeurIPS 2023).
> - Defects: first/second moments have complicated, tensor-dependent outlier patterns that block-wise quantization (8-bit, large blocks) cannot approximate; second moment suffers a zero-point problem (quantizing small values to zero badly distorts the 1/√v update direction). Fixes: smaller block size (B128), linear quantizer excluding zero, rank-1 normalization, optional second-moment factorization. Achieves 4-bit Adam/AdamW with accuracy matching 32-bit (GLUE, SQuAD, ImageNet/Swin-T, WMT, LLaMA fine-tune), memory savings ~43–58%. Limitations: optimal quantization may be task-dependent; only language/vision tasks tested (not RNNs, not your pixel tasks); 4-bit implementation not fused yet, so slower than 8-bit in some small-model cases.
> 
> **5. Anchor-free part–whole / part-body detection** — Read **"PBADet"** (doc 08b70bc3, ICLR 2024).
> - Defects: two-stage/anchored predecessors (BodyHands two-stage association, BPJDet body-to-part offsets) are inefficient: representation grows with number of parts and body-to-part offsets become invalid when parts are occluded. PBADet uses a single part-to-body center offset on anchor-free YOLO heads; one-to-one part↔body correspondence always valid. Validated on COCO-HumanParts (head/face/hands/feet; ~AP 42.7–43.0 all categories) and BodyHands (hand AP 89.1, cond. accuracy 92.6, joint AP 86.0), and CrowdHuman face–body association (leading body MR-2 ~36.5–37.5, competitive face AP). Defects/limitations: on single-part (face–body) CrowdHuman its advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced; ablation shows task-alignment and multi-scale offsets are required; extension to animals only qualitative.
> 
> **Not established in this collection:** any single paper evaluating all these together, and no evidence of MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR results for the JEPA-vs-MAE or video-pretraining methods. SVHN does not appear as a benchmark in the retrieved papers. The MNIST/CIFAR numbers found belong to the Hessian-spectrum paper (doc 582d138d), which is about optimization landscape structure (power-law Hessian spectra), not representation-learning choice. So I cannot confirm the "classic benchmarks (MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR)" evidence you hoped for — you'd need sources outside this collection.

### paperscope:gap:94 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building a resource-constrained edge AI system that must (a) associate hands/face to the right person in real time from video, (b) run on spiking/binary hardware with online updates, and (c) fine-tune large models under strict GPU memory using 4-bit optimizer states and LoRA-style end-to-end adaptation. I need research that shows anchor-free part–body association detection, online training for binary/spiking nets with temporal inputs, spectral diagnostics for EI-restricted recurrent blocks in time-series modeling (e.g., sequential MNIST), and self-supervised predictive encoders that avoid noisy features compared to reconstruction. Demonstrations on CIFAR-100 or similar and metrics like CE, Precision, and F1 would be ideal.Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

> {'answer': "- PBADet (one-stage, anchor-free part–body association)\n  - Gains are not uniform across settings: on CrowdHuman (single part, face–body) the advantage over prior art is \"not as pronounced\" as on multi-part datasets; several COCO-HumanParts APs are only on par with BPJDet rather than clearly better.\n  - Decoding and training depend on several hand-tuned hyperparameters (Top-K anchor assignment with K, α, β; scaling λ; multiple NMS thresholds τconf/τiou for parts and bodies). Performance is therefore sensitive to these choices.\n  - Requires dense part and body bounding-box annotations; method is evaluated with large input sizes and specific YOLO backbones, which may limit portability without re-tuning.\n\n- EI-constrained RNNs (ColEI vs. DANN; spectral analysis under Dale’s Law)\n  - Column EI (ColEI) RNNs exhibit poor learning due to a multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectrum (including large singular values), leading to unstable/inefficient training; they are highly sensitive to network size and E/I ratio (fewer inhibitory units and smaller networks perform worse) and show high variance across seeds.\n  - ColEI networks often require gradient clipping for stability and careful spectral-radius tuning; performance degrades at small spectral radii and depends on initialization.\n  - Even when spectral radius is controlled, large singular values remain; learning can still suffer from exploding/vanishing effects in certain directions.\n  - Theoretical and empirical results indicate sign constraints are not the main cause—spectral pathologies are—implying standard ColEI formulations have an inherent defect unless their spectra are explicitly regularized.\n\n- JEPA (deep linear self-distillation analysis of implicit bias)\n  - Analysis and claims rely on deep linear models with special initializations and the strong assumption that Σxx and Σyx are simultaneously diagonalizable; practical generalization to nonlinear encoders and non-diagonalizable data is not established.\n  - The beneficial implicit bias (prioritizing high regression-coefficient “influential” features) appears only with sufficiently deep encoders; with shallow encoders the effect largely disappears.\n  - Discussion notes potential vulnerability to “slow” or spurious features; JEPA may over-prioritize low-variance, slowly varying components relative to reconstruction-based methods.\n\n- 4-bit optimizer states (memory-efficient Adam/AdamW)\n  - Directly quantizing second moments to 4-bit fails due to a zero-point problem; without removing zero from the quantization map and changing normalization, training becomes unstable. Robust training requires specialized choices (e.g., DE-0 or Linear mapping, rank-1 normalization), reducing generality.\n  - Performance and stability are sensitive to block size and normalization strategy; smaller blocks (e.g., B128) and rank-1 normalization are needed to cope with heterogeneous outlier patterns.\n  - Overall memory savings can appear to “saturate” in end-to-end training because non-optimizer state (activations, data, fragmentation) still dominates footprint; speed can be lower than 8-bit until fused kernels are implemented.\n  - Reported evaluations are limited to language and vision; applicability to RL, audio, or graphs remains untested.\n\n- BSO / T-BSO (online training for Binary SNNs)\n  - Although T-BSO improves over BSO and binarized baselines, it underperforms strong online full-precision baselines (e.g., SLTT, OTTT) on ImageNet; accuracy remains several points lower at comparable time steps and backbone size.\n  - T-BSO introduces extra (though small) memory overhead for temporal second-moment tracking; it also depends on additional hyperparameters (γ, β1, β2), and still keeps first/last layers in full precision.\n  - Convergence guarantees are sublinear: average regret decays as O(1/√T) (BSO) and O(T^{-1/4}) (T-BSO), with T-BSO’s bound looser than BSO’s; practical convergence speed may thus lag in the worst case.\n  - Method efficacy hinges on thresholded, momentum-driven flips; inappropriate thresholds can slow learning or stall updates, necessitating per-task tuning despite reported robustness.\n"}

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved papers, here is a brief defect/limitation analysis of each method family relevant to your four requirements.
> 
> ## 1. Anchor-free part–body association (PBADet)
> - The single part-to-body offset works best for multi-part settings; on the single-part CrowdHuman face–body task, its advantage over anchor-based BPJDet is **less pronounced**.
> - Every component matters: ablations show dropping the association loss, multi-scale offset, or task-alignment learning each degrades hand AP, conditional accuracy, and joint AP (e.g., association loss removal drops conditional accuracy 92.62→80.78, joint AP 85.98→78.07). So the design is brittle to component removal.
> - It is a per-frame detector; nothing in the paper addresses online/temporal consistency across video frames, which you'd need for real-time person-ID association.
> 
> ## 2. Online training for binary spiking nets (BSO/T-BSO)
> - **BSO's core defect**: uniform gradient treatment across time steps discards BSNN temporal dynamics, which is why T-BSO was introduced.
> - **T-BSO's defects**: tracking per-timestep moments would make memory scale linearly with T, so it must average second-order moments (approximation); its regret bound is worse (O(T^3/4) vs BSO's O(√T)); it adds many hyperparameters (γ, β₁, β₂) and still stores extra computation state O(n²L+LT+nL); and scalability beyond image tasks (CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, DVS) is acknowledged as largely unexplored—T-BSO only reaches ~73% on CIFAR-100 (VGG-11, T=2), well below full-precision accuracy.
> 
> ## 3. Spectral diagnostics for EI-restricted recurrent blocks (ColEI/DANN)
> - The "defect" is in the EI-constrained architecture itself: ColEI recurrent nets learn worse on all tasks (sequential MNIST, adding, PTB, object recognition) with much higher seed variance; without gradient clipping they are highly unstable.
> - Root cause: the initial recurrent weight spectrum is multimodal/dispersed (rank-one column-mean nilpotent structure), unlike the Marchenko–Pastur/quarter-circle spectrum of standard RNNs and DANN RNNs; large singular-value modes deform activations/gradients even when the spectral radius is constrained.
> - Sign constraints contribute only ~1% vs ~2.3% total gap—so fixing signs is insufficient; the spectrum is the dominant defect, and smaller networks/fewer inhibitory units worsen it. NSE is only a heuristic diagnostic, and eigendecomposition is unreliable for non-symmetric matrices.
> 
> ## 4. JEPA predictive encoders vs reconstruction (MAE)
> - Theoretical claims are proven only for deep **linear** MLPs, restricted initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable Σ_yx, Σ_xx; real data distributions are expected to deviate significantly, and generalization to nonlinear/practical settings is explicitly unproven.
> - JEPA can still learn noisy features, but converges to lower-amplitude weights, making them less usable downstream; it is also vulnerable to **spurious or slow features** (prioritizes low-variance/"slow" features).
> - JEPA needs architectural tricks (stop-gradients, predictors, spectral/weight regularization) to avoid feature collapse; the analysis doesn't cover other joint-embedding variants.
> 
> ## 5. 4-bit optimizer states / LoRA-style adaptation (4-bit AdamW/AdamW-Factor)
> - Optimal quantization is **task-dependent** (block size, rank-1 vs linear mapping); the authors note task-specific settings might outperform theirs—a robustness gap.
> - Evaluation is limited to language/vision; applicability to RL, audio, graph learning is untested.
> - Second-moment quantization suffers a zero-point problem requiring zero-exclusion; moments have heterogeneous outlier patterns that block-wise quantization approximates poorly (smaller blocks/rank-1 normalization needed).
> - Memory savings saturate (total memory includes activations/data/fragments), and without fused kernels 4-bit is slower than 8-bit on small models.
> - Relatedly, the Hessian power-law study shows **LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the power-law Hessian structure** that full fine-tuning does, i.e., LoRA-style end-to-end adaptation changes optimization geometry and may limit how well the fine-tuned model matches full fine-tuning behavior.
> 
> ## Cross-cutting gaps for your system
> No retrieved paper demonstrates the full pipeline (anchor-free detection + online binary-spike training + EI-spectral diagnostics + JEPA pretraining + 4-bit LoRA fine-tuning) end-to-end, and none reports joint metrics (CE, Precision, F1) across all four components. The pieces are individually validated (PBADet: Precision/Recall/F1 vs ED-Pose; BSO: CIFAR-10/100 accuracy; ColEI: sequential MNIST error; JEPA: ImageNet CCA; 4-bit: GLUE/SQuAD/MMLU), but integration-level defects—e.g., whether anchor-free part–body association can run inside an online-trained BSNN, or whether JEPA features transfer to a 4-bit/LoRA fine-tuned head under GPU limits—are not established in this context.

**community 最终答案**

> 基于检索到的文献，各方法的开发缺陷（局限/不足）分析如下：
> 
> ## 1. PBADet（anchor-free 部件–人体关联检测）
> - **资源开销大，不天然适配边缘实时**：用 YOLOv7/YOLOv5l6 主干、1024×1024 输入，4 张 V100 训 100 epochs，且依赖预训练 YOLO 权重。
> - **对组件敏感**：消融显示去掉关联损失后条件准确率从 92.62% 掉到 80.78%；去掉多尺度中心偏移或 task-alignment 也均掉点，说明多尺度偏移、任务对齐都是关键依赖。
> - **解码仍需启发式后处理**：推理时用 NMS + 未分配且包含部件的身体中心的欧氏距离最近匹配，遮挡/密集场景下仍可能不稳。
> - **仅静态图像验证**：只在 BodyHands、COCOHumanParts、CrowdHuman、AnimalPose 等静态数据集上评测，无视频/时序验证。
> - **指标不直接覆盖 CE/Precision/F1**：主要报 AP、条件准确率、联合 AP、mMR⁻²（仅与 ED-Pose 对比时给出 Precision/Recall/F1）。
> - 在 CrowdHuman 单部件（脸–体）任务上相对 BPJDet 的优势不明显。
> 
> ## 2. BSO / T-BSO（二值脉冲网在线训练）
> - **与全精度仍有差距**：ImageNet 上 T-BSO 为 57.76%（模型仅 4.22MB），仍低于全精度在线方法 SLTT、OTTT；CIFAR-100 6 时间步为 74.27%。
> - **并非完全二值**：首层和末层仍需保留全精度权重。
> - **BSO 丢失时序信息**：对时间步做均匀梯度处理，必须靠 T-BSO 补，而 T-BSO 内存从 BSO 的 O(n²L/32) 升至 O(n²L+LT+nL)，训练内存 2.9GB→3.1GB，仍有时间步相关开销。
> - **符号翻转更新粒度粗**：只翻转符号、无幅度信息；需调阈值 γ、动量衰减 β₁/β₂，性能随时间步数波动；收敛证明依赖梯度有界及 β、γ 衰减假设。
> 
> ## 3. 谱诊断（Dale 定律/EI 约束循环块，sequential MNIST 等）
> - **诊断揭示的缺陷本身**：ColEI 网络在 adding、sequential MNIST、PTB、物体识别四个任务上均学得更差且跨种子方差更大；小网络、抑制性单元少时谱更病态、性能更差。
> - **不稳定**：无梯度裁剪时 ColEI 高度不稳定，需依赖梯度裁剪。
> - **仅初始化期诊断**：NSE（归一化 SVD 熵）在初始化时计算，只能预测训练前性能，不能纠正训练中的问题。
> - 谱分析需对循环权重做 SVD，大网络代价高；诊断与性能的关联是经验性的，属于"解释为什么差"而非修复手段。
> 
> ## 4. 4-bit 优化器状态（严格 GPU 内存 + LoRA 式适配）
> - **二阶矩零值问题**：值量化到 0 会经 1/√v 导致更新方向灾难性偏离；排除零后 DE-0 浪费 16 个量化点之一，线性映射最小可表示值仅 0.0625，逼近精度受限。
> - **离群模式复杂且逐层变化**：需更小 block（B128）或 rank-1 归一化，rank-1 对 1-D 张量退化为 per-tensor；小 block 增加额外内存。
> - **并非完全无损**：如 Swin-T 上 4-bit AdamW 80.8 vs 32-bit 81.2，存在轻微掉点。
> - **适用范围受限**：仅验证了语言/视觉任务，最优量化方案可能任务相关；收敛证明只针对量化的 SGD(M)，不覆盖 Adam 本身。
> - 配合 LoRA 时（Hessian 工作指出）：LoRA-only 微调不像全量微调那样诱导出 Hessian 幂律谱结构，谱诊断在 LoRA 适配器上行为会偏离预期（如 d_ks 先升后降、Tr(H) 才是更可靠泛化指标），说明谱类诊断对 LoRA 端到端适配的适用性存疑。
> 
> ## 5. JEPA（自监督预测编码器，避免噪声特征）
> - **易坍塌**：JEPA 目标可被"所有输入映射到同一向量"平凡极小化，须依赖 stop-grad 等机制。
> - **偏置有条件性**：对高影响力（高回归系数 ρ）特征的偏置只在**深层编码器**成立，浅层时明显减弱；且对虚假/慢特征存在脆弱性（"JEPAs vulnerability to spurious or slow features"）。
> - **可能反转学习顺序**：当 ρ 与 λ（协方差）趋势相反时，JEPA 相对 MAE 完全反转特征学习顺序，可能忽略高方差但有用的特征。
> - **理论局限**：仅对深度线性网络、平衡正交初始化、可同时对角化的数据严格成立，推广到非线性/真实分布是定性的。
> - 验证在 ImageNet-1K（CCA 度量），未提供 CIFAR-100 演示；没有给出 CE/Precision/F1 类指标。
> 
> ## 与需求匹配的整体缺陷提示
> - 用户想要的 CE、Precision、F1、CIFAR-100 演示：PBADet 主要用 AP/条件准确率/联合 AP/mMR⁻²，BSO 用 CIFAR-100 准确率（74.27%），4-bit 优化器 QA 任务报 F1 但分类用准确率，JEPA 用 ImageNet CCA——没有任何单一工作同时提供 CE+Precision+F1 的完整指标组合。
> - 各方法分别解决单一环节，尚无端到端联合（检测→二值脉冲在线→LoRA+4-bit 微调→自监督预训练）验证，集成时的组件相互影响（如二值权重与 4-bit 状态、谱诊断与 LoRA 的冲突）是未解决的开发缺陷。

</details>

### paperscope:gap:100 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building an edge‑constrained system that needs: (a) reliable hand/face‑to‑person association in crowded images at COCO scale; (b) label‑free pretraining that predicts one view’s representation from another instead of reconstructing pixels; (c) a recurrent controller that respects separate excitatory vs inhibitory units yet still trains well; (d) a policy learner that can start from a static log and keep improving with on‑policy updates while retaining theoretical stability; and (e) the ability to fine‑tune Transformer backbones/LLMs under tight VRAM using ~4‑bit AdamW states. Are there recent papers that collectively address these components, with experiments spanning COCO, CIFAR‑100/MNIST/PTB and common fine‑tuning setups?Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

**score：3→2（Δ-1）；rounds：4→2（Δ-2）。**

工具安排：naive 为第1轮5次、第2轮3次、第3轮3次；community 为第1轮5次。最终回答另占一轮。

轮次减少 2，工具总数 11→5、错误 0→0，整轮全部工具报错的轮数 0→0。这些计数把实际查询/读取安排与失败恢复分开；它们不支持将全部轮次差机械归因于社区。

每题内去重的 chunk 116→60、文档 overview 21→87；工具结果字符数 300,694→242,210，QA token 228,583→78,569。字符数不是 token，也不是多轮历史重复输入后的累计量。

首轮整组工具请求不同，这一差异发生在看到任何社区结果之前；首轮规划差不能反向归因于社区。

Gold 1：

> {'answer': 'Below are the main development defects and limitations explicitly indicated by the five cited methods, organized by component/method.\n\n(a) One‑stage anchor‑free part‑to‑person association (PBADet, ICLR 2024)\n- Enclosure assumption at decoding: the association step picks the body “that are unassigned and also enclose the part,” then chooses the nearest center. If a valid part box is not within any predicted body box (e.g., due to occlusion or annotation/box jitter), association cannot be made by design.\n- Benefits may be limited for single‑part association: the paper notes that in the face–body task (a single part), advantages over prior work are “not as pronounced” as in multi‑part settings.\n- Heavy resolution/compute: reported training uses 1024–1536 px inputs, multi‑scale heads, 100 epochs on 4×V100 GPUs; thresholds are tuned per‑dataset (e.g., very low part confidence on COCOHumanParts), implying non‑trivial resource and calibration costs.\n- Sensitivity to design choices: ablations show notable drops if multi‑scale offsets or task‑alignment are removed, indicating reliance on specific training recipes.\n- Detection AP parity rather than dominance: on COCOHumanParts, PBADet’s AP is “on par” with BPJDet (not consistently superior), so gains come mainly from association simplicity/robustness, not detection accuracy.\n\n(b) Label‑free JEPA‑style pretraining (How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features, NeurIPS 2024)\n- Theory restricted to a stylized setting: results are derived for deep linear encoders under special initializations and simultaneously‑diagonalizable Σxx and Σxy. The paper explicitly states that generalization to non‑linear models and non‑simultaneously‑diagonalizable data “remains unexplored.”\n- Depth required for the JEPA bias to emerge: the influential‑feature bias “takes hold only when the encoder is deep” and “diminishes substantially” for shallow encoders, reducing the expected advantage if depth is limited.\n- Possible vulnerability to slow/spurious features: the authors note that JEPA’s bias toward features with high regression coefficients can make it “vulnerable to spurious or slow features.”\n- Collapse avoidance still required: the method relies on StopGrad to prevent representation collapse; without such mechanisms, trivial solutions exist by construction.\n- Potential to deprioritize high‑variance but less predictive features: the analysis shows JEPA may reverse learning order relative to MAE when covariance and regression coefficients disagree; in such data regimes, JEPA can under‑emphasize highly covarying (but less predictive) features.\n\n(c) Recurrent controllers with Dale’s Law (Learning better with Dale’s Law: A Spectral Perspective, NeurIPS 2023)\n- ColEI (simple E/I column partition) pathologies: poor learning, higher variance, and instability without gradient clipping; multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra (including large singular values) cause exploding/vanishing gradients; performance is highly sensitive to network size and E:I ratio (small networks and fewer inhibitory units learn worse).\n- Hyperparameter sensitivity: performance depends strongly on spectral radius and gradient clipping; small changes can substantially affect stability and accuracy.\n- DANNs are better but not fully complete biologically: the recurrent DANNs used here omit features such as inhibitory‑to‑inhibitory connections and cell‑type‑specific time constants; they primarily model fast PV+ interneurons, so broader interneuron diversity is not captured.\n- Empirical scope: demonstrations are on adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Treebank, and a small natural‑object task; large‑scale/task‑diverse validation is not provided.\n- Open theoretical gaps: the paper notes open questions on the origin of ColEI’s unusual multimodal spectra and why large ColEI networks can learn despite large maximum singular values.\n\n(d) Hybrid offline‑enhanced on‑policy learner (HNPG/HAC, ICLR 2024)\n- Assumption‑dependent guarantees: “best‑of‑both‑worlds” rates rely on either (i) offline Bellman‑completeness/coverage for the pessimistic‑style bound or (ii) on‑policy coverage Cnpg for NPG‑style bounds; when these are weak, only the generic on‑policy bound applies.\n- Harsh theoretical constants: sample‑complexity bounds scale with large powers of 1/(1−γ) (e.g., 1/(1−γ)^14 in the corollaries), indicating pessimistic worst‑case sample needs.\n- Practical sample use: in the rich‑observation benchmarks, HNPG still needs substantial online data (tens of millions of steps for long horizons), and a strong offline set; off‑policy RLPD can be more sample‑efficient on short horizons (though less stable on images).\n- Implementation cost: every iteration requires collecting on‑policy rollouts to form Monte‑Carlo returns alongside fitting with offline TD targets; this dual pipeline increases complexity.\n- Empirical scope: validated on continuous Comblock (and a Cifar‑100 image‑based variant). Results on standard continuous‑control suites and broader domains are not reported.\n\n(e) 4‑bit state optimizers for fine‑tuning (Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4‑bit States, NeurIPS 2023)\n- Zero‑point failure for second moments: naive 4‑bit DE mapping pushes many v estimates to zero, causing catastrophic deviations in update directions (since updates use 1/sqrt(v)); requires zero‑excluding mappings (DE‑0) or linear mapping to avoid collapse.\n- Outlier‑pattern sensitivity: first/second moments exhibit heterogeneous row/column outliers varying by layer and model; large blocks (e.g., 2048) underfit these patterns. Accuracy requires smaller blocks (e.g., 128) and/or rank‑1 normalization, increasing scale‑storage and compute overhead.\n- Speed without fused ops: 4‑bit implementations can be slower than 8‑bit baselines unless specialized fused kernels are used; the paper reports slower runs prior to applying fused operators.\n- Small but present accuracy deltas in pretraining: on ImageNet (Swin‑T) and WMT14, 4‑bit AdamW is slightly below full‑precision (e.g., 80.8 vs 81.2 top‑1, 26.28 vs 26.61 SacreBLEU), showing a minor quality trade‑off in pretraining regimes.\n- Task dependence & coverage limits: the authors note optimal quantization settings “probably depend on task, datasets, and training details,” and their evaluation focuses on language/vision; applicability to RL, audio, and graphs remains to be studied.\n- Practical exclusions: tiny tensors (≤4096 elems) and certain layers (e.g., embeddings in some baselines) are left unquantized, which slightly limits peak memory savings and complicates parity across setups.'}

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Yes—collectively, but across five separate papers, not one unified method
> 
> Mapping your five components to the papers in this collection:
> 
> | Component | Paper | Benchmarks |
> |---|---|---|
> | (a) Hand/face↔person association | **PBADet** (ICLR 2024): one-stage anchor-free part-to-body association via a single part-to-body center offset | BodyHands, **COCO-HumanParts**, **COCO** val, **CrowdHuman** (face-body) |
> | (b) Label-free pretraining predicting one view's rep from another | **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (Apple, NeurIPS 2024): analyzes I-JEPA/BYOL-style self-distillation (predict in latent space) vs MAE (reconstruct pixels) | ImageNet-1K, ViT, CCA dynamics |
> | (c) Recurrent E/I controller that trains well | **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023) | adding, **sequential MNIST**, **Penn Tree Bank**, naturalistic object recognition |
> | (d) Policy learner from static log + on-policy updates with stability | **"Offline Data Enhanced On-Policy Policy Gradient with Provable Guarantees"** (ICLR 2024, HAC/HNPG); also **PPO-Clip two-timescale convergence** | rich-observation Comblock |
> | (e) ~4-bit AdamW states for VRAM-tight fine-tuning | **"4-bit Optimizers"** (NeurIPS 2023) | RoBERTa-L, Swin-T, GPT-2, Transformer, LLaMA-7B/13B/33B (GLUE, SQuAD, E2E, ImageNet, Alpaca) |
> 
> **Coverage caveat:** COCO is covered by (a); MNIST/PTB by (c); common fine-tuning by (e); **CIFAR-100 only appears in other SSL/optimizer papers** (the contrastive embedding-similarity paper and the Hessian paper), not in the JEPA paper—so no single combination here runs the full requested benchmark spread.
> 
> ## Development defects of each method
> 
> **(a) PBADet**
> - Its part-to-body offset is a regression from part center to body center; if a part is occluded or a box is speculative, the offset becomes meaningless—the paper admits pose-based baselines (ED-Pose) give "imprecise or speculative" limb predictions.
> - On the *single-part* face-body task (CrowdHuman) its advantage over BPJDet largely disappears; gains are only clear for multi-part settings.
> - Still requires hand-tuned NMS thresholds and post-processing heuristics (τ_body, τ_part), and every positive anchor inside a part box must also lie in the body box—a brittle geometry assumption for crowded, overlapping people.
> - It is fully supervised—no label-free signal to feed component (b).
> 
> **(b) JEPA self-distillation**
> - Objective is trivially collapsible; it survives only via stop-grad/EMA architectural tricks, not a principled constraint.
> - The paper's *theory* is restricted to deep linear encoders, special (balanced/orthogonal) initialization, and simultaneous diagonalizability; ImageNet results are only qualitative CCA confirmation at 64×64.
> - The bias to "influential/high-regression features" means JEPA can be *vulnerable to spurious or slow features*, and prioritizing low-variance subspaces can ignore genuinely informative high-variance signal.
> - It provides no CIFAR-100-scale validation and no drop-in pretrained model to connect to (a)/(c).
> 
> **(c) Dale's Law recurrent controllers**
> - The core defect the paper documents: *separating* units into E and I populations (ColEI) impairs learning—multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra at initialization → worse, high-variance final performance, and instability without gradient clipping. So the literal "separate E/I units" design is exactly what fails.
> - The fix (recurrent DANN) does *not* use separate E/I populations—it reparameterizes weights into non-negative E→E, E→I, I→E projections—so it only "respects Dale's Law" in a looser sense and doesn't satisfy the separate-unit requirement.
> - Small networks or biologically realistic (few-I) ratios still learn poorly; results are empirical with open theoretical questions about spectrum origin.
> 
> **(d) Hybrid on-policy + offline RL**
> - The best-of-both-worlds guarantee only holds when offline assumptions (realizability, Bellman-completeness, concentrability, reset distribution over state-action) hold; without completeness it degrades to vanilla on-policy NPG rates.
> - Offline component is inherently off-policy/bootstrap-based, so it can't escape the very instability the on-policy part is meant to hedge against.
> - PPO-Clip alternative only gives *subsequential* stationarity unless the policy-sync bias φ_n → 0; and per-sample off-policy reuse is bounded by the synchronization interval T.
> 
> **(e) 4-bit AdamW**
> - Optimal quantization is task-dependent; the authors concede lossless behavior isn't guaranteed, only "comparable" accuracy.
> - The convergence proof is for quantized **SGD(M)** only, not for the actual AdamW 4-bit update used in the experiments.
> - Quantizing both moments causes a marginal accuracy drop; 4-bitFactor (factorized second moment) trades slight accuracy for memory.
> - On small models (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2 Medium) it is *slower* than 8-bit AdamW until fused operators are added; memory savings saturate as bitwidth drops; only language/vision tasks were tested.
> 
> **Overall:** the five components exist in the literature and cover the requested domains, but they are disjoint research threads with no shared codebase, no end-to-end integration, and each carries its own known limitations—most notably that the "separate E/I units" requirement is (by the evidence here) fundamentally at odds with training well.

**community 最终答案**

> **Yes — collectively these components are covered by recent papers in the collection, though no single paper spans all of them.**
> 
> - **(a) Hand/face–person association at COCO scale:** PBADet (one-stage anchor-free part-to-body association) — evaluated on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, COCO val, CrowdHuman.
> - **(b) Label-free view-prediction (predict one view's representation from another, no pixel reconstruction):** the JEPA self-distillation analysis paper (I-JEPA-style, "Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features"), plus LDReg and the contrastive-embedding-similarity paper in the same SSL cluster (CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, COCO detection/segmentation).
> - **(c) Recurrent controller with separate E/I units that still trains:** "Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly" — ColEI vs recurrent DANN, experiments on adding task, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, object recognition.
> - **(d) Policy learner starting from a static log + on-policy improvement with provable stability:** HAC/HNPG ("Offline Data Enhanced On-Policy Policy Gradient") — best-of-both-worlds hybrid RL with NPG-style guarantees, tested on rich-observation Comblock.
> - **(e) 4-bit AdamW states for VRAM-constrained Transformer/LLM fine-tuning:** "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" — GLUE, SQuAD, E2E-NLG, WMT14, Swin-T ImageNet, LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning.
> 
> **Development defects of these methods:**
> 
> - **(a) PBADet:** advantage over BPJDet is small/less pronounced on CrowdHuman face-body association; face/head excluded from keypoint-level comparisons due to inconsistent annotations; comparisons use different training sets (COCO-HumanParts vs ED-Pose's COCO); anchor-free "all points in a box are positive" sampling can be noisy; multi-part representations grow rigidly in prior work, and occluded parts invalidate offsets.
> - **(b) JEPA analysis / SSL:** the JEPA paper is only a *theoretical analysis* (deep linear networks, special initialization, simultaneous diagonalizability), not a new pretraining method; LDReg's LID estimation degrades in high dimensions and relies on minibatch nearest neighbors, and forcing very low LID causes complete collapse.
> - **(c) Dale's-law RNNs:** ColEI networks still learn worse with higher variance; the initial recurrent spectrum is multimodal/dispersed (gradient clipping only mitigates, not fixes); small networks with few inhibitory units perform poorly; DANN lacks biological fidelity (no I→I connections, no cell-type time constants); normalised SVD entropy is only a correlational predictor.
> - **(d) HAC/HNPG:** offline gains require approximate Bellman completeness, realizability, smoothness and concentrability; when those fail it degrades to plain on-policy NPG rates; experiments are limited to Comblock-style environments (no standard benchmarks like D4RL/Atari), and the practical implementation (HPE regression, parameterized policies) is nontrivial.
> - **(e) 4-bit optimizers:** 4-bit variants were slower than 8-bit AdamW on smaller models due to missing fused operators; quantizing both moments costs a marginal accuracy drop; the best quantization scheme appears task-dependent; memory savings saturate (~57.7%) because activations/data dominate; only language/vision tasks were tested, and factorization only applies to the second moment.
> 
> Collectively, the COCO (PBADet/LDReg), CIFAR-100 (SSL similarity paper), MNIST/PTB (Dale's-law RNN), and standard fine-tuning (GLUE/SQuAD/Alpaca) coverage exists, but the pieces come from different papers with different assumptions — there is no integrated system, and the recurrent-controller paper addresses generic RNNs rather than an explicit "controller" use case.

> {'answer': '- PBADet (one-stage, anchor-free part–body association)\n  - Limited advantage on single-part association: On CrowdHuman’s face–body task (only one part), the gains over BPJDet are “not as pronounced,” indicating the method’s core scalability benefit shows less in single-part regimes.\n  - Sensitivity to design choices: Ablations show notable drops without the association loss, multi-scale formulation, or task-alignment learning, implying the method’s effectiveness depends on these components and their hyperparameters (e.g., K, α, β, λ for scaling; NMS thresholds per dataset).\n  - Dataset/threshold dependence: Inference relies on NMS with dataset-specific confidence/IoU thresholds; different settings were needed across BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, and CrowdHuman, suggesting tuning burden for deployment.\n\n- Contrastive learning via cosine similarity (full-/mini-batch analysis; SimCLR/DCL/DHEL, SigLIP)\n  - Mini-batch defect: Smaller batches provably induce higher variance of negative-pair similarities; negative pairs separate unevenly, degrading representation quality relative to full-batch training. With InfoNCE, the gradient that pushes negatives apart grows as batch size shrinks, amplifying the problem.\n  - Excessive separation under certain losses: For independently additive losses that only include cross-view negatives (c1=1, c2=0), such as SigLIP under specific hyperparameters, optimization can favor pushing negatives beyond the optimal −1/(n−1), forcing imperfect positive alignment.\n  - Mitigation trade-offs: The proposed variance-reduction auxiliary loss (L_VRNS) curbs the mini-batch variance but introduces a new hyperparameter (λ), has reduced impact with large batches, and can suppress semantically meaningful variance if overused.\n\n- How JEPA avoids noisy features (implicit bias in deep linear self-distillation)\n  - Scope limitations of the theory: Results rely on deep linear encoders, special balanced initializations, and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances; generalization to nonlinear encoders and realistic data distributions is unproven.\n  - Depth dependency: JEPA’s desirable bias toward “influential” (high-regression-coefficient) features emerges clearly only when the encoder is deep; shallow encoders behave more like MAE, implying increased depth/compute may be needed to realize the benefits.\n  - Potential vulnerability: The same bias that downweights noisy high-variance features can steer models toward slow or spurious features, as discussed by the authors, highlighting a risk in certain data regimes.\n\n- Memory-efficient optimizers with 4-bit states (Adam/AdamW-style)\n  - Zero-point failure mode in v (second moment): Mapping zero in low-bit formats pushes many v entries to 0; because updates scale by 1/sqrt(v), this causes update explosions and instability. Special mappings (exclude zero) or linear mapping are required to stabilize training.\n  - Outlier structure not uniformly handled: Large block sizes (e.g., 2048) miss common row/column outlier patterns in optimizer moments; while smaller blocks or rank-1 normalization help, they add scaling overhead and are not universally superior (authors show cases where rank‑1 underperforms block-wise).\n  - Task- and tensor-dependent settings: Optimal quantization choices (block size, mapping, rank‑1 vs. block-wise) vary with model/tensor statistics; stable operation requires heuristics (e.g., not quantizing small tensors or some embeddings), increasing tuning burden.\n  - Throughput trade-offs without kernel fusion: 4-bit variants can be slower than 8-bit/full-precision on smaller models unless fused operators are implemented; speed parity depends on systems engineering.\n  - Evaluation breadth: Demonstrated strong results on language and vision (e.g., RoBERTa-L, GPT‑2 M, Swin-T, Transformer), but applicability to RL, audio, or graphs remains to be validated per the authors.\n\n- Dale’s Law in RNNs (ColEI vs. recurrent DANNs)\n  - ColEI (naïve column-sign constraint) defects:\n    - Poor and unstable learning: Multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra with large modes cause exploding/vanishing dynamics; training is highly sensitive, often requiring gradient clipping and showing large variance across seeds.\n    - Sensitivity to network size and E/I ratio: Small networks or realistic E:I ratios (few inhibitory units) learn poorly; performance and spectra improve mainly with larger models and balanced E/I.\n    - Initialization/spectral-radius fragility: Performance depends acutely on spectral radius and initialization; stability windows differ from standard RNNs.\n  - Recurrent DANNs residual limitations:\n    - Biological specificity trade-off: While learning well with sign constraints, DANNs model fast feedforward inhibition (PV+‑like) and may not capture other inhibitory subtypes without architectural changes; authors suggest hybrids as future work.\n    - Open spectral questions: Despite good performance, theoretical understanding of spectrum origins and behavior (e.g., large max singular value in large nets) remains incomplete, complicating principled design.\n'}

**naive 最终答案**

> Here are the papers matching your four topics, with an analysis of their development defects.
> 
> **1. Contrastive learning geometry — "On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning"** (`160e1407...`)
> Covers cosine-similarity-based contrastive learning, the temperature parameter, and the mini-batch effect: smaller batches increase the variance of negative-pair similarities, causing "excessive separation."
> *Development defects:* The proposed variance-reduction auxiliary loss can suppress *meaningful* semantic variance (over-uniformizing embeddings hurts representation quality); its benefit diminishes as batch size grows; it adds a hyperparameter λ that needs careful tuning; the theory only covers specific loss forms (e.g., InfoNCE/SigLIP-style, simultaneously-diagonalizable assumptions), not all contrastive objectives.
> 
> **2. JEPA implicit bias — "Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features: A Deep Linear Network Analysis"** (`40fde037...`)
> Shows JEPA/self-distillation implicitly biases toward high-influence (high-regression-coefficient) features, whereas MAE is agnostic.
> *Development defects:* Analysis is restricted to deep *linear* networks with balanced orthogonal initialization and simultaneous-diagonalizable data; the bias toward influential features can make JEPA vulnerable to spurious or slow features, and it may prioritize low-variance "slow" features at the expense of other signal; the finding requires depth (diminishes for shallow encoders).
> 
> **3. Memory-efficient training — "4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States"** (`8d5e1455...`) and "Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure" (`582d138d...`)
> The 4-bit optimizer paper compresses AdamW/Adam optimizer states from 32→8→4-bit (sub-8-bit) for vision (Swin-T on ImageNet) and transformer/LLM models, and discusses low-rank factorization of states; the Hessian paper runs SGD/AdamW-style training with LoRA fine-tuning experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-100, and fine-tunes ViT-Base on CIFAR-100.
> *Development defects (4-bit optimizers):* Quantizing both moments still causes a small accuracy drop; the optimal quantization configuration is task/dataset-dependent; evaluation limited to language and vision (RL/audio/graphs untested); small models are slower than 8-bit without fused operators.
> *Development defects (Hessian paper):* The power-law Hessian structure is lost for small width/depth, limited data, noisy labels, and large-batch training; LoRA-only fine-tuning doesn't induce the structure as full fine-tuning does; SOTA LLMs were excluded because Hessian computation is too expensive.
> 
> **4. Part-body association — "PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association Detection"** (`08b70bc3...`)
> Anchor-free detector associating human parts to the correct person via a single learned part-to-body center offset.
> *Development defects:* Relies on the part-to-body offset being defined relative to multi-scale anchor points and requires task-alignment learning — ablations show accuracy drops without multi-scale offsets or task alignment, and without the association loss it degrades to heuristic Euclidean-distance matching; its advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced on the single-part CrowdHuman face-body task; depends on backbone choices (YOLOv5/v7).
> 
> **Connections to your broader interests:** The contrastive paper relates its variance reduction to temperature/regularization effects on embedding geometry (cross-entropy-like softmax loss), the 4-bit optimizer paper ties into practical AdamW/weight-decay choices and low-GPU-memory training (up to 57.7% memory savings), and the LoRA-related experiments (Hessian paper) connect fine-tuning efficiency and generalization structure to regularization.

**community 最终答案**

> I found four papers matching your four areas, plus a closely related regularizer.
> 
> **1. Contrastive embedding geometry (temperature, small-batch variance)**
> "On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning" (Lee et al., ICML 2025; doc `160e1407…`). It analyzes InfoNCE/SimCLR-style losses under cosine similarity with temperature: in full-batch settings the optimum is a simplex Equiangular Tight Frame (positive similarity 1, negative −1/(n−1)); in mini-batch settings smaller batches force higher variance in negative-pair similarities ("excessive separation"), which degrades representations. They fix this with an auxiliary variance-reduction loss (VRNS) and show it improves CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100/ImageNet accuracy and temperature robustness. Notably, the paper explicitly links the simplex-ETF optimum to **neural collapse under cross-entropy** (citing Papyan et al.; Lu & Steinerberger, "Neural collapse under cross-entropy loss") and to SigLIP temperature behavior—this is the cross-entropy/regularization link you asked about.
> 
> **2. JEPA implicit bias toward influential features**
> "Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features: A Deep Linear Network Analysis" (Littwin et al., NeurIPS 2024; doc `40fde037…`). It proves JEPA self-distillation has an implicit bias toward **high-influence features** (large regression coefficients), unlike MAE which prioritizes high-variance features even if noisy; the bias only takes hold with deep encoders. Confirmed on ImageNet-1K via CCA (I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance PCA subspace).
> 
> **3. Memory-efficient sub-8-bit optimizer states (CIFAR-100 / MNIST experiments)**
> Two complementary papers:
> - **"4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States"** (Li, Chen, Zhu; NeurIPS 2023; doc `8d5e1455…`) pushes Adam/AdamW states from 8-bit to 4-bit (smaller blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluding linear quantizer, factorization), with a convergence proof for quantized SGD(M), up to 57.7% memory savings, and LoRA discussed as a complementary low-rank technique. However, its experiments are on GLUE, SQuAD, ImageNet (Swin-T), WMT, and LLaMA/OPT — **not** CIFAR-100/MNIST.
> - **"Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure"** (doc `582d138d…`) provides exactly the CIFAR-100 + MNIST + ViT + LoRA experiments: LeNet/FCN/ResNet18/ViT-Base on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10/100 with many optimizer choices (SGD, Adam, AdamW, AMSGrad, Yogi, RAdam, Lookahead, etc.), ViT-Base fine-tuned on CIFAR-100 with Adam (0.9, 0.999), weight decay 0.1, and LoRA fine-tuning experiments. Its focus is Hessian power-law spectra and how they predict generalization and sharpness across optimizers, not memory reduction per se.
> 
> **4. One-stage anchor-free part–body association via learned offsets**
> "PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association" (Gao et al., ICLR 2024; doc `08b70bc3…`). It extends anchor-free dense detection with a single learned **part-to-body center offset** (2D displacement) per anchor point across multi-scale feature maps, with a dedicated association loss (top-K task-aligned anchors), guaranteeing one-to-one part→body correspondence. Outperforms BPJDet/HierR-CNN on BodyHands and COCO-HumanParts.
> 
> **Close additional match for topic 1's regularization theme:** "LDReg: Local Dimensionality Regularization for Self-Supervised Learning" (doc `51526068…`) regularizes against (local) dimensional collapse in SimCLR/BYOL/MAE — the geometry/regularization counterpart to the contrastive paper.
> 
> ---
> 
> **Development defects / limitations (from the papers themselves):**
> 
> - **Contrastive similarity paper (160e1407):** The VRNS auxiliary loss can *suppress semantically meaningful variance* in negative-pair similarities (over-regularization flattens informative structure); its benefit shrinks at large batch sizes where variance is naturally low; it adds a hyperparameter λ that needs careful tuning; and the theory covers specific loss families (InfoNCE-type) rather than all contrastive losses.
> 
> - **JEPA paper (40fde037):** Analysis is limited to **deep linear networks** with special (balanced orthogonal) initialization and simultaneously diagonalizable data; the qualitative claim rests on non-rigorous extrapolation to nonlinear models; the implicit bias toward influential/low-variance features can also be a **vulnerability to spurious or slow features** (the authors flag this), and the bias essentially disappears for shallow encoders, meaning depth is required to get the noise-suppression benefit.
> 
> - **4-bit optimizer paper (8d5e1455):** Optimal quantization settings are probably **task/dataset-dependent**; rank-1 normalization and linear second-moment mapping are not guaranteed lossless outside tested settings; without fused operators the 4-bit optimizers were *slower* than 8-bit on small models (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2); quantizing both moments still causes a marginal accuracy drop; evaluation is limited to language/vision (RL, audio, graph learning unverified); and 8-bit embedding layers were left unquantized in the 8-bit baseline, so the comparison is not fully apples-to-apples.
> 
> - **Hessian-structure paper (582d138d):** It is an *analysis* paper, not a memory-reduction method — Hessian computation (SLQ) is itself memory/GPU-expensive; power-law structure is **lost** with small width/depth, limited data, noisy labels, and large-batch training, so its diagnostics are not universally applicable; and the power-law/sharpness conclusions may not hold for very large SOTA LLMs (excluded by Hessian cost).
> 
> - **PBADet (08b70bc3):** Depends on task-alignment (TOOD-style) top-K anchor selection, which adds hyperparameters (α, β, K, λ_iou, λ_dfl, λ_cls, λ_assoc); the association loss's ablations show clear degradation when multi-scale offsets or task alignment are removed; on the single-part CrowdHuman face-body task its advantage over the anchor-based BPJDet is less pronounced; and its formulation assumes parts are inside body boxes, so heavily occluded/outside parts may still challenge the one-to-one association.
> 
> **Practical takeaways for your stated interests:** For regularization under cross-entropy/contrastive training, the simplex-ETF optimum (paper 1) is the shared structure behind both InfoNCE and neural collapse under cross-entropy, and LDReg (doc `51526068`) offers a geometric regularizer against collapse. For optimizer choice, the Hessian paper (`582d138d`) shows power-law sharpness correlates with generalization across SGD/Adam/AdamW on CIFAR/MNIST (practical for picking optimizers), while paper 3's 4-bit AdamW gives concrete GPU-memory savings (up to ~57.7%) that can be combined with LoRA, gradient checkpointing, activation compression, sharding, or offloading to keep GPU memory low.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below are the development defects and practical limitations explicitly reported or directly supported by the five referenced methods. Each item cites the concrete failure modes, sensitivities, or scope limits described in the papers themselves.
> 
> 1) PBADet (One‑stage, anchor‑free part–body association; ICLR 2024)
> - Advantage diminishes on single‑part association: On CrowdHuman (face–body is a single part), PBADet’s superiority over BPJDet is “not as pronounced” as in multi‑part settings; mMR−2 remains around ~50 (Tables 5–6), i.e., mismatches are still non‑trivial.
> - Training sensitivity to specific components: Ablations show the method relies on task‑alignment learning, multi‑scale supervision, and the association loss; removing these reduces conditional accuracy and joint AP (Table 4). This makes training more fragile to hyperparameter/branch choices (e.g., K, α, β for alignment; λ weights; scaling λ for offsets).
> - Dataset‑specific tuning and thresholds: Different NMS thresholds are required per dataset (BodyHands vs. COCOHumanParts vs. CrowdHuman), indicating non‑portable hyperparameters and added tuning effort.
> - High input resolution and compute: Experiments run at 1024×1024 or 1536×1536 with multi‑GPU (4×V100) and 100 epochs, which can be burdensome for real‑time deployment—even though the detector head is one‑stage.
> 
> 2) ColEI and DANN recurrent networks under Dale’s Law (NeurIPS 2023)
> - ColEI (column‑wise sign‑constrained) recurrent nets learn poorly by default: They exhibit multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra with large modes, causing exploding/vanishing directions, poor task performance, higher seed‑to‑seed variance, and strong instability without gradient clipping.
> - Small networks and realistic E:I ratios exacerbate failures: With fewer inhibitory units or small widths, spectra worsen (lower normalized SVD entropy), learning deteriorates, and training becomes less stable; performance becomes very sensitive to both EI ratio and network size.
> - Sign constraints alone don’t explain all failures: Even when sign constraints are lifted/added, most of the performance gap stems from spectral pathologies, implying basic ColEI design requires nontrivial spectrum control to learn well.
> - Dependence on careful initialization and clipping: ColEI training needs gradient clipping and spectral‑radius control; without them, training is highly unstable. This reduces robustness in practical development.
> - Scope limits of the analysis and model variants: Results rely on specific initializations and tasks (adding problem, sequential MNIST, PTB); theoretical questions remain open (origin of multimodal spectra; why large ColEI can work despite large max singular values). DANNs perform well but model only particular inhibitory circuitry (e.g., fast PV+) and omit other biological details (e.g., I→I connectivity) noted as future work.
> 
> 3) JEPA vs. MAE in deep linear self‑distillation (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Depth‑dependent bias can be undesirable: JEPA’s beneficial bias toward high‑influence (high regression‑coefficient) features grows with depth; for shallow encoders the bias weakens, limiting gains in small models. Conversely, JEPA may over‑prioritize “slow” or spurious features, potentially ignoring high‑variance but informative signals.
> - Theoretical scope constraints: Results require deep linear encoders, small initialization, special balancing, and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances; authors explicitly caution that generalization to nonlinear networks and realistic, non‑diagonalizable data is unproven.
> - Task/data‑model gap: Although JEPA avoids noisy features in the linear setting, the paper notes it remains unknown how fully these dynamics carry over to practical settings—highlighting a development risk if one assumes the same bias in real, nonlinear training.
> 
> 4) 4‑bit optimizers with rank‑1 normalization and zero‑point removal (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Hard failure mode (second moment zero‑point): Using standard dynamic‑exponent mapping that includes zero causes many second‑moment entries to quantize to zero; because updates scale with 1/√v̂, this produces catastrophic deviations and training instability. Smaller block sizes or stochastic rounding do not fix this; the zero point must be excluded (DE‑0 or linear mapping) to stabilize training (Table 1, Fig. 3 & Appendix C.1).
> - Sensitivity to quantization settings and outlier patterns: First/second moments exhibit heterogeneous outlier structures (row/column‑persistent, layer‑dependent), making large blocks (e.g., 2048) inaccurate; the method needs smaller blocks (e.g., 128) and/or rank‑1 normalization to avoid quality loss. This increases engineering complexity and per‑tensor decisions.
> - Stable Embedding layers only partially address instability: They can reduce instability in some settings but do not fully retain accuracy when the zero‑point issue persists; correct second‑moment mapping is still required (Table 1).
> - Throughput not always better without fused ops: For smaller models (e.g., RoBERTa‑Large, GPT‑2 Medium), the unfused 4‑bit implementation can be slower than 8‑bit until fused kernels are used (Table 4), reducing plug‑and‑play efficiency benefits.
> - Task scope and tuning overhead: Authors note optimal quantization choices may be task/dataset‑dependent; evaluation is limited to vision and language tasks, leaving RL/audio/graph applicability untested. This implies extra tuning/validation cost for new domains.
> 
> 5) Contrastive learning under cosine‑similarity analysis (ICML 2025) and the variance‑reduction auxiliary loss
> - Excessive negative separation and misalignment with certain losses: For independently additive losses that exclude within‑view negatives (e.g., Sigmoid‑based with (c1,c2)=(1,0)), specific hyperparameter regimes (e.g., small bias b) can push negative similarities below −1/(n−1); this prevents perfect positive alignment even at the full‑batch optimum (“excessive separation”), a structural defect of that loss class unless within‑view negatives are included.
> - Mini‑batch pathology: Small batches provably increase the variance of negative‑pair similarities; for InfoNCE, the gradient that pushes negatives apart grows as batch size shrinks. This explains frequent small‑batch degradation and is not present in full‑batch settings.
> - Auxiliary variance‑reduction loss has caveats: While it reduces this variance and improves accuracy in small‑batch regimes, the paper warns it may also suppress semantically meaningful variance in the data, has reduced impact at large batch sizes, and adds a new hyperparameter (λ) that requires tuning.
> - Temperature sensitivity remains: Baseline contrastive methods are sensitive to the loss temperature; although the variance‑reduction term improves robustness across temperatures, the underlying temperature dependence still needs attention and tuning.
> 
> Overall integration for the target HMI scenario
> - Cosine‑similarity and temperature (contrastive pretraining): The CL analysis shows that small batches amplify negative‑similarity variance and temperature sensitivity, degrading representation quality; eliminating within‑view negatives can also cause excessive separation. These are concrete defects to avoid when training under limited GPU/batch budgets.
> - Memory‑efficient end‑to‑end LoRA fine‑tuning: The 4‑bit optimizers reduce optimizer‑state memory but can fail without correct second‑moment mapping (zero‑point removal) and may require fused kernels to avoid speed regressions; quantization hyperparameters are task‑dependent and outlier‑pattern‑sensitive, implying extra tuning during LoRA/Transformer fine‑tuning.
> - Anchor‑free, one‑stage part–body association: PBADet reduces pipeline complexity but still needs high‑res inputs, dataset‑specific thresholds, task‑alignment hyperparameters, and shows only modest gains in single‑part cases, with non‑negligible residual association errors (mMR−2 ~50 on CrowdHuman).

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Recommended works
> 
> 1. **"On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning"** — explains cosine-similarity geometry and temperature in contrastive losses (InfoNCE/SigLIP/SimCLR): optimal embeddings align positives (similarity 1) and spread negatives uniformly at −1/(n−1); temperature shapes the similarity distribution and robustness. In mini-batch settings, **smaller batches induce higher variance of negative-pair similarities ("excessive separation")**, degrading representation quality — it proposes an auxiliary variance-reduction loss and shows it stabilizes performance across temperatures.
> 2. **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks"** — JEPA is biased to learn **high-influence features** (large regression coefficient ρ) rather than high-variance features, steering away from the top-variance subspace toward the semantically rich, low-variance subspace; MAE is mostly agnostic to this. This bias only holds with **deep encoders**.
> 3. **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** — 4-bit AdamW / 4-bit Factor quantize optimizer states (smaller block size, zero-point-excluding linear quantizer, rank-1 normalization, factorized second moment), cutting memory up to ~57.7% (e.g., LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU) while matching 32-bit AdamW on fine-tuning of transformers (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2, LLaMA), combinable with LoRA-style low-rank adaptation.
> 4. **PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association** — extends anchor-free detection with a **single part-to-body center offset**, giving one-to-one part↔body correspondence for hands/face in crowded scenes (BodyHands, CrowdHuman face-body) with compact compute (YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones).
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods
> 
> **Contrastive mini-batch analysis:**
> - The variance-reduction loss can **suppress semantically meaningful variance**, flattening informative structure between instances.
> - Gain **diminishes with large batches**; adds a **sensitive λ hyperparameter**; temperature tuning is still needed in practice.
> - Positive-pair perfect alignment is **unattainable** when negative similarity falls below the threshold −1/(n−1) (inherent alignment–separation trade-off).
> 
> **JEPA bias analysis:**
> - JEPA objective is **susceptible to representation collapse** (trivially minimized by constant output), requiring stop-grad/architectural tricks.
> - The bias toward predictive, low-variance features may explain **vulnerability to spurious or slow features**.
> - The analysis is restricted to **deep linear networks, special balanced orthogonal initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable data**; generalization to nonlinear models is not proven, and the bias **largely disappears with shallow encoders**.
> 
> **4-bit optimizers:**
> - Quantizing both first and second moments causes a **marginal accuracy drop** (e.g., CLS 81.2→80.8, MT 26.61→26.28).
> - **Optimal quantization scheme may be task-dependent**; only language/vision tasks were validated.
> - Without fused operators, 4-bit versions can be **slower than 8-bit AdamW** on smaller models (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2 Medium).
> - Second-moment quantization suffers a **zero-point problem** and moment outlier patterns that block-wise quantization cannot approximate well.
> 
> **PBADet:**
> - On the **single-part face-body task (CrowdHuman), its advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced** (competitive AP, though better MR-2).
> - Performance depends on its **association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and task-alignment learning** — ablations show metrics decline when any is removed (e.g., normalized absolute offset without multi-scale).
> - Inherits anchor-free dense-inference cost (per-pixel heads) and multi-scale feature-map handling, which still needs tuning under tight compute budgets; the part-to-body center offset assumes a detectable parent body, and occluded/truncated bodies can weaken association ground truth.
