> 1. **Mini-batch contrastive behavior + cosine similarity/temperature** — *On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning*: full-batch optimal encoders give positive-pair similarity 1 and negative-pair similarity −1/(n−1); temperature shapes the similarity distribution. In mini-batch settings, smaller batches increase the variance of negative-pair similarities ("excessive separation"), degrading representations; an auxiliary variance-reduction loss (with a temperature-robustness benefit) is proposed.
> 2. **JEPA's feature bias** — *Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features (Deep Linear Network Analysis)*: JEPA is implicitly biased to learn high-influence (high regression-coefficient) features and suppresses noisy ones, unlike MAE; the bias strengthens with encoder depth; JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features.
> 3. **4-bit optimizer states + low-rank adapters** — *4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States*: quantizes Adam/AdamW first/second moments to 4-bit (smaller block size, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer, rank-1 normalization, factorization), matching 32-bit accuracy on RoBERTa-L, Swin-T, GPT-2, Transformer, and LLaMA fine-tuning (including LoRA-based pipelines), with up to ~57.7% memory savings.
> 4. **Anchor-free one-stage part–body association** — *PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association*: a single part-to-body center offset on multi-scale feature maps links hands/face to bodies in one stage (YOLOv5/v7 backbones), handling multi-part association and crowded scenes (CrowdHuman face-body), suitable for tight compute budgets.
> 
> **Development defects of these methods**
> - **Contrastive-learning analysis**: the proposed variance-reduction loss can suppress not only mini-batch-induced variance but also variance that encodes meaningful data structure; it adds a hyperparameter λ; perfect positive alignment is unattainable when negative-pair similarity falls below the threshold; small batches inherently cause the excessive negative-pair separation.
> - **JEPA analysis**: theory is restricted to deep *linear* networks, balanced orthogonal initialization, and simultaneous diagonalizability; qualitative claims only supported by experiments; the JEPA objective itself is susceptible to trivial (collapse) solutions, requiring stop-gradients/architectural tricks, and JEPA still learns noisy features (just more slowly and with lower amplitude weights).
> - **4-bit optimizer**: quantization of both moments still causes a marginal accuracy drop; optimal quantization may be task-dependent; only language and vision tasks were tested; small-model runs are slower without fused operators; total memory savings saturate as bitwidth decreases, and the 4-bit Factor variant trades some accuracy.
> - **PBADet**: on COCOHumanParts its APs are only on par with BPJDet (leads mainly on person/feet metrics); on the single-part CrowdHuman face-body task its advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced; performance depends on the association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and task-alignment learning (removing any degrades results); anchor-free formulation relies on dense per-pixel prediction, which can be costly at high resolution.

</details>

<a id="case-paperscope-gap-109"></a>

### paperscope:gap:109 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively advance efficient and robust deep learning across: (1) one-stage, anchor-free part–body association; (2) spectral analysis of excitatory–inhibitory constrained recurrent nets under biological sign rules; (3) joint-embedding self-distillation in self-supervised learning that prioritizes influential features over noisy pixel reconstruction (contrasting cosine metrics with mean-squared error and cross-entropy); (4) memory-efficient training via low-bit (around 4-bit) optimizer states for Transformers/ResNet-50 with end-to-end LoRA-style fine-tuning; and (5) linear-time independence testing using learned Fourier feature embeddings. I care about practical runtime near O(n) in sample size, feature embeddings, and evaluation with F1/Precision.Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

**score：2→3（Δ+1）；rounds：4→3（Δ-1）。**

Gold 1：

> {'answer': "- PBADet (one-stage, anchor-free part–body association)\n  - Advantage is less pronounced when only a single part is annotated: on CrowdHuman (face–body only), authors note their gains over BPJDet are “not as pronounced” as in multi-part settings, since PBADet’s scalability benefit shows mainly when multiple parts exist.\n  - Dataset- and task-specific tuning required: inference depends on carefully chosen NMS thresholds that differ per dataset; training uses many hyperparameters (λiou, λdfl, λcls, λassoc, K, α, β, λ scaling), making deployment sensitive to settings.\n  - Computational cost: strong results rely on high-resolution inputs (e.g., 1024×1024, 1536×1536), pretrained YOLO backbones, and multi-GPU training, which raises training cost for practical adoption.\n  - Decoding choice can be brittle in very crowded scenes: association is resolved by nearest predicted body center among bodies that enclose the part; the paper shows success cases but also indicates that in crowded face–body scenarios benefits over BPJDet shrink, hinting remaining ambiguity in close-proximity cases.\n\n- EI-constrained RNNs under Dale’s Law (ColEI and DANN recurrent networks)\n  - ColEI (column-sign constrained) defects:\n    - Poor learning due to spectral pathology at initialization: multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra (with large modes) cause exploding/vanishing dynamics; performance lags standard RNNs and DANNs across tasks.\n    - High sensitivity to network size and E/I ratio: small networks and fewer inhibitory units degrade spectra (lower normalized SVD entropy) and hurt learning; greater variance across seeds.\n    - Training instability: markedly benefits from gradient clipping; without it, training can be highly unstable.\n    - Performance is better only at larger spectral radii, but still inferior to well-initialized baselines; no single ρ fixes the core issue.\n  - DANN (reparameterized EI) limitations:\n    - Still requires sign constraints (non-negative submatrices) with projection after updates; spectrum quality explains much of the gains, but sign constraints alone remain a mild detractor (authors measure small performance drops).\n    - Biological scope is limited: as discussed, DANNs naturally model fast PV+ interneurons and lack I→I connections and cell-type-specific time constants; extensions are needed for broader biological fidelity.\n    - Depend on spectral properties at initialization; careful initialization choices (and analysis via NSE) are key to good results.\n\n- Joint-Embedding Self-Distillation (JEPA) vs. MAE (deep linear analysis)\n  - Scope limitations of theory: results rely on deep linear models, special “balanced” initializations, and simultaneously diagonalizable covariance/correlation (Σxx, Σxy), limiting direct transfer to non-linear encoders and general real-world data.\n  - Depth dependence: JEPA’s desirable bias (prioritizing influential features via regression coefficients) becomes strong only with deeper encoders; for shallow encoders the effect diminishes substantially.\n  - Risk of bias to spurious/slow features: authors note JEPA’s focus on predictive, low-variance (often slowly varying) features could make it vulnerable to spurious or slow signals in practice.\n  - Empirical setting coverage: demonstrations are primarily synthetic/linear; broader validation in complex, non-diagonalizable and non-linear regimes remains open (acknowledged by authors).\n\n- 4-bit optimizer states (memory-efficient training for Transformers/ResNet-50 with end-to-end fine-tuning/LoRA)\n  - Runtime overheads without fused kernels: for smaller models, 4-bit optimizers can be slower than 8-bit (authors attribute to lack of fused operators; their fused version recovers speed, but this adds engineering dependence).\n  - Task- and data-dependence of quantization settings: optimal block size, mapping (DE-0 vs. Linear), and normalization (block-wise vs. rank-1) depend on outlier patterns that vary across layers/models; rank-1 can underperform block-wise in certain local multimodal cases (shown in appendices).\n  - Zero-point pitfall for second moments: naive low-bit quantization can collapse many entries to zero and destabilize updates; careful zero-excluding mappings are mandatory (increasing implementation complexity and sensitivity).\n  - Memory savings can appear to saturate in end-to-end training: total memory is dominated by activations/other buffers, so optimizer compression alone yields limited visible reduction in “total” footprint (authors’ tables show this effect), especially if other memory optimizations aren’t used.\n  - Reported scope: evaluations cover vision and language (Transformers/Swin/ResNet-50, LLaMA finetuning); RL, audio, and graph tasks are not evaluated (acknowledged limitation).\n\n- LFHSIC: Linear-time independence testing with learned Fourier feature embeddings\n  - Power–sample trade-off depends on D and dimensionality: although the statistic is O(nD(dx+dy+D)), increasing D (random Fourier features) raises compute; insufficient D lowers power, especially in high dimensions.\n  - Type I error control uses data splitting in continuous kernel-parameter learning: authors explicitly note continuous adaptation needs sample splitting (they use a 0.5 split), reducing sample efficiency; controlling Type I errors without splitting remains open.\n  - Threshold via gamma approximation: avoids expensive permutations, but relies on moment estimates and asymptotic approximation; approximation error may affect small-sample calibration.\n  - Restricted, smooth function classes and initialization: to curb overfitting and enable differentiable training, the method uses smooth, parameterized transforms (e.g., Gaussian/Mahalanobis); while practical and interpretable, they limit expressiveness vs. fully flexible models.\n  - Dataset-/setting-specific tuning: performance is sensitive to D, learning rate/steps, and frequency sampling; authors choose D and use different computational backends (CPU/GPU) depending on scale; gains require this tuning.\n"}

**naive 最终答案**

> Here are the five papers found and their development defects (limitations) as stated in the documents:
> 
> **1. PBADet (one-stage, anchor-free part–body association)** — PBADet outperforms BPJDet on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts and beats ED-Pose on hand/foot precision-recall-F1, but: its advantage over BPJDet is *less pronounced* on the single-part CrowhHuman face–body task; decoding depends on NMS thresholds plus greedy Euclidean nearest "enclosing unassigned body" matching, so association can fail when a part's body is missed or doesn't enclose it (crowded/occluded scenes); and multi-person pose estimators don't supply part boxes, which PBADet needs.
> 
> **2. EI-constrained RNN spectral analysis (Dale's Law)** — The constrained "ColEI" recurrent nets are shown to be defective: the column-mean rank-one nilpotent term yields a multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectrum (vs. unimodal random-matrix spectra for standard/DANN RNNs), which impairs learning more than the sign constraints themselves (sign constraints alone cost ~1% accuracy). Concretely: poor learning for small networks or few inhibitory units, high variance across initializations, and instability without gradient clipping. Normalized SVD entropy is proposed only as a diagnostic (NSE anti-correlates with error); no fix is given for ColEI spectra.
> 
> **3. Joint-embedding self-distillation (JEPA) analysis** — The theory is restricted to deep *linear* MLPs with constrained initialization and *simultaneously diagonalizable* covariances Σyx/Σxx, which real data distributions violate; generalizability to nonlinear models and practical settings is unexplored. JEPA objectives are susceptible to representation collapse (relying on StopGrad/non-contrastive tricks), and at large depth the encoder becomes low-rank until a single dominating eigenvalue remains. The paper flags JEPA's vulnerability to spurious/slow features. Note: the retrieved paper analyzes MSE-style latent prediction vs. pixel reconstruction; it does not explicitly contrast cosine metric vs. cross-entropy (that specific comparison isn't in the context).
> 
> **4. 4-bit optimizer states** — Defects/limitations: the optimal quantization settings appear task-dependent and only language/vision tasks were tested; without fused operators the 4-bit optimizers were *slower* than 8-bit ones; memory savings saturate as bitwidth drops (reported total memory includes activations/fragments). Crucially for your ask, coverage is a mismatch: experiments use Swin-T, Transformer-Base, RoBERTa-L, GPT-2, and LLaMA fine-tuning — *not ResNet-50*, and LoRA is only mentioned as related work, not evaluated end-to-end with 4-bit states on ResNet-50. That claimed capability cannot be established from this document.
> 
> **5. Linear-time independence testing (LFHSIC, learned Fourier feature pairs)** — Achieves O(n) time/space, runs within ~10s on 100k samples, and controls Type I error ≤0.05, but the key defect is that Type-I-error control in the continuous case *requires data splitting* (training/testing split), and designing tests without sample splitting remains open future work. NFSIC-type competitors need large sample sizes; no single test dominates all settings; linear-time tests have relatively lower power than quadratic ones in some low-dimensional settings (LFHSIC-M being an exception); and power depends on the number of Fourier features D.
> 
> Note: F1/Precision appear only in paper 1 (vs. ED-Pose) and paper 4 (F1 for SQuAD QA); no F1/Precision evaluation is reported in papers 2, 3, or 5.

**community 最终答案**

> 五个方向的论文均已找到，逐一给出方法简介及其发展缺陷（以检索到的证据为准）：
> 
> **1. PBADet（ICLR 2024）— 单阶段、anchor-free 部件-身体关联**
> 方法：在 anchor-free 多尺度特征图上用"部件到身体中心偏移"建立一对一关联，用 F1/Precision/Recall 等评估。
> 发展缺陷：
> - 其动机正来自 BPJDet 的缺陷——anchor-based 的 body-to-part 偏移会随部件数增多使表示膨胀、且部件被遮挡时偏移失效；而 anchor-based 学习部件-身体偏移时"偏移可能落在预设 anchor box 之外"，难以训练。
> - 单部件任务（CrowdHuman 脸-身体关联）相对 BPJDet 优势不明显。
> - 扩展到四足动物的实验主要是定性展示可行性，量化支撑弱。
> 
> **2. "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"（NeurIPS 2023）— 生物符号约束 E/I 循环网络的光谱分析**
> 方法：分析满足 Dale 定律（兴奋/抑制符号约束）的 RNN，提出 ColEI 与 DANN 两种实现，用归一化 SVD 熵（NSE）诊断初始权值谱。
> 发展缺陷：
> - 简单列约束的 ColEI 网络学习差、方差高，其奇异值谱呈多峰、分散的"病态"分布（源于列均值秩 1 幂零结构），小网络和抑制单元过少时更差；
> - 无梯度裁剪时高度不稳定；符号约束本身也小幅损害学习（尽管谱性质影响更大）；
> - 需要 NSE 这种诊断量才能事前预测性能，且该度量与架构超参耦合。
> 
> **3. "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"（NeurIPS 2024）— 联合嵌入自蒸馏**
> 方法：理论分析 JEPA（在隐空间做自蒸馏）相对 MAE（像素重建）的隐式偏置，说明 JEPA 优先学习高影响（低噪声）特征。
> 发展缺陷（含与你描述的差异）：
> - 论文中对比的是"隐空间 MSE 预测 vs 像素空间 MSE 重建"，**并未**如问题所述对比 cosine / cross-entropy；
> - 理论严格限于深度线性 MLP、特殊初始化、协方差可同时对角化，推广到非线性/一般数据分布尚未证实；
> - JEPA 目标本身易塌缩，需 stop-grad 等技巧；且可能对虚假（spurious）/慢特征脆弱。
> 
> **4. "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"（NeurIPS 2023）— 约 4-bit 优化器状态**
> 方法：对一阶/二阶矩用小块、rank-1 归一化、去零点线性量化压缩到 4-bit，在 RoBERTa-L、Swin-T、GPT-2、Transformer、LLaMA 上接近 32-bit 精度，最高省 57.7% 内存。
> 发展缺陷（含与你描述的差异）：
> - 论文并非问题所述的"ResNet-50 + 端到端 LoRA 式微调"：视觉验证用的是 Swin-T/ImageNet 分类，LLM 用 LLaMA 全参微调，仅引用了 LoRA 库进行 GPT-2 微调；
> - 小模型上比 8-bit 慢（未做算子融合），内存节省随位宽降低趋于饱和；
> - 一阶、二阶同时量化仍有微小精度损失，最优量化方案可能依赖任务，且仅测试了语言和视觉任务。
> 
> **5. "Efficiently Learning Significant Fourier Feature Pairs for Statistical Independence Testing"（LFHSIC，NeurIPS 2024）— 线性时间独立性检验**
> 方法：频域重释 HSIC，学习可训练傅里叶特征对，以线性时间 O(n) 优化目标建模检验功效，用 γ 近似阈值，100k 样本 10 秒内完成检验。
> 发展缺陷：
> - 作者明确承认"没有任何一个检验在所有设置下占优"，实际需结合多个检验；
> - 连续情形依赖数据切分来控 Type I error，不切分的数据驱动方案仍是开放问题；
> - 学习目标需要足够样本才稳定准确（小样本方差大），且特征不可学习的 FHSIC 等基线灵活性与性能不足。
> 
> 总体看，这些方法的共同"开发缺陷"是：泛化验证有限（线性/特定初始化、特定数据集）、存在额外的诊断或调参负担（NSE、任务相关量化、数据切分）、以及与你目标设定（cosine vs MSE/cross-entropy 对比、ResNet-50+LoRA 端到端）不完全吻合——这些具体设定在对应论文中未被直接覆盖。

</details>

<a id="case-paperscope-gap-187"></a>

### paperscope:gap:187 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively cover: (a) one-stage, anchor-free human part↔person association on COCO-style benchmarks; (b) adaptive graph message passing that mitigates oversmoothing, oversquashing, and underreaching; (c) self-distillation (JEPA-like) representation learning that favors high-influence latent features over pixel-space MSE; (d) spectral analyses of RNNs that respect excitatory/inhibitory sign rules (Dale’s Law); and (e) memory-lean training with 4-bit optimizer states (for Adam/SGD) that still match CE/MSE, cosine-similarity-based embeddings, Precision/F1 during fine-tuning on datasets such as CIFAR-100 and COCO with Transformer/ResNet-50 or feedforward classifiers.Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

**score：4→3（Δ-1）；rounds：6→4（Δ-2）。**

<details>
<summary>展开完整 gold 与两份最终答案</summary>

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Development defects by method:
> 
> 1) PBADet (one-stage, anchor-free part↔body association)
> - Benefits depend on multi-part settings: the paper reports that on CrowdHuman (a single-part face↔body association task) PBADet’s advantage over BPJDet is “not as pronounced,” i.e., improvements shrink when there is only one part to associate (Appendix A.1, Table 5/6 and discussion).
> - Heavy reliance on many training/inference hyperparameters: task-alignment parameters (K, α, β), multiple loss weights (λiou, λdfl, λcls, λassoc), scale λ for offsets, and separate NMS thresholds per class/dataset are all tuned; performance is sensitive to these choices (Sec. 3.3–4.1). While not unique to PBADet, this increases development complexity.
> - Comparable detection accuracy rather than universal gains: on COCOHumanParts, PBADet often matches rather than strictly exceeds the strongest YOLO-based baseline in certain AP metrics, with gains concentrated in association metrics (Tables 2–3). This indicates improvements are uneven across metrics and categories.
> 
> 2) Adaptive Message Passing (AMP) for mitigating oversmoothing/oversquashing/underreaching
> - Added computational and parameter overhead: AMP introduces layer-wise readouts and per-layer filtering, increasing the cost from O(|V|) or O(1) to O(|V|L) for readouts and adding extra parameters (Sec. 3.1; Sec. 5.3: “non‑negligible cost in terms of number of readout parameters”).
> - New hyperparameters and modeling choices: performance depends on selecting and initializing a truncated distribution over depth q(L) (Poisson, folded normal, mixtures) and a filtering strategy (input- vs. embedding-based), adding design/tuning burden (Sec. 3, E, 5.4).
> - Improvements can require deeper/wider models: on long-range chemical benchmarks, authors find that deeper networks and larger hidden sizes correlate with good results; under strict parameter budgets, gains may diminish (Sec. 5.1–5.3). Thus, achieving the reported improvements can demand higher model capacity.
> - Sensitivity behavior is heterogeneous: while filtering can reduce oversquashing, measured sensitivity (Jacobians) did not exhibit a universally improving trend across datasets; the authors caution against relying on sensitivity alone as a performance proxy (Sec. 5.2). This complicates diagnostics and tuning.
> 
> 3) JEPA-like self-distillation (deep linear analysis of implicit bias)
> - Theory restricted to simplified settings: results are derived for deep linear encoders/decoders under special initializations and simultaneously-diagonalizable data covariances; generalization to nonlinear encoders, realistic data, and broader architectures remains open (Limitations, Sec. 6; Preliminaries).
> - Depth-dependent advantage: the JEPA bias toward high-influence features “takes hold only when the encoder is deep” and “diminishes substantially” for shallow encoders (Abstract; Sec. 2–3). This limits the benefit if depth is constrained.
> - Potential vulnerability to slow/spurious features: the authors note JEPA’s focus on predictive, low-variance (slow) features “may shed light on [its] vulnerability to spurious or slow features” (Discussion, Sec. 7). In some regimes JEPA may underweight highly covarying yet informative features that MAE learns earlier (Sec. 2–3.2).
> 
> 4) Learning with Dale’s Law (ColEI vs. recurrent DANNs; spectral analysis)
> - Column EI (ColEI) partitions learn poorly and are unstable: ColEI yields multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra with large outlier modes, causing impaired learning and high variance across seeds; small networks and realistic E:I ratios exacerbate this; gradient clipping is often required (Sec. 3.1–3.4; Fig. 2, 3; App. Fig. 10).
> - Sensitivity to spectral radius and EI ratio: ColEI performance depends strongly on spectral radius ρ and E/I proportions—smaller networks or fewer inhibitory units worsen spectra and performance (Sec. 3.1, 3.4; Fig. 5–6). This increases tuning burden and reduces robustness.
> - Open theoretical gaps: the origin of ColEI’s unusual multimodal spectra and why large ColEI networks learn well despite large maximum singular values remain open questions (Discussion, Sec. 4). This limits principled design guidance for EI RNNs.
> - Biological fidelity limits in the presented DANNs: current recurrent DANNs omit inhibitory→inhibitory connections and cell-type specific time constants; thus they model specific fast PV+ interneuron circuitry rather than the full diversity of inhibitory cell types (Discussion, Sec. 4). This constrains biological realism and task fidelity.
> 
> 5) Memory-lean 4-bit optimizers (Adam/SGD states)
> - Zero-point failure mode for second moments: naive dynamic-exponent (DE) quantization pushes many v entries to zero, causing catastrophic update scaling (1/√v) and training instability; specialized mappings that exclude zero (DE‑0) or linear mapping are required (Sec. 4.1; Fig. 3; Tab. 1). This adds design constraints and failure cases if misconfigured.
> - Task/dataset-specific quantization settings: the authors note the “optimal quantization setting probably depends on task, datasets, and training details,” requiring choice among block size, rank‑1 normalization, mapping, and factorization. Broad applicability beyond vision/NLP (e.g., RL, audio, graphs) is untested (Limitations, Sec. 7).
> - Runtime overhead without fused kernels: for smaller models, 4‑bit optimizers can be slower than 8‑bit until fused implementations are used; speedups rely on fused ops and offloading scenarios (Tab. 4). This complicates practical deployment.
> - Factorization coverage limits: second-moment factorization applies only to tensors with dimension ≥2; 1D states must still be quantized, limiting maximum memory reduction (Sec. 4.3; D.1).
> - Accuracy is “comparable,” not universally lossless in pretraining: on some pretraining tasks (e.g., Swin-T ImageNet, WMT14), 4‑bit results are comparable but not strictly superior to 32‑bit/8‑bit baselines (Tab. 2, 4). Achieving parity may require careful mapping/normalization choices.
> 
> Overall: Across the five methods, the main development risks stem from (i) added computation/parameter overhead (AMP, PBADet hyperparameters), (ii) brittle or task-specific configurations (4‑bit mapping/normalization; AMP depth distributions), (iii) theory restricted to simplified regimes (JEPA linear analysis), and (iv) instability or sensitivity to spectra/ratios (ColEI under Dale’s Law). Each paper documents these constraints or open questions explicitly in its analysis, results, or limitations.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved collection, the five topics map to these papers:
> 
> (a) **PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association** (doc `08b70bc…`) — part↔body association via a single part-to-body center offset, evaluated on COCOHumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman.
> (b) **Adaptive Message Passing (AMP)** (doc `ef5f74e…`) — variational learning of message-passing depth and per-layer message filtering to mitigate oversmoothing, oversquashing, underreaching.
> (c) **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation** (doc `40fde03…`) — shows JEPA self-distillation prioritizes high-influence (large regression coefficient) latent features over pixel-space reconstruction (MAE).
> (d) **Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective** (doc `e63a94c…`) — spectral analysis of RNNs with excitatory/inhibitory sign constraints (ColEI vs. DANN), normalised SVD entropy.
> (e) **Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States** (doc `8d5e145…`) — 4-bit quantized first/second moments (B128, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear mapping, factorization) for Adam/AdamW matching 32-bit on fine-tuning tasks.
> 
> **Development defects / limitations:**
> 
> (a) **PBADet**: Per-category `mMR−2` on COCOHumanParts is *worse* than BPJDet for head/left-hand/right-hand/feet in several configurations (e.g., Ours-YOLOv7 41.1/42.7 vs BPJDet 50.2/51.4), and the YOLOv7 version uses more parameters (36.9M) than BPJDet-YOLOv5s6 (15.3M). Its advantage over BPJDet is "less pronounced" for the single-part (face-body) CrowdHuman task, and the association mechanism assumes a part's box lies inside its body box, making it fragile when parts are occluded or extend outside the body box.
> 
> (b) **AMP**: The learned-soft-filter approach applies filtering to *all* messages, which can add computational burden; it relies on variational inference with prior choices (Poisson/folded-normal/mixtures) and optional regularizers that introduce extra hyperparameters. Gains are demonstrated as improvements over base GNNs (GCN/GINE/GatedGCN/ADGN) rather than absolute state-of-the-art, and ablations show fixing depth to AMP's learned range does not improve performance — i.e., the learned depth/filtering is essential but costly.
> 
> (c) **JEPA paper**: Analysis is restricted to deep *linear* MLPs, special initialization, and *simultaneously diagonalizable* covariances Σyx/Σxx — assumptions the authors expect real data to violate. The distinct bias only appears for deep encoders and diminishes when the encoder is shallow. Non-linear models are unanalyzed, and JEPA's implicit bias may make it *vulnerable to spurious or slow features*.
> 
> (d) **Dale's Law RNNs**: ColEI networks learn worse with higher variance across seeds, are highly unstable without gradient clipping, and suffer multimodal/dispersed singular-value spectra with a large-singular-value mode (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure); small networks with few inhibitory units are worst. Sign constraints still independently impair learning (~0.7–1% error), and open questions remain (origin of the multimodal spectrum; why large ColEI learn well despite large σmax; only E→I partitioning studied, no I→I connections or cell-type-specific time constants).
> 
> (e) **4-bit optimizers**: Explicit limitations — the optimal quantization setting is task/data-dependent, and only language and vision tasks were tested (RL, audio, graph learning unverified); quantizing both moments causes a *marginal accuracy drop*; unfused 4-bit AdamW is *slower* than 8-bit AdamW on smaller models (RoBERTa-L 5.59 min vs 3.38 min; GPT-2M 2.43 h vs 2.04 h). Additionally, the user's description (CIFAR-100, COCO, ResNet-50, cosine-similarity embeddings, CE/MSE, feedforward classifiers, SGD) **does not match** this paper's actual evaluation: it uses Swin-T on ImageNet-1k, RoBERTa-L/GPT-2/Transformer/LLaMA fine-tuning (GLUE accuracy/correlation, SQuAD F1, BLEU, SacreBLEU); it covers AdamW (SGDM only in the framework/proofs), and no CIFAR-100/COCO/ResNet-50/cosine-embedding or CE/MSE results are reported — so those coverage claims are not supported by this document.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved documents, the five papers are:
> 
> **(a) PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association Detection** (doc `08b70bc3…`)
> **(b) Adaptive Message Passing (AMP)** (doc `ef5f74ee…`)
> **(c) How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation** (doc `40fde037…`)
> **(d) Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective** (doc `e63a94c4…`)
> **(e) Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States** (doc `8d5e1455…`)
> 
> Note on (e): this paper matches the 4-bit Adam/AdamW optimizer-state requirement (matching accuracy and F1 on RoBERTa/GLUE, Swin-T/ImageNet, GPT-2, Transformer WMT, LLaMA fine-tuning). However, the specific claims in your request about CIFAR-100/COCO, ResNet-50, cosine-similarity-based embeddings, MSE losses, or feedforward classifiers are **not supported** by the retrieved context; only language/vision benchmarks (NLU accuracy/correlation, CLS accuracy, BLEU, QA F1, SacreBleu) are evidenced.
> 
> **Development defects / limitations per the context:**
> 
> **(a) PBADet**
> - Its advantage over prior methods is less pronounced on single-part tasks (CrowdHuman face-body), where it is competitive but not clearly superior to BPJDet.
> - Performance depends on all design choices: ablations show dropping the association loss, using non-multi-scale center offsets, or removing task-alignment learning all degrade metrics; anchor-based backbones and body-to-part definitions underperform its anchor-free part-to-body design.
> 
> **(b) AMP**
> - It applies a learned (soft) filter to *all* existing messages and jointly learns depth via variational inference, which is more complex than fixed-depth architectures; the "right" depth/filtering must be learned per task rather than assumed.
> - The mitigation guarantee is asymptotic: a differentiable sigmoidal activation cannot propagate exactly the same value, only in the limit ϵ→0.
> - It avoids graph rewiring but does not impose strong inductive biases; whether learned message filtering is always preferable (vs. backtracking-avoidance or rewiring) remains an open question, and attention-style filters can add severe computational burden.
> 
> **(c) JEPA self-distillation analysis**
> - Results are limited to deep *linear* networks, special balanced-orthogonal initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable data; generalization to non-linear models/non-diagonalizable distributions is not proven.
> - The high-influence/low-variance bias appears only with deep encoders and diminishes for shallow ones.
> - The same bias that suppresses noisy features may make JEPA vulnerable to spurious or "slow" features, and noisy features are still learned (just with lower amplitude), so it is not a guaranteed cure.
> 
> **(d) Dale's-Law RNN spectral analysis**
> - Sign-constrained ColEI RNNs learn worse and with much higher variance across seeds; without gradient clipping they are highly unstable.
> - The root defect is spectral: column-mean rank-one nilpotent structure yields multimodal, dispersed singular values (pathology measured by NSE), which worsens for small networks and low inhibitory-unit ratios; spectral properties matter more than the sign constraints themselves.
> - Open theoretical questions remain (origin of multimodal spectra; why large ColEI networks train well despite a large maximal singular value), and the models are not fully biologically faithful (e.g., DANN lacks inhibitory-to-inhibitory connections, no cell-type time constants).
> 
> **(e) 4-bit optimizer states**
> - Quantizing both first and second moments causes a small accuracy drop; only a smaller block size (B128) plus rank-1 normalization and zero-point-excluded linear quantization recover near-lossless performance.
> - The optimal quantization appears task-dependent, and only language/vision tasks were tested.
> - On small models (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2) the unfused implementation is *slower* than 8-bit AdamW (speed only improves with fused operators / reduced communication); sublinear-memory optimizers (Adafactor, SM3) are more memory-efficient but suffer performance degradation, especially on image classification.

Gold 1：

> {'answer': 'Below are the main development defects and limitations, method by method, drawn only from the provided papers.\n\nPBADet (ICLR 2024)\n- Benefits are task-dependent and diminish on single-part association: On CrowdHuman’s face–body (single-part) association, the authors explicitly note “the advantages of our method over BPJDet are not as pronounced” (A.1). \n- Not uniformly superior across categories/metrics: On COCOHumanParts, PBADet is “on par” with BPJDet in overall APs, and per-part association errors (mMR−2) are not consistently lower for every part (e.g., YOLOv7 right-hand worse than BPJDet; Table 3). \n- Heavy reliance on many training/inference hyperparameters: The approach requires tuning multiple task-alignment and NMS thresholds (λiou, λdfl, λcls, λassoc; λ; K, α, β; τconf, τiou), which increases setup complexity (Sec. 3.3–3.4, 4.1). \n\nLearning with Dale’s Law (NeurIPS 2023)\n- Strong modeling/initialization assumptions: Core analyses and performance claims rely on special initializations (orthogonal/balanced weights) and projected gradient updates to enforce signs; empirical insights may not directly transfer to typical initializations (Sec. 2.2, 3.1). \n- Data distribution simplifications: Key results assume simultaneously diagonalizable Σxx and Σxy and use synthetic/temporal linear generative models; authors acknowledge generalization to realistic, non-simultaneously-diagonalizable data is untested (Sec. 2.3.2, Limitations in Discussion). \n- Biological scope incomplete: DANN RNNs omit biologically relevant features (e.g., inhibitory–inhibitory connections, cell-type-specific time constants), and hybridizing ColEI and DANNs is left to future work (Discussion). \n\nJEPA implicit bias (NeurIPS 2024)\n- Theoretical scope restricted: Results are derived for deep linear networks under small initialization and gradient-flow dynamics; extension to non-linear encoders and practical training regimes remains open (Limitations). \n- Strong covariance assumptions: Analyses often require Σxx and Σxy to be simultaneously diagonalizable; authors note real data likely violates this, limiting direct applicability (Limitations). \n- Bias toward “influential/slow” features: JEPA prioritizes features with large regression coefficients and tends to focus on slow/low-variance directions; authors caution this may make JEPA vulnerable to spurious/slow features and neglect highly covarying high-variance (potentially noisy) features (Discussion, Sec. 3.2–4.1). \n\n4-bit Optimizers (NeurIPS 2023)\n- Instability with naïve 4-bit quantization: Using dynamic exponent (DE) mapping with zero-point at 4-bit caused frequent training instabilities (e.g., 33–66% unstable runs on GPT-2/E2E-NLG); stability required removing the zero point or switching to linear mapping (Table 1). \n- Performance/throughput gaps without kernel fusion: For smaller models, 4-bit optimizers were slower than 8-bit baselines until fused operators were used; speed currently depends on implementation maturity (Tab. 4). \n- Task-dependent quantization design: Authors state the “optimal quantization setting depends on task, datasets, and training details”; rank‑1 normalization/linear mapping were robust in reported tasks, but may not universally yield lossless performance (Limitations). \n- Scope limited to vision/language: Evaluation excludes reinforcement learning, audio, and graph learning; applicability to these domains remains to be studied (Limitations). \n- Factorization benefits are situational: Second-moment factorization cannot be applied in some sharded settings (e.g., FSDP packing of parameters), limiting memory gains (Sec. D.2, LLaMA setup). \n- Apparent memory savings saturation: Reported total GPU memory savings may “saturate” when activations dominate footprint, so optimizer-state compression does not proportionally reduce end-to-end memory (Tab. 4 note). \n\nAdaptive Message Passing (ICML 2025)\n- Additional computational overhead: Filtering is O(|V|), but AMP’s layer-wise readouts add O(|V|L) cost and “non-negligible” parameter overhead versus single-readout MPNNs (Sec. 3.1). \n- More parameters/depth often required: On long-range chemical tasks, AMP frequently learns deeper models; the authors note parameter budgets used in prior work “might limit progress,” but AMP’s deeper networks increase training/inference cost (Sec. 5.1, 5.3). \n- Variational family selection remains a hyper-parameter: Choosing/truncating q(L) (e.g., Poisson, folded normal, mixtures) and its initialization still requires manual selection; while believed to have smaller effect, it is an extra design step (Practical Considerations, Sec. B). \n- Filtering choice is empirical and not universally beneficial: Input-based vs embedding-based filters improve results in most but not all cases; ablations show some points with no gains (“grey area”), so filter type must be tuned per task (Fig. 5). \n- Sensitivity is not a reliable single metric: Authors show heterogeneous sensitivity profiles and caution that reducing sensitivity via filtering can still improve outcomes, implying standard sensitivity-based diagnostics may misjudge oversquashing mitigation (Sec. 5.2, Theorem 3.1). \n- Dynamic depth maintenance complexity: Growing/shrinking nets as q(L)’s support changes (retaining excess layers) introduces engineering and memory management complexity (Practical Considerations).'}

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Works that address the needs
> 
> **1. Hand/face→person linking in crowded COCO-like scenes: PBADet** (one-stage anchor-free part-body association)
> - Uses a single part-to-body center offset; evaluated on COCO-HumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman; reports AP, precision/recall/F1 for hands/feet vs ED-Pose, and body MR-2/AP on CrowdHuman.
> - Development defects: on the single-part face-body task (CrowdHuman) its advantage over BPJDet is not pronounced; for body detection it is only *comparable* to DETR-based detectors (PED-DETR, Iter-E2EDET), not clearly better; it is YOLOv5/YOLOv7-based (not Transformer/ResNet-50 backbones, which your pipeline mentions); the ED-Pose comparison was partly favorable to ED-Pose (GT part boxes) yet PBADet still wins.
> 
> **2. Graph long-range dependencies without oversmoothing/oversquashing: Adaptive Message Passing (AMP)**
> - Variational framework that learns message-passing depth and per-layer soft message filtering; proven sensitivity bound; mitigates oversmoothing/oversquashing/underreaching.
> - Development defects: the family of depth distributions (Poisson, folded normal, mixtures) is a hyper-parameter that must be tuned; relies on variational inference assumptions; learned depth after training does not help further (fixing depth gives no gain); improvements shown only on five node/graph datasets, with no guarantee of the learned filtering being optimal per task.
> 
> **3. Self-supervised latent-space prediction avoiding noisy pixels: "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (+ LDReg)
> - Shows JEPA-style self-distillation predicts in latent space and is implicitly biased to high-influence features, learning noisy features more slowly than MAE pixel reconstruction; LDReg additionally regularizes local dimensionality (works on ResNet-50/ViT-B and improves COCO detection).
> - Development defects (JEPA paper): theory limited to deep *linear* networks, balanced orthogonal initialization, and simultaneous diagonalizability; qualitative generalization only; JEPA still eventually learns noisy features, just with lower amplitude. LDReg: LID estimation degrades in high dimensions and uses minibatch nearest neighbors; forcing very low LID can cause full collapse.
> 
> **4. 4-bit optimizer states under tight GPU memory: Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States**
> - 4-bit Adam/AdamW with B128/DE first moment, rank-1/linear zero-excluded second moment, optional factorization; matches 32-bit AdamW on GLUE/SQuAD/ImageNet(NLU)/MT and LLaMA fine-tuning, saving up to ~57.7% memory.
> - Development defects: optimal quantization is task/dataset dependent; evaluated only on language/vision tasks (RL/audio/graphs untested); without fused operators 4-bit is slower than 8-bit on smaller models; quantizing both moments causes a marginal accuracy drop; memory savings saturate because total memory includes activations/data.
> 
> **Caveat:** no single work covers the full pipeline end-to-end — these are four separate papers. CIFAR-100 and SGD with 4-bit states are not covered in these documents (the optimizer paper tests AdamW; CIFAR-100 appears nowhere).

**community 最终答案**

> **Works matching each need (no single paper covers the whole pipeline):**
> 
> 1. **Hand/face→person association in crowded, COCO-like scenes:** *PBADet* (one-stage anchor-free part-body association; part-to-body center offset; evaluated on COCO-HumanParts, CrowdHuman, BodyHands with AP/Precision/Recall/F1 on YOLOv5/YOLOv7).
> 2. **Graph long-range dependencies w/o oversmoothing/oversquashing:** *Adaptive Message Passing (AMP)* — variational learning of message-passing depth + message filtering, explicitly mitigates oversmoothing, oversquashing, underreaching.
> 3. **Latent-space SSL avoiding noisy pixels:** *"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features"* (JEPA's latent prediction biases toward high-influence, low-noise features vs MAE's pixel reconstruction). Complementary: *LDReg* (prevents local dimensional collapse).
> 4. **Tight-memory Adam/SGD fine-tuning with 4-bit states:** *"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"* (4-bit Adam/AdamW quantization, B128 + rank-1 normalization + zero-point exclusion, up to 57.7% memory savings, lossless fine-tuning, quantized-SGD convergence proof).
> 5. **CE/accuracy + F1/Precision on CIFAR-100/COCO with Transformer/ResNet-50:** *LDReg* (ResNet-50/ViT-B, ImageNet linear eval + COCO detection/segmentation) and *"On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning"* (CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet top-1). Note: the 4-bit optimizer evaluates Swin-T/ImageNet, not CIFAR-100/COCO-ResNet-50, so that exact eval coverage is only partial.
> 
> **Development defects (from the context):**
> 
> - **PBADet:** association relies on anchor points inside a part box also lying inside the body box — ambiguous under occlusion/overlap in crowds; its advantage over BPJDet on CrowdHuman face-body is "less pronounced"; animal experiments derive body boxes from ground truth (not fully end-to-end); face/head excluded from some COCO comparisons due to inconsistent keypoint counts.
> - **AMP:** "non-negligible cost in terms of number of readout parameters"; the filtering-strategy choice (input- vs embedding-based) "remains a matter of empirical investigations"; sensitivity is unreliable as the *sole* oversquashing metric; fixing depth after the learned range doesn't improve performance.
> - **JEPA analysis:** theory restricted to deep linear MLPs, special initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances; generalization to nonlinear models and real data distributions "remains unexplored"; JEPA can still learn noisy features at lower amplitude and may be vulnerable to spurious/slow features; it is an analysis, not a new pretraining method.
> - **LDReg:** LID estimation accuracy "degrades as dimensionality increases" and uses minibatch nearest neighbors; requires tuning β; assumes higher dimensionality is desirable; forcing very low LID can trigger complete collapse.
> - **4-bit optimizer:** optimal quantization settings are task/dataset-dependent; slower than 8-bit AdamW on small models without fused kernels; quantizing both moments yields a marginal accuracy drop; only language and vision tasks were tested.
> - **Contrastive-embeddings paper:** extra hyperparameter and possible "suppression of meaningful semantic variance."

### paperscope:gap:193 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers on improving training and inference efficiency and stability in deep networks that collectively cover: (a) making adaptive moment methods (e.g., decoupled-weight-decay variants of Adam) and first-order SGD usable with sub-byte state storage for full-precision accuracy; (b) curvature-aware regularization beyond quadratic for hyper-parameter search when the objective is non-differentiable or discrete (e.g., maximizing F1/Precision on standard vision benchmarks like MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR-100) and gradients are unavailable; (c) explaining the inductive bias of non-contrastive joint-embedding self-supervised learning (teacher–student in latent space) toward useful feature embeddings rather than pixel noise under CE/MSE losses; (d) understanding how enforcing excitatory/inhibitory sign constraints changes the spectrum and learning dynamics of deep recurrent models; and (e) anchor-free, one-stage part-to-body association detectors that report metrics such as Precision/F1. I’m especially interested in works that discuss regularization choices, approximations, and how these methods integrate with AdamW/SGD and end-to-end fine-tuning (including low-rank adapters).Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

<summary>展开完整 gold 与两份最终答案</summary>

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below are the main development defects and limitations explicitly stated or clearly evidenced in the five provided works. Each item only reflects constraints, caveats, or unresolved issues documented in the papers themselves.
> 
> 1) PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part–Body Association (ICLR 2024)
> - Limited advantage on single-part association: The authors emphasize that on CrowdHuman (face–body is a single-part association), PBADet’s edge over BPJDet is “not as pronounced” as in multi-part settings; performance is only comparable on that benchmark, so gains are not uniform across tasks.
> - Sensitivity to task/dataset configuration: Reported improvements are tied to specific datasets (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts). On some categories/metrics they are merely “on par,” not consistently superior.
> - Heavy reliance on detector hyperparameters and NMS: The method’s training/inference pipeline depends on anchor alignment and several NMS thresholds, which the paper sets but does not show as robust across settings (a potential tuning burden).
> 
> 2) Learning Better with Dale’s Law: A Spectral Perspective (NeurIPS 2023)
> - ColEI (simple excitatory/inhibitory column partition) defects: (i) Poor learning and higher variance across seeds; (ii) strong instability without gradient clipping; (iii) degraded learning for small networks and when inhibitory proportion is small; (iv) performance depends on spectral radius settings; (v) multimodal and dispersed singular-value spectra that correlate with poor training.
> - DANN (recurrent Dale’s ANN) and analysis limitations: While DANNs learn well, the paper acknowledges biological and modeling gaps (e.g., lack of inhibitory-to-inhibitory connections, no cell-type-specific time constants), and notes open theoretical questions behind multimodal spectra and large maximum singular values. Thus, the current EI formulations are still simplified and not fully biologically faithful.
> 
> 3) How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Theory restricted to a simplified regime: Results are proven only for deep linear models under special initializations and the strong assumption that Σ_yx and Σ_xx are simultaneously diagonalizable; generalization to nonlinear encoders or realistic data that violate this assumption is not established.
> - Practical generalization unresolved: The authors explicitly state that extending the analysis to fully practical, non-simultaneously-diagonalizable data and nonlinear networks remains future work.
> - Potential bias risk: The paper itself notes that the same bias that steers JEPA toward predictive low-variance (“slow”) features may also render it vulnerable to spurious/slow signals; this trade-off is not resolved here.
> 
> 4) Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Domain and setting coverage: The authors state their evaluation is limited to language and vision; applicability to RL, audio, and graphs is untested.
> - Task-dependence of quantization: They caution the optimal quantization settings (e.g., block size, normalization, mapping) can be task/dataset dependent; achieving lossless performance may require tuning.
> - Throughput/latency constraints in practice: Without fused kernels, 4-bit AdamW can be slower than 8-bit baselines; speed parity requires implementation-level fusion.
> - Quantization design constraints: Second-moment quantization must exclude zero (to avoid catastrophic inverse-square-root blow-up), forcing specific mappings (e.g., linear map with a nonzero minimum representable value). Rank-1 normalization grants accuracy but adds extra normalization metadata and complexity. Factorization–quantization hybrid helps memory but only applies to second moments; 1D tensors are still quantized.
> - Incomplete coverage of tiny tensors: They explicitly do not quantize very small tensors (≤4096 elements), adding special-case handling that slightly reduces the total attainable memory win.
> 
> 5) Efficient Hyper-parameter Optimization with Cubic Regularization (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Dominant lower-level cost: The most expensive step is training lower-level models. Each outer iteration samples K hyper-parameters and (re)trains models, which can be very time-consuming (empirically dwarfing the cubic subproblem time) and may limit scalability.
> - Convergence hinges on accuracy and sampling: The theoretical guarantees require (i) sufficiently accurate (or many) samples K for gradient/Hessian estimates of the relaxed objective, and (ii) sufficiently accurate lower-level solutions. If either is weak, convergence may degrade.
> - Assumption-heavy analysis: Convergence relies on a ρ-Lipschitz Hessian for the relaxed objective and bounded errors/variances; these conditions can be restrictive in complex ML pipelines.
> - Practical burden of second-order modeling: Even if θ is low-dimensional, the approach still needs Hessian-related construction and a cubic-regularized subproblem per outer step, increasing implementation complexity relative to first-order relaxations.
> 
> Cross-cutting observations (grounded in the papers):
> - Optimizer/memory methods vs. speed: The 4-bit optimizer shows that memory savings do not automatically yield faster training; implementation-level fusion is needed to avoid slowdowns.
> - Spectral/curvature reliance: The Dale’s Law work and cubic-regularization HPO both hinge on spectral/second-order properties; in practice, this can add hyper-parameters and computation (e.g., spectral radius control; Hessian surrogates) that must be tuned or approximated with care.
> - Dataset/task specificity: PBADet’s advantage shrinks on single-part association; 4-bit optimizers require task-specific quantization settings; JEPA theory is tied to toy linear regimes. These papers explicitly caution against universal performance assumptions without retuning or extending the methods.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the context, the following papers collectively cover (a)–(e):
> 
> **(a) Sub-byte optimizer states** — *"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"*: compresses Adam/AdamW first/second moments to 4 bits (block B128, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear mapping, optional factorization), matching 32-bit accuracy across NLU/vision/MT/LLaMA fine-tuning; also gives a convergence proof for quantized SGD(M). Mentions LoRA/end-to-end fine-tuning context.
> **(b) Curvature-aware (beyond-quadratic) HPO without gradients** — *"Hyper-Parameter Optimization via Stochastic Relaxation and Cubic Regularization"*: handles discrete hyper-parameters and non-differentiable metrics via stochastic relaxation + cubic regularization (Hessian-based, saddle-point escaping), with experiments on CIFAR-10 noisy-label schedule search, feature selection, KG completion.
> **(c) Inductive bias of non-contrastive joint-embedding SSL** — *"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features: A Deep Linear Network Analysis"*: explains teacher–student latent-space (JEPA) dynamics under MSE-type losses, showing implicit bias toward high-influence/low-variance ("slow") features and depth-strengthened noise suppression versus MAE pixel reconstruction.
> **(d) E/I sign constraints, spectrum and dynamics** — *"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"*: shows ColEI sign-constrained RNNs learn worse due to multimodal/dispersed initial singular-value spectra (rank-one column-mean structure), not sign constraints per se; normalized SVD entropy predicts performance.
> **(e) Anchor-free one-stage part-to-body detector** — *"PBADet"*: single part-to-body center offset on anchor-free multi-scale heads; outperforms BPJDet/HierR-CNN, reports AP plus higher precision/recall/F1 (e.g., vs ED-Pose for hands/feet).
> 
> **Development defects (from the context):**
> 
> - **(a)** Optimal quantization may be task-dependent; only language/vision tasks tested; second-moment quantization is unstable (zero-point problem); the convergence guarantee covers quantized SGD(M), not Adam itself.
> - **(b)** Runtime is dominated by lower-level training; Hessian computation limits it to low-dimensional hyper-parameter spaces; convergence is only to approximate second-order stationary points with inexact lower-level solves; experiments don't cover MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR-100 F1/Precision as requested.
> - **(c)** Analysis is restricted to deep linear networks, special (balanced orthogonal) initialization, and simultaneous diagonalizability; beyond that only qualitative generalization via ImageNet CCA experiments.
> - **(d)** Sign constraints still impair learning (0.7% RNN / 1% ColEI); ColEI networks are unstable without gradient clipping, show high variance across seeds/initializations, and degrade with small size or few inhibitory units; DANN reparameterization is needed to recover standard-RNN-like spectra.
> - **(e)** On single-part tasks (CrowdHuman face-body) the advantage over BPJDet is marginal; anchor-free detection inherently risks lower recall (near-center points); association quality depends on task-alignment top-K anchor selection; the quadrupeds extension is only qualitatively validated.
> 
> Overall, no single paper covers all requested settings jointly (e.g., (a) lacks true SGD sub-byte state beyond the analysis; (b) lacks the exact vision F1/Precision benchmarks; (c) is a toy-model theory; (d) is empirical and RNN-specific; (e) emphasizes AP/MR-2 more than F1), so the five requirements are met as a collection rather than by any one work.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, here are the matching papers for each criterion:
> 
> **(a) Sub-byte optimizer states for AdamW/SGD** — "4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States" (doc 8d5e1455): pushes optimizer states to 4-bit (below 8-bit) for Adam/AdamW and is stated as applicable to SGDM and Adam/AdamW. Uses smaller blocks (B128), rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluding linear quantizer, and factorization of the second moment; matches full-precision accuracy across GLUE, SQuAD, ImageNet (Swin-T), MT, and LLaMA fine-tuning, with memory savings up to 57.7%. It discusses integration with LoRA (as related work), delta tuning, offloading, and sharding.
> 
> **(b) Curvature-aware regularization beyond quadratic for non-differentiable/discrete objectives** — "Hyper-Parameter Optimization via Stochastic Relaxation and Cubic Regularization" (doc 2d57d4ed): handles hyper-gradients unavailable (non-differentiable metrics such as MRR/NDCG, discrete hyper-parameters) via stochastic relaxation + cubic regularization (beyond quadratic), converging to approximate second-order stationary points with inexact lower-level solves; validated on knowledge-graph completion and noisy-label schedule search (CIFAR-10). Note: the collection does not contain a paper explicitly maximizing F1/Precision on MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR-100; this is the closest match for the stated setting.
> 
> **(c) Inductive bias of non-contrastive joint-embedding SSL (teacher–student, latent space)** — "Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features: A Deep Linear Network Analysis" (doc 40fde037): analyzes JEPA (stop-gradient teacher–student self-distillation) vs MAE; shows JEPA prioritizes high-influence features and suppresses pixel/feature noise with depth, learning "slow" low-variance features rather than noise. Also relevant: "LDReg: Local Dimensionality Regularization for Self-Supervised Learning" (doc 51526068) on preventing dimensional collapse via local intrinsic dimensionality regularization.
> 
> **(d) E/I sign constraints, spectrum and learning dynamics of recurrent models** — "Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly" (doc e63a94c4): compares sign-constrained ColEI and DANN RNNs with standard RNNs; shows the initial singular-value spectrum (multimodal, dispersed, rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure) matters more than the sign constraints themselves, with normalized SVD entropy predicting performance; documents instability without gradient clipping and worse learning for small networks/few inhibitory units.
> 
> **(e) Anchor-free, one-stage part-to-body association detector with Precision/F1** — "PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association" (doc 08b70bc3): one-stage, anchor-free, single part-to-body center offset on YOLOv5/YOLOv7; reports AP, MR-2, and Precision/Recall/F1 (beating ED-Pose on hands/feet) on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman; extends to quadruped AnimalPose/AP-10K.
> 
> Additionally, for your interest in regularization/approximations and integration with SGD/AdamW, LoRA, and end-to-end fine-tuning: "Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure" (doc 582d138d) analyzes Hessian power-law spectra across SGD/Adam-family optimizers on MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/CIFAR-10/100 and shows LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the power-law structure that full fine-tuning does (Hessian trace is a more reliable generalization indicator for LoRA adapters).
> 
> **Development defects of these methods:**
> 
> **(a) 4-bit optimizers**: optimal quantization settings are task/data dependent and out-of-scope settings might beat them; evaluation limited to language and vision (no RL/audio/graph); without fused operators, 4-bit AdamW is slower than 8-bit on smaller models; only "comparable/lossless" accuracy, with marginal drops when both moments are quantized.
> 
> **(b) HPO with cubic regularization**: requires Hessian computation (cubic regularization), feasible only because hyper-parameters are low-dimensional; runtime is dominated by lower-level training; performance depends on number of sampled hyper-parameters K and accuracy of (inexact) lower-level solves; only approximate second-order stationarity is guaranteed, and the non-differentiable F1/Precision-on-vision-benchmarks case is not directly demonstrated.
> 
> **(c) JEPA analysis**: restricted to deep linear MLPs, balanced orthogonal initialization, and simultaneous diagonalizability; the mechanism is only qualitatively supported for real networks; CE (cross-entropy) teacher–student variants are not analyzed (MSE-style self-distillation is); LDReg's LID estimation degrades in high dimensions and relies on minibatch neighbors, and forcing very low LID can cause complete collapse.
> 
> **(d) Dale's-law RNNs**: ColEI networks show high variance across initializations and during training, are highly unstable without gradient clipping; performance degrades sharply for small networks or low inhibitory fractions; the origin of the multi-modal spectrum and why large ColEI networks learn well despite large maximal singular values remain open questions; DANN's robustness trades off biological fidelity (no I→I connections, specific interneuron types).
> 
> **(e) PBADet**: the advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced for single-part face-body association (CrowdHuman); per-part association accuracy depends on the association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and task-alignment learning (ablations show each is needed); anchor-free detection relies on dense in-box positive sampling, and association offset regression can be affected by multi-scale feature-anchor interpretation.

</details>

### paperscope:gap:199 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find a compact set of papers that, taken together, cover: (1) anchor-free, one-stage human part–to–body association on common object benchmarks (think the dataset used in mainstream detection challenges like COCO) with Transformer-style backbones; (2) memory-lean training via quantizing stateful optimizer buffers to around 4 bits while preserving Adam/AdamW or SGD behavior; (3) self-supervised joint-embedding objectives that prefer predictive, high-influence features over pixel-level MSE reconstruction (with analyses in deep linear nets and cosine-similarity space); (4) per-prompt interpretability for alignment—measuring how much supervised fine-tuning contributes at inference and relating it to jailbreak success (e.g., AUROC/F1/Precision reporting); and (5) recurrent models constrained by excitatory/inhibitory partitions (Dale-like) analyzed through spectra/entropy of singular values. Prefer works that touch standard datasets (MNIST/CIFAR-100/COCO), use Transformers/RNNs, and discuss common losses (cross-entropy, MSE) and feature embeddings.Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

<summary>展开完整 gold 与两份最终答案</summary>

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Here’s a clear, concise summary of the **development defects** in *TuCo*’s method, as stated in the paper:
> 
> 1. **Dependence on Pre-Trained Model Access**  
>    - Computing TuCo requires access to *both* the original pre-trained and the fine-tuned model.
>    - This requirement limits applicability in settings where only the fine-tuned weights are available (e.g., many closed-source APIs).
> 
> 2. **High Computational Overhead**  
>    - TuCo’s computation cost is essentially two full forward passes per prompt (fine-tuned model + pre-trained model), which is significant for large LLMs.
>    - This overhead makes it less suitable for real-time or large-scale production monitoring.
> 
> 3. **Limited to Residual-Stream Additive Architectures**  
>    - The decomposition into PTC and FTC assumes a residual, additive Transformer block design, which may limit applicability to architectures that deviate from this structure.
> 
> 4. **Not a Detection or Defense Mechanism**  
>    - TuCo is designed for *analysis*, not for prevention or detection of jailbreaks.
>    - Although it correlates with jailbreak success, it’s not directly usable as a standalone security safeguard without further processing.
> 
> 5. **Final-Token Focus**  
>    - The metric is computed only on the final token’s hidden state to avoid dilution, which may miss fine-tuning effects manifesting in earlier token positions.
> 
> 6. **No Behaviour Attribution to Specific Fine-Tuning Data**  
>    - TuCo quantifies *overall fine-tuning influence*, but cannot identify which fine-tuning examples/datasets are responsible for observed effects.
> 
> 7. **Benchmark & Domain Limitations**  
>    - Validation is on specific datasets (e.g., MMLU, MWE, HH-RLHF) and jailbreak attack types, leaving generalization to other domains, languages, or attack styles untested.
> 
> These constraints mean that while TuCo is insightful for *offline interpretability and safety research*, it has limited immediacy for closed-source models, low-latency use cases, or direct deployment as a defense.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Compact Paper Set
> 
> 1. **PBADet (ICLR 2024)** — one-stage anchor-free part–body association; single part-to-body center offset; evaluated on **COCO-HumanParts, COCO-WholeBody-derived, CrowdHuman, BodyHands** with AP/Precision/Recall/F1 (beats BPJDet, HierR-CNN, ED-Pose). Caveat: backbones are **YOLOv5/v7/v8 CNNs**, not Transformers; no Transformer-backbone part–body paper exists in this collection (ED-Pose with Swin-L appears only as a competitor).
> 2. **4-bit Optimizers (NeurIPS 2023)** — quantizes Adam/AdamW (and SGDM) optimizer states to **4 bits** via smaller blocks (B128), zero-point-excluding linear quantizer, rank-1 normalization, factorized second moment; lossless vs 32-bit on GLUE/SQuAD/ImageNet (Swin-T)/WMT/Alpaca; up to 57.7% memory savings; framework covers SGD(M).
> 3. **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features (NeurIPS 2024)** — joint-embedding predictive (self-distillation) objective vs MAE pixel reconstruction, analyzed in **deep linear networks**: JEPA is biased toward high-influence (high-regression-coefficient) features while MAE prioritizes high-variance/noisy features; validated on ImageNet-1K I-JEPA vs MAE (CCA).
> 4. **On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning** — analysis in **cosine-similarity space** (positive/negative-pair similarities, expectation/variance; InfoNCE/SigLIP) with a variance-reduction loss; experiments on **CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100**, cross-entropy/InfoNCE losses. (Together with #3, this covers the "deep linear nets + cosine-similarity space" analyses.)
> 5. **TuCo (ICML 2025)** — per-prompt interpretability for alignment: exact decomposition of fine-tuned Transformer LLM into pre-training (PTC) and fine-tuning (FTC) components; measures fine-tuning's contribution at inference; jailbreaks (GCG, conjugate, many-shot) attenuate TuCo, with **AUROC >0.8** (up to 0.87) for most models and per-prompt AUC/F1-style reporting.
> 6. **Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly (NeurIPS 2023)** — recurrent E/I (Dale-like) networks: column-partitioned ColEI vs DANN; analyzes singular-value spectra and **normalised SVD entropy (NSE)**; ColEI shows multimodal, dispersed spectra (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure) vs unimodal random-matrix spectra; NSE anti-correlates with test error; tasks: adding problem, **sequential MNIST**, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition.
> 
> ## Development Defects of These Methods
> 
> **1. PBADet**
> - No Transformer backbone: it relies on YOLO-style CNN backbones adapted to anchor-free heads (the paper itself notes YOLOv5/v7 needed adaptation), so the Transformer-style requirement is unmet.
> - Association is a single center-offset regression: occluded/overlapping parts and one-to-many part-to-body cases rely on the offset validity assumption; performance on the single-part CrowdHuman face-body task is only marginally better than BPJDet.
> - On COCO-HumanParts it is competitive but not uniformly best per-category; body-detection AP is only comparable to (not above) DETR-family detectors like PED-DETR.
> - Ablations show dependence on the association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment; without them accuracy drops.
> 
> **2. 4-bit Optimizers**
> - Optimal quantization settings are task/dataset-dependent; authors admit task-specific settings could outperform.
> - Quantizing both moments still causes a marginal accuracy drop; the convergence proof covers only quantized SGD(M), not Adam/AdamW.
> - Slower than 8-bit on small models (no fused kernels); memory savings saturate as bitwidth decreases; evaluation limited to language and vision tasks (no RL/audio/graph).
> 
> **3. JEPA deep-linear analysis**
> - Restricted to deep linear networks, balanced orthogonal initialization, and simultaneous diagonalizability; nonlinear generalization is only qualitative.
> - JEPA objective is prone to collapse (needs stop-grad/architectural tricks); the bias toward high-influence features may also make JEPA vulnerable to spurious/slow features.
> - Empirical confirmation limited to ImageNet-1K I-JEPA-vs-MAE alignment analysis.
> 
> **4. Embedding-similarity analysis**
> - Analysis targets InfoNCE-style (and SigLIP) losses only; mini-batch results rely on specific assumptions.
> - The proposed variance-reduction loss adds a tunable hyperparameter and may suppress meaningful semantic variance; experiments limited to CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet-100 with ResNets (no large-scale full ImageNet validation).
> 
> **5. TuCo**
> - Requires access to **both** the pretrained and fine-tuned models plus an extra forward pass (2× compute) — not applicable when only the fine-tuned model is available.
> - Not a defense; detection quality varies (AUROC 0.66 for Vicuna-13B, negligible for Llama-3-8B with 0.24% jailbreak rate); α-scaling needs 5-fold CV per model; validated only on models ≤13B.
> 
> **6. Dale's Law RNNs**
> - Findings are architecture-specific (ColEI vs DANN); ColEI is highly unstable without gradient clipping and shows high variance across seeds/initializations.
> - NSE is an empirical diagnostic, not a theoretical guarantee; open questions remain on the origin of the multimodal spectrum and why large ColEI networks learn well despite large max singular values; no formal theory linking NSE to trainability.
> - Limited task coverage (MNIST, PTB, adding, one object-recognition task); small networks and low I-unit ratios degrade both spectra and performance.

**community 最终答案**

> ## Compact paper set
> 
> **1. Anchor-free one-stage part–body association** — *PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association* (ICLR 2024; doc `08b70bc3…`). One-stage, anchor-free detector with a single part-to-body center offset; evaluated on COCO-HumanParts, COCO-WholeBody-derived BodyHands, CrowdHuman, AnimalPose; reports AP, MR-2, Precision/Recall/F1. **Caveat:** it uses YOLOv5/YOLOv7 **CNN** backbones, not Transformer-style backbones (DETR variants such as PED-DETR/ED-Pose appear only as comparisons). No paper in the collection matches "anchor-free + Transformer backbone" exactly.
> 
> **2. 4-bit optimizer states** — *Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States* (NeurIPS 2023; doc `8d5e1455…`). Quantizes first/second moments (B128, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer, factorization) for Adam/AdamW/SGDM; matches 32-bit AdamW on ImageNet-1k (Swin-T), GLUE, SQuAD, E2E-NLG, WMT14, LLaMA fine-tuning; ~57.7% memory savings.
> 
> **3. Self-supervised joint-embedding vs. reconstruction** — two papers: *How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features* (NeurIPS 2024; doc `40fde037…`) — JEPA-style self-distillation prioritized over pixel-level MAE reconstruction, analyzed with **deep linear networks** (critical times, high-influence features), validated on ImageNet-1K via CCA; and *On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning* (doc `160e1407…`) — analysis in **cosine-similarity space** (optimal positive/negative similarities, mini-batch variance), improved top-1 on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet.
> 
> **4. Per-prompt interpretability for alignment** — *TuCo: Measuring the Contribution of Fine-Tuning to Individual Responses of LLMs* (ICML 2025; doc `e20e7624…`). Decomposes any fine-tuned Transformer into pre-training/fine-tuning components; measures per-prompt fine-tuning contribution at inference; jailbreaks lower TuCo, successful jailbreaks more so (AUC 0.87 for Llama-13B; GCG AUC >0.78 on 4/5 models); also MMLU/MWE behavior steering.
> 
> **5. Dale's-law RNNs via spectra** — *Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective* (NeurIPS 2023; doc `e63a94c4…`). ColEI (column-constrained E/I partitioning) vs. DANN RNNs on adding problem, **sequential MNIST**, PTB, object recognition; attributes poor learning to multimodal/dispersed singular-value spectra, quantified by **normalised SVD entropy (NSE)**.
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods
> 
> - **PBADet:** backbone is CNN-based (YOLO) rather than the requested Transformer; advantage over BPJDet shrinks on the single-part CrowdHuman face-body task; performance degrades without the association loss, multi-scale offsets, or task-alignment learning (ablations); dense per-pixel formulation is heavier than sparse DETR-style heads; hyperparameters (offset scaling λ, task alignment) need tuning.
> - **4-bit optimizers:** optimal quantization setting is task/dataset-dependent (no lossless guarantee for untested settings); evaluated only on language/vision — not RL, audio, or graph learning; without fused kernels it is *slower* than 8-bit AdamW on small models; memory savings saturate since activations/data still dominate; quantizing both moments causes a marginal accuracy drop.
> - **JEPA/contrastive analyses:** JEPA theory restricted to deep **linear** networks, special balanced-orthogonal initialization and simultaneous diagonalizability; leap to nonlinear models is heuristic; JEPA remains vulnerable to spurious/slow features; the contrastive-similarity variance-reduction loss adds a tuning hyperparameter and may suppress meaningful semantic variance.
> - **TuCo:** requires access to *both* the pre-trained and fine-tuned models (not available for closed APIs) plus an extra forward pass (~2× cost); it is an analysis metric, not a robust attack detector (GCG AUC >0.78 only on 4/5 models; needs a threshold); decomposition assumes residual (additive) transformer layers.
> - **Dale's-law RNNs:** ColEI networks train worse and with high seed variance, are unstable without gradient clipping; performance and spectra worsen for small networks and few inhibitory units; NSE is a diagnostic heuristic (anti-correlation), not a causal guarantee; DANN omits inhibitory-to-inhibitory connections and cell-type-specific time constants, limiting biological fidelity.

</details>

I’d prefer Transformer/RNN solutions and possibly adapter‑style, end‑to‑end parameter‑efficient fine‑tuning. Which papers should I read to cover all these pieces?Please analyze the development defects of these methods.
