**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below we summarize, for each work, the key development defects or limitations explicitly evidenced in the provided papers.
> 
> 1) PBADet: One-stage, anchor-free part–body association (ICLR 2024)
> - Limited advantage on single-part settings: The authors explicitly note that on the face–body association task in CrowdHuman (a single-part case), PBADet’s advantages over BPJDet are “not as pronounced” as in multi-part scenarios (Appendix A.1).
> - Hyperparameter and pipeline sensitivity: The method relies on task-alignment (K, α, β), NMS thresholds for body/part, and a Top-K assignment strategy; while not claimed as failures, the paper fixes these values and does not demonstrate robustness to their variation, suggesting potential sensitivity in practice (Sec. 3.3–3.4, 4.1).
> - Association decoding still heuristic in crowded scenes: Although simpler than BPJDet, inference picks the nearest enclosing body to the predicted body-center offset (Sec. 3.4). In dense scenes this nearest-center rule can be ambiguous; the paper does not analyze failure cases of this heuristic.
> - Gains are dataset/task-dependent: Strong gains are shown for multi-part human parts and several metrics, but for single-part association the improvement is small, showing the benefit is not uniform (Table 5, Appendix A.1).
> 
> 2) Training Dale-constrained deep networks: spectral perspective (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Column EI (ColEI) RNNs suffer spectral pathologies: At initialization their singular value spectra are multimodal and dispersed with large singular modes, causing poor/unstable learning, especially versus standard RNNs and DANNs (Fig. 3D–F; Sec. 3.2–3.3).
> - High variance and instability without gradient clipping: ColEI networks show higher training variance and can be highly unstable without gradient clipping (Sec. 4 Discussion; Appendix Fig. 10 referenced), indicating practical fragility.
> - Performance degrades for small networks or few inhibitory units: Small ColEI networks and those with realistic low I-fractions learn poorly, matching worse spectral properties (Sec. 3.4; Fig. 5–6). NSE (normalized SVD entropy) diagnostically drops with such settings.
> - Heavy dependence on careful initialization/spectral control: Good learning is tied to spectral properties; ColEI needs spectrum “transplant” or careful designs. The study finds spectra matter more than sign constraints, but fixing spectra in ColEI is nontrivial (Sec. 3.3).
> - Theoretical analysis assumptions limit generality: Key results (ODE equivalence, critical times) require special initializations and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances; while experiments support insights, these assumptions restrict formal guarantees (Assumption 3.1; Sec. 3, Appendices B.1–B.5).
> 
> 3) JEPA vs MAE: implicit bias in deep linear self-distillation (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Scope restricted to deep linear encoders and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances: Core theorems depend on strong assumptions (linear networks, special inits, diagonalizable Σxx, Σxy), limiting direct applicability to realistic non-linear settings (Sec. 6 Limitations).
> - JEPA’s bias requires depth and may fail for shallow encoders: The “influential feature” prioritization emerges only when the encoder is deep; with shallow encoders the distinct advantage largely diminishes (Sec. 3, 3.2; Corollary 3.6).
> - Potential vulnerability to spurious/slow features: The paper notes the implicit bias that helps JEPA focus on predictive, low-variance features may also render it vulnerable to “spurious or slow features,” depending on data (Sec. 7 Discussion).
> - Collapse prevention and objective design still critical: The analysis uses stop-gradient and specific JEPA formulations; in practice, collapse-avoidance and predictor design remain delicate and can affect outcomes (Sec. 1, 2).
> 
> 4) Active, anytime-valid RCPS with online calibration and label budgeting (NeurIPS 2024)
> - i.i.d. data assumption: Guarantees are derived under i.i.d. sampling; the paper recognizes that handling distribution shift (covariate/label shift) requires new machinery (Sec. 6 Conclusion/Limitations).
> - Label-policy constraints and existence conditions: The active e-process requires labeling probabilities bounded away from zero (qt(x) ≥ ε) and relies on existence of optimal policies/predictors; these assumptions can be restrictive in practice (Prop. 2; Assumption 2; Prop. 5; Sec. 6).
> - Utility depends on predictor quality: While safety guarantees hold regardless, poor risk predictors rb increase variance and slow “wealth” growth, making the procedure label-inefficient even if valid (Sec. 2.2; Proposition 3; Sec. 3 Theorem 3).
> - Anytime-validity can be conservative: Though not framed as a failure, the use of Ville’s inequality and e-process thresholds (1/α) can make tests conservative, potentially increasing sample/label needs for utility (Def. 2; Fact 1; Theorem 1/2).
> - Expected-budget control (not per-instance): The framework controls the expected fraction of queried labels under a budget B, not per-sequence guarantees; this may be misaligned with hard, per-instance budget constraints (Sec. 2.1, 3).
> 
> 5) Text-space Graph Foundation Models (TS-GFMs): benchmarked methods such as OFA, Prodigy, LLaGA, GraphMAE (NeurIPS 2024 D&B)
> - Limited or negative transfer on node-level co-training: Across diverse graphs, co-training often underperforms training-from-scratch GCNs; gains are inconsistent and heavily dataset-dependent (Table 1; Observation 1). Hyperparameter preferences vary by dataset, complicating unified backbones.
> - Catastrophic forgetting across domains/tasks (LLM+projector): LLaGA matches single-task in-domain performance but degrades with broad cross-domain co-training, consistent with catastrophic forgetting (Sec. 4.2.1, Observation 1; [49] cited in the paper).
> - Weakness on link prediction: GFMs offer no advantage vs link-specific models and struggle to scale to large graphs; best-in-class performance requires explicit structural/inductive biases (e.g., BUDDY with structural embeddings) (Sec. 4.2.2; Observation 2; Fig. 4, Tables 3–4).
> - Gains largely confined to graph-level tasks: Clear benefits are shown on molecular graph classification when co-training in text space, but not reliably for node-level/link-level tasks (Sec. 4.2.3; Observation 3).
> - Cross-task co-training can hurt node/link performance: Combining node/link/graph tasks often improves graph-level results but degrades node/link tasks, indicating task interference without careful inductive bias alignment (Sec. 4.3; Table 6; Observation 4).
> - Pre-training transfer and in-context learning are far from solved: Cross-graph, cross-task ICL remains weak; even same-task transfer via fine-tuning yields limited gains when LLM embeddings already perform well (Sec. 4.4; Tables 7–8; Observations 5–6).
> - Text-space conversion can introduce feature loss: Converting non-text attributes (e.g., atomics, categorical) to text may degrade performance, although co-training can mitigate some loss (Appendix B, Table 10).
> - Practicality issues in prior formulations: OFA’s original dataset-weighting needs extensive tuning and is impractical at scale; the benchmark uses equal weights, highlighting sensitivity in earlier designs (Sec. 4.1 Models).
> - Compute and scalability: Several GFM pipelines (e.g., OFA, LLaGA) are computationally heavy and struggle with large graphs or many datasets, limiting practical pre-training/co-training breadth (Sec. 4.2.2; Table 3 training times; remarks around scalability).
> - Encoder dependency: Performance depends strongly on the chosen text encoder (e.g., MiniLM vs MPNet), implying sensitivity to language backbone quality (Appendix G.2, Table 16).
> 
> Overall synthesis across the five topics
> - Methods that rely on unified, general-purpose backbones (anchor-free part–body association; Dale-constrained networks; self-distillation JEPA; anytime-valid RCPS; text-space GFMs) often achieve their guarantees or certain advantages only under specific regimes/assumptions (e.g., multi-part association, favorable spectra, deep encoders, i.i.d. data, or graph-level tasks). Outside these regimes, the papers candidly report weaker gains, instability, or significant engineering sensitivity (hyperparameters, encoder choice, structural biases, or scalability)—pinpointing the main development defects that future work must address.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, here is a small set of works covering the five areas, followed by an analysis of their development defects.
> 
> ## The set of works
> 
> 1. **Part-body association — PBADet** (ICLR 2024): one-stage, anchor-free, uses a single part-to-body center offset (representation length 5+K+2 vs BPJDet's 6+K+2K), contrasting with heavier two-stage/heuristic pipelines. (doc `08b70b…90`)
> 2. **E/I-constrained networks — "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023): trains ColEI and DANN RNNs under Dale's Law, analyzes singular-value spectra and uses normalized SVD entropy (NSE) to predict performance; gradient clipping stabilizes. (doc `e63a94…c8`)
> 3. **Implicit bias of SSL — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024): contrasts joint-embedding self-distillation (JEPA) vs reconstruction (MAE) via deep linear networks, showing JEPA favors high-influence features while MAE favors high-variance/noisy features; ImageNet CCA experiments. (doc `40fde0…03`)
> 4. **Active anytime-valid risk control** (NeurIPS 2024): extends RCPS to sequential, adaptive data with anytime-valid guarantees (e-processes/betting), active labeling under a label budget, ML predictors as control variates, regret bounds, label-efficient experiments. (doc `cda0aa…16d`)
> 5. **Text-space Graph Foundation Models** (TSGFM benchmark): unifies diverse graphs via language feature space using LLM encoders, graph prompts, graph SSL, and graph→text projectors; studies co-training, few-shot/zero-shot, in-context learning and fine-tuning. (doc `403fea…51f`)
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods
> 
> **PBADet**
> - Advantage shrinks on single-part tasks: on CrowdHuman face-body association its body MR-2 is best but AP is only competitive with BPJDet.
> - Gains are fragile: ablations show removing the association loss, using single-scale (non-multi-scale) center offsets, or dropping task-alignment all degrade metrics; the anchor-based variant underperforms its anchor-free version.
> - Works only at bounding-box level for parts/bodies; it does not provide part keypoints, limiting use where fine pose detail matters.
> 
> **Dale's Law/EI networks**
> - ColEI networks inherently learn poorly with high variance across seeds and are highly unstable without gradient clipping — the sign-constrained objective itself impairs learning.
> - Performance is predicted by (but not guaranteed from) NSE at initialization; the multi-modal spectrum origin and why large ColEI nets train well despite large σ_max remain open questions (empirical rather than fully explained).
> - Results are limited to RNNs and specific architectures (DANN models only fast PV+ interneurons, no I-to-I connections), so generalization to conv/feedforward/spiking settings is unproven.
> 
> **JEPA vs MAE (SSL implicit bias)**
> - The theoretical analysis only holds for deep linear networks, simultaneously-diagonalizable data, and special initialization — not for nonlinear models.
> - JEPA's bias to "influential" features also makes it vulnerable to spurious or slow features, and the objective is susceptible to collapse (needs StopGrad).
> - MAE-style reconstruction remains prone to dimensional collapse and to prioritizing noisy, high-variance subspaces, which is exactly the defect the paper highlights.
> 
> **Active anytime-valid risk control**
> - Valid only under the i.i.d. stream assumption; distribution/covariate/label shift at test time is not handled.
> - Relies on restrictive assumptions (bounded label policies, existence in Proposition 5) that the authors note could be removed only with more careful analysis.
> - Label efficiency depends on accurate conditional-risk predictors; the risk estimate treats unqueried labels as zero risk, which can bias variance reduction.
> 
> **Text-space GFMs**
> - Projecting features into text space can hurt performance (e.g., categorical Tolokers degrades); non-text attributes need multimodal (text-chemistry) encoders, and projection itself incurs a performance loss.
> - Negative transfer is data-trait-dependent and hard to predict from dataset ratios; models like SGC fail on heterophilous graphs, and strong LLM encoders are required just to mitigate feature heterogeneity.
> - Capability is limited on structure-dominated tasks (link prediction, graph classification); evaluation is weakened by single-seed runs, limiting robust comparison.
> 
> Overall, the common development gaps across the set: (1) theoretical results are derived in simplified/linearized or i.i.d. settings with unproven generalization; (2) stability/robustness depends on sensitive components (gradient clipping, task alignment, accurate predictors, strong encoders) that can fail silently; (3) evaluation is often incomplete (single seeds, no distribution shift, limited ablations), so the claimed efficiency/robustness is not always robustly validated.

**community 最终答案**

> ## Works matching the five topics
> 
> 1. **PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association** (ICLR 2024) — one-stage anchor-free detection with a single part-to-body center offset, contrasting with two-stage/anchor-based (BPJDet, Hier-R-CNN) pipelines; YOLOv5/v7 backbones, TOOD task alignment, IoU/DFL/classification + association losses, SGD, evaluated on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman.
> 
> 2. **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023) — RNNs under E/I (Dale-like) constraints (ColEI vs DANN), spectral analysis via normalised SVD entropy (NSE), spectrum-transplant experiments, gradient clipping; tasks: adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition.
> 
> 3. **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks"** (NeurIPS 2024) — JEPA self-distillation vs MAE reconstruction on deep linear networks; implicit bias to high-influence (low-variance) features; CCA validation on ImageNet. Related: **"On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning"** covers cosine-similarity geometry (optimal negative-pair similarity −1/(n−1)) and mini-batch variance on CIFAR-10/100/ImageNet.
> 
> 4. **"Active, Anytime-Valid Risk-Controlling Prediction Sets"** (NeurIPS 2024) — extends RCPS to sequential/adaptive data via e-processes and betting; active labeling with label budgets, IPW, optimal predictors/policies, regret bounds; ImageNet + simulations.
> 
> 5. **"Text-space Graph Foundation Models: Comprehensive Benchmarks and New Insights"** (NeurIPS 2024 D&B) — benchmark of 23 text-attributed datasets aligning diverse graphs in a unified LLM feature space; GFM building blocks (graph SSL, graph prompts, LLM-with-projectors), zero/few-shot, fine-tuning, co-training, in-context learning.
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods
> 
> **PBADet**
> - Association is still resolved by a heuristic at inference: Euclidean distance from predicted body center to the nearest *unassigned enclosing* body, plus NMS — decoding is not end-to-end learned.
> - Anchor-free training only supervises points inside ground-truth boxes (per FCOS), and the method relies on multi-scale feature maps; ablations show dropping multi-scale offsets or task-alignment clearly degrades AP/conditional accuracy.
> - Advantage over BPJDet is much less pronounced on the single-part CrowdHuman task; animal experiments are only qualitative.
> - Heavy training cost (100 epochs, 4×V100, AMP); anchor-based variants of the same backbone underperform the anchor-free one.
> 
> **Dale's-law RNNs**
> - ColEI networks learn worse on all four tasks with much higher seed-to-seed variance; without gradient clipping they are highly unstable (clipping helps them far more than standard/DANN nets).
> - Performance is worst for small networks with few inhibitory units; the initial spectrum is multimodal/dispersed, and constraining the spectral radius does not constrain the rank-one column-mean (nilpotent) component that drives the singular-value pathology.
> - Sign constraints themselves also impair learning, so the fix (DANN reparameterization) only partially addresses the problem; spectral analysis relies on eigen/singular-value assumptions (non-orthogonal eigenvectors of non-symmetric matrices), and the origin of the multimodal spectra plus why large networks tolerate large σmax remain open.
> - Biologically, DANNs lack I-to-I connections and cell-type time constants.
> 
> **JEPA vs MAE analysis**
> - The theoretical result is confined to deep *linear* networks, balanced orthogonal initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable data; nonlinear models and general data are not covered.
> - The distinct bias only appears when the encoder is deep — it substantially diminishes for shallow encoders; the JEPA objective is itself collapse-prone (needs stop-gradient), and JEPA may be vulnerable to spurious/slow features.
> - The requested CE-vs-MSE comparison is not explicitly covered in the retrieved material; the cosine-similarity analysis (contrastive paper) additionally notes small-batch training inflates negative-pair similarity variance, degrading representations, and its proposed fix adds a tuning hyperparameter that can suppress meaningful semantic variance.
> 
> **Active anytime-valid RCPS**
> - Assumes i.i.d. data; distribution shift (covariate/label shift) is not handled — only "average-risk" extensions via empirical-Bernstein supermartingales are suggested.
> - Requires a bounded label policy (q*(x) ≥ ε) and an existence assumption (Prop. 5) for the optimal-policy characterization; the reported evaluation uses safety-violation rate, β̂ convergence and label efficiency — it does *not* report AUROC/Precision/F1 as the request asks, and results are on CPU simulations/ImageNet with θ=0.1, α=0.05, B=0.3.
> 
> **Text-space GFMs**
> - Most experiments are single-seed due to compute cost (OneForAll/LLaGA take days), inflating variance; the benchmark focuses on co-training and largely skips large-scale pre-training/transfer.
> - Transfer to new data is either infeasible (co-training requires retraining) or weak (fine-tuning/ICL has not shown promising cross-graph, cross-task results; "we are still far away from cross-graph, cross-task in-context learning").
> - Text-space projection itself causes performance loss (e.g., Tolokers 83.25→78.16; gap between LLM and original features on graph-level tasks), and negative transfer depends on intrinsic dataset traits rather than size; MPNN backbones (e.g., SGC) fail on heterophilous graphs, and graph-transformer generalization remains open; label embeddings are critical for prompt transferability, otherwise prompts fail.
> 
> Overall: the set covers all five topics (with the caveats that the CE-vs-MSE comparison and AUROC/Precision/F1 metrics requested are not present in the retrieved context), and the main recurring development defects are heuristic/approximate components (PBADet decoding, RCPS assumptions), high variance and instability (ColEI), limited theoretical scope (linear-only JEPA analysis, i.i.d./bounded-policy assumptions in RCPS), and evaluation/transfer weaknesses (single-seed GFM benchmarking, negative transfer, text-projection loss).

</details>

### paperscope:gap:220 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building a multi-modal system that: (a) detects and tracks hands/face relative to a person in real time, (b) fuses heterogeneous graph data by mapping attributes to text and then learns across datasets with a unified backbone, (c) pretrains representations with self-supervised objectives that avoid noisy features (favoring joint-embedding over masked reconstruction), (d) guarantees online safety via anytime-valid risk control while actively budgeting labels, and (e) uses recurrent controllers for time-series modeling that respect excitatory/inhibitory sign constraints yet remain trainable and stable. We fine-tune Transformers/vision-language models (possibly with LoRA), optimize with Adam/SGD and CE losses, compare cosine similarity, and monitor AUROC/F1. Can you point me to papers that jointly address these components end-to-end so I can design the detection, SSL, graph unification, and online calibration stack?Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Development defects and limitations by method/paper:
> 
> 1) PBADet (one-stage, anchor-free part–body association detection)
> - Limited advantage in single-part settings: The method’s benefits over body-to-part approaches are not pronounced when only one body part is involved; on CrowdHuman (face–body association), improvements are modest because the task is singular in nature (Appendix A.1: “the advantages of our method over BPJDet are not as pronounced as seen in scenarios with multiple parts-to-body associations”).
> - Sensitivity to training/inference hyperparameters: Performance relies on carefully chosen anchor alignment parameters (K, α, β), scaling factor λ, and NMS thresholds (τconf, τiou) per dataset, indicating non-trivial tuning needs across domains (Sec. 3.3, 3.4, 4.1).
> - Assumptions that can break in edge cases: The design assumes part anchor points fall within both part and enclosing body boxes; crowded occlusions or annotation edge cases that violate this geometry could impair association (Sec. 3.1). The paper does not report robustness under such violations.
> - Mixed gains across datasets/metrics: On COCOHumanParts, overall AP is on par with BPJDet and gains concentrate in some scales/categories; association mMR gains vary by part (Tables 2–3), suggesting non-uniform benefits across scenarios.
> 
> 2) EI RNNs under Dale’s Law (ColEI vs DANNs)
> - ColEI (column-signed RNNs) learn poorly primarily due to spectral pathologies: Multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra (with modes of large singular values) at initialization harm learning and stability, more so than mere sign constraints (Sec. 3.2–3.3; Fig. 3D–F, Fig. 4). This causes higher variance across seeds and strong reliance on gradient clipping for stability (Sec. 3.1; Appendix Fig. 10).
> - Strong dependence on network size and E/I ratio: Small networks and realistic low inhibitory proportions degrade learning and spectra (lower normalized SVD entropy), with performance improving only as networks get wider and EI ratios balanced (Sec. 3.4; Figs. 5–7). Hence, practical small-scale EI RNNs with few inhibitory units are especially brittle.
> - Initialization fragility and tuning burden: Performance hinges on spectral radius choices and special initializations to align spectra (Sec. 3.1; Appendix §2.2, §3.1), indicating sensitivity that complicates development.
> - Limited biological realism and scope for DANNs: While DANNs learn well and are robust to sign constraints, the paper notes missing inhibitory–inhibitory connectivity and other biological details, and different interneuron subtypes may require hybrid models (Sec. 4 Discussion).
> 
> 3) JEPA vs. MAE (deep linear self-distillation analysis)
> - Restricted theoretical setting: Results rely on deep linear networks with special initializations and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances; extension to nonlinear, practical models and non-diagonalizable settings is unproven (Sec. 6 Limitations). 
> - Depth-dependent bias and vulnerability: JEPA’s favorable bias toward “influential” (high-regression-coefficient) features emerges only with deep encoders; shallow JEPA resembles MAE and loses this advantage (Cor. 3.3, Sec. 3.2). The same bias may make JEPA prone to over-emphasizing slow/spurious features in some data (Sec. 7 Discussion).
> - Collapse avoidance and reliance on tricks: Non-contrastive JEPA requires stop-gradient or similar mechanisms to prevent collapse; poor choices can compromise training (Sec. 1, Eq. 5), adding design complexity.
> - Unclear generalization beyond the linear regime: Although suggestive experiments are provided, the paper explicitly cautions that real-world generality remains to be demonstrated (Sec. 6 Limitations, Sec. 7 Discussion).
> 
> 4) Active, anytime-valid risk-controlling prediction sets (RCPS)
> - i.i.d. assumption and distribution shift: Guarantees are derived under i.i.d. data; handling production distribution shift is left to future work (Sec. 6 Conclusion/Limitations). 
> - Label policy constraints: The theory requires a lower bound on labeling probabilities (q_min/ε) and existence of an optimal policy satisfying q*(x)≥ε (Assumption 2; Prop. 5). These constraints may be restrictive in practice and can complicate deployment under tight label budgets.
> - Predictor quality directly affects efficiency: Inaccurate conditional risk predictors increase variance and slow e-process growth, delaying safe calibration under a label budget (Sec. 2.2; Theorem 3), implying a dependency on reliable auxiliary models.
> - Hyperparameter and algorithmic complexity: Designing λ_t (betting rates) and learning label policies/predictors to maximize growth-rate lower bounds entails online optimization and regret trade-offs (Defs./Thm. in Sec. 3), increasing implementation complexity.
> 
> 5) Text-space Graph Foundation Models (TS-GFMs) and benchmark findings
> - Node classification co-training often underperforms task-specific models: Across citation/e-commerce graphs, co-training with OFA/DGI/GraphMAE/LLaGA frequently trails training-from-scratch GCNs; hyperparameters optimal per-graph do not transfer, and negative transfer is common (Sec. 4.2.1; Table 1). LLaGA also exhibits cross-domain forgetting (Sec. 4.2.1), matching reports of catastrophic forgetting in multimodal LLMs.
> - Limited scalability and weak link-prediction performance: GFM methods (OFA, LLaGA, GraphMAE) show no advantage over specialized link predictors (SEAL, BUDDY) and scale poorly—e.g., much longer training times than BUDDY on small datasets (Table 3), and difficulty extending to large graphs (Sec. 4.2.2). Effective link prediction requires task-specific structural inductive biases (e.g., structural embeddings), which generic GFM backbones lack (Tables 3–4; Observation 2).
> - Text projection can lose information: Mapping non-text attributes (e.g., molecular atomics, categorical fields) to text can reduce performance relative to original features, unless compensated by co-training (Appendix B; Table 10). 
> - Cross-task co-training trade-offs: Joint node/link/graph training improves graph-level tasks but can hurt node/link performance due to an inductive bias shift towards higher-order structure (Sec. 4.3.1; Table 6; Observation 4), complicating “one-backbone-for-all” aspirations.
> - Pre-train/fine-tune and in-context learning are inconsistent: Pre-training often yields limited gains versus strong text encoders with simple propagation; zero/few-shot in-context learning on graphs remains weak, especially cross-task (Tables 7–8; Observation 6). Performance depends heavily on the text encoder choice (Appendix G.2), indicating susceptibility to foundation encoder quality.
> - Sensitivity to dataset scale and imbalance: Negative transfer correlates with small training splits and dataset interactions rather than only scale ratios; improvements appear only in certain settings (Appendix G.5; Table 19–20), increasing the tuning burden.
> 
> Overall cross-paper takeaways relevant to system design
> - Methods that assume idealized conditions (e.g., i.i.d., special spectral properties, deep linearity, or strict geometric inclusion of parts within bodies) can face practical brittleness under distribution shift, occlusion/crowding, or small-scale regimes.
> - Unified backbones without task-specific inductive biases (e.g., for link prediction) struggle to match specialized models—scaling and efficiency limitations further impede deployment.
> - Text-space unification is promising but not universally beneficial; performance can regress for non-text attributes and in node-level co-training, and depends strongly on encoder quality and careful hyperparameterization.
> - For EI-constrained RNNs, spectral initialization and architecture choices (e.g., DANNs vs ColEI) are critical; naïve sign constraints alone are insufficient and can lead to instability, poor learning, and high variance.
> - Active risk control is theoretically sound but hinges on policy/predictor estimation quality and i.i.d. assumptions; relaxing these while maintaining label budgets is an open challenge.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Answer
> 
> **No paper in this collection jointly addresses all five components end-to-end.** Each component is covered by a separate, unintegrated paper — you would have to assemble the stack yourself:
> 
> | Component | Paper |
> |---|---|
> | (a) Hand/face/body detection & association | **PBADet** — one-stage anchor-free part-body association (part-to-body center offset; hands, face, feet vs. person) |
> | (b) Graph unification via text mapping | **Text-space Graph Foundation Models benchmark** — attributes→text via LLM encoders, unified backbone, cross-dataset/cross-task co-training |
> | (c) SSL favoring joint embedding over masked reconstruction | **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** — shows JEPA self-distillation biases toward high-influence (less noisy) features vs. MAE |
> | (d) Online safety + active label budgeting | **"Anytime-Valid Risk-Controlling Active Labeling"** — RCPS extended to sequential/adaptive data via e-processes/betting, with label-budget policies |
> | (e) Recurrent E/I sign-constrained controllers | **"Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly"** — DANN-style EI RNNs are trainable/stable; ColEI partitioning is not |
> 
> Caveats on coverage: PBADet is single-image detection/association, not multi-frame real-time tracking. Fine-tuning/LoRA, Adam/SGD, CE, cosine, AUROC/F1 are generic practice not jointly treated by any of these papers (NEFTune, on noisy embeddings for instruction fine-tuning incl. QLoRA, is the only LoRA-adjacent item).
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods
> 
> - **PBADet**: its advantage over BPJDet is not pronounced for single-part tasks (face–body); only comparable AP to DETR-based detectors; association quality suffers when parts are occluded, and part-to-body offsets scale in complexity with more parts.
> - **Text-space GFMs**: text-space conversion can cause significant performance loss on non-text attributes (Tolokers accuracy 83.25→78.16); negative transfer on small datasets under co-training; how to model the graph-structure–LLM-feature interaction is still open; SGC fails on heterophilous graphs; results are single-seed.
> - **JEPA analysis**: proof restricted to deep linear networks, special balanced orthogonal initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable data; generalization to nonlinear models is only qualitative; JEPA itself is vulnerable to spurious/slow features, and depth-based noise suppression isn't established beyond the linear regime.
> - **Anytime-valid RCPS**: assumes i.i.d. streaming data; doesn't handle distribution shift at test time (only hinted at via empirical Bernstein supermartingales); label policies must be bounded; guarantees rest on e-process/Ville's-inequality machinery that requires monotone risk/utility assumptions.
> - **Dale's-law RNNs**: sign constraints inherently impair learning (ColEI worse and higher-variance); ColEI is highly unstable without gradient clipping; performance degrades for small networks and low inhibitory ratios due to multimodal/dispersed spectra; the analysis is confined to initialization spectra; DANN models omit I→I connections and cell-type time constants, limiting biological fidelity.

**community 最终答案**

> ## No single paper covers the whole stack
> 
> Based on the collection, **no paper jointly addresses all five components end-to-end**. Each component maps to a separate paper; the stack must be assembled manually:
> 
> - **(a) Detection**: PBADet — one-stage anchor-free part-body association (hands/face relative to person), real-time via YOLOv5/v7 backbones.
> - **(b) Graph unification**: Text-space Graph Foundation Models (TSGFM) benchmark — maps node attributes to text via LLM encoders and co-trains across datasets with a unified backbone; also Graph World Model (GWM-T/GWM-E, converts multi-modal graph data to text/embedding space) and GEEA (generative entity alignment).
> - **(c) SSL**: "Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features" — exactly the joint-embedding-vs-masked-reconstruction (MAE) comparison you want; plus LDReg (anti-collapse regularization) and HASSOD (self-supervised object detection).
> - **(d) Online calibration**: "Active, Anytime-Valid Risk Controlling Prediction Sets" — e-process/betting-based risk control with active labeling and label budgets.
> - **(e) Recurrent E/I controllers**: "Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly" — E/I sign-constrained RNNs (ColEI vs DANN), trainability, stability, gradient clipping.
> 
> Your LoRA/Adam/CE/AUROC-F1/cosine-similarity details are not jointly treated by any one paper either (only tangential work, e.g., Hessian-spectrum analysis notes LoRA-only fine-tuning doesn't induce full fine-tuning's power-law structure).
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods
> 
> **(a) PBADet**: Part-to-body offsets become invalid when parts are occluded; performance degrades as part-set complexity grows; on CrowdHuman face-body, its advantage over BPJDet is marginal; gains over pose estimators rely on evaluation details (keypoint-in-box criterion).
> 
> **(b) Graph unification (TSGFM/GWM)**: Text-space transformation itself causes performance loss (e.g., Tolokers accuracy drops 83.25→78.16; molecular AUC 75.52→74.20); negative transfer depends on dataset traits rather than data ratios; SGC/inductive-bias backbones fail on heterophilous graphs; results from single-seed runs. GWM only handles text/image/table and homophilous graphs; too many hops cause over-smoothing; GWM-T has high token cost. GEEA's synthesis fails when KGs have sparse attributes or missing images.
> 
> **(c) SSL (JEPA/LDReg/HASSOD)**: The JEPA analysis relies on deep linear networks, special initializations, and simultaneous diagonalizability — generalization is qualitative. LDReg's LID estimation degrades in high dimensions and uses minibatch nearest neighbors; pushing LID too low triggers complete collapse. HASSOD suffers hierarchy misalignment with human perception and fails on overlapping similar objects, heterogeneous wholes, and text.
> 
> **(d) Anytime-valid active labeling**: Assumes i.i.d. data — explicitly flagged as not handling test-time distribution shift (covariate/label shift); requires bounded label policies; guarantees depend on the monotonicity/continuity assumptions on risk and utility.
> 
> **(e) Dale's-law RNNs**: Sign constraints themselves measurably impair learning (~0.7–1% error increase); naive ColEI partitioning gives multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra causing instability without gradient clipping and higher variance across seeds; small networks with few inhibitory units train poorly; only initialization spectra (NSE) are used as a diagnostic — no fix for the pathological spectra is proposed (left as future work, e.g., I→I connections, cell-type time constants).
> 
> **Bottom line**: assemble the stack from (a) PBADet, (b) TSGFM/GWM, (c) JEPA-analysis + LDReg/HASSOD, (d) anytime-valid active labeling, (e) DANN-style recurrent E/I networks — and account for each method's known failure modes above, since no integrated end-to-end system exists in this collection.

### paperscope:gap:223 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that, together, cover: (1) self-supervised learning analyses comparing Mean Squared Error (MSE) vs cross-entropy (CE) objectives (e.g., JEPA/self-distillation) and their implicit bias in deep networks; (2) memory-efficient training with Adam/AdamW using quantized first/second-moment states for fine-tuning; (3) one-stage, anchor-free detection on COCO-style benchmarks for part-body association with metrics like Precision/F1; (4) hierarchical generative pipelines that combine Transformers and Diffusion models with GNN training and prediction for property-guided structure generation; and (5) interpretability of recurrent models via spectral analysis under excitatory/inhibitory constraints. Ideally these works also discuss feature embeddings, End-to-end LoRA fine-tuning, and practical evaluation on datasets beyond MNIST/CIFAR-100.Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

**score：2→4（Δ+2）；rounds：3→3（Δ+0）。**

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Development defects and limitations per method
> 
> 1) PBADet (one-stage, anchor-free part–body association)
> - Limited advantage in single-part settings: The authors note that on CrowdHuman’s face–body task (only one part), PBADet’s advantage over BPJDet is “not as pronounced” as in multi-part scenarios, indicating reduced relative benefit when only one part type is present.
> - Enclosure assumption at decoding: The association step selects the body that both encloses the part and has the smallest distance to the predicted body center. This relies on the part box being inside a detected body box; under heavy occlusion, truncation, or missed body detections, this constraint can fail and break association.
> - Sensitivity to task-alignment and multi-scale choices: Ablations show noticeable drops without task alignment and multi-scale formulation, implying dependence on these design choices and their hyperparameters.
> - Dataset- and setting-specific thresholds: Inference uses dataset-specific NMS/confidence/IoU thresholds (different for BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, and CrowdHuman), suggesting non-trivial tuning to maintain performance across datasets.
> 
> 2) Learning with Dale’s Law via spectral analysis (recurrent EI models)
> - Instability and high variance in ColEI: Column-sign-constrained EI (ColEI) RNNs train poorly, are highly unstable without gradient clipping, and show higher variance across seeds—pointing to practical fragility.
> - Performance sensitivity to EI ratio and size: ColEI networks learn worse for small networks and for biologically realistic low proportions of inhibitory units; performance improves only for wider networks with more balanced E/I ratios.
> - Pathological spectra in ColEI: ColEI initializations produce dispersed, multimodal singular-value spectra (including large modes), which correlate with poor learning; fixing this is non-trivial and remains an open design challenge.
> - Open theoretical gaps: The origin of the multimodal spectra in ColEI and why large ColEI networks can learn despite large maximum singular values are explicitly left as open questions.
> - Biological coverage limitations of DANNs: While DANN RNNs learn well, they specifically model fast PV+ feedforward inhibition; they do not capture the diversity of inhibitory subtypes or I→I connectivity and cell-type-specific time constants discussed as needed for more faithful biological modeling.
> 
> 3) How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features (implicit bias of deep linear self-distillation)
> - Restricted theoretical setting: Results rely on deep linear encoders, special balanced/orthogonal initializations, small initialization scale, and simultaneously diagonalizable data covariances; generalization to nonlinear networks and non-diagonalizable data is explicitly unproven.
> - Depth dependence: The JEPA-vs-MAE bias separation largely appears when the encoder is deep; for shallow encoders (e.g., L=1), behaviors converge, limiting applicability of the claimed implicit bias in shallow settings.
> - Potential vulnerability to slow/spurious features: The discussion explicitly notes JEPA’s tendency to focus on slow/low-variance features may make it vulnerable to spurious or slow signals in some regimes.
> - Synthetic/idealized experiments: Empirical validations primarily use synthetic Gaussian data and controlled linear generative models; broader practical implications are suggested but not established.
> 
> 4) Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States (4-bit Adam/AdamW states)
> - Zero-point failure mode for v (second moment): Quantizing the second moment with mappings that include zero causes catastrophic errors in the update direction (observed as large spikes in 1/√v); avoiding this requires careful, custom quantization (e.g., linear mapping without zero), increasing implementation complexity.
> - Trade-offs from smaller blocks and rank-1 normalization: Improving accuracy requires smaller block sizes (e.g., B=128) and/or rank-1 normalization, which increases bookkeeping (more scales) and can add memory/implementation overhead versus coarser, simpler schemes.
> - Operator/implementation dependency for speed: Without fused kernels, 4-bit optimizers can run slower than 8-bit on some fine-tuning tasks; speed parity required operator fusion, highlighting engineering sensitivity.
> - Partial coverage of states/tensors: Rank-1 normalization falls back to block-wise for 1D tensors; factorization applies only to second-moment tensors with dimension >1; small tensors (≤4096), norms, and biases are left unquantized—so the solution is not uniformly 4-bit across all optimizer states.
> - Task dependence and domain coverage: The paper explicitly notes that optimal quantization settings may be task-dependent and that evaluation is limited to language/vision; applicability to RL, audio, or graph learning remains untested.
> - Total memory reduction saturation: Reported total memory savings can “saturate” because activations/data dominate; optimizer compression alone cannot always translate to proportionate end-to-end memory gains.
> 
> 5) GenMS (LLM + diffusion + GNN hierarchical materials generation)
> - Limited uniqueness and complexity: Although GenMS meets instructions and yields low-energy candidates, uniqueness of generated compositions is modest for some families (e.g., pyrochlore and spinel), and the authors note difficulty generating more complex structures (e.g., MXenes, Kagome lattices).
> - Heuristic exploitation and OOD risks in selection: Selection relies on a GNN property predictor (trained on unrelaxed structures) and thresholds to avoid out-of-range predictions. The paper explicitly cautions about possible exploitation/out-of-distribution issues and mitigates them heuristically, indicating residual risk remains.
> - Compute–quality trade-off: Lower formation energies require larger branching factors (more formulae/structures), which raises inference cost; practical use may be constrained by available compute (and downstream DFT budgets).
> - No synthesizability/experimental validation: The pipeline does not assess synthesizability, and utility for specific application targets (e.g., electrodes, superconductors) still requires experimental verification.
> - Matching/evaluation caveats: The structure-matching procedure can yield false positives due to how reference sets are curated—acknowledged in the paper—so some “match” successes may overestimate exact structural fidelity.
> - Data gap necessitating factorization: Absence of paired language→structure data forces factorization into language→formula and formula→structure modules; while pragmatic, it limits direct end-to-end learning of language-conditioned structural details.
> 
> Overall cross-cutting observations
> - Several methods depend on non-trivial hyperparameter choices and dataset-specific tuning (PBADet thresholds; 4-bit quantization block sizes/mappings; GenMS tree-search widths and thresholds).
> - Multiple works highlight theoretical or evaluation constraints (JEPA’s linear/diagonalizability assumptions; Dale-law spectral open questions; GenMS matching caveats and lack of synthesis validation) that should be addressed before broader deployment.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, here are the matching papers and their development defects:
> 
> **1. MSE vs CE objectives / JEPA implicit bias** — *Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features* (NeurIPS 2024, doc `40fde037…`). Analyzes JEPA (latent-space MSE prediction, self-distillation) vs MAE (input reconstruction), showing JEPA's implicit bias toward high-influence features. **Defects:** analysis limited to deep *linear* networks, special balanced-orthogonal initialization, and simultaneous diagonalizability of data covariances; results don't generalize to nonlinear models or non-self-distillation joint-embedding architectures; the bias may make JEPA vulnerable to spurious/slow features. (Feature embeddings & ImageNet-1K evaluation are covered.)
> 
> **2. Memory-efficient Adam/AdamW with quantized moments** — *4-bit Optimizers* (NeurIPS 2023, doc `8d5e1455…`). Quantizes first/second moments (smaller blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion, factorization) for fine-tuning. **Defects:** optimal quantization settings are probably task-dependent (not explored); evaluated only on language/vision tasks (RL, audio, graph untested); quantizing both moments causes a marginal accuracy drop; slower than 8-bit optimizers on small models without fused operators. LoRA is referenced in its fine-tuning context.
> 
> **3. One-stage, anchor-free part-body association detection** — *PBADet* (ICLR 2024, doc `08b70bc3…`). Single part-to-body center offset on COCO-style benchmarks (COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman, BodyHands) with AP, Precision/Recall/F1 vs ED-Pose. **Defects:** its advantage over anchor-based BPJDet shrinks on single-part tasks like CrowdHuman face-body association; performance depends on task-alignment loss and multi-scale offsets (ablations degrade without them); association branch adds complexity; qualitative generalization to animals only.
> 
> **4. Hierarchical Transformer + Diffusion + GNN generative pipeline** — *GenMS* (ICLR 2024, doc `277849d4…`). LLM (transformer) → chemical formulae → diffusion model → structures; GNN predicts formation energy, used in forward tree search for property-guided generation, DFT-verified. **Defects:** weak on complex structures (MXenes, Kagome lattices); no synthesizability check; target-property suggestions (batteries, semiconductors) still need experimental verification.
> 
> **5. Spectral interpretability of RNNs under E/I constraints** — *Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective* (NeurIPS 2023, doc `e63a94c4…`). Shows ColEI (sign-constrained excitatory/inhibitory) RNNs learn poorly due to multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra, not sign constraints. **Defects:** ColEI networks show high variance across initializations and instability without gradient clipping; performance worsens for small networks/few inhibitory units; only RNN/feedforward settings tested, without spiking models; spectral diagnosis is empirical, not theoretical.
> 
> **Additional relevant works for the "ideally also" criteria:** *LDReg* (doc `51526068…`) covers SSL feature embeddings, dimensional collapse, and ImageNet/COCO evaluation; *NEFTune* (doc `fad0fb20…`) covers noisy embeddings in instruction fine-tuning (works with QLoRA); *Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure* (doc `582d138d…`) analyzes LoRA-only fine-tuning (notes it does not induce the power-law Hessian structure that full fine-tuning does).
> 
> **Cross-cutting development defects:** The JEPA analysis and the spectral RNN work both rely on simplified/linear or initialization-dependent settings, limiting transfer; the 4-bit optimizer and GenMS both admit limited domain coverage (task/data-dependent, no experimental validation); PBADet's gains are task-specific rather than universal; LoRA-based fine-tuning may not reproduce full fine-tuning's learned structure, and SSL methods remain susceptible to (local) dimensional collapse.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, here are the papers that together cover the five requested topics, followed by a brief analysis of their development defects (limitations).
> 
> ## Matching papers
> 
> 1. **SSL objective analysis & implicit bias** — *Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features: A Deep Linear Network Analysis* (40fde037…): analyzes the implicit bias of JEPA/self-distillation vs MAE in deep linear networks (JEPA biased toward high-influence "slow" features, MAE toward high-variance/noisy ones). Note: the context compares JEPA (latent-space, MSE-like) vs MAE reconstruction; a direct explicit MSE-vs-cross-entropy comparison is not present.
> 
> 2. **Memory-efficient Adam/AdamW fine-tuning** — *4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States* (8d5e1455…): quantizes first/second moments (B128, rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion), covering LLaMA/RoBERTa/GPT-2 fine-tuning, and references LoRA.
> 
> 3. **One-stage anchor-free detection with Precision/F1** — *PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association Detection* (08b70bc3…): one-stage anchor-free detector on COCOHumanParts/BodyHands with part-to-body center offset, reporting Hand AP, Precision/Recall/F1.
> 
> 4. **Hierarchical Transformer+Diffusion+GNN generation** — *GenMS: Generative Hierarchical Materials Search* (277849d4…): LLM (transformer) proposes formulae → diffusion model generates structures → GNN predicts properties (formation energy) → forward tree search for property-guided generation.
> 
> 5. **Spectral interpretability of recurrent models under E/I constraints** — *Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly* (e63a94c4…): spectral (singular value) analysis of E/I-constrained RNNs, normalised SVD entropy as a predictor of performance.
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods
> 
> 1. **JEPA implicit bias analysis**: analysis restricted to deep *linear* networks with special balanced initialization and simultaneous-diagonalizability assumptions; doesn't rigorously extend to nonlinear models; the bias may make JEPA vulnerable to spurious/slow features; generalization to other joint-embedding architectures is left open.
> 
> 2. **4-bit optimizers**: optimal quantization setting appears task/dataset-dependent; evaluation limited to language/vision (RL, audio, graph learning untested); quantizing both moments causes a marginal accuracy drop; on smaller models the method is slower than 8-bit optimizers until fused operators are implemented.
> 
> 3. **PBADet**: its advantage over anchor-based BPJDet is less pronounced on single-part tasks (e.g., CrowdHuman face-body); performance depends on all components (association loss, multi-scale center offsets, task-alignment learning — removing any of them degrades metrics).
> 
> 4. **GenMS**: weaker on certain structure classes (MXenes, Kagome lattices); no synthesizability check; experimental/DFT validation still needed; relies on pretrained LLMs that lack low-level structural detail, hence the need for the diffusion/GNN hierarchy.
> 
> 5. **Dale's-law RNNs**: EI-partitioned (ColEI) networks show higher variance across initializations and are highly unstable without gradient clipping; the origin of the multimodal spectrum and why large ColEI networks learn well despite large maximal singular values remain open theoretical questions; results are limited to RNNs (not convolutional/spiking or more faithful E/I models).
> 
> The context does not establish a direct MSE-vs-CE objective comparison paper, nor dedicated papers explicitly combining "feature embeddings, End-to-end LoRA fine-tuning, and non-MNIST/CIFAR-100" evaluation across all five topics; only partial overlap exists (e.g., LoRA referenced in the 4-bit optimizer work, and ImageNet/LLaMA/COCO-level benchmarks rather than MNIST/CIFAR).

### paperscope:gap:226 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building a resource-constrained AI stack for materials discovery and human–robot interfaces: we need (a) self-supervised pretraining that avoids noisy features (MSE vs CE) before fine-tuning, (b) a one-stage anchor-free detector that associates hands/faces to bodies on COCO-like data with strong Precision/F1, (c) a language-to-structure generator that uses Transformers, Diffusion models, and a GNN to propose low-energy crystals, (d) Adam/AdamW variants with tiny optimizer states for efficient updates, and (e) guidance on designing EI-constrained RNNs with spectral diagnostics for interpretability. Which papers collectively address these needs, including tips for End-to-end LoRA fine-tuning?Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below are the development defects or stated limitations for each method, strictly as described in the papers themselves.
> 
> 1) PBADet (one-stage anchor-free part–body association)
> - Diminished advantage on single-part association: On CrowdHuman’s face–body association (only one part), the paper explicitly notes that “the advantages of our method over BPJDet are not as pronounced” compared to multi-part settings (Appendix A.1). In practice, PBADet’s strengths show up more clearly when multiple parts must be associated to a body.
> 
> 2) Learning with Dale’s Law in RNNs (ColEI vs. DANN; spectral perspective)
> - ColEI networks: learning defects tied to spectral pathologies
>   • Poor learning and high variance: ColEI RNNs “did not learn as well as DANNs and standard RNNs,” with worse final performance and larger variability across seeds (Fig. 2, §3.1).
>   • Instability without gradient clipping: “Gradient clipping benefitted ColEI networks substantially more,” and without clipping they are “highly unstable,” consistent with pathological singular value distributions (§3.1, Discussion).
>   • Sensitive to EI ratio and size: Reducing inhibitory units (larger E:I) worsens spectral clustering (lower normalised SVD entropy) and harms learning; small networks suffer more. Performance improves mainly in larger, more balanced networks (Figs. 5–7, §3.4).
>   • Spectral-radius tuning helps but does not close the gap: While ColEI can perform better at larger spectral radii ρ, it still does not match the best performance of DANNs/standard RNNs across ρ (§3.1).
> - Theoretical scope limitations of the analysis (for both ColEI and DANN conclusions)
>   • Assumptions restrict generality: Core theoretical results rely on deep linear RNNs, special balanced/orthogonal initializations, and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances (Assumption 3.1; lemmas/theorems in §3).
>   • Open questions remain: The origin of ColEI’s multimodal singular-value spectra and why large ColEI networks learn well despite large maximum singular values are left as open theoretical questions (Discussion).
> 
> 3) How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features (JEPA vs. MAE)
> - Scope and assumptions of the theory
>   • Limited setting: Results are restricted to deep linear networks with particular initializations and the simultaneously-diagonalizable case for Σxx and Σyx; generalizability to practical, non-linear settings “remains unexplored” (Limitations §6).
>   • Depth dependence: The “distinct implicit bias” (JEPA prioritizing high-regression-coefficient ‘influential’ features) “takes hold only when the encoder is deep and diminishes substantially when the encoder is shallow” (§1, §3.2), so shallow encoders lose this advantage.
>   • Data-model mismatch risk: The paper cautions that real data may deviate from simultaneous diagonalizability and that their claims’ applicability to general architectures and datasets is untested (Limitations §6).
> - Potential vulnerability of JEPA’s bias
>   • Sensitivity to spurious/slow features: The authors note that the bias towards predictive, low-variance (slow) features “may shed light on JEPAs vulnerability to spurious or slow features” (Discussion §7).
> - MAE’s reconstructive bias (for contrast)
>   • Tendency to emphasize high-variance (possibly uninformative) features, as also argued in recent literature; by design MAE’s prioritization is largely set by covariance λ rather than information content (Introduction, §3.2).
> 
> 4) Memory-Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States
> - Performance and applicability constraints
>   • Task-dependent quantization: The authors state “The optimal quantization setting probably depends on task, datasets, and training details,” implying extra tuning may be needed (Limitations §7).
>   • Domain coverage: Current evaluation is “limited to language and vision tasks;” applicability to reinforcement learning, audio, and graph learning is “still needs further study” (Limitations §7).
>   • Speed overhead without fused kernels: In measured wall-clock time, 4-bit AdamW can be slower than 8-bit baselines unless kernel fusion is applied (Table 4). The paper notes it “should match or surpass 8-bit optimizers after operator fusion,” but without fusion it’s a drawback.
> - Methodological caveats
>   • Rank-1 normalization is not universally superior: The appendix shows cases where Rank‑1 normalization approximates worse than small-block quantization, depending on distribution patterns (Appendix C.2, Figs. 24, 26, 28).
>   • Factorization applicability: The combined ‘4-bit Factor’ variant factorizes only 2D+ second-moment tensors; 1D moments still rely on quantization (Sec. 4.3, D.1), so memory savings are shape-dependent.
> 
> 5) GenMS: Generative Hierarchical Materials Search (language→formula→structure with GNN selection)
> - Explicitly stated limitations
>   • Difficulty with complex lattices: “Less effective in generating complex structures such as Mxenes and Kagome lattices” (Conclusion §5: Generating complex structures).
>   • Experimental impact not yet validated: While GenMS proposes viable candidates and low energies, its practical effectiveness in suggesting specific materials with target properties “requires further experimental verification” (Conclusion §5: Impact on experimental exploration).
>   • No synthesizability assessment: Synthesizability is not included in the pipeline; assessing it will require added tools and multimodal integrations (Conclusion §5: Synthesizability).
>   • Generalization to other chemical systems left open: Extension to molecules/proteins is only posited as future work (Conclusion §5: Extension to other chemical systems).
> - Heuristic selection risks and mitigations
>   • Potential heuristic exploitation: Using a learned energy GNN could exploit irregularities in out-of-manifold structures; the authors mitigate by using a GNN trained on unrelaxed structures and discarding samples with out-of-range predictions (§2.2). Nonetheless, this underscores a dependence on heuristic reliability rather than first-principles guarantees.
> 
> These are the stated defects and limitations drawn directly from the papers’ own descriptions of shortcomings, scope constraints, or open issues for their respective methods.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Papers that address each need
> 
> **(a) Noisy-feature-free self-supervised pretraining (MSE vs CE)** → *"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features: A Deep Linear Network Analysis"* (40fde037). It contrasts JEPA (MSE-style latent prediction) with MAE (reconstruction/CE-style) and shows JEPA is implicitly biased toward high-influence features, suppressing noise better; MAE's ordering depends mainly on eigenvalues. Complements it: *LDReg* (51526068) prevents local dimensional collapse that degrades downstream fine-tuning.
> 
> **(b) One-stage anchor-free detector for hand/face↔body association** → *PBADet* (08b70bc3). A single part-to-body center offset on anchor-free heads (YOLOv5/7). On COCO-HumanParts/BodyHands it beats BPJDet/HierR-CNN, and on COCO val it gives far higher Precision/Recall/F1 than ED-Pose for hands/feet (e.g., all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51).
> 
> **(c) Language-to-structure generator with Transformers+Diffusion+GNN** → *GenMS* (277849d4). An LLM generates candidate formulae, a diffusion model generates low-level structures (compact A×4 representation), and a GNN ranks them via forward tree search; produces low-formation-energy (DFT-verified) double perovskites/spinels from language.
> 
> **(d) Adam/AdamW variants with tiny optimizer states** → *4-bit Optimizers* (8d5e1455). Quantizes Adam/AdamW first/second moments to 4-bit (B128 block, rank-1/DE-0 linear, optional factorization), matching full-precision accuracy with up to 57.7% memory savings (LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU).
> 
> **(e) EI-constrained RNN design with spectral diagnostics** → *"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"* (e63a94c4). Shows EI (excitatory-inhibitory) RNNs fail mainly due to multimodal/dispersed singular-value spectra at initialization, not sign constraints; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) is a pre-training diagnostic that predicts performance.
> 
> **(End-to-end LoRA fine-tuning tips)** → *"Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure"* (582d138d): LoRA fine-tuning improves task performance but does *not* induce the power-law Hessian structure that full fine-tuning does, and the Hessian trace Tr(H) is a more reliable generalization indicator for LoRA adapters than the power-law slope. Supporting tips: *NEFTune* (fad0fb20) shows noisy embeddings (alpha/√(Ld), α≈10) improve instruction/QLoRA fine-tuning; *RTB* (756d1e62) shows LoRA plus stochastic timestep subsampling and batched gradient computation keeps diffusion fine-tuning memory-efficient.
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods
> 
> **(a) JEPA analysis**: limited to deep *linear* MLPs, requires special balanced-orthogonal initialization and simultaneous diagonalizability; only qualitative generalization is confirmed empirically. **LDReg**: LID estimation degrades in high dimensions and uses minibatch nearest neighbors; over-forcing low LID can trigger full collapse.
> 
> **(b) PBADet**: on CrowdHuman single-part face-body association its edge over BPJDet is small; body detection only reaches AP comparable (not superior) to DETR-style detectors; evaluations often use a COCO val subset with fixed ground-truth part boxes.
> 
> **(c) GenMS**: uniqueness is weak (<50% unique formulae for pyrochlore/spinel); weaker on MXenes/Kagome lattices; no synthesizability check, and experimental validation is still pending; direct LLM-to-structure baselines near 0% success show the framework is complex and hierarchical by necessity.
> 
> **(d) 4-bit optimizers**: optimal quantization settings may be task-dependent (only language/vision tasks tested); unfused implementations are slower than 8-bit on small models; quantizing both moments causes a marginal accuracy drop; factorized versions lose accuracy on some tasks (e.g., Swin-T ImageNet).
> 
> **(e) EI RNNs**: ColEI networks need gradient clipping, show high seed-to-seed variance and worse small-network behavior; sign constraints still cause some degradation even after fixing spectra; the origin of the multimodal ColEI spectrum and why large networks learn despite large σmax remain open.
> 
> **(LoRA/Hessian)**: LoRA's failure to reproduce full fine-tuning's power-law Hessian structure implies different (potentially weaker) generalization; the Hessian trace diverges from expected patterns on well-pretrained models, and computing Hessian spectra of SOTA LLMs is too expensive. **NEFTune**: gains rely on GPT-4-based judging, limited 30B/70B validation, and no conclusive mechanism. **RTB**: even with LoRA, full-trajectory gradients barely fit in memory; discrete-diffusion infilling is limited by a weak prior and reward models that favor repetition.

**community 最终答案**

> ## Papers addressing each need
> 
> **(a) Self-supervised pretraining avoiding noisy features** — *"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features"* (doc `40fde037…`). JEPA (predicting latent representations, MSE in latent space) is biased toward high-influence features and suppresses noise, whereas MAE (reconstruction MSE in data space) chases high-variance, often noisy, features. Note: the analysis compares MSE objectives (JEPA latent vs MAE reconstruction); **no CE-based pretraining comparison appears in the context**. Complement with *LDReg* (`51526068…`) to counter local dimensional collapse.
> 
> **(b) One-stage anchor-free part-body detector** — **PBADet** (`08b70bc3…`): one-stage, anchor-free, single part-to-body center offset associating hands/faces/feet to bodies. On COCO-HumanParts it outperforms BPJDet/HierR-CNN, and on COCO against ED-Pose it gives much higher Precision/Recall/F1 (e.g., left hand 37.63/60.82/46.50 vs 18.36/30.34/22.87).
> 
> **(c) Language-to-structure crystal generator** — **GenMS** (`277849d4…`): LLM proposes formulae → diffusion model (compact A×4 representation) generates structures → GNN predicts formation energy; forward tree search yields low-energy crystals (DFT-verified), satisfying user requests >80%.
> 
> **(d) Adam/AdamW with tiny optimizer states** — **4-bit Optimizers** (`8d5e1455…`): quantized 4-bit AdamW/Adam states (smaller blocks for m, rank-1 normalization + zero-point-excluded linear mapping for v, optional factorization), up to 57.7% memory savings with accuracy matching 32-bit, including LLaMA fine-tuning.
> 
> **(e) EI-constrained RNNs with spectral diagnostics** — *"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"* (`e63a94c4…`): ColEI RNNs learn poorly due to multimodal/dispersed singular-value spectra at initialization, not just sign constraints; **normalised SVD entropy (NSE)** predicts training performance and guides EI architecture design (DANN-style networks keep healthy spectra).
> 
> **End-to-end LoRA fine-tuning tips (context sources)**:
> - **NEFTune** (`fad0fb20…`): add noise α/√(Ld) to embeddings during LoRA/QLoRA instruction tuning — AlpacaEval 29.8→64.7%, reduces overfitting (α=10, uniform noise, longer sequences; dropout/weight decay don't replicate the gains).
> - **4-bit optimizers**: use 4-bit AdamW states for LoRA fine-tuning for memory savings without hurting LLaMA instruction tuning.
> - **Hessian structure** (`582d138d…`): LoRA-only fine-tuning does **not** induce the power-law Hessian spectrum that full fine-tuning does — treat Hessian trace Tr(H) (not power-law slope) as the more reliable generalization indicator during LoRA adaptation.
> - **Agreement-on-the-Line** (`f6089dba…`): random LoRA initialization supplies model diversity giving reliable ID/OOD agreement lines, aligning with full fine-tuning under random heads.
> - **RTB** (`756d1e62…`): LoRA for diffusion fine-tuning with stochastic timestep subsampling and batched gradients to stay memory-efficient.
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods
> 
> - **(a) JEPA paper**: analysis restricted to deep *linear* MLPs with special balanced orthogonal init and simultaneous diagonalizability; only qualitatively extended to real networks. LDReg: LID estimation degrades in high dimensions and relies on minibatch nearest neighbors; forcing very low LID collapses representations.
> - **(b) PBADet**: advantage over BPJDet is small on CrowdHuman's single-part face task; anchor-free/low-recall tradeoff; metrics mostly VOC AP@0.5 and mMR−2, and the authors elsewhere argue COCO AP misleads class-agnostic detection (HASSOD); depends on COCO-style part annotations.
> - **(c) GenMS**: weak on MXenes/Kagome lattices; uniqueness of generated formulae <50% for pyrochlore/spinel; no synthesizability check and no experimental validation; LLM prompting baselines often produce invalid/unusable structures.
> - **(d) 4-bit optimizers**: optimal quantization likely task-dependent; tested only on language/vision (not RL/audio/graph); un-fused implementation slower than 8-bit on small models; small accuracy drop when quantizing both moments.
> - **(e) Dale's Law RNNs**: ColEI networks train worse and with higher variance (needing gradient clipping); sign constraints themselves still impair learning; NSE diagnostic is computed only at initialization; small networks with few inhibitory units have pathological spectra.
> - **LoRA-related**: NEFTune's evaluation relies on GPT-4 judging with no conclusive mechanism or safety analysis; Hessian study can't cover SOTA LLMs (cost) and LoRA's divergent Hessian behavior signals possibly different generalization than full FT; 4-bit quantization optimality is task-dependent; AGL depends on specific diversity sources and settings.

### paperscope:gap:229 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that, taken together, cover: (1) one-stage, anchor‑free part–body association evaluated on COCO/COCO‑WholeBody style benchmarks; (2) the implicit bias of label‑free representation learning (JEPA/self‑distillation) versus masked reconstruction, contrasting MSE vs cross‑entropy losses and using cosine similarity on feature embeddings; (3) spectral analyses of excitatory–inhibitory recurrent deep networks for time‑series modeling, explaining stability via singular‑value properties; (4) memory‑efficient training via 4‑bit optimizer states for Adam/AdamW and stochastic gradient methods, including end‑to‑end LoRA fine‑tuning; and (5) diffusion models with Transformer‑based conditional guidance that improve cross‑domain deepfake detection, using attention and reporting Precision/F1. Prefer works that reference COCO, use SGD/Adam variants, and discuss practical architectures (e.g., ResNet‑50/ViT).Please analyze the development defects of these methods.
