**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> {'answer': 'Below are the main development defects or limitations explicitly reported (or directly implied by the authors’ formulations and experiments) for each method/paper.\n\n1) PBADet (One-stage anchor-free part–body association detector)\n- Gains depend on multi-part association: The advantages over BPJDet are “not as pronounced” on single-part tasks such as face–body association in CrowdHuman, where only one part is involved (authors’ own finding).\n- Formulation relies on anchor-free positive samples within bounding boxes: Training and decoding assume that any anchor point inside a part box also belongs to the body box; at inference, the body is selected among those that “enclose the part.” This design constraint can be brittle in cases where part boxes extend beyond body boxes (as reflected in their decoding rule), and requires careful NMS and threshold selection (authors specify τconf/τiou per dataset).\n- Evaluation scope and outputs: The method focuses on bounding boxes (not segmentation or keypoint heatmaps) and was evaluated mainly on BodyHands, COCO-HumanParts, and CrowdHuman; benefits on broader association types or dense occlusion scenarios are not shown in the paper.\n\n2) Learning better with Dale’s Law (recurrent EI networks; ColEI vs. DANN)\n- Theoretical scope limitations: Results are derived for deep linear networks with special, balanced initializations and simultaneously diagonalizable Σxx and Σyx; the authors explicitly note these are strong assumptions and the generalization to realistic non-linear settings remains unexplored (Limitations section).\n- ColEI performance defects: Column-wise EI-constrained RNNs (“ColEI”) train poorly overall, show higher variance across seeds, and are highly unstable without gradient clipping (empirical findings). Performance degrades for small networks and when the ratio of excitatory to inhibitory units is large (few inhibitory units), with “pathological” multimodal singular value spectra.\n- Sensitivity to spectrum and network size: The method shows large maximum singular values and requires spectral properties (high Normalised SVD Entropy) to predict trainability. Small or imbalanced EI networks yield dispersed spectra correlated with worse learning (authors’ main result).\n- Open theoretical questions: The origin of multimodal spectra in ColEI and why large ColEI networks learn well despite increasing max singular value are acknowledged as open issues (Discussion).\n\n3) How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features (deep linear self-distillation analysis)\n- Analytical setting limitations: Theoretical results rely on deep linear encoders/decoders, special initializations, and the strong assumption that Σxx and Σyx are simultaneously diagonalizable; authors state generalizability to non-linear, practical training remains untested (Limitations section).\n- Depth dependence and bias: The JEPA objective’s beneficial bias (toward high regression-coefficient features that avoid noisy pixels) emerges only with sufficiently deep encoders; for shallow encoders (L=1), the advantage largely vanishes (Corollary and experiments). This implies sensitivity to network depth.\n- Potential vulnerability to “slow/spurious” features: The authors discuss that JEPA’s implicit bias toward slowly varying, influential features may render it vulnerable to spurious or slow signals (Discussion), even though this can also help avoid noisy pixels.\n- Collapse avoidance is architectural: Non-contrastive JEPA requires mechanisms like StopGrad to avoid trivial collapse; the analysis assumes such design is in place.\n\n4) Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States\n- Zero-point problem in second moment: Quantizing the second moment with mappings that include zero (e.g., DE with zero) causes catastrophic deviations in update directions (the inverse square root explodes), necessitating special mappings (DE-0 or linear) and careful normalization (authors’ own identification and fix).\n- Rank-1 normalization is not universally superior: Empirical histograms show rank‑1 normalization can outperform or underperform block-wise normalization depending on distribution structure (Appendix C.2), so choice is task/data dependent.\n- Task-specific tuning: Authors state that “optimal quantization setting probably depends on task, datasets, and training details,” and their evaluation is limited to language and vision benchmarks; applicability to RL, audio, and graph tasks is untested (Limitations section).\n- Practical exclusions and overheads: They do not quantize small tensors (≤4096) and often exclude embedding layers; factorization is applied only to ≥2D second-moment tensors, implying implementation complexity and some residual memory overheads.\n- Pretraining parity not guaranteed: While finetuning results are typically lossless, pretraining (e.g., image classification, translation) is only “comparable,” not uniformly equal to 32‑bit baselines (main results table), indicating residual performance gap in some settings.\n\n5) VLM4Bio (Benchmark dataset for trait discovery)\n- Coverage limitations: Only three organism groups (fish, birds, butterflies) are included. Trait grounding/referring are annotated on subsets (Fish‑500 and Bird‑500), limiting breadth of traits and images (Dataset description).\n- Class imbalance and image biases: Fish‑10K and Butterfly‑10K are imbalanced and drawn from museum collections with artificial backgrounds and artifacts, while Bird‑10K (CUB subset) has in‑the‑wild backgrounds that likely align with common training data of VLMs; this can inflate bird performance and depress museum-image performance (Results and Dataset distribution figures).\n- Label noise acknowledged: Manual curation plus source-label reliance may introduce noise; authors explicitly acknowledge potential label noise and plan future cleaning (Limitations section).\n- Model coverage limits: Proprietary VLMs requiring paid APIs (e.g., Gemini variants, Claude Opus) are not evaluated; thus, benchmark comparisons exclude some leading systems (Limitations section).\n- Zero-shot focus: The evaluation centers on zero-shot VLMs; finetuning/RAG or knowledge-infused prompting is left to future work, so practical utility may be understated for models that benefit from domain finetuning (Conclusion/Future Work).\n\nThese defects are taken directly from the authors’ methodological choices, stated limitations, experimental scope, and empirical findings across the five works.'}

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the available documents, the pieces map to these papers:
> 
> 1. **Species classification + trait grounding/counting/reasoning benchmark (Transformer/VLM-based)** — **VLM4Bio** (doc `29594c71…`): covers species classification, trait identification (fins, beaks etc.), trait grounding/referring, trait counting, and reasoning tests (CoT, FCT, NOTA) on museum fish/bird/butterfly images.
> 2. **Low-memory fine-tuning / parameter-efficient updates** — **4-bit Optimizers** (doc `8d5e1455…`): 4-bit optimizer states for Adam/AdamW (up to ~57.7% memory savings, LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU); **NFTS** (doc `aa60be77…`): NAS over adapters/frozen layers for parameter-efficient few-shot fine-tuning of ViT/ResNet.
> 3. **Stable RNN with biological E/I dynamics** — **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (doc `e63a94c4…`): recurrent Dale's ANNs (DANN) and ColEI networks aligned with excitation/inhibition balance.
> 4. **Self-supervised pretraining avoiding noisy pixels** — **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (doc `40fde037…`): JEPA/self-distillation implicitly prefers high-influence features over pixel noise vs MAE reconstruction; **LDReg** (doc `51526068…`) additionally counters local dimensional collapse.
> 5. **Anchor-free part-to-whole detector with COCO-style evaluation** — **PBADet** (doc `08b70bc3…`): one-stage anchor-free part-body association (part-to-body center offset), evaluated with COCO AP/AR, Precision/Recall/F1.
> 6. **Rigorous VLM reasoning/trait-grounding benchmark** — **VLM4Bio** again, plus PBADet's Precision/Recall/F1 metrics.
> 
> **Development defects of these methods:**
> 
> - **VLM4Bio**: uses only micro-averaged accuracy — it does **not** report F1/Precision/AUROC as you require; limited to three taxa (no amphibians/mammals); possible label noise; background removal via GroundingDINO/SAM can introduce artifacts/bias; fish/butterfly sets are class-imbalanced (rare species underrepresented); VLMs struggle badly with grounding/referring and counting (can identify "eye" but fail to localize it); GPT-4V often refuses/"Other" answers rather than answering; prompting helps only larger models (CoT/dense captions hurt smaller ones); no Gemini/Claude evaluated.
> - **4-bit optimizers**: optimal quantization is task-dependent; 4-bit approximation of moments has outlier patterns a block-wise quantizer can't capture; second-moment zero-point problem; sublinear-memory baselines (Adafactor/SM3) still degrade accuracy; validated only on language/vision tasks.
> - **NFTS**: expensive evolutionary search; per-layer decisions are complex/no simple pattern (risks over-tuning to the source domain); same meta-test hyperparameters across domains; combining adapters with full fine-tuning was needed — adapter-only variants underperform.
> - **Dale's Law RNNs**: simple E/I (ColEI) partitioning inherently impairs learning (multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectrum; worse with few inhibitory units or small networks), requiring gradient clipping; DANN needs post-update weight clipping; E/I sign constraints limit the solution space.
> - **JEPA (noisy-feature avoidance)**: non-contrastive self-distillation is susceptible to representation collapse without stop-grad; theoretical guarantees hold only for deep linear nets with special initialization/diagonalizability; MAE still prioritizes high-variance pixel subspaces; needs predictor/EMA machinery.
> - **LDReg**: local intrinsic dimensionality estimation degrades in high dimensions and relies on minibatch nearest neighbors; over-regularizing (forcing very low LID) can trigger complete collapse; global covariance/variance regularizers barely helped.
> - **PBADet**: anchor-free detection generally has lower recall than anchor-based counterparts; part-to-body offset can fall far outside part anchor boxes; gains shrink on single-part tasks (face-body on CrowdHuman); without the association loss, association falls back to heuristic Euclidean matching; the whole-part hierarchy can misalign with human perception (overlapping similar objects, heterogeneous wholes, text fail), and it argues COCO AP is misleading for class-agnostic detection (advocates AR instead).
> 
> So no single paper covers your pipeline end-to-end: VLM4Bio gives the tasks/benchmark, and the training-efficiency, E/I-RNN, SSL, and detector pieces each come from separate papers with the defects above.

**community 最终答案**

> ## Papers covering each piece
> 
> 1. **VLM4Bio** (`29594c71…`) — VLM benchmark on museum fish/bird/butterfly images covering exactly your tasks: species classification, trait identification (fins, beak traits), trait grounding/referring (bounding boxes), trait counting, plus reasoning tests (Chain-of-Thought, Dense Caption, False Confidence Test, None-of-the-Above). Evaluates 12 VLMs (GPT-4V, LLaVA, BioCLIP, etc.).
> 2. **4-bit Optimizers** (`8d5e1455…`) — low-memory fine-tuning: compresses Adam/AdamW optimizer states to 4-bit (with LoRA/delta-tuning context), enabling LLaMA-7B fine-tuning on one 80GB GPU.
> 3. **Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly** (`e63a94c4…`) — stable E/I-aligned RNNs: compares standard RNNs, column-constrained E/I (ColEI) and Dale's ANNs (DANN) via spectral analysis (normalised SVD entropy), explaining training instability.
> 4. **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features** (`40fde037…`) — self-supervised pretraining that avoids latching onto noisy pixels: shows JEPA self-distillation biases toward high-influence features vs MAE reconstructing pixels.
> 5. **PBADet** (`08b70bc3…`) — one-stage **anchor-free** detector for part-to-body association (a single part-to-body center offset), evaluated on COCO-HumanParts/BodyHands/CrowdHuman/AnimalPose with AP, Precision, Recall, F1.
> 
> Note: no paper in the collection reports **AUROC** for trait grounding; VLM4Bio uses micro-averaged accuracy, and PBADet uses AP/F1/Precision/Recall.
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods
> 
> **VLM4Bio**
> - Only three taxa; possible label noise; Gemini/Claude not tested.
> - Fish-10K/Butterfly-10K are imbalanced (bias toward common species like *Heliconius*), limiting rare-class conclusions; background removed with SAM, introducing artificial backgrounds/imaging artifacts.
> - Reports only micro-averaged accuracy — no F1/Precision/AUROC; zero-shot evaluation only.
> - All VLMs drop sharply on grounding/referring/counting vs identification; CoT/context only helps large models (GPT-4V/4o), not LLaVA/BLIP; GPT-4V produces many "Other" responses (refusals, "insufficient data"), and smaller models are error-prone.
> 
> **4-bit Optimizers**
> - Optimal quantization is task-dependent; validated only on language/vision tasks; moment outlier patterns are complex, so block-wise 4-bit approximation can degrade accuracy in untested settings and needs stochastic rounding/rank-1 factorization to stay competitive.
> 
> **E/I RNN**
> - ColEI networks learn worse and with higher variance across all four benchmarks; gradient clipping only mitigates the deficit.
> - Small networks with few inhibitory units worsen spectra and performance; analysis limited to RNNs (not conv/feedforward/spiking), no I→I connections, and the paper diagnoses the problem but does not provide the improved ColEI initialization (left as future work).
> 
> **JEPA**
> - Analysis restricted to deep *linear* networks, special balanced-orthogonal initialization, and simultaneous diagonalizability; the noise-avoidance claim is only qualitatively supported by ImageNet experiments.
> - The bias favors high *regression-coefficient* features — if noise is influential, suppression is not guaranteed; the flickering-image model shows a noise-vs-temporal-correlation trade-off.
> 
> **PBADet**
> - Anchor-free dense prediction historically yields lower recall than anchor-based detectors; per-pixel heads add compute.
> - On single-part tasks (face–body, CrowdHuman) its advantage over BPJDet shrinks; performance depends on ablations (association loss, multi-scale offsets, task-alignment) — removing any degrades results; animal (AP-10K/AnimalPose) results are qualitative only; occluded/invisible parts limit part detection even though the part-to-body offset stays valid.

### paperscope:gap:265 — 同轮数、更多概览仍不能保证缺陷细节齐全

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively address principled uncertainty and inductive-bias–aware learning across deep networks: (a) distributional approaches and ensemble disagreement for exploration in reinforcement learning, (b) joint-embedding self-distillation that prioritizes informative features in self-supervised learning, (c) spectral or structural constraints (e.g., excitatory/inhibitory partitions) that affect RNN training dynamics, (d) anytime-valid calibration that controls prediction risk under adaptive data collection, and (e) anchor-free perception models that associate human parts to bodies in images. Prefer works that use standard optimizers (SGD/Adam), common losses (cross-entropy or mean squared error), CNN/Transformer backbones, and evaluations on familiar vision benchmarks (e.g., COCO, MNIST), reporting metrics like precision/F1 or AUROC and analyzing feature embeddings or cosine similarity.Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

**score：4→2（Δ-2）；rounds：3→3（Δ+0）。**

两边都为 3 轮，naive 9 次工具、community 8 次工具，overview 12→65；两边都找到 PE-DQN、JEPA、Dale’s-law、RCPS 和 PBADet。community 将篇幅用于重新介绍论文与补充 LDReg，但 judge 指出投影偏差/收缩条件、预测器反噬、深度依赖等缺项。naive 第二轮读了 RCPS 文档，community 第二轮只读 PE-DQN、JEPA、PBADet，体现核验重心不同。不能据此断言全部 −2 分都是社区噪声：两份答案共同存在若干未展开细节，judge 对遗漏重要性的尺度也需要复核。

<details>
<summary>展开完整 gold 与两份最终答案</summary>

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> - PBADet (ICLR 2024, one-stage anchor-free part–body association)
>   - Advantage not pronounced in single-part association: On CrowdHuman’s face–body (single-part) task, the paper notes PBADet’s advantage over BPJDet is “not as pronounced” as in multi-part settings, indicating limited benefit in scenarios with only one part class.
>   - Sensitivity to design choices: Ablations show removing task-alignment learning or the multi-scale formulation degrades Conditional Accuracy and Joint AP, implying dependence on these components and associated hyperparameters (e.g., K, α, β for anchor assignment; λ weights for losses; NMS thresholds).
>   - Operational tuning overhead: The method relies on several hand-set hyperparameters (loss weights λiou, λdfl, λcls, λassoc; scaling factor λ; multiple NMS thresholds per class/dataset), which the paper specifies but must be tuned per dataset.
> 
> - Dale’s Law in RNNs (NeurIPS 2023: ColEI vs. recurrent DANNs)
>   - ColEI (column excitatory–inhibitory partition) defects:
>     - Poor and unstable learning: Empirically underperforms standard RNNs and DANNs across tasks, with higher variance across seeds and pronounced instability without gradient clipping.
>     - Spectral pathology: Multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra (with large modes) cause training pathologies; learning worsens for small networks and for biologically realistic E:I ratios (few inhibitory units).
>     - Sensitivity to network size/E:I ratio: Performance and spectrum improve only with larger models and more balanced E:I; small networks and fewer I units lead to degraded learning.
>   - Recurrent DANNs: While they learn well, they require specific reparameterization and initialization to maintain Dale’s Law; the paper emphasizes performance hinges on having “good” spectral properties rather than merely imposing sign constraints.
> 
> - JEPA vs. MAE (NeurIPS 2024, deep linear self-distillation)
>   - Restricted theoretical setting: Main results rely on deep linear networks, gradient flow, small-initialization regime, and especially the simultaneously diagonalizable assumption for Σxx and Σyx; the paper explicitly notes real data “significantly deviate” from these assumptions, so generalization to nonlinear, practical settings is unproven.
>   - Depth-dependent benefit: JEPA’s desirable implicit bias (prioritizing influential/high-ρ features) “takes hold only when the encoder is deep” and diminishes for shallow encoders, limiting applicability when using shallow backbones.
>   - Potential vulnerability to slow/spurious features: The discussion highlights JEPA’s tendency to focus on slow features, noting possible vulnerability to spurious or slow signals.
> 
> - Active, anytime-valid RCPS (NeurIPS 2024)
>   - IID requirement and distribution shift: Guarantees are derived under i.i.d. data; the paper acknowledges extending to distribution shift (e.g., covariate/label shift) is future work, so safety under shifting test-time distributions is not covered.
>   - Label-policy constraints: The theory requires a lower bound on labeling probability (q_min) and a bounded labeling policy (Assumption 2); in practice, such bounds may be hard to ensure, and optimal policies may not exist under all constraints.
>   - Dependence on predictor quality: The predictor-based variance reduction can backfire—“bad predictions can increase the variance… and lead to slower growth of the e-process,” delaying risk certification.
>   - Regret bounds are conditional: Growth-rate/regret guarantees hinge on accurate estimation of the optimal labeling policy and predictor; deviations directly degrade the wealth process, potentially slowing or weakening anytime-valid guarantees.
> 
> - Diverse Projection Ensembles for Distributional RL (ICLR 2024; PE-DQN)
>   - Residual approximation bias: Projections (categorical/quantile) induce irreducible approximation errors; even at the fixed point, ensemble disagreement does not vanish, and optimism bonuses can persist unless the number of atoms K is increased (the paper provides explicit bounds).
>   - Disagreement targets TD error, not true return error: With shared TD targets, raw ensemble disagreement reflects distributional TD error rather than error to the true return distribution; an extra uncertainty propagation scheme is required to align bonuses with true epistemic uncertainty.
>   - Convergence depends on projection contractivity: Theoretical guarantees require the combined operator Ω_M T^π to be a contraction (c̄_p γ < 1); if constituent projections are not sufficiently non-expansive in aggregate, the guarantee does not apply.
>   - Exploration bonus sensitivity: The paper notes β is a sensitive parameter for UCB-style exploration (wrong β can “prevent proper convergence”); they resort to a decay schedule across tasks, indicating tuning burden.
>   - Ensemble overhead: Although smaller than some baselines, the method fundamentally requires multiple distributional models and computing average 1‑Wasserstein disagreements and propagated bonuses, adding computational and implementation complexity.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the context, here are the five papers and an analysis of their development defects:
> 
> **(a) PE-DQN – "Diverse Projection Ensembles for Distributional Reinforcement Learning" (ICLR 2024)**
> Distributional RL using ensembles of categorical/quantile projections; exploration bonus = ensemble disagreement (average 1-Wasserstein distance) propagated via distributional TD errors.
> Development defects:
> - Only uniform mixtures over ensembles are considered; no mechanism to exploit strengths of particular models in specific state-action regions.
> - With TD backups, ensemble disagreement measures error w.r.t. the bootstrapped target, not the true return distribution, so uncertainty quantification is only indirect (motivates the whole propagation scheme).
> - The exploration bonus is only expected to vanish in the limit of infinite iterations; no guarantee of bounded-error calibration in practice.
> - Evaluated only on bsuite/VizDoom; no standard vision benchmarks (COCO/MNIST), no feature-embedding/cosine-similarity analysis; uses CNN DQN rather than Transformer backbones.
> 
> **(b) "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks" (NeurIPS 2024)**
> Joint-embedding self-distillation analysis showing JEPA prioritizes high-influence (informative, low-noise) features while MAE prioritizes high-variance features.
> Development defects:
> - Theory restricted to deep linear MLPs, balanced-orthogonal initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances Σyx, Σxx; real data distributions deviate substantially from this assumption.
> - Generalization to nonlinear models/practical scenarios remains unexplored; the implicit bias also makes JEPA vulnerable to spurious or slow features.
> - Only ImageNet CCA-based experiments confirm the mechanism; no precision/F1/AUROC-style downstream metrics, no standard loss-based training analysis (uses gradient-flow ODEs rather than SGD/Adam).
> 
> **(c) "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023)**
> Spectral/structural analysis of excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) partitions in RNNs (ColEI vs DANN vs standard RNNs).
> Development defects:
> - Simple column-constrained E/I partitioning (ColEI) trains substantially worse, with higher variance across seeds, multimodal/dispersed singular-value spectra, and instability without gradient clipping.
> - Performance degrades further for small networks and fewer inhibitory units; sign constraints themselves also impair learning (though less than spectra).
> - Analysis limited to 1-layer RNNs (100 units) on adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and object recognition; no CNN/Transformer backbones, no COCO-scale evaluation, no embedding/cosine-similarity analysis, and the origin of ColEI multimodal spectra and why large ColEI networks learn well despite large σmax remain open.
> 
> **(d) "Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets" (NeurIPS 2024)**
> Extends RCPS to anytime-valid, active-labeling settings, guaranteeing simultaneous risk control on adaptively collected data via e-processes/betting.
> Development defects:
> - Guarantees hold only under the i.i.d. assumption; distribution shift (covariate/label shift) at test time is not handled.
> - Requires bounded label-policy assumptions (Assumption 2) and an existence assumption (Prop. 5); authors note these could be removed with more careful analysis.
> - Risk is controlled only in expectation (miscoverage rate); stronger average-sense guarantees via empirical Bernstein supermartingales are left as future work.
> - It is a calibration wrapper (no SGD/Adam training, no CNN/Transformer losses, no embedding analysis); experiments limited to simulations and ImageNet miscoverage, reporting violation rates and β̂t rather than precision/F1 or AUROC.
> 
> **(e) PBADet – "A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association" (ICLR 2024)**
> Anchor-free detector using a single part-to-body center offset to associate parts (hands, feet, face) with bodies.
> Development defects:
> - One-to-one part→body correspondence becomes invalid/less effective when parts are invisible or occluded (the failure mode it highlights in BPJDet's body-to-part offsets is only partially solved; multi-part occlusion remains a challenge).
> - On the single-part CrowdHuman face-body task, its advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced; anchor-free detection relies on points inside boxes and shows lower recall than anchor-based counterparts in general.
> - Evaluated on COCO-HumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman with AP/precision/recall/F1 and MR-2; no AUROC, no explicit feature-embedding/cosine-similarity analysis; uses YOLOv5/YOLOv7 CNN backbones (task-alignment + classification/regression losses), not Transformer backbones.
> 
> **Cross-cutting development defects:** All five are evaluated on limited or non-overlapping benchmarks (bsuite/VizDoom, ImageNet, MNIST/PTB, COCO-HumanParts), with none reporting AUROC or detailed feature-embedding/cosine-similarity diagnostics except the JEPA paper (CCA on ImageNet). None combines standard SGD/Adam training with all the requested common losses, and each has restrictive assumptions (linear models, i.i.d. data, uniform ensembles, sign/spectral constraints, one-to-one part correspondence) that limit robustness and generalization.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, here are the matching papers and an analysis of their development defects.
> 
> ## Papers found (one per topic)
> 
> **(a) Distributional RL + ensemble disagreement for exploration**
> - **PE-DQN / "Projection Ensembles for Deep Q-Learning"** (ICLR 2024, doc `5ebc98c7...`): diverse projection ensembles (categorical/quantile) with 1-Wasserstein disagreement bonus, tested on bsuite and VizDoom.
> 
> **(b) Joint-embedding self-distillation prioritizing informative features**
> - **"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024, doc `40fde037...`): shows JEPA biases toward high-influence, low-noise (slow) features vs MAE.
> - Related: **LDReg** (`51526068...`) regularizes local dimensional collapse in SSL (SimCLR/BYOL/MAE).
> 
> **(c) Spectral/structural constraints (excitatory/inhibitory) in RNNs**
> - **"Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly"** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `e63a94c4...`): ColEI E/I partitioning impairs learning due to multimodal singular-value spectra, not sign constraints.
> 
> **(d) Anytime-valid calibration / risk control under adaptive collection**
> - **"Active, Anytime-Valid Risk Controlling Prediction Sets"** (NeurIPS 2024, doc `cda0aa75...`): e-process/betting-based RCPS valid under adaptive (active) labeling, tested on ImageNet.
> 
> **(e) Anchor-free human part–body association**
> - **PBADet** (ICLR 2024, doc `08b70bc3...`): one-stage anchor-free part-to-body center offset; COCOHumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman; YOLOv5/v7 backbones.
> 
> ## Development defects / limitations
> 
> **(a) PE-DQN**: Only uniform mixtures over distributional ensembles are considered — no adaptive/non-uniform weighting to exploit model strengths in specific state-action regions; limited to categorical and quantile projections (no other representation families); ensemble disagreement can be biased to distributional TD errors rather than true return errors, requiring an elaborate uncertainty-propagation scheme; exploration bonuses must vanish asymptotically for convergence, so the method targets the exploration regime specifically.
> 
> **(b) JEPA paper**: Theory restricted to deep *linear* MLPs, a special (balanced orthogonal) initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances Σyx, Σxx — a strong assumption real data likely violates; generalization to non-linear models and non-diagonalizable distributions is unproven (only qualitative ImageNet-1K support via CCA); implicit bias toward slow/low-variance features could be a vulnerability to spurious or slow features. **LDReg**: LID estimation degrades in high dimensions and uses minibatch nearest neighbors; forcing very low LID triggers complete collapse; global covariance/variance regularizers barely help, showing the defect is hard to correct with existing losses.
> 
> **(c) Dale's Law RNNs**: ColEI networks show high variance across seeds, need gradient clipping (unstable otherwise), and have pathological dispersed/multimodal spectra — an initialization defect that predicts poor training via normalized SVD entropy; the origin of the multi-modal spectrum and why large ColEI nets learn well despite large singular values remain open; only ReLU 1-layer RNNs studied; DANN and ColEI have different neurobiological interpretations, so results don't fully transfer between E/I modeling choices.
> 
> **(d) Anytime-valid RCPS**: Assumes i.i.d. data — no coverage of test-time distribution shift (covariate/label shift); requires bounded label policies (Assumption 2) and an existence assumption (Prop. 5); control is in an average-risk sense with no stronger guarantees under realistic distributional assumptions; label-efficiency gains depend on learned/pretrained policies whose deviation from log-optimality only enters via regret bounds.
> 
> **(e) PBADet**: Advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced for single-part (face-body on CrowdHuman) tasks; qualitative unreliability for limb parts (legs/arms) can obscure body-part relationships; ablations show the association loss is essential (conditional accuracy drops from 92.62 to 80.78 without it), multi-scale offsets and task-alignment each matter — i.e., performance is sensitive to these design components; association relies on anchor points inside part boxes, inheriting the anchor-free dense-inference assumption that all such points are positive samples.
> 
> Note: the collection contains no single paper spanning all five topics; the above set collectively covers them. Some requested preferences (e.g., AUROC/cosine-similarity analyses) are not reported in these works, and metrics are instead regret/AP/F1/conditional accuracy etc.

</details>

### paperscope:gap:268 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building an end-to-end system where a robot must read hand/pose cues from cameras, explore a new environment safely, and provide predictions with statistically controlled risk while learning on the fly. I need: a robust anchor-free detector that links body parts to the correct person (COCO-scale images, CNN/Transformer backbones, CE/MSE training with Adam/SGD); an exploration module that uses distributional value functions and ensemble diversity to handle epistemic vs. aleatoric uncertainty; a recurrent controller whose stability benefits from biologically inspired E/I constraints and good spectral properties; a self-supervised pretraining recipe (joint-embedding) that avoids noisy features in learned representations; and an anytime-valid calibration method that guarantees low risk under adaptive labeling. Can you point me to research that ties these pieces together and reports standard metrics like precision/F1 or AUROC on benchmarks (e.g., MNIST/COCO), leveraging feature embeddings and cosine similarity?Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

<details>
<summary>展开完整 gold 与两份最终答案</summary>

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> - PBADet (one-stage anchor-free part–body association detector)
>   - Advantages are not pronounced on single-part association tasks: the authors explicitly note that in the CrowdHuman face–body association (a singular, one-part case), PBADet’s benefits over BPJDet are “not as pronounced” compared to multi-part settings. This reveals a scenario where the proposed design provides limited gains (Appendix A.1).
>   - Sensitivity to task-alignment and multi-scale supervision: ablations show that removing task-alignment learning or multi-scale anchor points degrades conditional accuracy and joint AP. The method’s performance is therefore dependent on these components (Table 4).
>   - Dataset- and pipeline-specific tuning: inference relies on dataset-specific NMS thresholds (different τ_conf and τ_iou for BodyHands vs. COCOHumanParts) and tuned loss/assignment hyperparameters (K, α, β, λ), indicating non-trivial per-dataset calibration needs (Section 3.3–3.4; Implementation Specifics).
>   - Heavy training resources and pretrained backbone dependence: training uses 4×V100 GPUs, AMP over 100 epochs, and relies on pretrained YOLO weights. This raises practical development costs and ties results to specific CNN/YOLO backbones (Implementation Specifics).
> 
> - Dale’s Law RNNs (ColEI vs. recurrent DANNs)
>   - ColEI (simple column-wise E/I sign constraints) learns poorly and is unstable: it exhibits multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra with large singular values, leading to exploding/vanishing gradients, high variance across seeds, and strong dependence on gradient clipping (Figures 2–3; text in Section 3.1–3.3).
>   - Strong sensitivity to EI ratio and network size: small networks and few inhibitory units reduce normalised SVD entropy (NSE) and impair learning; larger E/I imbalance worsens spectral properties and performance (Figures 5–6; text in Section 3.4).
>   - Performance depends on spectral radius and special initialisation: ColEI requires setting spectral radius (e.g., 1.5) and specific initialisation schemes to function at all; performance still lags behind DANNs and standard RNNs across tasks (Figure 2; Appendix).
>   - DANNs mitigate sign-constraint harms but still rely on initial spectral properties: the paper shows performance gains stem mainly from better spectra rather than sign constraints alone; achieving good spectra and NSE remains a prerequisite (Section 3.3–3.4).
> 
> - JEPA vs. MAE (deep linear analysis of self-distillation and reconstruction)
>   - Applicability limited by theoretical setting: the main claims rely on deep linear networks and simultaneously diagonalizable Σ_xx and Σ_yx; generalisation to non-linear encoders and real data distributions remains unproven (Section 6: Limitations).
>   - JEPA’s beneficial bias requires depth: the distinctive bias towards influential (high-regression-coefficient) features diminishes substantially with shallow encoders, reducing JEPA’s advantage versus MAE (Corollary 3.6; Section 3.2–3.3).
>   - Potential vulnerability to spurious/slow features: the authors caution that JEPA’s implicit bias can favour slowly varying or spurious features, which may be undesirable depending on the task (Section 7: Discussion).
>   - MAE prioritises high-variance features: reconstruction-based methods tend to learn subspaces that explain bulk variance, which may yield uninformative features for perception tasks (Introduction; Related Work; Section 7).
> 
> - Active, anytime-valid RCPS (risk-controlling prediction sets under adaptive labeling)
>   - IID data assumption: the anytime-valid guarantees are derived under an i.i.d. data model; handling distribution shift is left for future work (Section 6: Conclusion, limitations).
>   - Lower-bounded labeling probability constraint: guarantees and e-process nonnegativity require a minimum labeling probability q_min ≥ ε; very low or highly variable labeling rates violate assumptions (Proposition 2; Section 2.1; Assumption 2).
>   - Dependence on predictor quality: variance-reduction via risk predictors (r̂) helps only if predictions are accurate; poor predictors increase variance and slow rejection of unsafe β, reducing label-efficiency (Proposition 3; Theorem 3).
>   - Regret bound depends on policy/predictor estimation error: the growth-rate (power) of the underlying e-process is explicitly degraded by deviations from the optimal labeling policy q* and predictor r*, so practical performance hinges on learning these well under a label budget (Theorem 3; Section 3).
> 
> - Diverse projection ensembles for distributional RL (PE-DQN)
>   - Residual epistemic uncertainty at convergence: because each projection (categorical/quantile) incurs irreducible approximation error, ensemble disagreement may not vanish even when the mixture reaches its fixed point; this necessitates careful bonus decay to avoid over-exploration (A.4: Propositions 8–9, Lemmas 10–11; Corollary 12).
>   - Contraction requires bounded projection moduli: ensemble convergence depends on each projection being bounded in Wasserstein metrics; poor choices can break contraction, harming stability (Proposition 1).
>   - Approximation capacity bound by atom count/grid: categorical/quantile projections introduce bounded errors that scale with grid spacing and number of atoms K; insufficient K or poorly chosen supports degrade accuracy (A.4: Lemmas 10–11; Corollary 12).
>   - Bonus estimation complexity and target mismatch: using joint TD targets means ensemble disagreement measures TD error, not true return error; the paper must add a separate uncertainty-propagation scheme to reconcile this (Theorem 3; Section 4.2–5.1).
>   - Computational demands remain non-trivial: despite fewer models than some baselines, the method uses large CNN backbones, prioritized replay, target nets, and spectral normalization; experiments report multi-hour wall-clock times per seed/environment (Appendix B: Table 7), indicating practical training costs.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Mapping to the research collection
> 
> No single paper in this collection ties all five components together end-to-end. Each requirement maps to a separate work:
> 
> 1. **Anchor-free part-body detector** — PBADet (ICLR 2024): one-stage anchor-free detection with a single part-to-body center offset; YOLOv5/YOLOv7 (CNN) backbones, focal/CE + IoU + association losses, SGD. Reports **AP on COCO-HumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman**, and **Precision/Recall/F1 vs. ED-Pose** on COCO val (e.g., all parts 39.41/63.09/48.52 vs. 24.09/45.51/31.51).
> 
> 2. **Distributional-value exploration with ensemble diversity** — PE-DQN / Diverse Projection Ensembles (ICLR 2024): ensembles of quantile + categorical projections; ensemble disagreement (1-Wasserstein) as epistemic bonus propagated through distributional TD errors; separates epistemic vs. aleatoric. Evaluated on bsuite (468 envs) and VizDoom; **no COCO/MNIST/precision metrics**.
> 
> 3. **E/I-constrained recurrent controller with spectral stability** — "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023): ColEI vs. DANN vs. standard RNNs; **sequential MNIST error, adding problem, Penn Tree Bank**; normalised SVD entropy predicts performance.
> 
> 4. **Joint-embedding pretraining avoiding noisy features** — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (deep-linear self-distillation analysis; ImageNet-1K, features compared via **CCA**, not cosine similarity or AUROC) and LDReg (local-dimensionality regularization; ImageNet linear eval + **COCO detection/segmentation AP**).
> 
> 5. **Anytime-valid calibration under adaptive labeling** — "Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets": e-process/betting-based RCPS, valid at all times under active/IPW labeling; simulations + **ImageNet** (safety violation rate ≤ α=0.05, label efficiency); guarantees risk, not precision/F1/AUROC.
> 
> **Gap vs. your request:** nothing in the collection reports AUROC, or uses cosine similarity on embeddings as the primary metric. The closest standard metrics are precision/F1/AP (PBADet), MNIST error (E/I RNNs), CCA alignment (JEPA), and risk-violation rates (RCPS).
> 
> ## Development defects of the methods
> 
> **PBADet**
> - Anchor-free dense prediction inherits FCOS/TOOD issues: independent classification/localization need task-alignment to avoid inconsistent predictions; lower recall than anchor-based methods when relying on near-center points.
> - Advantage over BPJDet is small on the single-part CrowdHuman face-body task (mMR−2 50.8 vs. 50.1), i.e., the gain concentrates on multi-part settings.
> - Relies on NMS/confidence thresholds tuned per dataset (τ differs between BodyHands and COCOHumanParts); a one-to-one part-to-body offset assumes parts lie inside the body box.
> - No transformer-backbone experiments, no uncertainty quantification, no AUROC/cosine-similarity evaluation.
> 
> **PE-DQN (projection ensembles)**
> - **Residual approximation error**: finite-dimensional projections make the fixed point ≠ true return distribution (bias) and ensemble disagreement never vanishes, so the epistemic bonus can frustrate exploration or yield overconfident predictions; errors are only upper-bounded via atom count K.
> - Ensemble disagreement with shared TD targets measures distributional TD error w.r.t. bootstrapped targets, not the true return distribution.
> - Only uniform mixtures of quantile/categorical projections; greedy-policy and contraction assumptions; no use of precision/F1 or detection benchmarks.
> 
> **E/I-constrained RNNs**
> - Naive Dale's-law (ColEI) sign constraints give multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra (rank-one column-mean structure), causing poor learning, high variance across seeds, and instability (gradient clipping required); sign constraints also shrink the solution space.
> - Performance degrades sharply for small networks or skewed E/I ratios; NSE is a diagnostic at initialization only, not a training mechanism; only linear-spectrum intuition, no theory for why large networks escape pathology.
> 
> **JEPA self-distillation**
> - Theory limited to deep linear MLPs, special initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances — real data violate this; nonlinear generalization unproven.
> - The implicit bias is toward predictive, low-variance ("slow"/influential) features, which makes JEPA **vulnerable to spurious or slow features**; at large depth the encoder can become low-rank toward a single dominant feature.
> - ImageNet evidence is correlational (CCA alignment), not a benchmark metric like AUROC/F1.
> 
> **Anytime-valid RCPS with active labeling**
> - i.i.d. stream assumption; no distribution-shift guarantee (covariate/label shift left to future work with empirical-Bernstein supermartingales).
> - Requires bounded label policies (q_t ≥ q_min) and monotonicity/right-continuity of risk and utility (Assumption 1); label-policy/predictor estimation error enters the regret bound.
> - Controls expected risk only (P(ρ(β̂_t) ≤ θ for all t) ≥ 1−α), not per-prediction calibration; "all"/"oblivious" baselines are label-inefficient, and learned policies need accurate conditional-risk/standard-deviation estimates.
> 
> **Bottom line:** the collection supports each module individually, but there is no integrated system paper, and the specific metric set you request (AUROC, cosine-similarity-based evaluation tying all modules) is not reported anywhere in the context.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the document collection, no single paper ties all five components together, but each piece maps to specific research:
> 
> **Component research (with reported metrics):**
> - **Anchor-free part-body association**: PBADet (ICLR 2024) — one-stage anchor-free detector with part-to-body center offset (YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones). On COCOHumanParts: all-categories AP 43.0/41.8 (AP.5:.95 original/subordinate); vs ED-Pose reports per-part Precision/Recall/F1 (e.g., left hand 37.63/60.82/46.50, all parts 39.41/63.09/48.52). BodyHands ablations: Hand AP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98.
> - **Exploration with distributional values + ensemble diversity**: PE-DQN (ICLR 2024) — ensembles of quantile/categorical projections separate epistemic from aleatoric uncertainty; evaluated on bsuite (468 envs) and VizDoom (only method succeeding on all 10 seeds).
> - **Recurrent controller with E/I constraints and spectral properties**: "Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly" (NeurIPS 2023) — recurrent DANNs match standard RNNs; normalised SVD entropy predicts performance on adding problem, sequential MNIST, PTB.
> - **Self-supervised joint-embedding pretraining avoiding noisy features**: JEPA deep-linear analysis (Apple) — JEPA suppresses noisy features vs MAE; LDReg (ICLR 2024) counters dimensional collapse and improves COCO detection/segmentation transfer. Cosine-similarity analysis exists in "On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning" (CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet top-1).
> - **Anytime-valid calibration under adaptive labeling**: "Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets" (NeurIPS 2024) — e-processes/betting, IPW active labeling; ImageNet experiments keep violation rates below α=0.05.
> 
> **Development defects of these methods (from the context):**
> 
> 1. **PBADet**: (a) On COCOHumanParts mMR−2 it is worse than BPJDet for right-hand/right-foot/left-foot (e.g., 52.6/52.5 vs 49.1/50.4); (b) its advantage over BPJDet shrinks on the single-part CrowdHuman face-body task; (c) ablations show removing the association loss collapses Joint AP from 85.98 to 78.07 — the framework degrades without task alignment and multi-scale offsets; (d) still uses two-stage-style post-processing (Euclidean distance matching when association head removed), and YOLO-scale inputs (1024–1536).
> 
> 2. **PE-DQN**: (a) Residual projection approximation errors persist even in convergence, so epistemic-uncertainty estimates are biased and ensemble disagreement never vanishes — this "can frustrate exploration or lead to overconfident predictions"; (b) TD backups make consistent uncertainty quantification fundamentally hard; (c) errors are only controllable via projection-error bounds (e.g., number of atoms K); (d) limited to uniform mixtures over the ensemble — noted as conservative/under-exploiting.
> 
> 3. **ColEI-style E/I RNNs**: (a) multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra with a large-singular-value mode cause exploding activations/gradients — highly unstable without gradient clipping; (b) much higher variance across seeds; (c) small networks or skewed E/I ratios (few inhibitory units) learn poorly; (d) sign constraints themselves still cost ~0.7–1% error even when spectra are fixed; (e) NSE at initialization is only a diagnostic — it must be measured before training and does not fix the pathology (DANN reparameterization does).
> 
> 4. **Self-supervised pretraining**: JEPA analysis is limited to deep linear networks, special balanced-orthogonal initialization, and simultaneous-diagonalizability assumptions — "less than rigorous leap to practical settings," and JEPA may be vulnerable to spurious/slow features. LDReg: LID estimation degrades in high dimensions and uses minibatch nearest neighbors (accuracy loss); needs a tuned hyperparameter β; assumes higher dimensionality is always desirable, and forcing very low LID can trigger complete collapse. The contrastive variance-reduction loss suppresses "semantically meaningful variance," has reduced benefit at large batch sizes, and adds a hyperparameter λ.
> 
> 5. **Anytime-valid risk control**: (a) assumes i.i.d. data — no guarantee under covariate/label shift at test time (extension is future work); (b) relies on a bounded-label-policy assumption and an existence assumption (Proposition 5) that the authors want to remove; (c) non-queried points are treated as incurring zero risk, which can bias estimates; (d) guarantees are only in expectation/with probability 1−α over the stream, not per-instance.
> 
> Additionally, if self-supervised detection is part of the pipeline (HASSOD): learned hierarchies misalign with human perception — overlapping similar objects merge into one, heterogeneous wholes (e.g., a motorcycle) are not grouped, and text is not localized; these failures persist in prior methods like CutLER.

</details>

<summary>展开完整 gold 与两份最终答案</summary>

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Development defects and limitations, by method:
> 
> 1) PBADet (one-stage, anchor-free part–body association)
> - Benefits diminish on single-part association: On CrowdHuman (face–body), the authors note the task is “singular in nature… Consequently, the advantages of our method over BPJDet are not as pronounced,” with comparable mMR−2 and AP to prior work. This indicates gains rely on multi-part scenarios and are limited when only one part type is present.
> - Sensitivity to training design choices: Ablations show removing multi-scale anchoring (w/o Multi-scale) or task-alignment learning (w/o Task-align) reduces conditional accuracy and joint AP, implying dependence on these components and associated hyperparameters (e.g., K, α, β, λ, NMS thresholds) for best results.
> - Formulation relies on anchor-free enclosure assumption: The method “utilizes” that any anchor point in a part’s box also belongs to the body’s box to learn the part-to-body center offset; this design assumption constrains applicability to settings where the part box is contained in the person box.
> - Generality claims beyond humans are not empirically validated: While presented as a “universal framework” (e.g., wheel–car), non-human evaluations are qualitative only (animal results), with no quantitative benchmarks provided.
> 
> 2) Learning better with Dale’s Law (spectral perspective on EI RNNs)
> - Stability/performance issues in simple EI partitioning (ColEI): ColEI networks learn poorly without gradient clipping and exhibit high variance across seeds; they are especially weak for small networks and realistic E/I ratios (few inhibitory units).
> - Dependence on spectral properties at initialization: The study shows initial singular value spectra strongly affect learning; large, multimodal spectra (ColEI) correlate with poor performance, but this relies on specific initializations and may not capture training-time spectral evolution.
> - Open theoretical gaps: The origin of ColEI’s multimodal spectrum and why large ColEI networks can learn despite large maximum singular values remain unresolved, limiting prescriptive guidance.
> - Biological fidelity limitations: Recurrent DANNs lack features like inhibitory-to-inhibitory connections and cell-type-specific time constants; models could be more biologically faithful.
> - Scope constraints: Results are shown on a limited task suite (adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Treebank, a small naturalistic recognition task), with ReLU RNNs; generality to other architectures and tasks is not established.
> 
> 3) How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features (implicit bias of deep linear self-distillation)
> - Strong modeling assumptions: Theory is restricted to deep linear networks with special orthogonal/small initializations and StopGrad, and assumes Σxx and Σyx are simultaneously diagonalizable. These conditions are rarely met in practice.
> - Limited external validity: The authors explicitly note that extending results to nonlinear encoders/decoders and practical JEPA/MAE systems remains open; conclusions may not hold for real-world data where simultaneity and linearity break.
> - Depth dependence: The JEPA bias toward high-influence features diminishes with shallow encoders; benefits depend on encoder depth and small-initialization dynamics.
> 
> 4) Memory-Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States
> - Configuration sensitivity and added complexity: To avoid catastrophic errors (zero-point problem) when quantizing the second moment, the method needs specific mappings excluding zero (e.g., Linear, DE-0) and specialized normalization (rank-1). Inappropriate block sizes or mappings (e.g., large B2048 with DE) degrade performance, revealing sensitivity to quantization design.
> - Practical speed overheads without kernel fusion: The authors report 4-bit optimizers “appear to be slower than 8-bit AdamW” on some finetuning tasks unless fused operators are used (they later add fused variants to close the gap), indicating implementation complexity for efficiency.
> - Incomplete coverage of parameters: Heuristics skip quantization for small tensors (≤4096) and apply factorization only to tensors with dimension ≥2, leaving some states uncompressed.
> - Limited domain evaluation: Experiments cover language and vision (RoBERTa, GPT-2, Swin, Transformer) but not reinforcement learning, audio, or graphs; applicability beyond these domains is untested.
> - Memory savings bounded by total training footprint: While optimizer-state memory shrinks markedly, total training memory includes activations/data/fragments, so overall gains can saturate, limiting end-to-end savings depending on workload.
> 
> 5) GROOVE (meta-learned RL optimizers via adversarial environment design)
> - Heavy compute and simple training domains: Meta-training requires “a huge number of environment interactions,” so the study relies on fast, simple Grid-Worlds; conclusions may not generalize to more complex training domains without further evidence.
> - Limited evaluation breadth and gap to SOTA RL: Despite strong transfer versus LPG, GROOVE lags state-of-the-art, manually designed RL algorithms on Atari; broader benchmarks (beyond Atari/MinAtar/small Procgen subset) are not covered.
> - Sensitivity to AR antagonist choice: Algorithmic Regret works best with particular antagonists (A2C), while PPO, random, or expert antagonists can underperform; this adds a design dependency and potential brittleness.
> - Additional system complexity: AR requires co-training an antagonist agent and a PLR-style curation loop; although chosen for sample efficiency over generator-based UED, this increases implementation and tuning complexity.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Matching papers and their development defects
> 
> **1. One-stage anchor-free part-body perception** → **PBADet** (08b70bc…, ICLR 2024). A single part-to-body center offset links any part to its parent body, avoiding BPJDet-style body-to-part offsets. Defects: prior body-part offsets become invalid when parts are occluded and scale poorly with more parts; on the single-part CrowdHuman face-body task PBADet's advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced; accuracy in complex/crowded scenes remains challenging, and part boxes often must be derived from keypoint annotations.
> 
> **2. Spectral view of Dale's-Law RNNs** → **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (e63a94c…, NeurIPS 2023). Defects it exposes: simple column-constrained ColEI RNNs have multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra (rank-one column-mean/nilpotent structure) causing poor, high-variance learning; they are highly unstable without gradient clipping; small networks or few inhibitory units learn worse. Note the paper's own limitations for your request: it uses **projected gradient descent with sign-clipping plus gradient clipping, not explicit SGD/AdamW**, so the "influence of spectra on SGD/AdamW dynamics" is not directly demonstrated—only that sign constraints and, more strongly, initial spectra determine learning.
> 
> **3. JEPA vs pixel reconstruction** → **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks"** (40fde03…, NeurIPS 2024). Shows JEPA prioritizes high-influence (high-ρ) features and suppresses noisy low-ρ features with depth, while MAE orders features mainly by covariance λ and learns high-variance/noisy subspaces. Defects/limits: analysis restricted to deep linear networks under balanced-orthogonal initialization and simultaneous diagonalizability; no proof for nonlinear models; JEPA is susceptible to representation collapse (needs stop-grad) and to spurious/slow features; MAE produces uninformative perceptual features.
> 
> **4. ~4-bit optimizer states** → **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (8d5e145…, NeurIPS 2023). Defects: quantizing both moments gives marginal accuracy drop; second-moment quantization suffers a zero-point problem (solved by zero-exclusion/rank-1/factorized schemes); smaller models run slower than 8-bit because operators are not fused; optimal quantization may be task-dependent; only language/vision tasks were tested. Directly relevant caveat: its benchmarks are **Swin-T on ImageNet, RoBERTa-L, GPT-2, Transformer, and LLaMA—not MNIST/CIFAR-100**. The MNIST/CIFAR-100 + ViT-Base/CIFAR-100 fine-tuning with AdamW/SGD appears in the Hessian-spectra paper (582d138…) about generalization/sharpness, which is not a 4-bit memory-frugal method.
> 
> **5. General RL updates via adversarial/teacher curricula** → **GROOVE** (319440a3…, NeurIPS 2023). Uses UED + algorithmic regret to curate meta-training levels for policy meta-optimization. Defects: meta-training is computationally constrained and limited to simple GPU-based Grid-Worlds, so conclusions may not transfer to complex environments; meta-testing variety limited by Atari cost; a generalization gap still remains; prior UED metrics (PLR/LPG) alone are insufficient and require AR; generator-based UED (PAIRED) is less sample-efficient, hence PLR-style curation.
> 
> **Cross-cutting gaps for your stated emphasis:** interpretability/attention is only implicitly covered (PBADet's anchor-free task alignment, ViT use in the JEPA/ImageNet and CIFAR-100 ViT experiments); online implementation is addressed only by GROOVE's single-V100 JAX training; none of the papers jointly connects spectral/optimizer analysis with attention backbones.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, the papers that collectively cover your five topics are:
> 
> **1. One-stage, anchor-free part→instance association**
> - **PBADet** (08b70bc…) — extends anchor-free detection (YOLOv5/v7 heads) with a single *part-to-body* center offset linking hands/face/feet to the parent body on COCO-WholeBody/BodyHands/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman.
> 
> **2. Spectral view of Dale's-Law RNNs + spectra affecting SGD/AdamW learning dynamics**
> - **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (e63a94c4…) — shows ColEI (E/I sign-constrained) RNNs learn poorly not because of sign constraints but because of pathological (multimodal, dispersed) singular-value spectra at initialization; NSE predicts performance; gradient clipping stabilizes.
> - **"Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure"** (582d138d…) — power-law Hessian spectra hold across SGD/Adam/AdamW (LeNet on MNIST/CIFAR-10/100, ViT on CIFAR-100) and predict generalization; explains low-dimensional learning dynamics.
> 
> **3. Joint-embedding SSL vs pixel reconstruction**
> - **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (40fde037…) — proves JEPA self-distillation implicitly biases toward high-influence features and suppresses noise, unlike MAE reconstruction (deep-linear analysis + ImageNet I-JEPA/MAE CCA).
> - **LDReg** (51526068…) — counters local dimensional collapse in SSL representations.
> 
> **4. ~4-bit optimizer states for AdamW/SGD fine-tuning**
> - **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (8d5e1455…) — 4-bit first/second-moment quantization (B128/rank-1, zero-point exclusion) for Adam/AdamW matching 32-bit accuracy; evaluated on Swin-T (ImageNet), RoBERTa, GPT-2, Transformer-Base, LLaMA-7B/13B/33B. Note: it does **not** use MNIST/CIFAR-100; those benchmarks + ViT/SGD/AdamW appear instead in the Hessian paper (582d138d…), so no single paper unifies "4-bit states + MNIST/CIFAR-100" exactly.
> 
> **5. General RL updates via adversarial/teacher curricula**
> - **GROOVE** (319440a3…) — meta-learns a general RL optimizer via Unsupervised Environment Design, using a novel *algorithmic regret* metric and PLR-style adversarial level curation; outperforms LPG on unseen Grid-Worlds, Min-Atar, Atari, Procgen.
> 
> ---
> 
> **Development defects / limitations of each method:**
> 
> 1. **PBADet**: requires anchor-based YOLOv5/v7 backbones to be adapted to anchor-free heads; its gain over BPJDet is small on the single-part face-body task (CrowdHuman, Table 5); ablations show it needs multi-scale offsets and task-alignment supervision (both hurt if removed); one-to-one part-to-body correspondence may fail with heavily occluded/invisible parts, and representation length still grows with the number of classes.
> 
> 2. **Dale's Law spectral paper**: only empirical (no closed-form origin of the multimodal spectrum); ColEI shows high seed variance and is unstable without gradient clipping; performance degrades sharply for small networks or few inhibitory units; analysis is limited to a few tasks (adding, sMNIST, PTB, object recognition); NSE is only a correlational diagnostic, not a causal guarantee.
> 
> 3. **JEPA/MAE analysis**: theory holds only for deep *linear* networks with special balanced-orthogonal initialization and simultaneous diagonalizability; "noise suppression" claims generalize only qualitatively to ImageNet; LDReg's LID estimation degrades in high dimensions and relies on minibatch nearest neighbors; forcing too-low LID causes full collapse.
> 
> 4. **4-bit optimizers**: optimal quantizer (block size, rank-1 vs B128) may be task-dependent; quantizing both moments still causes a marginal accuracy drop; slower than 8-bit on small models because fused operators are missing; not validated on MNIST/CIFAR-100 or on SGD states; only language/vision tasks tested.
> 
> 5. **GROOVE**: meta-training uses only simple Grid-Worlds (limited distribution), PLR-style curation rather than generative environment models; algorithmic regret is an approximation; generalization to truly novel, high-dimensional real-world environments remains unproven (gap still exists vs. human-designed algorithms); heavy compute, though JAX implementation reduces it.

</details>

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Development defects summarized per method:
> 
> PBADet (one-stage anchor-free part–body association)
> - Limited benefit on single-part association: authors note that on CrowdHuman (face–body only) “the advantages of our method over BPJDet are not as pronounced,” indicating gains depend on multi-part scenarios.
> - Association decoding assumption: inference picks the body “that are unassigned and also enclose the part,” so parts detected outside any body box (due to occlusion or localization error) cannot be associated.
> - Sensitivity to hyperparameters/heads: performance relies on task-alignment learning (α, β, K), multi-scale features, and a fixed offset scaling factor (λ). Ablations show drops “w/o Multi-scale” and “w/o Task-align,” implying sensitivity to these design choices.
> - Compute/resource demands: training used large inputs (e.g., 1024–1536 resolution) and 4×V100 GPUs for 100 epochs; indicates non-trivial memory/compute during development.
> 
> Dale’s Law RNNs (ColEI vs DANN; spectral perspective)
> - ColEI networks train poorly: exhibit “multimodal, dispersed” singular-value spectra, leading to unstable learning, higher variance across seeds, and strong dependence on gradient clipping.
> - Scaling sensitivity: ColEI performance degrades in small networks and with few inhibitory units; authors show worse spectra/performance with biologically realistic E/I ratios and small sizes.
> - Hyperparameter fragility: ColEI needs careful spectral-radius (ρ) tuning; good performance only at certain ρ, and instability otherwise.
> - Architectural constraints and projections: enforcing Dale’s Law via projected gradient descent (zeroing sign-violating weights) introduces non-smooth updates; DANNs in the paper omit I→I connections (acknowledged as missing biology), limiting biological fidelity.
> 
> JEPA self-distillation (deep linear analysis of JEPA vs MAE)
> - Theory restricted setting: results rely on deep linear encoders, shallow linear decoders, specific small-initialization regimes, and “simultaneously diagonalizable” data covariances; generalization to nonlinear networks and real data is not established (explicitly acknowledged in Limitations).
> - Depth dependency: the beneficial implicit bias (favoring high-regression-coefficient/influential features) “takes hold only when the encoder is deep,” reducing advantages for shallow encoders.
> - Potential vulnerability to slow/spurious features: authors note JEPA’s bias toward predictive low-variance/slow features “may shed light on JEPAs vulnerability to spurious or slow features.”
> 
> 4-bit optimizers (memory-efficient AdamW variants)
> - Training instability without special handling: naive 4-bit quantization suffers a “zero-point problem” for second moments; many runs become unstable unless zero is excluded from the quantization map (DE-0/linear) and small blocks or rank-1 normalization are used.
> - Sensitivity to quantization configuration: optimal settings (block size, mapping, rank-1 vs block-wise) are task dependent; authors state “optimal quantization setting probably depends on task, datasets, and training details.”
> - Representation trade-offs: excluding zero means smallest representable second-moment values are bounded (e.g., 0.0625 for 4-bit linear), potentially limiting very small values.
> - Slight accuracy regressions in some pretraining: small but consistent drops vs 32-bit on vision/MT pretraining (e.g., Swin-T ImageNet top-1 81.2→~80.8–80.9; WMT14 26.61→~26.28–26.45).
> - Throughput overheads without kernel fusion: 4-bit versions can be slower than 8-bit until fused operators are used; indicates extra engineering needed for speed.
> - Coverage limits and exclusions: certain small or sensitive tensors (e.g., biases/normalizations, small tensors ≤4096) are left in higher precision; factorization applied only to ≥2D tensors—leaving some memory on the table.
> - Scope limitations: evaluations focused on language/vision fine-tuning/pretraining; applicability to RL, audio, and graph tasks is not established (stated limitation).
> 
> GROOVE (adversarial environment design for policy meta-optimization)
> - Computational overhead and scope limits: meta-training relies on fast Grid-Worlds; authors acknowledge conclusions “cannot be guaranteed to generalize to more complex environments,” and meta-testing breadth is limited by Atari evaluation cost.
> - Still below SOTA handcrafted RL on Atari: despite gains over LPG, performance remains inferior to top model-free baselines (e.g., Rainbow), showing the discovered optimizer is not yet competitive with best manual algorithms.
> - Curriculum metric overhead/choice sensitivity: algorithmic regret (AR) requires training an additional antagonist (e.g., A2C) during meta-training—extra compute—and performance depends on antagonist choice (A2C>PPO>random/expert in their tests).
> - Static-curation dilution: with static high-AR level sets, the advantage over random curricula “decreases as the number of levels grows,” necessitating continual environment adaptation.
> - PLR-only design trade-off: using curation (PLR) avoids generator training but inherits PMO’s sample-inefficiency for regret estimation (train-to-convergence to score levels) and may miss novel levels a learned generator could propose.
> - Robustness gains are uneven: on in-distribution Grid-Worlds, improvements concentrate on the “lower-scoring half” of tasks, with parity on easier tasks—indicating robustness is improved but not uniformly.

**naive 最终答案**

> Yes — each need maps to a specific work in the context, though no single work addresses all five together. Here are the matches and their development defects.
> 
> **1. Anchor-free part–body association — PBADet (ICLR 2024).** One-stage anchor-free detector using a single part-to-body center offset to associate hands, face, feet with the correct body, outperforming BPJDet/HierR-CNN on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman. *Defects:* predictions are unreliable for limbs (legs/arms), which clouds body–part relationships; the advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced on the single-part CrowdHuman face–body task; ablations show it depends on association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment (removing any degrades conditional accuracy/JointAP); anchor-free performance still varies by backbone.
> 
> **2. 4-bit optimizer states with AdamW — "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (NeurIPS 2023).** Quantizes first/second moments (B128/DE, rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion), matching 32-bit AdamW with up to 57.7% memory savings. *Defects:* optimal quantization settings are task- and dataset-dependent; evaluation is limited to language/vision — applicability to RL, audio, graphs is explicitly unverified; unfused 4-bit AdamW is slower than 8-bit (only fusion closes the gap); memory savings saturate as bitwidth drops (activations/data dominate); quantizing both moments still causes a marginal accuracy drop.
> 
> **3. Joint-embedding SSL avoiding pixel noise — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024), plus LDReg (ICLR 2024).** Shows JEPA self-distillation implicitly biases toward high-influence (high regression coefficient) features and suppresses noisy/pixel-level variance, unlike MAE reconstruction; LDReg counters local dimensional collapse via local intrinsic dimensionality regularization. *Defects:* the JEPA analysis is limited to deep *linear* networks with special initialization and simultaneous-diagonalizability assumptions — only qualitative generalization to real models; LDReg's LID estimation degrades in high dimensions and relies on minibatch nearest neighbors, and forcing very low LID can trigger complete collapse.
> 
> **4. E/I constraints and spectral properties — "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023).** Extends Dale's-constrained E/I networks (ColEI vs DANN RNNs) and shows initial singular-value spectrum, not sign constraints, mainly determines learning; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) predicts performance. *Defects:* ColEI networks learn worse with higher variance across seeds; their multimodal, dispersed spectra make them highly unstable without gradient clipping; performance degrades for small networks and fewer inhibitory units; the rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure escapes spectral-radius control; NSE is only an empirical diagnostic, not a cure, and sign constraints still contribute some impairment.
> 
> **5. Adversarial environment design for RL algorithm discovery — GROOVE (ICLR 2024).** Extends UED to policy meta-optimization (Meta-UPOMDP), proposing algorithmic regret (AR) to meta-learn RL update rules that transfer to unseen Atari/Procgen better than LPG. *Defects:* meta-training uses only simple Grid-World environments (sparse coverage of exploration/credit-assignment challenges); compute constraints force PLR-style level curation rather than generative level models (generators are less sample-efficient); AR requires co-training an antagonist agent with a hand-designed algorithm; generalization beyond tested domains remains open.
> 
> Overall: the components exist and are individually strong, but each carries task-specific scope limits (small datasets like MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR-100 are not directly validated for the 4-bit optimizer or PBADet; RL use of 4-bit optimizers is explicitly untested), and integration across the five needs is not demonstrated in any single work in the context.

**community 最终答案**

> Yes — each of your five needs is addressed by a separate paper in this collection (no single work covers all of them together):
> 
> 1. **Anchor-free part–body association** → **PBADet** (ICLR 2024): one-stage, anchor-free detector linking hands, face, feet to bodies via a single part-to-body center offset.
> 2. **4-bit optimizer states with AdamW** → **"4-bit Optimizers"** (NeurIPS 2023): 4-bit first/second moments for AdamW, up to 57.7% memory savings, lossless fine-tuning.
> 3. **Joint-embedding SSL avoiding pixel noise** → **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024): shows JEPA self-distillation (joint-embedding) suppresses pixel-level noise vs. MAE reconstruction; plus **LDReg** (ICLR 2024) counters dimensional collapse in SSL.
> 4. **E/I constraints with spectral properties (Dale's Law)** → **"Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly"** (NeurIPS 2023): shows performance of E/I RNNs is governed by initial singular-value spectra, not sign constraints; normalised SVD entropy predicts learning.
> 5. **Adversarial curriculum design for RL algorithm discovery** → **GROOVE** (ICLR 2024): meta-learns general RL update rules via UED-style regret-maximizing (algorithmic regret) curricula, improving OOD transfer vs. LPG.
> 
> **Development defects of these methods:**
> 
> - **PBADet**: Association relies on the part lying inside the body box and on a single center offset; ablations show the association loss, multi-scale offset, and task-alignment are all required (removing any degrades accuracy). Its advantage over BPJDet shrinks on single-part (CrowdHuman face-body) tasks; it builds on adapted YOLO backbones and adds branches/complexity; invisible or occluded parts still weaken body-part detection.
> 
> - **4-bit optimizers**: Authors state optimal quantization is likely task-, dataset-, and training-detail-dependent; only language/vision tasks were tested (no robotics/control); uncompressed (unfused) versions are slower than 8-bit on small models; memory savings saturate as bitwidth drops because data/activations/fragmentation dominate; 4-bit Factor's gains depend on tensor dimensionality.
> 
> - **JEPA analysis / LDReg**: JEPA objective is prone to trivial collapse (requires stop-grad/non-contrastive tricks); the analysis is limited to deep *linear* networks, special initialization, and simultaneous diagonalizability — only qualitative extrapolation to real nets. LDReg's LID estimation degrades in high dimensions, relies on minibatch nearest neighbors, and over-aggressive regularization can trigger complete collapse; global covariance/variance regularizers barely help.
> 
> - **Dale's Law RNNs**: Traditional ColEI networks learn poorly, with high variance and instability without gradient clipping, and degrade badly for small networks or few inhibitory units (multimodal, dispersed spectra); DANN models omit inhibitory-to-inhibitory connections and represent only fast PV+ interneurons — limited biological fidelity; results are empirical (spectrum transplants, no full theory of spectrum origin).
> 
> - **GROOVE**: Meta-trained only on simple Grid-Worlds; both GROOVE and LPG still underperform manually designed SOTA RL algorithms; prior UED value-loss metrics fail in this setting, and even optimal-policy regret underperforms algorithmic regret with an A2C antagonist (difficulty of selecting a good antagonist); performance gap vs. random levels narrows as level count grows, and compute constraints limit scale.

</details>

### paperscope:gap:277 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively cover: (a) spectral/curvature analyses of deep networks (e.g., power‑law Hessian spectra and eigengaps) to explain how SGD/Adam/AdamW training relates to generalization across CNNs and Transformers on standard small‑image and detection benchmarks; (b) biologically constrained E/I recurrent networks obeying Dale’s principle, analyzed through singular/eigenvalue spectra; (c) joint‑embedding self‑distillation (JEPA) showing why predicting in latent space (vs reconstruction with MSE) prioritizes informative features in deep linear nets; (d) memory‑efficient training via 4‑bit optimizer states using block/rank‑1 quantization that retain accuracy during fine‑tuning and adapter‑based updates; and (e) a one‑stage anchor‑free detector that associates human parts with their bodies on whole‑body datasets. Please include works that discuss cross‑entropy vs MSE losses, attention backbones, LoRA‑style fine‑tuning, and report results on common digit/object benchmarks.Please analyze the development defects of these methods.
