**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below are the development defects/limitations explicitly stated or directly implied in each method as reported in the papers you provided.
> 
> 1) PBADet: One‑stage anchor‑free part‑to‑body association (ICLR 2024)
> - Advantage diminishes on single‑part association: On CrowdHuman (face–body only), the benefit over BPJDet is “not as pronounced,” since the task involves just one part (Appendix A.1).
> - Dataset‑ and threshold‑sensitive decoding: Inference depends on NMS confidence/IoU thresholds tuned differently per dataset (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman), indicating sensitivity of association quality to these settings.
> - Heavy reliance on anchor‑free multi‑scale heads: Ablations show performance drops when the center‑offset is defined without multi‑scale anchors or task‑alignment (Table 4), implying the method’s gains depend on these design choices.
> - Generality not validated outside human parts: Although claimed as a “universal framework” (e.g., wheel‑and‑car), experiments are reported only on human whole‑body datasets (COCO‑WholeBody/HumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman); broader applicability is unverified.
> - Implementation‑level constraints: Large input resolutions (1024–1536) and dataset‑specific hyperparameters (e.g., K, α, β for task alignment; λ for scaling) may increase tuning burden and compute.
> 
> 2) Dale’s Law in EI RNNs (ColEI vs DANN RNNs) (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Column EI (ColEI) defects: 
>   • Poor learning and instability: Performs worse than standard RNNs/DANNs across tasks, needs gradient clipping for stability, and exhibits higher seed variance.
>   • Pathological spectra: Multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra (large modes and large max singular values) correlate with poor learning; spectrum pathology worsens for small networks and more realistic E/I ratios (few inhibitory units).
>   • Hyperparameter sensitivity: Learning degrades as inhibitory fraction decreases; small models learn less effectively and display worse spectral properties.
> - DANN RNNs caveats: 
>   • Biological scope: Models fast PV+ interneurons; does not capture other inhibitory types or I–I connections and cell‑type‑specific time constants (not yet included).
>   • Initialization/architectural assumptions: Good learning is tied to spectral properties at initialization and specific reparameterization; generalization to alternative bio‑faithful designs is suggested but not shown.
> - Open theoretical gaps: Origin of ColEI multimodal spectra and why large ColEI networks can learn despite large max singular values remain open questions.
> 
> 3) JEPA implicit bias in deep linear self‑distillation (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Scope limited to a solvable regime: Results are derived for deep linear encoders/decoders under balanced orthogonal initializations, small‑init gradient flow, and (crucially) simultaneously diagonalizable Σxx and Σyx; practical nonlinear/real‑data settings may violate these assumptions.
> - Depth‑dependence of the advantage: The “influential‑feature” bias (prioritizing large regression coefficients ρ) “takes hold only when the encoder is deep” and “diminishes substantially when the encoder is shallow,” reducing JEPA’s claimed advantage in shallow models.
> - Collapse avoidance is architectural: JEPA requires mechanisms like StopGrad to prevent representational collapse; without them, the objective is susceptible to trivial solutions.
> - Generalization to non‑diagonalizable or nonlinear generative processes remains unverified; the paper explicitly notes this as future work.
> 
> 4) Memory‑efficient 4‑bit optimizer states (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Zero‑point failure mode in 2nd moment: Standard dynamic‑exponent quantization maps many small v̂ entries to zero, causing catastrophic deviation in the update direction (1/√v̂). The fix (exclude zero; linear map) is essential; without it, training can become unstable or degrade.
> - Task/hyperparameter dependence: Best quantization settings (e.g., block size B=128, rank‑1 normalization vs block‑wise, linear vs DE‑0 mapping) depend on task/model; authors note optimal settings may vary and were only systematically validated on language/vision.
> - Limited domain coverage: Evaluation is on NLU/QA/NLG, image classification, WMT MT, and LLaMA instruction tuning; applicability to reinforcement learning, audio, and graph learning remains unknown.
> - Speed trade‑offs on small models: 4‑bit variants can be slower than 8‑bit without fused kernels; speed parity requires operator fusion (they report separate “fused” results).
> - Accuracy trade‑offs in pretraining: Small, but measurable degradations on some pretraining tasks (e.g., Swin‑T ImageNet and WMT14 en‑de) compared with 32‑bit AdamW.
> - Factorization limits: Factorization applies only to second moment; first‑moment quantization remains necessary, and factorization may introduce different approximations than pure quantization.
> 
> 5) Power‑law Hessian structure and spectral analysis (ICML 2025)
> - Computational/memory cost: Exact/approximate Hessian spectrum estimation (Lanczos/SLQ) is heavy; authors could not include state‑of‑the‑art LLMs due to “extremely large” cost.
> - Partial spectrum and cutoffs: Statistical tests and fits are performed only on top eigenvalues above a cutoff (∼1000 largest), leaving the bulk of near‑zero spectrum untested/unused; results may depend on the cutoff and SLQ accuracy.
> - Generalization predictor not robust: While KS distance (power‑law goodness) predicts LLM generalization in some cases (and when sharpness fails), the authors explicitly note it is “not a robust generalization measure.”
> - Dataset/model coverage limits: CNNs (MNIST/Fashion/CIFAR) and mid‑scale GPT‑2/TinyLlama are studied; findings may not directly transfer to larger models or other modalities.
> - Methodological sensitivity: Reported “phases” (e.g., large‑batch transitions) and many claims rely on training time, batch size, and under/over‑parameterization regimes; these require careful replication and could be sensitive to training schedules.
> 
> Cross‑paper development risks to keep in view
> - Heavy dependence on spectral/curvature proxies: Several methods lean on Hessian/singular value structure (Dale’s Law analysis, power‑law spectral goodness) that are expensive to compute and may be sensitive to initialization, model size, and task scale.
> - Assumption gaps between theory and practice: JEPA results require deep linear networks and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances; power‑law Hessian tests focus on top eigenvalues; conclusions may weaken under realistic nonlinear/attention backbones or non‑diagonalizable data.
> - Engineering sensitivity: PBADet’s thresholds and training hyperparameters, 4‑bit optimizers’ quantization settings (block size, mapping, normalization), and DANN/ColEI initializations can materially affect outcomes, raising tuning burden for new datasets or backbones.

**naive 最终答案**

> I found the relevant papers covering all five topics.
> 
> **Papers found:**
> 
> **(a) Spectral/curvature analysis of deep networks** — *Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure: From CNNs to LLMs* (ICML 2025). It shows power-law Hessian spectra and eigengaps hold across SGD/Adam/AMSGrad etc., CNNs (LeNet, ResNet18) and Transformers (ViT-base on CIFAR-100, GPT-2, TinyLlama); the slope predicts generalization on MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/CIFAR-10/100; also covers Adam vs SGD for Transformers and LoRA fine-tuning of TinyLlama (LoRA fine-tuning does **not** induce the power-law structure that full fine-tuning does).
> 
> **(b) Biologically constrained E/I recurrent networks** — *Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly* (NeurIPS 2023). Analyzes ColEI and DANN networks obeying Dale's principle via singular/eigenvalue spectra (multimodal vs unimodal spectra, normalised SVD entropy) on sequential MNIST, adding, PTB, and object recognition.
> 
> **(c) JEPA self-distillation** — *How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks* (NeurIPS 2024). In deep linear nets, JEPA (latent prediction, MSE) prioritizes high-influence/informative features, whereas MAE (reconstruction with MSE) prioritizes high-variance/noisy features.
> 
> **(d) Memory-efficient 4-bit optimizer states** — *Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States* (NeurIPS 2023). Uses smaller block size (B128) and rank-1 normalization/linear quantization (zero-point exclusion) for Adam/AdamW states, retaining accuracy in fine-tuning (GLUE, SQuAD, E2E-NLG, Alpaca) and pretraining (ImageNet/Swin-T, WMT14); LoRA mentioned as a related parameter-efficient approach.
> 
> **(e) One-stage anchor-free part-body detector** — *PBADet* (ICLR 2024). A one-stage anchor-free detector using a single part-to-body center offset, evaluated on BodyHands, COCO-HumanParts, COCO-WholeBody, and CrowdHuman (face-body association).
> 
> **Regarding cross-entropy vs MSE, attention backbones, LoRA, digit/object benchmarks:** CE-vs-MSE is only touched indirectly (JEPA vs MAE compare MSE-based objectives; the ReLU-network theory paper uses square loss). Attention backbones appear in the Hessian paper (ViT-base, GPT-2/TinyLlama) and PBADet (compares DETR-based detectors); LoRA is covered in the Hessian paper and mentioned in the 4-bit optimizer paper. Digit/object benchmarks (MNIST, CIFAR, ImageNet, COCO) are reported across these works. No dedicated paper in the collection directly analyzes cross-entropy vs MSE losses.
> 
> **Development defects / limitations:**
> 
> - **(a) Hessian analysis:** cannot analyze state-of-the-art LLMs due to the huge memory/computation cost of Hessian computation; experiments are largely restricted to top eigenvalues or the last layer. Power-law goodness is *not* a robust generalization predictor (sharpness measures fail for LLMs; power-law correlation also unreliable in some cases). The structure breaks with small width/depth, limited data, noisy labels, or large-batch training. LoRA-only fine-tuning fails to form the power-law spectrum, suggesting LoRA adapters have different (possibly limited) generalization behavior.
> - **(b) EI networks:** ColEI networks learn poorly with high variance across seeds and are unstable without gradient clipping; performance worsens for small networks with few inhibitory units; the origin of the multimodal spectra and why large ColEI networks learn well despite large singular values remain open questions; DANN lacks I→I connections and cell-type time constants.
> - **(c) JEPA:** analysis is restricted to deep *linear* networks with balanced orthogonal initialization and simultaneously diagonalizable data; JEPA is susceptible to representation collapse (needs stop-gradient) and may be vulnerable to spurious/slow features; generalization to non-linear models is not established.
> - **(d) 4-bit optimizers:** the optimal quantization scheme is task/dataset-dependent; only language and vision tasks were tested (not RL/audio/graph); unoptimized (non-fused) implementation is slower than 8-bit; total memory savings saturate at low bitwidths because data/activations/fragments dominate; slight accuracy drops occur (e.g., Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2; WMT14 26.28 vs 26.61).
> - **(e) PBADet:** its advantage over BPJDet is small for single-part tasks (face-body on CrowdHuman); it relies on YOLO (convolutional) backbones while DETR-based detectors remain competitive in body AP; task-alignment learning is necessary (performance drops without it); the single center-offset association may be less reliable for small/occluded parts.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the papers that collectively cover your five topics:
> 
> **1. (a) Spectral/curvature analyses — "Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure: From CNNs to LLMs"** (doc `582d138d...`)
> - Power-law Hessian spectra and power-law eigengaps across SGD, Adam, AMSGrad, RAdam, etc.; slope magnitude correlates with sharpness/generalization (LeNet on MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/CIFAR-10/100; ResNet18; ViT; GPT-2/TinyLlama).
> - Covers attention backbones (ViT, GPT-2), cross-entropy-trained classifiers on digit benchmarks, AdamW, and LoRA fine-tuning (LoRA-only tuning fails to induce the power-law that full fine-tuning does; Tr(H) more reliable for pretrained models).
> 
> **2. (b) Dale's-law E/I recurrent networks — "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (doc `e63a94c4...`)
> - ColEI (sign-constrained columns) vs DANN RNNs; eigenvalue/singular-value spectra at initialization, normalised SVD entropy, on sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, object recognition.
> 
> **3. (c) JEPA vs reconstruction — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks"** (doc `40fde037...`)
> - Shows deep linear JEPA (self-distillation, latent-space prediction) prioritizes high-influence features, whereas MAE-style MSE reconstruction prioritizes high-variance/noisy features; depth strengthens this bias; ImageNet-1K I-JEPA validation.
> 
> **4. (d) 4-bit optimizer states — "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (doc `8d5e1455...`)
> - 4-bit Adam/AdamW with small block (B128) quantization for first moment and rank-1 normalization + zero-point-excluding linear quantizer (optionally factorized second moment); matches 32-bit accuracy on GLUE, SQuAD, ImageNet-1k (Swin-T attention backbone), E2E-NLG, WMT14, LLaMA fine-tuning; up to ~57.7% memory savings; explicitly relates to LoRA-style tuning.
> 
> **5. (e) One-stage anchor-free part-body detector — "PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association"** (doc `08b70bc3...`)
> - Single part-to-body center offset on anchor-free YOLOv5/v7 backbones; outperforms BPJDet/HierR-CNN on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman (face-body), and extends to quadruped datasets.
> 
> ---
> 
> **Development defects / limitations of these methods:**
> 
> - **Hessian paper:** cannot analyze SOTA LLMs due to Hessian memory/compute cost; power-law goodness is *not* a robust generalization predictor in all cases (sharpness-based measures fail on LLMs); analysis limited to top ~1,000 eigenvalues (tail estimation inaccurate); LoRA-only fine-tuning does not reproduce the power-law structure of full fine-tuning.
> - **Dale's-law paper:** ColEI networks learn worse and with higher variance; sign constraints alone still hurt (gradient clipping needed); spectra worsen for small networks/fewer inhibitory units; eigenvalue analysis is limited because non-symmetric eigenvectors are non-orthogonal (motivating SVD/NSE); DANNs lack biological details such as I→I connections and cell-type time constants.
> - **JEPA paper:** analysis limited to deep *linear* MLPs, balanced-orthogonal initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable data; JEPA can be vulnerable to spurious/slow features and requires stop-gradient tricks to avoid collapse; noisy features are still learned (just at lower weight amplitude).
> - **4-bit optimizer paper:** optimal quantization scheme is task/dataset dependent; only language and vision tasks were evaluated (RL, audio, graph untested); implementation was not fused, so small models ran slower than 8-bit optimizers; memory savings saturate at low bitwidths because total memory (activations, fragments) dominates; LoRA noted as applicable mainly to language-model fine-tuning.
> - **PBADet:** its advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced on the single-part (face-body) CrowdHuman task; anchor-free design and association branch rely on task-alignment learning and multi-scale offsets (ablations show degradation without them); one-to-one part-to-body correspondence limits handling of occluded/multiple part configurations compared to body-to-part designs.

### paperscope:gap:280 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building a low‑memory, real‑time gesture interface for a multi‑person scene (e.g., a clinical setting) and need: a one‑pass detector that reliably links hands/face to the correct person; training on limited‑VRAM GPUs using optimizers with tiny state (≈4‑bit) during end‑to‑end or adapter‑based fine‑tuning; guidance on avoiding noisy pixel cues when using self‑supervised distillation (preferring predictive latent features over raw reconstruction with MSE); and practical ways to track/forecast generalization by inspecting curvature/spectral properties while training with CE under SGD/AdamW on transformer/CNN backbones. Point me to papers that demonstrate these pieces on typical digit/object and whole‑body datasets and discuss metrics like Precision/F1 or cosine‑style similarity where relevant.Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

**score：4→2（Δ-2）；rounds：4→3（Δ-1）。**

工具安排：naive 为第1轮4次、第2轮2次、第3轮2次；community 为第1轮4次、第2轮4次。最终回答另占一轮。

Gold 1：

> Below are the development defects and stated limitations for each method, based strictly on the provided papers.
> 
> 1) PBADet (ICLR 2024, one‑stage anchor‑free part‑body association)
> - Limited gain on single‑part tasks: The advantage over BPJDet is not pronounced when the task involves a single part (e.g., face–body association on CrowdHuman), as explicitly noted in Appendix A.1.
> - Dataset/threshold sensitivity: Inference requires separate NMS thresholds for bodies and parts and per‑dataset tuning (e.g., different τconf/τiou for COCOHumanParts vs. BodyHands), implying sensitivity to dataset conditions. (Paper text shows they use different thresholds per dataset.)
> - Dependency on anchor‑free heads and specific hyperparameters: The method is implemented via anchor‑free YOLO heads with specific loss weights (λiou, λdfl, λcls, λassoc), scaling factor (λ), and task‑alignment parameters (K, α, β). While effective, it ties the approach to those design choices and training recipes (e.g., 4× V100, AMP, 100 epochs, 1024×1024), which may constrain portability without re‑tuning. (Stated training setup and ablation show drops when removing task‑alignment or multi‑scale.)
> 
> 2) Dale’s Law in RNNs (NeurIPS 2023, ColEI vs. recurrent DANNs; spectral perspective)
> - ColEI instability and variance: ColEI RNNs show high variance across initializations and are highly unstable without gradient clipping; they also benefit substantially more from clipping than other models. (Explicitly reported.)
> - Sensitivity to network size and E:I ratio: Small ColEI networks and those with fewer inhibitory units learn less effectively; their spectral properties worsen (multimodal, dispersed singular‑value spectra) and learning degrades. (Explicitly demonstrated.)
> - Spectral pathologies persist despite sign constraints control: Even after relaxing sign constraints or transplanting singular vectors, the singular‑value spectrum itself has stronger impact; poor spectra in ColEI remain a core issue. (Shown in spectrum transplant experiments.)
> - Theoretical scope limitations: Key derivations rely on special initializations/assumptions (Assumption 3.1), and open theoretical questions remain (origin of ColEI’s multi‑modal spectra; why large ColEI learns well despite large maximum singular values). (Explicitly stated.)
> - Biological modeling scope: The work focuses on ColEI and DANN abstractions; other interneuron subtypes and more biologically faithful features (e.g., I→I connections, cell‑type‑specific time constants) are not explored; hybrid designs are left for future work. (Explicitly noted as future directions.)
> 
> 3) JEPA vs. MAE in deep linear self‑distillation (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Strong assumptions limit generality: Theory requires deep linear encoders, simultaneously diagonalizable Σxx and Σyx, specific balanced/orthogonal initializations, and gradient flow analysis. The authors explicitly note generalization to nonlinear networks and non‑simultaneously‑diagonalizable data remains open.
> - Depth‑dependent bias: JEPA’s favorable “influential‑feature” bias (toward high regression coefficients) takes hold only when encoders are deep, and diminishes substantially for shallow encoders; this reduces the robustness of the claimed advantage in shallow settings. (Explicitly shown.)
> - Potential vulnerability to spurious/slow features: The paper notes JEPA’s bias toward predictive low‑variance (slow) features can be a drawback—making JEPA vulnerable to spurious or slow features in some scenarios. (Explicitly discussed in the paper’s discussion.)
> - Empirical scope: Experiments are mainly in linear settings and controlled toy generative processes (plus a small‑scale ImageNet‑64 representation check); broader validation in practical nonlinear architectures is outside scope. (Explicitly acknowledged.)
> 
> 4) Memory‑efficient 4‑bit optimizers (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Task‑specific tuning likely needed: Authors state the optimal quantization configuration can depend on task/data; although rank‑1 normalization + linear mapping worked well in their tests, there is no guarantee of lossless performance universally.
> - Limited domain coverage: Evaluation focuses on language/vision; applicability to RL, audio, and graphs is not established. (Explicit limitation.)
> - Implementation caveat (performance): Without fused kernels, their 4‑bit implementation can be slower than 8‑bit; they therefore add a fused version to recover speed. (Explicitly reported in Table 4.)
> - Structural constraints: Rank‑1 normalization falls back to per‑tensor for 1D second‑moment tensors (where they use B128 block‑wise instead), implying mixed schemes and potential sensitivity to tensor shape. (Method detail as stated.)
> - Zero‑point failure mode in second‑moment quantization: The paper identifies that including zero in the quantization map catastrophically breaks Adam’s update (most entries quantize to zero, blowing up 1/√v), necessitating zero‑excluding mappings. While they solve this, it underscores a failure mode that must be avoided in practice. (Explicitly demonstrated.)
> 
> 5) Power‑law Hessian structure in CNNs and LLMs (ICML 2025)
> - Computational/memory limits: The main limitation stated is the inability to include state‑of‑the‑art, very large LLMs in Hessian analysis due to prohibitive memory/compute costs. (Explicit.)
> - Partial spectrum focus: The empirical analysis and KS tests focus on the top portion of the Hessian spectrum (∼ up to 1,000 eigenvalues above a cutoff) because estimating many near‑zero eigenvalues is inaccurate/expensive. This truncation is a methodological constraint. (Explicitly explained.)
> - Generalization predictor is not robust: Although the KS distance (power‑law goodness) can correlate strongly with generalization in several LLM settings where sharpness fails, the authors explicitly state it is not a robust generalization measure in all cases. (Explicit.)
> - Informal theory: The maximum‑entropy interpretation of the power‑law spectrum is presented as an informal explanation (not a full proof), indicating theoretical incompleteness. (Explicitly framed as an interpretation.)
> - Model/data scope: Several conclusions are demonstrated on specific CNNs/LLMs and datasets; while coverage includes multiple tasks and scales, broader universality is not claimed. (Implied by experimental scope; authors note room for future work.)
> 
> Summary: Across these works, the main development defects/limitations center on (i) task/model‑specific scope and assumptions (JEPA theory; 4‑bit optimizer task dependence; Hessian truncation and compute limits), (ii) stability and scaling sensitivities (ColEI instability, dependence on EI ratio/size; PBADet’s limited gains on single‑part association; 4‑bit implementation speed without fused ops), and (iii) predictors that are not universally reliable (Hessian power‑law goodness as a non‑robust generalization metric; sharpness failing for LLMs). These are all explicitly reported or constrained within the papers’ own analyses.

**naive 最终答案**

> Here are the papers from the collection that map onto each piece of your pipeline, followed by an analysis of each method's development defects.
> 
> ## 1. One-pass part→body association detector
> **PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association** (ICLR 2024). A single anchor-free YOLO-style detector links parts (face, left/right hands, feet) to the correct parent body via a single part-to-body center offset, with branches for classification, localization and displacement. On **BodyHands** (hand-body) and **COCOHumanParts** (whole-body, six parts) it beats SOTA (BPJDet, HierR-CNN), and it is extended to **CrowdHuman** (face-body) and **AnimalPose/AP-10K** (quadrupeds). Metrics: AP (IoU=0.5), conditional accuracy, joint AP, mMR−2 (part-body mismatch), and Precision/Recall/F1 vs ED-Pose (e.g., left hand P/R/F1 37.63/60.82/46.50 vs 18.36/30.34/22.87). Real-time claim rests on the YOLOv7 backbone (1024×1024 input).
> 
> **Development defects:**
> - Evaluated/compared in ways that favor it: vs ED-Pose it uses ground-truth part boxes for the competitor but requires its own predicted boxes with IoU>0.5; on CrowdHuman (single face part) the advantage over BPJDet is "not as pronounced."
> - BodyHands has only one part type (no left/right hand distinction), so multi-part generality is only partially validated there.
> - Association relies on a body center/box being present; occluded or heavily crowded bodies (the clinical multi-person case) stress the single-offset assumption; NMS thresholds (τ_conf, τ_iou) must be hand-tuned per dataset.
> - Trained with plain SGD/AMP on 4×V100 at 100 epochs — the paper does not address low-VRAM or 4-bit optimizers at all.
> 
> ## 2. ≈4-bit optimizer states for low-VRAM fine-tuning
> **Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States** (NeurIPS 2023). Compresses Adam/AdamW first/second moments to 4-bit via smaller block size (B128), rank-1 normalization, and zero-point-excluding linear quantization (optionally factorizing the second moment, "4-bitFactor"). Validated on image classification (Swin-T/ImageNet-1K), NLU (RoBERTa-L/GLUE), QA (SQuAD), NLG (GPT-2/E2E), MT (Transformer/WMT14), and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning (Alpaca) — matching 32-bit AdamW, cutting total memory up to 57.7% and enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU. Works for both end-to-end and (via LoRA-related parameter-efficient tuning) adapter-style adaptation.
> 
> **Development defects:**
> - Only reduces optimizer-state memory; activations/data/fragments remain, so savings "saturate" — it does not compress activations (that needs GACT/checkpointing, referenced but separate).
> - On small models (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2M) it is *slower* than 8-bit AdamW unless fused operators are used.
> - Quantizing both moments causes a marginal accuracy drop; the paper's convergence proof covers quantized SGD(M), not AdamW formally.
> - Authors state the optimal quantization scheme is task/dataset-dependent and untested beyond language/vision; factorization of the second moment adds overhead/complexity.
> 
> ## 3. Predictive latent features vs. noisy pixel reconstruction
> **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks** (NeurIPS 2024). Shows self-distillation (JEPA-style, predicting target-encoder outputs in latent space) is implicitly biased to learn high-ρ "influential" features and suppresses noise, whereas MAE-style reconstruction (MSE in pixel space) prioritizes whatever explains bulk variance, which is often uninformative/noisy. Depth strengthens JEPA's noise suppression; validated on ImageNet-1K where I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance perceptual PCA subspace than MAE (measured by CCA/cosine-style similarity of embeddings).
> 
> **Development defects:**
> - Theory restricted to deep **linear** MLPs with balanced orthogonal initialization and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances Σ_yx, Σ_xx — assumptions real data violate; results only "qualitatively" generalize.
> - JEPA can still learn noisy/spurious/slow features (it converges to lower-amplitude weights); collapse prevention needs stop-gradients/extra tricks.
> - No direct evaluation on digit/object or whole-body datasets — evidence is linear-model simulation + ImageNet; the claim about perception-level noise avoidance is partly speculative.
> 
> ## 4. Tracking generalization via curvature/spectral analysis (CE, SGD/AdamW)
> **Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure: From CNNs to LLMs** (ICML 2025). Hessian spectra of well-trained networks follow a power law; the fitted slope ŝ correlates with sharpness and generalization, and the KS-statistic d_ks can forecast LLM generalization during training (up to 0.98 correlation). Datasets include **MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-1K** (LeNet/ResNet/ViT and GPT-2/TinyLlama with CE under SGD, Adam, AdamW, etc.). The appendix analyzes **LoRA adapter fine-tuning** (TinyLlama/MathQA): power-law forms early in early layers, but for pretrained+LoRA models d_ks initially rises then falls with test loss, and the Hessian **trace Tr(H)** is often the more reliable generalization indicator.
> 
> **Development defects:**
> - Not a robust predictor: power-law "goodness" fails in some regimes (sharpness measures work on CNNs but fail for LLMs); needs overparameterized models and breaks with limited data, large batches, and noisy labels.
> - SOTA LLMs were excluded because Hessian computation is too memory/GPU expensive — a real practical barrier for your low-memory setting.
> - LoRA-only fine-tuning does *not* induce the power-law structure the way full fine-tuning does, so the forecasting method needs care for adapter-based training.
> 
> ## Additional cosine-similarity metric reference
> **On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning** analyzes cosine similarities of positive/negative pairs (optimum 1 and −1/(n−1)), noting mini-batch settings increase negative-pair similarity variance and degrade representations; proposed an auxiliary variance-reduction loss, tested on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100, ImageNet with ResNet backbones under SGD. Useful if you want a cosine-style monitoring metric, with the defect that the extra loss hyperparameter can suppress meaningful semantic variance.
> 
> **Overall gap:** no single paper in this collection demonstrates all four pieces together on digit/object + whole-body datasets; PBADet (part 1) never uses 4-bit optimizers or spectral analysis, and the SSL/Hessian papers are validated mainly on ImageNet/LLMs, not on hand/face whole-body data.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the relevant papers from the collection for each requirement, with their development defects.
> 
> **1. One-pass detector linking hands/face to the correct person**
> - **PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association (ICLR 2024)** — one-stage, anchor-free; a single part-to-body center offset links hands/face/feet to the correct body. Demonstrated on BodyHands (hand AP, conditional accuracy, joint AP), COCOHumanParts (AP per part), CrowdHuman (face-body MR-2/AP), and quadruped AnimalPose/AP-10K; vs ED-Pose it reports **Precision/Recall/F1** (e.g., all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51). Related context: BPJDet, BodyHands (two-stage), Associative Embedding.
> - **Defects:** advantage over BPJDet shrinks for single-part (face-body) tasks on CrowdHuman; ablations show association head, multi-scale offsets and task-alignment are each essential (without the association loss conditional accuracy drops ~80.8→92.6 range), so accuracy depends on detection quality; the ED-Pose comparison is favorable to ED-Pose (GT part boxes used, no part detector); NMS thresholding is still needed; heavy 1024–1536px inputs for accuracy.
> 
> **2. Tiny-state (≈4-bit) optimizers for limited-VRAM GPUs**
> - **Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States (NeurIPS 2023)** — 4-bit AdamW / 4-bit Factor via B128/DE first-moment and rank-1/linear (zero-excluded) second-moment quantization. Tested on Swin-T/ImageNet-1k (CLS), RoBERTa-L GLUE/SQuAD, GPT-2 E2E-NLG, Transformer WMT14, LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning; up to 57.7% memory saving; supports end-to-end and fine-tuning (adapter-style tasks included).
> - **Defects:** slower than 8-bit AdamW on small models because fused operators are not implemented yet (speed expected to match after fusion); quantizing both moments causes a marginal accuracy drop; second moment suffers a zero-point problem — naive 4-bit (B2048/DE) can be unstable (33–66% unstable runs) unless zero is excluded/factorized; optimal quantization scheme may be task-dependent; only language/vision tasks tested.
> 
> **3. Self-supervised distillation avoiding noisy pixel cues (latent prediction over MSE reconstruction)**
> - **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks (NeurIPS 2024)** — explains why JEPA-style self-distillation prioritizes high-influence predictive latent features and suppresses noise vs MAE-style reconstruction; ImageNet-1K experiments show I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance PCA/perceptual subspace than MAE (CCA measurements). Related: **LDReg** (counters local dimensional collapse of SSL features), and **On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning** (cosine-style negative-pair similarity analysis, InfoNCE/SigLIP, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100/ImageNet).
> - **Defects:** theory limited to deep linear networks, balanced orthogonal initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable data — non-linear/non-diagonalizable generalization is unproven; JEPA's bias toward predictive low-variance features also makes it "vulnerable to spurious or slow features" and it can still learn noisy features (at lower weight amplitude); feature-prioritization efficiency claims are qualitative. LDReg's LID estimation degrades in high dimensions; forcing very low LID can trigger full collapse.
> 
> **4. Tracking/forecasting generalization via curvature/spectral properties under CE with SGD/AdamW**
> - **Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure (ICML 2025)** — Hessian spectra of well-trained CNNs and LLMs follow a power law (MLE + Kolmogorov-Smirnov test); power-law slope correlates with sharpness/generalization (LeNet on MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/CIFAR-10/100 under SGD and Adam-family optimizers; GPT-2/TinyLlama with AdamW pretraining/fine-tuning), and can predict LLM generalization during training where conventional sharpness fails (d_ks up to ~0.98 correlation).
> - **Defects:** generalization prediction works only "sometimes" — conventional sharpness-based measures largely fail as LLM generalization predictors; power-law structure is lost with small width/depth, limited data, noisy labels, and large-batch training; LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the power-law structure as full fine-tuning does; Hessian computation is expensive (SOTA LLMs excluded by cost); power-law goodness and sharpness capture different regimes. (Related spectral-property analysis: normalised SVD entropy of initial weights anti-correlates with final test error in RNNs.)
> 
> **Summary of the main cross-cutting defects:** PBADet's association gains degrade for single-part/crowded cases and depend on detection/offsets; 4-bit optimizers trade speed and slight accuracy for memory and need careful zero-point handling; JEPA's noise-avoidance benefit is proven only in simplified linear settings and can suppress useful spurious/slow features; Hessian power-law forecasting is dataset/optimizer/regime-dependent, expensive, and unreliable as a universal generalization predictor.

</details>

### paperscope:gap:283 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that, across vision and language, study how representation-level choices and training procedures influence reliability and performance: for example, adding noise to learned token embeddings during post-training adaptation of attention-based models; joint-embedding predictive setups in self-supervised learning analyzed under mean‑squared vs softmax cross‑entropy losses; biologically constrained recurrent nets with separate excitatory/inhibitory units examined through their singular-value spectra; and sequential calibration methods that give anytime‑valid risk control with active labeling. I’m also looking for a one‑stage detector without anchors that associates human parts to their parent person on standard detection benchmarks, trained with stochastic gradient descent or adaptive moment optimizers on convolutional backbones with multi‑scale features, and evaluated with metrics like AUROC/F1 or perplexity.Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

**score：4→2（Δ-2）；rounds：3→4（Δ+1）。**

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below are the main development defects or limitations explicitly stated or clearly supported by the provided papers, organized by method.
> 
> 1) PBADet (ICLR 2024): One‑stage anchor‑free part‑to‑body association detection
> - Advantage diminishes in single‑part settings: On CrowdHuman’s face‑body association (a single-part task), the paper notes “the advantages of our method over BPJDet are not as pronounced,” indicating limited gains when only one part is involved.
> - Reliance on paired detection quality and dataset‑specific thresholds: The method decodes associations via predicted offsets and NMS with dataset‑specific thresholds; while standard practice, performance depends on robust detection of both parts and bodies and threshold tuning (reported different thresholds per dataset), which can limit portability across domains.
> 
> 2) Column EI (ColEI) RNNs enforcing Dale’s Law via signed columns (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Poor learning and instability without special care: ColEI networks “did not learn as well” as standard RNNs/DANNs across adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and naturalistic object recognition; they showed higher variance across seeds and benefited “substantially more” from gradient clipping, indicating training instability.
> - Spectral pathologies at initialization: They exhibit a multimodal, dispersed singular‑value spectrum with a mode of large singular values (even with eigenvalue radius constrained), which deforms activations/gradients and impairs learning.
> - Sensitivity to E/I ratio and size: Small ColEI networks and/or fewer inhibitory units degrade both spectrum (lower normalized SVD entropy, larger max singular values) and performance; performance improves only with larger networks and balanced E/I ratios, reducing practicality in small‑scale settings.
> - Initialization dependence and practicality: The strong conclusions rely on specific “balanced,” orthogonal initializations and spectral‑radius setting; training requires projected gradient steps to maintain signs, adding complexity.
> 
> 3) DANN RNNs (recurrent Dale’s ANNs)
> - Scope/assumption limitations in analysis: Although DANNs match standard RNNs’ spectra and learn well empirically, the theoretical comparisons rely on special initializations and on diagonal/alignable data covariance assumptions; generality to broader settings is not established within the paper.
> - Biological fidelity trade‑offs: DANNs specifically model fast PV+ interneurons; the authors note other inhibitory subtypes (e.g., SOM+, CCK+) are not directly captured, and hybrid/extended architectures are left for future work.
> 
> 4) JEPA (non‑contrastive self‑distillation, e.g., BYOL/SimSiam/I‑JEPA/V‑JEPA) vs MAE (NeurIPS 2024)
> - JEPA
>   - Collapse risk: The paper reiterates that the basic JEPA objective is “susceptible to collapse,” requiring tricks such as StopGrad; stability depends on such design choices.
>   - Implicit‑bias downside: While JEPA prioritizes high‑influence (predictive) features, the authors warn this may make JEPAs “vulnerable to spurious or slow features,” especially in realistic settings where such features exist.
>   - Theory scope limits: Results are for deep linear encoders with special initializations and simultaneously diagonalizable Σxx and Σxy; behavior with non‑diagonalizable or nonlinear models is unproven.
> - MAE
>   - Biased toward high‑variance (possibly noisy) subspaces: The paper (and related evidence it cites) shows MAE “learns uninformative features” for perception tasks and, in the linear analysis, prioritizes features by covariance (λ) rather than predictive influence (ρ), so it can favor noisy/high‑variance directions.
>   - Depth insensitivity in feature priority: In their dynamics, MAE’s feature learning order depends mainly on λ even as encoder depth grows, limiting its ability to focus earlier on influential but lower‑variance features.
> 
> 5) Active, anytime‑valid risk‑controlling prediction sets (NeurIPS 2024)
> - IID and shift assumptions: Guarantees are proved for IID streams; the authors note extension to distribution shift (e.g., covariate/label shift) is future work, so guarantees may not hold under shift without additional assumptions.
> - Label‑policy constraints: The approach requires a lower bound on labeling propensities (Assumption 2: qt(x) ≥ ε) and an existence/feasibility condition for the optimal policy form; these constraints may be restrictive in practice.
> - Dependence on predictors/estimation quality: Anytime‑validity is preserved, but label efficiency (growth rate) hinges on the accuracy of the conditional risk predictor and of the learned labeling policy; the regret bounds explicitly degrade with estimation error.
> - Conservativeness and operational complexity: Using e‑processes imposes time‑uniform guarantees but can be conservative, and the method adds operational overhead (online betting parameters, normalization for budget, inverse‑propensity weighting).
> 
> 6) NEFTune (ICLR 2024): Noisy Embedding Instruction Fine‑Tuning for LLMs
> - Evaluation bias and scope: Main gains are reported on AlpacaEval, a model‑judged benchmark (GPT‑4/ChatGPT). Authors acknowledge reliance on a single judge and limited compute prevented broad validation at larger model sizes/datasets.
> - Safety and alignment not rigorously assessed: The paper explicitly states it “does not rigorously evaluate the impact on model safety and reliability (toxicity/refusals),” and for further finetuning of LLaMA‑2‑Chat notes “some capabilities… may be affected like its ability to refrain from outputting toxic behavior.”
> - Gains concentrated in conversational quality: On OpenLLM Leaderboard tasks (ARC/HellaSwag/MMLU/TruthfulQA), performance is “the same,” indicating little to no improvement in factual QA/reasoning; improvements are largely in verbosity/fluency.
> - Weaker gains in resource‑constrained settings: With QLoRA (4‑bit), improvements are “milder” than full finetuning, suggesting sensitivity to quantization and/or training budget.
> - Mechanistic understanding incomplete: Authors state they lack a conclusive explanation for why NEFTune works; the observed effects (e.g., longer outputs) do not fully explain the performance gains.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Papers found (matching each method you described)
> 
> 1. **Noise added to token embeddings during post-training adaptation** → *NEFTune: Noisy Embeddings Improve Instruction Finetuning* (ICLR 2024). Adds scaled uniform noise α/√(Ld) to embeddings during instruction fine-tuning of LLaMA/OPT models.
> 2. **Joint-embedding predictive setups (JEPA) under MSE vs. predictive losses** → *Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features: A Deep Linear Network Analysis* (NeurIPS 2024). Analyzes JEPA vs. MAE (MSE reconstruction) dynamics with deep linear networks. (The specific MSE-vs-softmax-cross-entropy analysis of Tian et al. 2021 appears only as a citation, not as retrievable content here.)
> 3. **Biologically constrained recurrent nets with E/I units, singular-value spectra** → *Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective* (NeurIPS 2023). Compares ColEI vs. DANN vs. standard RNNs via singular-value spectra and normalized SVD entropy.
> 4. **Sequential calibration with anytime-valid risk control + active labeling** → *Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets* (NeurIPS 2024). Uses e-processes/betting for time-uniform risk control with active label queries.
> 5. **One-stage anchor-free detector for part–body association** → *PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association* (ICLR 2024). Uses a single part-to-body center offset on multi-scale feature maps with YOLOv5/v7 backbones. Note: it is evaluated with AP/MR-2/precision/recall/F1, not AUROC/perplexity.
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods
> 
> **NEFTune**
> - Gains are limited to conversational quality; OpenLLM-benchmark performance is unchanged.
> - Evaluation relies heavily on GPT-4/human judges (biased, no conclusive mechanism); no safety evaluation; limited validation on 30B/70B models.
> - Noise scale α is sensitive (α=100 destroys training; best α must be tuned); benefits are not reproduced by dropout/weight decay; noise at inference can regenerate training data (memorization risk).
> 
> **JEPA/MSE analysis**
> - JEPA objectives are prone to trivial collapse without stop-gradient/architectural tricks; MAE is trivially minimized by constant encoders.
> - JEPA suppresses noisy features, but is vulnerable to spurious/slow features; MAE prioritizes high-variance subspaces that may be uninformative for perception.
> - Theory holds only for deep linear networks with balanced orthogonal initialization and simultaneous diagonalizability — generalization to real nonlinear models is qualitative.
> 
> **Dale's Law EI RNNs**
> - ColEI networks train worse and with much higher seed variance; multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra at initialization create pathological dynamics (need gradient clipping).
> - Performance degrades sharply for small networks and few inhibitory units; sign constraints themselves also impair learning.
> - Normalized SVD entropy is only a correlational diagnostic; origins of the multimodal spectrum and why large ColEI works despite large σmax remain open.
> 
> **Anytime-valid risk-controlling active labeling**
> - Guarantees hold only in the i.i.d. setting; distribution shift (covariate/label shift) is left to future work.
> - Label policies require a positive query-probability lower bound q_min (can never fully stop labeling); relies on monotonicity/right-continuity assumptions; safety is only probabilistic (1−α).
> 
> **PBADet**
> - Advantage over BPJDet is much less pronounced on single-part tasks (e.g., face–body on CrowdHuman).
> - Ablations show association quality depends on multi-scale center-offset interpretation and task-alignment learning; removing either degrades performance.
> - Association accuracy is coupled to detection quality, and extension to non-human (quadruped) part–body association is less thoroughly validated.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the papers matching your descriptions, along with their development defects (limitations) as reported in the context.
> 
> **1. NEFTune: Noisy Embeddings Improve Instruction Finetuning** (ICLR 2024)
> - Matches: adding noise to token embeddings during instruction fine-tuning of attention-based LLMs (LLaMA-2-7B, OPT-6.7B), noise scaled α/√(Ld).
> - Defects: relies heavily on GPT-4 judging; limited validation at 30B/70B scale; no conclusive mechanism established; no safety evaluation; gains appear mainly in conversational quality while OpenLLM benchmark scores are unchanged; increased verbosity is a visible side-effect, and noise scaling/hyperparameters need tuning.
> 
> **2. "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks"** (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Matches: joint-embedding predictive (JEPA) self-supervised setups analyzed via solvable deep linear networks; compares objectives (MSE-based JEPA prediction in latent space vs MAE reconstruction in data space).
> - Note: the analysis contrasts MSE objectives (JEPA vs MAE), not "mean-squared vs softmax cross-entropy"; no paper in the collection analyzes JEPA under a softmax cross-entropy loss.
> - Defects: theory restricted to deep linear MLPs, special (balanced orthogonal) initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable data; nonlinear models/general distributions not covered; the implicit bias toward influential features also implies vulnerability to spurious/slow features; results generalize only qualitatively.
> 
> **3. "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Matches: biologically constrained RNNs with separate excitatory/inhibitory units (ColEI, DANN) analyzed through singular-value spectra (multimodal/dispersed spectra, normalised SVD entropy).
> - Defects: ColEI networks learn worse and with much higher variance across seeds; they are highly unstable without gradient clipping; spectra worsen for small networks with few inhibitory units; only two EI formulations considered, leaving open theoretical questions (origin of multi-modal spectra, why large ColEI networks still learn); models could be more biologically faithful (e.g., no I-to-I connections in DANNs, no cell-type-specific time constants).
> 
> **4. "Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets"** (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Matches: sequential calibration with anytime-valid risk control via e-processes/betting, plus active labeling policies under a label budget, with regret bounds and ImageNet experiments.
> - Defects: assumes i.i.d. data; label policies must be lower-bounded; distribution shift (covariate/label shift) during test time is not handled; guarantees rely on monotonicity/right-continuity assumptions.
> 
> **5. PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association** (ICLR 2024)
> - Matches: anchor-free one-stage detector associating human parts to parent bodies on standard benchmarks (BodyHands, COCO-HumanParts, CrowdHuman), multi-scale feature maps, convolutional YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones, task-alignment loss; evaluated with AP, conditional accuracy, and F1/precision/recall (e.g., vs ED-Pose).
> - Note: it is evaluated with AP/F1, not AUROC or perplexity.
> - Defects: on the single-part CrowdHuman face-body task its advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced; dependence on task-alignment learning, association loss, and multi-scale offset design (ablations show removing any hurts); compared mainly to YOLO-family backbones.
> 
> In sum, none of the collection's papers match "mean-squared vs softmax cross-entropy" for JEPA or "AUROC/perplexity" evaluation for the detector — those details are not supported by the context.

### paperscope:gap:286 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building a real-world system that needs: (1) a lightweight single-pass model to detect hands/face and link them to the correct person in crowded scenes; (2) a practical way to boost a transformer assistant’s instruction-following via a simple fine-tuning tweak on feature embeddings; (3) online, label-efficient calibration that guarantees low risk at every time step; and (4) guidance on designing recurrent controllers that respect excitatory/inhibitory constraints. I’d also like theory explaining why predicting in a learned representation space can avoid noisy cues in self-supervised pipelines. Are there works that collectively cover these needs?Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

**score：4→2（Δ-2）；rounds：4→4（Δ+0）。**

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below are the main development defects and limitations explicitly stated or implied by the five methods in the provided papers. Each list is restricted to issues the papers themselves acknowledge or demonstrate.
> 
> 1) PBADet (one-stage anchor-free part–body association)
> - Advantage not pronounced in single-part settings: On CrowdHuman (face–body association), PBADet’s benefit over BPJDet diminishes because the task involves only one part; gains showed up mainly with multiple parts-to-body associations.
> - Sensitivity to design hyperparameters and dataset-specific tuning: Training and inference rely on numerous, dataset-tuned knobs (e.g., loss weights λiou/λdfl/λcls/λassoc, scaling factor λ for offsets, alignment parameters K, α, β, and NMS thresholds τconf/τiou that differ across datasets). Ablations show performance drops without multi-scale supervision or task-alignment learning, indicating sensitivity.
> - Decoding assumption: Inference assigns each part to an unassigned body that encloses it and minimizes a distance to the predicted body center. This assumes the part box is contained in a body box; the method does not discuss failures when this enclosure assumption is violated (e.g., annotation noise or extreme occlusions).
> 
> 2) Dale-constrained RNNs: ColEI vs recurrent DANNs (Dale’s ANNs)
> - ColEI (column sign-constrained EI RNNs) defects:
>   • Poor learning and instability: Empirically underperform standard RNNs/DANNs across tasks; more variable across seeds; substantially benefit from gradient clipping (indicating instability).
>   • Spectral pathology: Multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra with large outlier singular values cause exploding/vanishing dynamics and impaired learning; pathology worsens in small networks and with few inhibitory units (high E:I ratios).
>   • Heavy dependence on network size and E/I ratio: Small ColEI networks and realistic low fractions of I units learn significantly worse; performance improves mainly for larger, more balanced networks.
>   • Tuning burden: Outcomes depend on spectral radius ρ; ColEI’s best region differs from standard/DANN RNNs and requires careful choice.
> - Recurrent DANNs (EI architecture) caveats the paper notes:
>   • Biological scope: DANNs most naturally model fast PV+ circuits; they may not capture other inhibitory subtypes (the authors suggest hybrid models for broader biological fidelity).
>   • Open theory gaps: The origins of ColEI’s multimodal spectra and why large max singular values do not preclude learning in large ColEI networks remain unresolved; results guide design but do not fully fix ColEI training without new initializations.
> 
> 3) JEPA vs MAE in deep linear self-distillation (implicit bias analysis)
> - Restricted theoretical scope: Results rely on deep linear networks, special orthogonal/balanced initializations, and simultaneously diagonalizable Σxx and Σyx. Generalization to nonlinear encoders/decoders and real data not guaranteed.
> - Depth dependence: The JEPA advantage (prioritizing high-regression-coefficient, low-noise features) only clearly manifests with deep encoders; the effect diminishes with shallow encoders.
> - Potential bias to slow/spurious features: The authors note the discovered bias could explain JEPA’s tendency to focus on slow or spurious features in some settings.
> 
> 4) Active, anytime-valid Risk-Controlling Prediction Sets (RCPS)
> - i.i.d. assumption: Guarantees assume i.i.d. (X, Y) over time; handling distribution shift is left to future work.
> - Label-policy constraints: The method assumes a positive lower bound on the labeling probability (Assumption 2) and existence of an optimal policy form; removing these assumptions requires additional analysis.
> - Predictor dependence: Using a conditional risk predictor r̂ can substantially reduce variance and improve label efficiency, but poor predictions increase variance and slow the e-process growth (while not invalidating risk control).
> - Practical tuning: Requires setting a label budget B, lower bounds q_min, and managing betting parameters; mis-specification slows convergence to the optimal β* even though validity is maintained.
> 
> 5) NEFTune (noisy-embedding instruction finetuning)
> - Evaluation dependence and potential length confound: Main gains are reported on AlpacaEval using GPT-4/ChatGPT as judges. Although the authors show length alone does not fully explain improvements, longer outputs do correlate with higher scores; reliance on model-based judges introduces bias.
> - Limited validation scope: Due to compute limits, extensive validation on larger models/datasets is incomplete; many runs used fixed hyperparameters rather than thorough sweeps. Gains on QLoRA are smaller.
> - Safety/behavioral unknowns: The impact on safety, toxicity, and refusal behavior is not rigorously evaluated; the authors note that additional finetuning of LLaMA-2-Chat may affect refusal/toxicity safeguards.
> - Hyperparameter sensitivity and failure modes: Performance depends on noise scale α; very large α (e.g., 100) can break training, and benefits plateau or decrease with excessive epochs. Gains are primarily in conversational quality; standard factual/MC benchmarks (ARC/HellaSwag/MMLU/TruthfulQA) remain largely unchanged.
> 
> Overall integration
> - Methods targeting representation/regularization (JEPA, NEFTune) deliver strong, task-specific gains but come with scope constraints (linear/deep-theory assumptions or evaluation biases) and tuning sensitivity.
> - Biologically constrained training (ColEI) faces practical learning defects tied to spectral pathologies; DANNs alleviate these but raise modeling-scope questions for broader inhibitory diversity.
> - The anchor-free detection design (PBADet) yields robust multi-part association but requires dataset-specific hyperparameter tuning and its decoding depends on containment assumptions.
> - Anytime-valid RCPS delivers rigorous sequential guarantees, but label-efficiency and speed hinge on predictive quality and policy constraints under i.i.d.; robust handling of distribution shift remains open.

**naive 最终答案**

> Yes — the collection covers all four needs plus the theory, but each paper has development defects you should weigh.
> 
> **1. Hands/face detection + person linking in crowds — PBADet** (doc `08b70bc…`)
> One-stage, anchor-free, part-to-body center offset linking hands/face to the correct person; lightweight YOLOv5/7 backbones; beats BPJDet/BodyHands/HierR-CNN on BodyHands & COCO-HumanParts and leads body MR-2 on CrowdHuman.
> - **Defects:** it is a single image (not video) detector; on the *single*-part face-body CrowdHuman task its advantage over BPJDet is small (best MR-2 but comparable AP); hands/feet gains vs. ED-Pose rely on comparing box-based detection with keypoints (evaluation bias in its favor); requires 1024–1536 px input and large YOLOv5l6/YOLOv7 variants for best results (86.1M/36.9M params), so true "lightweight" needs the small s6 variant with lower accuracy; center-offset linking can degrade with occlusion.
> 
> **2. Instruction-following boost via embedding tweak — NEFTune** (doc `fad0fb…`)
> Adds scaled uniform noise (α/√(Ld)) to embeddings during fine-tuning; LLaMA-2-7B AlpacaEval win rate 29.8→64.7, +8–10% on Evol-Instruct/ShareGPT/OpenPlatypus, works with QLoRA/RLHF models, no OpenLLM regression.
> - **Defects:** primary metric AlpacaEval depends on a single GPT-4 judge (biased); validated mainly at 7B (30B/70B not swept); no conclusive mechanism for why it works; safety/toxicity/refusal not rigorously evaluated, and it may weaken a chat model's ability to refuse toxic behavior; gains partly correlate with longer outputs; hyperparameters (α, noise type) fixed rather than swept.
> 
> **3. Online label-efficient calibration with anytime-valid risk — Active, Anytime-Valid RCPS** (doc `cda0aa…`)
> Extends RCPS to streaming with active labeling (query labels per budget), guaranteeing risk ≤ θ *for all t simultaneously* with prob. ≥ 1−α via e-processes/betting; learned/pretrained labeling policies cut labels while keeping violation rate ≤ α (simulations + ImageNet).
> - **Defects:** assumes i.i.d. data and bounded label policies (stated limitations); guarantees rely on monotone risk and safe β=1 start; risk control is over the *parameterized* set, not raw model errors; label-policy/predictor models must be re-estimated online (computational overhead); empirical validation is limited to synthetic + ImageNet classification (no deployed use cases).
> 
> **4. Recurrent controllers with E/I constraints — "Why Dale's Law RNNs Learn Poorly"** (doc `e63a94…`)
> Explains ColEI (column-sign-constrained) RNNs train poorly due to multimodal/dispersed singular-value spectra at initialization (rank-one nilpotent column-mean term), while recurrent DANN architectures preserve unimodal spectra and learn as well as standard RNNs; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) predicts performance; gradient clipping mitigates ColEI instability.
> - **Defects:** it is a diagnosis/guidance study, not a controller-design algorithm; small 1-layer RNNs dominate, larger networks behave differently (bigger ColEI learn despite large σmax, unexplained); no theory for the origin of the spectra; no E→I connections/time constants in DANN; no downstream controller/robot validation.
> 
> **5. Theory: why predicting in latent space avoids noisy cues — "Why JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (doc `40fde0…`)
> Analyzes deep linear self-distillation: JEPA is implicitly biased toward high-influence (high regression-coefficient) features and suppresses noise with depth, whereas MAE orders features mainly by eigenvalue (variance), so it wastes capacity on noisy high-variance cues; ImageNet-1K confirms I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance perceptual PCA subspace.
> - **Defects:** theory only for deep *linear* networks, balanced orthogonal initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable data; no rigorous proof for nonlinear models; an implicit bias toward predictive low-variance features may also make JEPA vulnerable to spurious/slow features; the transfer to non-self-distillation joint-embedding architectures is untested.
> 
> **Bottom line:** the collection collectively covers all five needs, but (1) is not video-scale or fully lightweight at top accuracy, (2) lacks safety validation and large-scale verification, (3) is i.i.d.-only with modest empirical scope, (4) gives diagnostic guidance rather than a deployable controller, and (5) is a linear-theory explanation with limited generalization evidence.

**community 最终答案**

> 是的，这些需求可被以下五篇文献集体覆盖（均来自该语料库）：
> 
> 1. **手/脸检测与人物关联**：PBADet（one-stage anchor-free part-body association，基于 YOLOv7/YOLOv5，单中心偏移实现 part→body 关联，在 BodyHands/COCO-HumanParts/CrowdHuman 上优于 SOTA）。
> 2. **指令跟随微调**：NEFTune——训练时向 embedding 加 α/√(Ld) 缩放均匀噪声，LLaMA-2-7B 在 AlpacaEval 上胜率 29.8%→64.7%，几乎无额外开销。
> 3. **在线、标签高效的任意时刻风险控制**：Anytime-Valid Risk-Controlling Active Labeling（基于 e-process/testing-by-betting 与主动标签策略，保证 P(ρ(β̂t)≤θ, ∀t)≥1−α，且标签预算受限）。
> 4. **满足兴奋/抑制（Dale 律）约束的递归控制器设计**：Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective（ColEI vs DANN RNN；指出奇异值谱比符号约束更关键，提出 NSE 作为训练前诊断指标）。
> 5. **潜在空间预测避免噪声特征的理论**：How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features（深度线性网络分析证明 JEPA 偏向高回归系数、低方差“高影响力”特征，而 MAE 偏向高协变特征，从而抑制噪声）。
> 
> ---
> 
> **这些方法的开发缺陷（依据上下文）：**
> 
> - **PBADet**：在单部件任务（CrowdHuman 面部-身体关联）上相对 BPJDet 优势不明显；仅测试 YOLO 骨干；需手工设定 NMS 阈值；与 ED-Pose 的对比评估使用了其自身 COCO GT 部件框，存在评估口径偏置风险。
> - **NEFTune**：主要评测依赖 GPT-4/AlpacaEval 单一裁判，有偏见风险；未在 30B/70B 大模型上充分验证；缺少安全评估；机制（降低对指令分布过拟合）仅为假设、无定论；人类评估规模很小（140 条、作者自评）；更长的输出部分解释增益但无法完全复现（强制加长仅边际提升，Gaussian 噪声只加长不提质）。
> - **Anytime-valid risk control**：假设数据 i.i.d.；要求标签策略有下界 q_min 且 ρ(1)=0；使用 IPW 修正；风险保证是概率性的（1−α），对标签预算和策略偏差敏感。
> - **Dale 律 RNN**：ColEI 网络学习差且方差大、需梯度裁剪才能稳定；仅给出经验性谱分析，理论问题未解（ColEI 多模态谱的起源、大网络为何仍能学好）；DANN 缺少 I→I 连接、未建模细胞类型特异时间常数，生物保真度有限。
> - **JEPA 理论**：仅限深度线性 MLP、特殊初始化、Σyx/Σxx 可同时对角化；向非线性/真实分布推广未经验证；理论本身还提示 JEPA 可能对虚假/缓慢特征存在脆弱性（该点未被充分研究）。

### paperscope:gap:289 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively cover: (1) an anchor‑free, one‑stage part/body association detector built on multi‑scale features (rather than anchors) for reliable hand/face/body linking; (2) analyses of deep network training dynamics showing how excitatory–inhibitory constraints impact recurrent models via spectral properties and how this interacts with common losses (e.g., MSE vs cross‑entropy) and optimizers (SGD/AdamW); (3) self‑supervised learning works contrasting joint‑embedding prediction vs input reconstruction and their implicit biases; (4) memory‑efficient training that compresses optimizer states to ≈4‑bit using quantization/factorization while preserving accuracy; and (5) instruction tuning of Transformer code models on permissive data (with SFT/LoRA style end‑to‑end fine‑tuning). I’m especially interested in attention‑based backbones, cosine‑similarity style probes, evaluation with Precision/F1, and methods with near‑linear O(n·D(…)) complexity under practical backbones (e.g., ResNet‑50/Transformer).Please analyze the development defects of these methods.
