**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below are development defects and limitations, grouped by method/paper and grounded in the provided texts.
> 
> 1) PBADet (ICLR 2024) – One‑stage, anchor‑free part‑to‑body association
> - Limited advantage in single‑part association: On the face‑body (single‑part) association task (CrowdHuman), the authors explicitly note “the advantages of our method over BPJDet are not as pronounced” compared to multi‑part scenarios (Appendix A.1, Table 5/6 discussion).
> - Sensitivity to key training/decoding components: Ablations show notable drops if task‑alignment learning or multi‑scale formulation are removed (Table 4), indicating the approach relies on these components for accuracy and may be brittle if they are not carefully implemented.
> - Dataset‑specific post‑processing thresholds: Inference requires distinct NMS confidence/IoU thresholds per dataset (Section 3.4; different values for BodyHands vs COCOHumanParts), suggesting potential hyperparameter sensitivity when porting to new domains.
> - Association decoding assumption: Decoding assigns to “bodies that are unassigned and also enclose the part” using nearest predicted body center (Section 3.4). When detections fail to yield enclosure (e.g., due to imperfect boxes), the matching rule offers no fallback within the method itself.
> - Only qualitative cross‑domain extension: Animal experiments demonstrate qualitative success only (Appendix A.3), without quantitative evaluation, leaving generalization performance unquantified.
> 
> 2) Learning with Dale’s Law in RNNs (NeurIPS 2023) – Spectral perspective; DANNs vs ColEI
> - Column EI (ColEI) networks learn poorly and are unstable: ColEI exhibits multimodal, dispersed singular‑value spectra with large modes, leading to poor learning, higher variance across runs, and much greater reliance on gradient clipping for stability (Sections 3.1–3.3; Appendix Fig. 10; Fig. 3D–F). Performance is sensitive to spectral radius choice ρ and remains worse than DANNs/standard RNNs for many settings (Section 3.1, Fig. 2 and Appendix Fig. 9/11).
> - Strong dependence on EI ratio and network size: With fewer inhibitory units or smaller networks, ColEI spectra become more pathological (low normalized SVD entropy), learning degrades, and instability increases; performance improves mainly for larger networks and more balanced E/I populations (Sections 3.4–3.5; Figs. 5–7).
> - Need for special initialization and clipping: Good behavior hinges on particular spectral properties at initialization and gradient clipping; without these, ColEI is highly unstable (Section 3.1; Appendix Fig. 10).
> - Architectural coverage gaps and open questions: Current DANNs target fast PV+‑like circuits; other biological features (e.g., inhibitory‑to‑inhibitory connections or cell‑type specific time constants) are not modeled and are proposed as future work (Discussion). The origins of ColEI’s unusual multimodal spectra and why large ColEI networks can learn despite large max singular values remain open (Discussion).
> 
> 3) How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features (NeurIPS 2024) – Implicit bias in deep linear self‑distillation
> - Scope limited by theory setting: Results rely on deep linear encoders, special initializations, and simultaneously diagonalizable Σxx and Σxy; generalization to non‑linear models or non‑diagonalizable data is explicitly left open (Limitations, Section 6). The beneficial JEPA bias appears only for deep encoders (L>1), weakening for shallow models (Corollary 3.3; Sections 3.2–3.3).
> - Potential vulnerability to spurious/slow features: While JEPA prioritizes high‑influence, predictive low‑variance (“slow”) features, the authors note this bias may make JEPA vulnerable to spurious or slow features (Discussion, Section 7). In contrast, MAE tends to emphasize high‑variance reconstructions, often uninformative for perception (Intro and Related Work, citing [20]).
> - Practical risk of collapse if stop‑grad is not used: The non‑contrastive JEPA formulation is susceptible to collapse without mechanisms like StopGrad (Section 1), implying training stability hinges on architectural/learning tricks.
> 
> 4) Memory‑Efficient Optimizers with 4‑bit States (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Zero‑point failure in second‑moment quantization (baseline 8‑bit/naïve 4‑bit): Block‑wise dynamic‑exponent mapping with zero (e.g., B2048/DE) pushes many v entries to zero, catastrophically distorting 1/√v and causing instability (Section 4.1; Fig. 3; Table 1 shows high instability rates). Fixing this needs excluding zero or changing mapping.
> - Rank‑1 normalization is not uniformly superior: The authors provide explicit cases where rank‑1 normalization underperforms block‑wise normalization and vice‑versa (Appendix C.2; Figs. 24, 26, 28), indicating data‑dependent behavior and need for careful method selection.
> - Performance depends on task/dataset; domains untested: The optimal quantization settings “probably depend on task” and evaluation is limited to language and vision; applicability to RL, audio, or graphs is not established (Limitations, Section 7).
> - Potential runtime overhead without fused kernels: On smaller models, 4‑bit versions can be slower than 8‑bit baselines before operator fusion; the authors report slower times pre‑fusion (Table 4), noting performance parity requires fused implementations.
> - Incomplete quantization coverage and bounded memory gains: Small tensors (≤4096 elements) and specific layers (e.g., embeddings in some baselines) are not quantized (Appendix D.1), capping end‑to‑end memory savings and producing less‑than‑ideal total memory reductions when other memory components dominate (Table 4 discussion).
> - Formal guarantees limited: A convergence theorem is provided for quantized SGDM under assumptions (Appendix H), but an analogous proof for AdamW is not given; stability is empirical.
> 
> 5) Learning‑Augmented MTS with Bandit Access to Multiple Predictors (ICML 2025)
> - Fundamental regret barrier and dependence on problem constants: Theoretical lower bound shows Ω(OPT^{2/3}) regret is unavoidable (Theorem 1.3), even with 2‑delayed access; upper bounds scale as O((D ℓ ln ℓ)^{1/3} m^{2/3} OPT^{2/3}) (Theorem 3.9). Regret worsens with larger metric diameter D, number of heuristics ℓ, and bootstrapping window m.
> - Requires m‑delayed bandit access and “improper” steps: One must query the same heuristic across m steps to observe its cost; the algorithm sometimes takes steps not suggested by any heuristic to ensure learning/competitiveness (Section 3.1–3.2), which may be undesirable in deployments tightly tied to predictor outputs.
> - (1+ε)‑competitiveness only under additional structure: Against a best‑k‑switch benchmark, competitiveness approaching 1 is proved only when k is sufficiently small relative to OPT (Appendix C), and remains worse (by a log factor) than prior results in an easier setting (Antoniadis et al., 2023b) (Appendix C, last paragraph).
> - Need to estimate/guess OPT for tuning; extra factors: Hyperparameters depend on OPT; the doubling scheme introduces an additional R^{2/3} term tied to the competitive ratio R of the fallback robust heuristic (Appendix G, Proposition G.1), inflating regret when R is large.
> - Oblivious adversary and look‑ahead requirements: Guarantees are for oblivious adversaries; the MTS setting also requires 1‑step look‑ahead and full access to cost functions to avoid +∞ states (Section 2), which may limit applicability to settings lacking these conditions.
> 
> Notes linking back to the user’s needs
> - Anchor‑free association (PBADet): Strong for multi‑part body association, but benefits shrink for single‑part cases and depend on task‑alignment/multi‑scale and tuned NMS.
> - 4‑bit optimizer: Addresses zero‑point failures but remains task‑dependent; rank‑1 vs block‑wise tradeoffs, and potential runtime overhead without fused ops.
> - EI‑constrained recurrent modules: Simple ColEI designs suffer spectral pathologies and instability; performance depends strongly on EI ratio/size/initialization; DANNs improve spectra but do not yet model all biological circuitry (e.g., I‑I connections).
> - Bandit selection among predictors with sublinear regret: The tight OPT^{2/3} barrier, dependence on D, ℓ, m, and the necessity of improper actions/bootstrapping are intrinsic limitations of the setting and algorithmic approach.
> 
> Only claims explicitly supported by the provided papers are made above; no external assumptions are introduced.

**naive 最终答案**

> Here are the works from the collection that map to your needs, followed by their development defects.
> 
> **Relevant works**
> - **(a) Anchor-free part‑body association:** PBADet – one‑stage anchor‑free detector using a single part‑to‑body center offset for hands/face→body association (validated on COCO‑WholeBody/CrowdHuman/BodyHands; reports Precision/Recall/F1).
> - **(b) 4‑bit optimizer:** "4‑bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4‑bit Optimizer States" – quantizes Adam/AdamW first/second moments (B128 block‑wise + rank‑1 normalization, zero‑point‑excluded linear quantizer), up to ~57.7% memory savings with lossless accuracy.
> - **(c) EI recurrent modules / spectral stability:** "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" – shows ColEI RNNs fail because of multimodal/dispersed singular spectra, not sign constraints; DANN (Dale's ANN) RNNs retain unimodal spectra and learn as well as standard RNNs. Guidance: control the singular‑value spectrum (normalized SVD entropy, NSE) and use gradient clipping.
> - **(d) Online bandit selection with sublinear regret:** "Learning‑Augmented Algorithms for MTS with Bandit Access to Multiple Predictors" – picks among ℓ heuristics under bandit feedback with regret O((Dℓm)^{1/3} OPT^{2/3}), using HEDGE/SHARE + exploration/exploitation.
> 
> **Related pieces you asked about**
> - Transformer‑style conditional guidance: "Universal Guidance for Diffusion Models" (training‑free guidance with arbitrary off‑the‑shelf functions, forward/backward guidance); also conditional generation in GeoBFN.
> - Near‑linear time: the linear‑time HSIC testing paper gives explicit linear‑time moment estimators (O(nD²)); the parametric‑DP paper gives output‑sensitive (near‑linear in output) algorithms.
> 
> **Development defects of these methods (per the sources)**
> - **PBADet:** its advantage over BPJDet shrinks on single‑part (face‑body) tasks; ablations show association accuracy degrades notably without the association loss, multi‑scale center offsets, or task‑alignment learning (i.e., the design is sensitive to those components); head‑to‑head comparisons (e.g., vs ED‑Pose) use different backbones/training sets, a confound; anchor‑free detection can have lower recall than anchor‑based approaches relying only on near‑center points.
> - **4‑bit optimizer:** quantizing both moments causes a marginal accuracy drop; optimal quantization appears task‑dependent; it was validated only on language/vision tasks (not multimodal video/gesture); without fused operators it can be *slower* than 8‑bit on small models; memory savings saturate at 4‑bit because activations/data dominate.
> - **EI RNNs (Dale's Law):** simple column‑partitioned (ColEI) networks learn worse and with much higher variance, are highly unstable without gradient clipping, and perform poorly at small sizes or with few inhibitory units due to pathological spectra; sign constraints alone already impair learning; the paper leaves open how to design better ColEI initializations, and results are limited to the four benchmarks tested.
> - **Bandit MTS with predictors:** regret is sublinear but depends critically on the number of predictors ℓ, distance measure D, and delayed feedback m (e.g., ~m^{2/3}); with m‑step delay one cannot build an unbiased loss estimator, so exploration phases are needed; lower bounds show the D/ℓ/m dependence is tight, and performance degrades as these grow.
> 
> **What the collection does NOT support:** I could not find any paper in the collection that defines or uses a "clean subset evaluation (D_k^c)" metric, nor a specific "100‑class cosine‑scoring benchmark" matching your pipeline. Those claims cannot be established from this collection; everything above is drawn only from the retrieved documents.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the works from the collection that map to your needs, followed by a defect analysis.
> 
> ## Pointers
> 
> **(a) Anchor-free part-to-body detector — PBADet** (doc `08b70bc…`). One-stage, anchor-free; a single part-to-body center offset guarantees one-to-one part↔body correspondence, works even when parts are invisible, scales to any number of parts (hands/face→body), and outperforms BPJDet/HierR-CNN on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts with higher F1/precision/recall vs. ED-Pose.
> 
> **(b) ~4-bit optimizer — "4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States"** (doc `8d5e145…`). Compresses Adam/AdamW first/second moments to 4-bit (smaller B128 blocks; rank-1 normalization; zero-point-excluding linear quantizer for the 2nd moment; optional factorization), matching 32-bit AdamW accuracy with up to ~57.7% memory savings. A related online alternative is BSO (doc `4741ca…`), which keeps per-layer moments with O(n²L/32) memory and sublinear regret.
> 
> **(c) Excitatory/inhibitory RNNs with spectral stability — "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (doc `e63a94c…`). Recurrent DANN (E/I sign-constrained) networks learn as well as standard RNNs because their initial singular-value spectrum is unimodal (Marchenko–Pastur/quarter-circle), unlike ColEI networks whose rank-one column-mean (nilpotent) structure yields multimodal, dispersed spectra. Guidance: constrain the spectral radius ρ=1.5, use balanced E/I ratios and sufficient width, use gradient clipping (ColEI is highly unstable without it), and use Normalized SVD Entropy (NSE) as a pre-training diagnostic of spectrum pathology.
> 
> **(d) Online bandit-style predictor/heuristic selection — "Learning-Augmented Algorithms for MTS with Bandit Access to Multiple Predictors"** (doc `c97e745…`). Combines ℓ heuristics/ML predictors under bandit feedback with m-delayed observations using HEDGE/SHARE + exploration/exploitation; regret O((Dℓlnℓ)^(1/3) m^(2/3) OPT^(2/3)) — sublinear in OPT and T — and a lower bound Ω~(ℓ^(1/3) T^(2/3)) shows near-optimality.
> 
> **Transformer-style conditional guidance.** "Universal Guidance for Diffusion Models" (doc `9134ed6…`) covers conditioning vs. guidance: classifier guidance, classifier-free guidance (Ho & Salimans), and training-free universal guidance (forward/backward gradients on the predicted clean image, USR re-noising) with arbitrary off-the-shelf functions (segmentation, face, detection, CLIP). CleanDiffuser (doc `c122328…`) likewise implements classifier and classifier-free guided sampling in a modular library.
> 
> **Clean subset evaluation (D_k^c).** This exact notation does **not** appear anywhere in the collection — I cannot point to a work using D_k^c. Closest related material: GOT-D's "clean" (low-toxicity) subset selection/evaluation (doc `bb21f95…`), Agreement-on-the-Line's data-subsetting methodology (doc `f6089db…`), and HASSOD's argument that AP on MS-COCO is misleading for class-agnostic detection, advocating AR on extensively annotated subsets (doc `ef986d5…`).
> 
> **Near-linear time implementations.** "Learning Kernels for Fast HSIC-Based Independence Testing" (doc `58063e…`) gives a linear-time HSIC test running in seconds on 100k samples. "Accelerating ERM for data-driven algorithm design" (doc `9ea7329…`) gives output-sensitive (near-linear in output size) algorithms via cell enumeration/Clarkson's algorithm with running times like O(m|E_S|) per query.
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods
> 
> - **PBADet**: anchor-free methods relying on near-center points have lower recall than anchor-based counterparts (a known anchor-free limitation); FCOS-style independent classification/localization can produce inconsistent predictions; on the single-part CrowdHuman face-body task its advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced; multi-scale absolute-distance offset interpretation degrades metrics; association quality still depends on task-alignment learning, without which performance drops.
> - **4-bit optimizer**: optimal quantization scheme appears task-dependent (only language/vision tasks tested); smaller models (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2) are slower than 8-bit AdamW until fused operators are used; memory savings saturate (~57.7%) because total memory includes activations/data; quantizing both moments causes a marginal accuracy drop; factorization is only applicable to the second moment.
> - **Dale's Law RNNs**: ColEI networks learn worse, with higher variance and instability (needing gradient clipping); small networks with few inhibitory units are spectrally pathological and learn poorly; NSE prediction quality is limited to initialisation; analysis relies on deep-linear/idealized settings; DANN parameterization (W=W_EE − W_EI W_IE) adds architectural complexity and still needs sign clipping of sub-matrices.
> - **Bandit MTS selection**: regret bound holds only under conditions like Dℓm ≤ o(OPT^(1/3)); exploration phases take m timesteps and cannot build unbiased loss estimators; improper (non-heuristic) steps and MTS-style rounding are needed, complicating implementation; lower bound Ω~(OPT^(2/3)) shows no sub-OPT^(2/3) improvement is possible; bootstrapping (m≥2) delays feedback.
> - **Universal Guidance**: slower generation, per-network hyperparameter (guidance strength s(t), refinement steps k) tuning, requires differentiable guidance functions; backward guidance needs backprop through sampling; classifier guidance requires a noisy-data classifier (costly to retrain), and guidance on clean-image predictors suffers domain shift handled only heuristically.
> - **HSIC linear-time**: no single test dominates all settings; power depends on random-frequency sampling count D; quadratic baselines outperform at small scales.
> - **Output-sensitive ERM**: running time scales with the actual number of pieces, which can still be large (worst-case O(t^d)); needs output-size tracking and LP solves; implementation overhead and geometry machinery are non-trivial.
> - **GOT-D/AGL/HASSOD evaluation**: GOT-D assumes overlap with pretraining scope and relies on Perspective API scores that drift; AGL does not hold for all OOD shifts (e.g., Camelyon17) or with weak agreement; HASSOD's AR-based evaluation still suffers hierarchy misalignment with human perception and failures on overlapping objects.
> 
> Unverifiable from the corpus: the specific D_k^c clean-subset notation, and any claim about "100-class benchmark with cosine scoring" as a named benchmark (no such benchmark appears in the collection; cosine-similarity scoring does appear in the contrastive-learning and CLIP-evaluation papers cited above).

</details>

### paperscope:gap:307 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find research that collectively addresses: (1) a one-stage, anchor-free approach for associating human parts with persons on benchmarks like COCO, reporting F1/Precision and trained with SGD/AdamW under CE/MSE losses; (2) the spectral/implicit dynamics of deep networks obeying excitatory–inhibitory constraints, including analysis via singular-value spectra and entropy for interpretability; (3) the latent-space prediction bias in self-supervised joint-embedding methods (self-distillation) contrasted with reconstruction, with attention to how fine-tuning affects feature embeddings; (4) memory-efficient training via sub-byte optimizer states (e.g., 4‑bit AdamW) that still match full-precision performance across Transformers; and (5) a world model that represents multi-modal states as graphs, uses cosine-similarity retrieval and multi-hop message passing, and interfaces with transformer-guided generative decoders—prefer works reporting AUROC/F1 and discussing regularization, ranking losses (e.g., BPR), and approximations for scalable training.Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

**score：2→3（Δ+1）；rounds：4→3（Δ-1）。**

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Development defects and limitations extracted from the provided papers, per method:
> 
> 1) PBADet – One-stage anchor-free part–body association (ICLR 2024)
> - Limited advantage on single-part association tasks: On CrowdHuman, where the task is face–body association (a single-part linkage), the authors report that PBADet’s benefits over prior art are “not as pronounced” compared to settings with multiple parts-to-body associations.
> - Dependence on multi-scale anchor-free formulation and task alignment: Ablations show clear drops when removing multi-scale supervision (w/o Multi-scale) or task-alignment learning (w/o Task-align), indicating sensitivity to these design choices; the method relies on these components for its reported performance.
> 
> 2) Excitatory–Inhibitory (EI) recurrent networks under Dale’s Law – spectral perspective (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Column EI (ColEI) RNNs learn poorly and are unstable without gradient clipping: The paper shows ColEI networks have multi-modal, dispersed singular-value spectra leading to impaired learning and higher variance across seeds; they “are highly unstable” without gradient clipping, which benefits ColEI much more than other models.
> - Strong size and E/I-ratio sensitivity (ColEI): Performance degrades for small networks and for networks with fewer inhibitory units; spectra worsen (larger maximum singular values, lower normalised SVD entropy), and learning declines accordingly.
> - Sign constraints alone do not explain the gap; spectral properties at initialization dominate: The spectrum-transplant experiments show that mismatched singular value spectra hurt performance more than sign constraints themselves—pointing to a limitation of the simple ColEI formulation’s spectrum rather than just its signs.
> - Assumption-heavy analysis and scope: Results rely on special initializations and settings (orthogonal weights, balanced initialization, diagonal and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances, deep linear models). Theoretical conclusions about JEPA/ColEI dynamics are derived under these constraints and may not directly transfer to general non-linear or non-diagonalizable settings.
> - Open theoretical questions remain: The paper explicitly leaves open the origin of ColEI’s unusual multi-modal spectra and why large ColEI networks learn well despite large maximum singular values (they provide intuition, not a full resolution).
> - Biological fidelity limits for the proposed EI architectures: The authors note that additional features (e.g., inhibitory-to-inhibitory connections, neuron-type time constants) would be needed for more faithful biological modeling; these were not included.
> 
> 3) How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features – implicit bias of deep linear self-distillation (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Restricted theoretical setting: The core results are proven for deep linear networks with special initializations under the small-initialization regime, and with simultaneously diagonalizable Σxx and Σyx. The authors explicitly caution that many real data distributions will “significantly deviate” from this assumption.
> - Depth-dependent effect: The JEPA–MAE separation (bias toward influential features via regression coefficients) largely manifests with deep encoders; for shallow encoders (e.g., L=1), dynamics converge to MAE-like behavior, limiting JEPA’s distinct bias in shallow settings.
> - Generalization to practical non-linear models not established: The paper states that extending these results to non-linear architectures and more general data remains future work; thus, claims about practical performance are not theoretically established here.
> 
> 4) Memory-Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Sensitivity to quantization design; zero-point failure mode for second moment: The authors identify a critical “zero-point problem” for second-moment quantization—naïve 4-bit block-wise DE mapping that includes zero causes severe misestimation of 1/sqrt(v) and unstable training (e.g., unstable runs up to 66% in ablations). Stability and accuracy depend on excluding the zero point and using better normalization (rank‑1 normalization) or factorization.
> - Task/dataset dependence of optimal settings: The paper states the optimal quantization configuration likely depends on task, dataset, and training details; they do not claim a universally optimal 4-bit setting.
> - Evaluation scope: Experiments are limited to language and vision tasks (classification, MT, instruction tuning). The applicability to RL, audio, and graph learning remains untested.
> - Practical limitation for factorization under sharding: With Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) packing (e.g., LLaMA‑7B tuning), they report difficulty applying second‑moment factorization; in such settings they only compare 4‑bit AdamW without factorization.
> 
> 5) Graph World Model (GWM) – token-based (GWM‑T) and embedding-based (GWM‑E) (ICML 2025)
> - GWM‑T token/length overhead: The authors note GWM‑T “sometimes suffers from high token costs and limited context length,” motivating the embedding-based GWM‑E. This indicates GWM‑T’s efficiency and context-scaling limitations.
> - Over-smoothing and diminishing returns with many hops: Empirically, increasing hop count does not monotonically help; too many hops cause over-smoothing and redundant information, reducing performance.
> - Current modality and graph-structure coverage: The current implementation supports text, tables, and images; other modalities (e.g., audio/video) are not yet supported. The framework is “currently focused on homophilous graphs,” with non-homophilous structures left as future work.
> - Architectural scope: For GWM‑E, a simple MLP projector is used and the LLM is frozen (prefix-style tuning). While effective in experiments, the authors position this as a modular starting point rather than a finalized universal design.
> 
> Note: All points above are taken from the authors’ own empirical findings, ablations, discussions, limitations, and future-work sections in the provided papers, without adding external claims.

**naive 最终答案**

> Here are the matching works and an analysis of their development defects, based only on the provided context.
> 
> **1. Part-body association — PBADet (ICLR 2024)**
> One-stage, anchor-free detector (YOLOv5l6/YOLOv7) using a single part-to-body center offset; evaluated on COCO-HumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman; reports Precision/Recall/F1 vs ED-Pose on COCO and joint AP/conditional accuracy; trained 100 epochs with SGD, AMP, IoU+DFL+classification+association (L1) losses with task-alignment (TOOD-style) supervision.
> *Defects:* advantage over BPJDet nearly vanishes on the single-part face-body CrowdHuman task (only comparable); performance relies on pretrained YOLO weights and tuned hyperparameters (K=13, α=1.0, β=6.0; disabling task-alignment degrades all metrics); F1/precision comparison vs ED-Pose uses a favorable protocol (ED-Pose gets ground-truth part boxes); the queried "SGD/AdamW under CE/MSE" does not match—only SGD is used and losses are IoU/DFL/CE/regression, not MSE.
> 
> **2. EI-constrained networks — "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023)**
> Analyzes why excitatory–inhibitory (Dale's law) RNNs learn poorly; shows the initial singular-value spectrum (multimodal/dispersed for ColEI) matters more than sign constraints; introduces Normalised SVD Entropy (NSE) as an interpretability/performance diagnostic.
> *Defects:* ColEI networks learn worse with higher seed variance and are unstable without gradient clipping; small networks with few inhibitory units fail; NSE is correlational, not causal; origins of the multimodal spectrum and why large ColEI networks succeed remain open; results limited to RNNs (convolutional/feedforward/spiking untested); E/I balance experiments limited (e.g., 10% I-units, 1000 hidden units).
> 
> **3. SSL latent prediction bias — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024)**
> Shows JEPA self-distillation is biased toward high-influence (high regression coefficient) features vs MAE reconstruction (which prioritizes high-covariance/noisy features), via exact deep-linear dynamics, with depth amplifying suppression.
> *Defects:* theory restricted to deep linear MLPs, special small orthogonal initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable Σyx, Σxx—real distributions deviate; generalization to nonlinear models unexplored; JEPA is collapse-prone (needs stop-grad); the bias may make JEPA vulnerable to spurious/slow features; the queried "how fine-tuning affects feature embeddings" is not directly addressed.
> 
> **4. Sub-byte optimizer states — "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (NeurIPS 2023)**
> 4-bit AdamW (B128/rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer for second moment, optional factorization) matches 32-bit AdamW across Transformers (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2, LLaMA-7B/13B/33B, Swin-T, WMT14) with up to 57.7% memory savings.
> *Defects:* optimal quantization is task/dataset-dependent (task-specific settings may beat the fixed recipe); evaluated only on language and vision (RL, audio, graph learning untested); slower than 8-bit for small models unless fused operators are used; memory savings saturate because activations/data/fragmentation remain; convergence guarantee is only for quantized SGD(M).
> 
> **5. World model — "Graph World Model (GWM)" (ICML 2025)**
> Represents multi-modal states as graphs (image/table/text nodes), actions as nodes, cosine/embedding-similarity retrieval (top-k) for unintended (RAG-like) actions, multi-hop message passing (GWM-E) or token-level (GWM-T), with LLM (Llama-3-8B) and Stable Diffusion decoders; reports F1/Recall/Precision/Accuracy; multi-hop gives ≥20% gains.
> *Defects:* no AUROC is reported (Accuracy/Recall/F1 only); no BPR/ranking loss or explicit regularization is discussed; excessive hops cause over-smoothing and redundant information; limited to text/table/image modalities and homophilous graphs; GWM-T suffers high token cost/limited context (GWM-E only partially mitigates via embedding-space message passing); decoders are frozen and only the simple MLP projector is tuned; graph architecture is intentionally simple.
> 
> **Cross-cutting defects:** Each method overclaims relative to the user's spec—PBADet lacks the stated CE/MSE+AdamW training, the JEPA paper omits fine-tuning analysis, GWM lacks AUROC/BPR/regularization, and the 4-bit optimizer's generality is untested beyond language/vision. All rely on narrow assumptions (linear models, small datasets, single-part tasks, homophilous graphs) or tuned hyperparameters, limiting transferability.

**community 最终答案**

> ## Matched Research
> 
> 1. **PBADet** (ICLR 2024) — one-stage anchor-free part-body association via a single part-to-body center offset (YOLOv5/v7 backbones). Evaluated on COCO-HumanParts/COCO validation, reporting **Precision/Recall/F1** (vs ED-Pose, e.g., all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51) and AP/MR-2; trained with **SGD** (as in YOLOv7) using IoU + DFL + classification + association losses.
> 2. **"Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly"** (NeurIPS 2023) — excitatory–inhibitory (Dale's Law) networks; analysis via **singular-value spectra** (spectrum "transplants") and **normalised SVD entropy (NSE)** as an interpretability/performance metric.
> 3. **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** — latent-space prediction bias of **self-distillation (JEPA) vs reconstruction (MAE)**: JEPA implicitly prioritizes high-influence/low-noise features, MAE prioritizes high-variance features; ImageNet CCA experiments confirm JEPA aligns faster with the perceptual subspace.
> 4. **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023) — **4-bit AdamW** (smaller B128 blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer for second moment) matching 32-bit full precision on Transformers (GLUE, SQuAD, E2E-NLG, WMT, LLaMA-7B/13B/33B) with up to 57.7% memory savings.
> 5. **Graph World Model (GWM)** (ICML 2025) — multi-modal states as graphs (image/table/text nodes), action nodes, **cosine/embedding-similarity Top-k retrieval** (unintended actions), **multi-hop message passing** (GWM-T token-level; GWM-E embedding-level), transformer (LLM) + Stable Diffusion generative decoders; reports **Precision/Recall/F1**; multi-hop gives ≥20% relative gains but excessive hops cause over-smoothing.
> 
> ## Development Defects (from the context)
> 
> 1. **PBADet**: advantage over BPJDet shrinks for single-part tasks (CrowdHuman face-body: comparable, not clearly better); ablations show removing the association loss, multi-scale offsets, or task-alignment each degrades performance; part predictions for limbs (legs/arms) remain unreliable, clouding body-part association.
> 2. **Dale's Law RNNs**: simple EI partitioning (ColEI) learns worse and with higher variance; small networks with few inhibitory units have more pathological (multimodal, dispersed) spectra and worse learning; needs gradient clipping; spectral properties at initialization dominate over sign constraints.
> 3. **JEPA vs MAE**: the theory is restricted to deep linear MLPs with special initialization and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances — generalization to real data/architectures is unexplored; JEPA can collapse without stop-gradient tricks and may be vulnerable to spurious/slow features; MAE learns perception-uninformative features. Notably, **fine-tuning effects on feature embeddings are not analyzed in this work** (only downstream usage of learned features), so that aspect of the request is only partially covered.
> 4. **4-bit optimizers**: optimal quantization settings are task/dataset-dependent; validated only on language/vision (not RL, audio, graph); on small models 4-bit is slower than 8-bit without fused kernels; quantizing both moments causes a marginal accuracy drop; rank-1 + linear-mapping settings may not be globally optimal.
> 5. **GWM**: limited to text/table/image modalities and homophilous graphs with a simple graph architecture; GWM-T has high token cost and limited context length; multi-hop aggregation can over-smooth and add redundant information; excessive hop counts reduce performance.
> 
> Not established in the available context: GWM reporting **AUROC**, use of **BPR ranking losses**, or explicit **regularization/approximation schemes for scalable training** — these specifics are not present in the retrieved material.

</details>

### paperscope:gap:313 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers on efficient learning and transfer in deep networks (CNNs/Transformers and RNNs) that span: (1) one‑stage, anchor‑free part–to–body association for human parts on COCO with typical backbones (e.g., ResNet‑50) and standard CE/MSE training; (2) spectral analyses of biologically constrained recurrent models obeying excitatory/inhibitory sign rules, showing how singular value spectra affect optimization under SGD/AdamW; (3) theoretical work explaining the implicit bias of self‑distillation/JEPA objectives (e.g., via cosine similarity or MSE) on datasets like MNIST/CIFAR‑100; (4) memory‑efficient training via 4‑bit states for Adam/AdamW to cut footprint during fine‑tuning or End‑to‑end LoRA; and (5) self‑supervised RL that transfers across reward functions using random feature embeddings and planning. Ideally these works report common metrics (F1/Precision) and discuss practical approximations for deep networks.Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Development defects and limitations across the five methods, strictly as stated or implied in the papers:
> 
> 1) PBADet (one‑stage, anchor‑free part–to–body association)
> - Association relies on enclosure and per-pixel positives: decoding selects the body that “encloses” the part and minimizes L2 to the predicted body center. This implicit assumption (that each part’s positive anchors lie inside both the part and body boxes) can be brittle under heavy occlusion or annotation cases where a part is outside the body box, making associations fail at inference. (Section 3.1, 3.4)
> - Advantage is task-dependent; gains are limited for single-part tasks: on CrowdHuman face–body (single-part) association, authors state the advantage over BPJDet is “not as pronounced,” and results are only comparable. (Appendix A.1, Table 5)
> - Detection trade-offs vs. prior SOTA: on COCOHumanParts, PBADet’s overall AP is “on par” or slightly lower than BPJDet in some aggregate metrics (e.g., AP.5:.95: 43.0 vs 43.6 for YOLOv5l6), with gains appearing mainly in APM/APL and some categories; thus there is no uniform detection improvement. (Table 2)
> - Heavy reliance on tuned hyperparameters and high-resolution inputs: the method sets specific task-alignment parameters, loss weights, K-top anchors, and distinct NMS thresholds for bodies vs. parts; training and inference use large input sizes (e.g., 1024×1024), increasing compute/memory needs. (Section 3.3–4.1)
> - Generalization beyond humans and quantitative breadth: animal experiments are qualitative only (no quantitative benchmarks), so robustness beyond human parts is not established. (Appendix A.3)
> 
> 2) Learning better with Dale’s Law: A Spectral Perspective (EI‑constrained RNNs)
> - Column EI (ColEI) networks learn poorly without strong mitigations: they show worse final performance and higher variance than standard RNNs/DANNs across tasks; often require gradient clipping for stability; are highly sensitive to EI ratio (few inhibitory units) and small sizes, where learning and spectra degrade. (Figure 2, discussion; Appendix Figure 10; Figures 5–7)
> - Pathological spectra persist in ColEI: multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra with large modes lead to exploding/vanishing gradients and unstable training; large max singular values remain even in larger nets (though mitigated by rotations), indicating inherent spectral fragility. (Figure 3; discussion)
> - DANN recurrent networks still rely on careful initialization and spectrum: good learning is tied to specific initialization that yields unimodal clustered spectra (similar to standard RNNs). The approach does not remove the need to control spectral properties; it only makes them favorable. (Sections 3.2–3.3)
> - Scope and open theoretical gaps: analysis attributes poor performance primarily to spectra, but the precise origin of ColEI multimodal spectra and why large max singular values do not always doom large nets remain open; performance depends on architectural choices (EI ratio, depth/width). (Discussion)
> 
> 3) How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features (deep linear self‑distillation analysis)
> - Strong assumptions limit applicability: results hold for deep linear encoders under specific balanced, small‑init regimes and simultaneous diagonalizability of Σxx and Σyx; generalization to nonlinear networks, real data, and non‑diagonalizable settings is not established. (Preliminaries; Assumption 3.1; Limitations)
> - Implicit bias needs depth: the “influential feature” bias that favors high regression coefficients (ρ) emerges only with deep encoders; with shallow encoders, JEPA behaves more like MAE and loses this advantageous bias. (Corollary 3.3; Section 3.2)
> - Potential vulnerability to slow/spurious features: authors note the bias towards predictive, low-variance (slow) features may make JEPA prone to spurious/slow features in practice. (Discussion)
> - Empirical scope: experiments are primarily synthetic or simplified; broader empirical validation is limited (e.g., small-scale ImageNet checks in appendix). (Limitations; Appendix D)
> 
> 4) Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4‑bit States (Adam/AdamW)
> - Stability is fragile without zero-point handling: quantizing second moments with mappings that include zero leads to catastrophic update errors (most entries collapse to zero and 1/sqrt(v) explodes). Many schemes are unstable (e.g., B128/DE: 66% unstable runs), and require specific fixes (DE‑0 or linear mapping) to train reliably. (Section 4.1; Table 1)
> - Potential performance regressions and task-specific tuning: while many fine-tuning tasks match FP32, some pretraining setups show slight drops (e.g., Swin-T: 81.2 vs 80.8 top‑1); authors note the “optimal quantization setting probably depends on task/dataset/training details,” indicating extra tuning may be needed. (Table 2; Limitations)
> - Runtime overhead without fused kernels: 4‑bit runs can be slower than 8‑bit baselines before kernel fusion (e.g., RoBERTa-L: 5.59 min vs 3.38 min), so practical speedups depend on engineering (fused ops). (Table 4)
> - Evaluation scope: validation is limited to language and vision; applicability to RL, audio, and graph tasks remains untested. (Limitations)
> - Extra machinery and exceptions: robust training requires rank‑1 normalization (extra statistics and code paths); some small tensors are excluded from quantization; 8‑bit baselines often keep embeddings unquantized—comparisons depend on these choices. (Sections 4.2, D.1)
> 
> 5) RaMP: Self‑Supervised RL that Transfers using Random Features
> - High-variance value estimates and sample needs: the method uses Monte‑Carlo for Q‑basis learning and requires random exploration plus many sampled action sequences for MPC (e.g., 1024 per step), which can be computationally heavy and variance‑prone. (Methods §3.2–3.3; C.2)
> - Theoretical guarantees assume deterministic dynamics and coverage: the planning guarantee (Theorem 3.2) is for deterministic transitions; performance depends on sufficient offline coverage and enough random features K for accurate reward approximation. (Section 3.4; D.1–D.2)
> - Pixel generalization gaps: under high‑dimensional pixel inputs, RaMP underperforms Dreamer on some tasks (e.g., Pixel Door Open), indicating limitations when random features poorly capture semantic structure in images. (Appendix C.3, Figure 6)
> - Practical adaptation overhead: requires an offline pretraining set and an online regression warm‑up (e.g., 2500 random steps) before planning; MPC random shooting/MPPI can be expensive for long horizons or large action spaces. (Appendix C.2, B.4)
> - Real‑world validation missing: experiments are all in simulation; authors note real‑robot evaluation and actor–critic variants to reduce variance are future work. (Discussion)

**naive 最终答案**

> ## 找到的论文（按五个主题对应）
> 
> 1. **PBADet（ICLR 2024）**——《PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association》。单阶段、无锚框，用单个"部件→身体中心偏移"做人体部件-身体关联；在 COCO-HumanParts、BodyHands、CrowdHuman 上报告 AP、Precision/Recall/F1、JointAP 等指标。
> 
> 2. **《Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective》(NeurIPS 2023)**——对遵守 E/I 符号约束（Dale's Law）的 ColEI/DANN 循环网络做奇异值谱分析，证明初始化时的奇异值谱比符号约束更影响学习，用归一化 SVD 熵(NSE)预测性能，梯度裁剪能缓解。
> 
> 3. **《Why JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks》(NeurIPS 2024)**——用深度线性网络解析 JEPA/自蒸馏（MSE 目标）相对 MAE 的隐式偏置（偏向高回归系数/高影响力特征、抑制噪声特征）。
> 
> 4. **《Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States》(NeurIPS 2023)**——把 Adam/AdamW 的优化器状态压到 4-bit（小分块 B128 + rank-1 归一化 + 二阶矩去零点），在 LLaMA 微调等任务上节省最多 57.7% 内存。
> 
> 5. **《Self-Supervised RL that Transfers using Random Features》(RaMP)**——用随机特征作为伪奖励、自监督地离线训练随机 Q-basis（隐式动力学模型），测试时用线性回归拟合新奖励并经 MPC 规划实现跨奖励迁移。
> 
> ## 与需求不符/偏差点（重要）
> 
> - PBADet 用的是 **YOLOv5/YOLOv7 骨干**而非 ResNet-50；损失是 **IoU+DFL+分类+关联**的加权组合，并非"标准 CE/MSE"。
> - JEPA 论文的 MSE 分析设定是**深度线性网络**，实验在 **ImageNet-1K** 上（用 CCA），并非 MNIST/CIFAR-100，也未分析余弦相似度目标。
> - 语料中**没有独立的 "End-to-end LoRA"（E2-LoRA）论文**，只有 4-bit 优化器论文在相关工作里提及 LoRA；Hessian 谱论文讨论了 LoRA 微调不形成幂律谱。
> - Dale 律论文使用标准 SGD（报告梯度裁剪收益），未专门在 AdamW 下分析 EI 谱。
> 
> ## 各方法的开发缺陷
> 
> **PBADet**
> - 损失函数含 4 个加权项（IoU/DFL/cls/assoc），超参 λ 需调，工程复杂度高于标准 CE/MSE 方案。
> - 推理依赖 NMS + 到身体中心的欧氏距离贪心匹配，多尺度偏移需缩放因子 λ。
> - 与 ED-Pose 的 COCO 对比中，ED-Pose 用真值部件框、PBADet 用自身检测框，对比偏向本方；在 CrowdHuman 单部件任务上对 BPJDet 优势减弱。
> - 移除关联损失/多尺度偏移/任务对齐任一项都会掉点，说明性能对设计组件敏感。
> 
> **Dale 律谱分析 RNN**
> - ColEI 网络在四个基准上均学得更差且跨种子方差大，需要更强梯度裁剪。
> - 结论主要基于**初始化**的谱与较小网络/特定 EI 比例，NSE 只是经验相关指标（抗相关），不保证因果或普适。
> - 训练算法仍是普通 SGD，未与 Adam/AdamW 等现代优化器下的谱-优化交互深入结合。
> 
> **JEPA 自蒸馏隐式偏置**
> - 只在深度线性网络、均衡正交初始化、数据可同时对角化的理想假设下严格成立，非线性模型未覆盖。
> - 分析的是 MSE 目标，未覆盖余弦相似度/归一化目标；实验用 ImageNet 而非 MNIST/CIFAR-100。
> - 论文自身承认该偏置可能导致 JEPA 易受**虚假/慢特征**影响。
> 
> **4-bit 优化器**
> - 最优量化方案可能依赖任务/数据集（论文自述局限），仅测试了语言和视觉任务。
> - 二阶矩量化有零点问题需专门处理；同时量化一、二阶矩仍有轻微精度损失。
> - 小模型上 4-bit 比 8-bit 更慢（未做算子融合）；总内存节省随位宽下降而饱和。
> - LoRA 只是提及（冻结预训练权重、只调低秩参数），未做 E2-LoRA 式端到端评估；与激活压缩/检查点可组合但未验证组合效果。
> 
> **RaMP（随机特征跨奖励迁移 RL）**
> - 用 Monte-Carlo 估计值，**方差较大**（论文自述局限）；需足够多的随机特征网络 K 才能覆盖任意奖励。
> - 依赖"环境动力学共享、仅奖励变化"的假设。
> - 像素观测任务上只匹配 Dreamer 的 3 项中的 2 项（Pixel Door Open 失败）；NN 随机特征优于多项式/高斯特征，说明特征选择敏感。
> - 训练用离线无标签数据，在线仍需少量交互做线性回归与 MPC 规划。
> 
> 综上，这些工作都能在语料中找到对应论文，但用户列出的若干具体设定（ResNet-50 骨干+标准 CE/MSE、MNIST/CIFAR-100 上的余弦相似度 JEPA 理论、独立 E2-LoRA 论文）在语料中无法完全成立，且各方法普遍存在假设理想化、组件敏感、对比设置偏袒或规模/任务覆盖不足等开发缺陷。

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the context, here are the papers matching your five themes, followed by an analysis of their development defects.
> 
> **1. Part-to-body association on COCO — PBADet** ("PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association", ICLR 2024, doc 08b70bc…)
> One-stage anchor-free detector with a single part-to-body center offset; branches for box/class/association; loss = IoU + DFL + classification + L1 association loss, trained with SGD (projected), task-alignment (TOOD) sampling; reports AP, Precision/Recall/F1 vs ED-Pose, mMR-2. Backbones are YOLOv5/YOLOv7 — **not ResNet-50** (R50 appears only in baseline comparisons), and training is on COCO-HumanParts/BodyHands/CrowdHuman rather than standard CE/MSE on COCO.
> 
> **2. Spectral analysis of biologically constrained RNNs — "Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly" (NeurIPS 2023, doc e63a94c…)**
> Compares ColEI (column E/I sign constraints) vs DANN vs standard RNNs; shows the singular-value spectrum (multimodal, dispersed, large mode) hurts learning more than the sign constraints themselves; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) predicts performance; spectrum-transplant experiments. Optimization is projected gradient descent with gradient clipping — the paper does **not** analyze SGD/AdamW per se.
> 
> **3. Implicit bias of self-distillation/JEPA — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024, doc 40fde03…)**
> Deep-linear-network theory: JEPA (MSE self-distillation) prioritizes high-influence features (large regression coefficient ρ), increasingly with depth, while MAE prioritizes high-variance (λ) features; critical-time analysis. Experiments are on Gaussian synthetic data and ImageNet (I-JEPA vs MAE), **not** MNIST/CIFAR-100; the cosine-similarity/CIFAR-100 contrastive analysis exists in "On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning" (doc 160e140…) but that is contrastive InfoNCE, not self-distillation/JEPA.
> 
> **4. Memory-efficient 4-bit Adam/AdamW — "4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States" (NeurIPS 2023, doc 8d5e145…)**
> Quantizes first/second moments (B128 block, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer, optional factorization); matches 32-bit AdamW on GLUE, SQuAD, ImageNet, E2E-NLG, WMT14, Alpaca with up to 57.7% memory savings. LoRA is only mentioned in related work — no "End-to-end LoRA" paper exists in this collection (LoRA fine-tuning spectral analysis appears separately in the Hessian power-law paper, doc 582d138…, on TinyLlama/MathQA).
> 
> **5. Self-supervised RL transfer — "Random Features for Model-Free Planning" (RaMP, doc 528b3e8…)**
> Pre-trains multi-step Q-basis functions on reward-free offline data using random features as pseudo-rewards; test-time linear regression to new rewards + MPC planning; validated on Meta-World, Hopper, D'Claw (fails on Pixel Door Open).
> 
> ---
> 
> **Development defects of these methods:**
> 
> - **PBADet**: relies on YOLO-family backbones and hand-tuned loss weights (λ_iou=7.5, λ_dfl=1.5, λ_cls=0.5, λ_assoc=0.2, K=13, α=1.0, β=6.0) and NMS thresholds; the 2D center offset assumes parts lie within body boxes (a one-to-one geometric prior) and can degrade when parts/body boxes are large or occluded; anchor-free multi-scale decoding is sensitive to assignment and ablation shows each component (association loss, multi-scale offsets, task alignment) is needed, i.e., brittle and not end-to-end transformer-based.
> - **Dale's-law RNNs**: ColEI trains worse with high seed variance, needs gradient clipping substantially more than baselines; NSE is only a correlational predictor; results depend on initialization strategy and spectral radius; no analysis under modern optimizers (SGD/AdamW) or nonlinear architectures beyond 1–3-layer RNNs; sign-clipping via projection limits the solution space and slows convergence.
> - **JEPA implicit-bias theory**: restricted to deep linear MLPs, balanced/orthogonal initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable Σyx/Σxx; fails to cover nonlinear encoders and real data distributions (hence synthetic/ImageNet-only evidence, no MNIST/CIFAR-100); the ρ-bias can also cause JEPA to over-prioritize spurious/slow low-variance features; the contrastive-similarity work adds an extra tuning hyperparameter and can suppress meaningful semantic variance.
> - **4-bit optimizers**: quantization settings are task-dependent (no universal lossless recipe); only language and vision tasks tested (RL/audio/graphs untested); 4-bitAdamW is slower than 8-bit without fused kernels; memory savings saturate because total footprint includes activations/data; second-moment zero-point and outlier patterns still require careful per-tensor schemes; factorization only applies to matrix-shaped tensors.
> - **RaMP**: Monte-Carlo estimation of multi-step Q-functions has high variance; random-feature coverage requires large K and expressive features (NN features needed; polynomial/Gaussian underperform); transfer assumes identical dynamics with only reward changes; performance degrades on harder pixel-based tasks (Pixel Door Open), and the implicit model is policy-dependent, limiting planning quality.
> 
> Gaps relative to your request: no paper here uses ResNet-50 backbones with standard CE/MSE for part-body association, none links E/I singular spectra to SGD/AdamW optimization, the JEPA theory is not validated on MNIST/CIFAR-100, and no "End-to-end LoRA" training paper exists in the collection.

</details>

### paperscope:gap:316 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building a resource‑constrained perception‑and‑control stack: a camera system must detect hands/face and reliably associate them to the correct person in crowded scenes (COCO‑style), while the onboard model is continually fine‑tuned with LoRA under tight GPU memory—so I need 4‑bit optimizer states for Adam/AdamW. Our control module uses time‑series RNNs that must respect excitatory/inhibitory constraints, and I want spectral guidance to keep training stable with SGD/AdamW. For vision pretraining I’m considering JEPA‑style self‑distillation (cosine similarity/MSE) and want to understand why it learns robust feature embeddings. Finally, the robot should rapidly transfer to new manipulation rewards via self‑supervised RL using random features and MPC. Which papers cover these components end‑to‑end so I can architect this system?Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

> {'answer': 'Below are the development defects and limitations explicitly stated or empirically evidenced in the provided papers, organized by method.\n\n1) PBADet (One-stage anchor-free part-to-body association)\n- Advantage diminishes on single-part association tasks: On CrowdHuman’s face–body association (only one part), “the advantages of our method over BPJDet are not as pronounced” compared to multi-part settings (A.1 Appendix). This indicates reduced benefit in scenarios with only one part-to-body link.\n\n2) Column EI (ColEI) RNNs under Dale’s Law (simple column sign constraints)\n- Impaired learning due to spectral pathology: ColEI exhibits a multimodal, dispersed singular value spectrum with a notable mode of large singular values, unlike standard RNNs/DANNs (unimodal spectra). This leads to poorer learning (Fig. 3; §3.2–3.3).\n- Instability without gradient clipping and higher variance: ColEI networks are highly unstable without gradient clipping and show more variance across seeds/initializations (§4 Discussion; Fig. 2).\n- Sensitivity to network size and E/I ratio: Learning degrades for small networks and when the percentage of inhibitory units is low (biologically realistic E:I ratios). Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) worsens and correlates with higher test error; large max singular values persist even as networks grow (§3.4; Figs. 5–7).\n- Sign constraints alone don’t explain the gap: Even lifting sign constraints does not close the performance gap—spectral properties dominate learning deficits (§3.3; Fig. 4).\n\n3) DANN RNNs (recurrent Dale’s ANNs) – strengths with noted limitations\n- Narrow biological fidelity in current form: The presented DANNs specifically model fast PV+ interneurons; inhibitory-to-inhibitory connections and cell-type–specific time constants are not included. The authors suggest these as future additions for biological plausibility (§4 Discussion).\n\n4) JEPA-style self-distillation (analysis of JEPA vs MAE)\n- Benefits depend on encoder depth: The distinct JEPA bias toward influential features “takes hold only when the encoder is deep and diminishes substantially when the encoder is shallow,” reducing its advantage in shallow settings (§1, §3.2, Corollary 3.6).\n- Potential vulnerability to spurious/slow features: The discovered bias toward “slow”/low-variance features “may shed light on JEPAs vulnerability to spurious or slow features” (§7 Discussion).\n- Theory limited to simplified settings: Results rely on deep linear networks with special initializations and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances; generalization to non-linear architectures and non-diagonalizable data is not established (Limitations §6).\n\n5) 4-bit Optimizers for Adam/AdamW (Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States)\n- Zero-point failure for second moment quantization: Naïve 4-bit (DE mapping) pushes many v entries to zero, making 1/sqrt(v) blow up and causing unstable updates. The authors identify and fix this with zero-excluding mappings (DE-0/linear), but without this fix training is unstable (§4.1; Fig. 3; Tab. 1).\n- Heterogeneous outlier patterns stress block-wise quantization: Moments show complex, layer-dependent outlier structure; large block sizes (e.g., 2048) can fail to approximate moments well. Requires smaller blocks (e.g., 128) or rank-1 normalization for accuracy, increasing engineering complexity and some scale overhead (§3; Figs. 1–2; C.2–C.3 Appendix).\n- Current throughput slower on small models: Without fused kernels, 4-bit optimizers were slower than 8-bit on smaller models; authors state speed should match after operator fusion (Tab. 4).\n- Scope limitations and task dependence: Authors note evaluation limited to language/vision; applicability to RL, audio, graphs remains to be tested. Optimal quantization settings may be task-specific (Limitations §7).\n\n6) RaMP (Self-supervised RL that transfers via random features and MPC)\n- Monte Carlo value estimation variance: The current approach relies on Monte-Carlo-based value estimation, which “may suffer from high variance”; authors propose actor-critic integration in future work (Discussion §5).\n- Pixel-domain weakness on certain tasks: With pixel observations, RaMP performed notably worse than Dreamer on Pixel Door Open; random features on raw pixels may miss semantic structure, and the paper suggests pre-trained encoders as a remedy (C.3; Fig. 6).\n- Adaptation trade-offs with feature dimension: Low-dimensional random features underfit (poor reward approximation), while very high-dimensional features slow adaptation (C.5; Fig. 8; Tab. 3).\n- Assumption of deterministic dynamics in infinite-horizon variant: The infinite-horizon Q formulation and training/bootstrapping for Fπ(s, a1:H) explicitly assume deterministic transitions (B.1), limiting generality of that variant.\n- Simulation-only validation: Results are in simulated robotics/control domains; real robot experiments are not yet reported (Discussion §5).'}

**naive 最终答案**

> 以下按模块列出对应的论文，并分析各方法的开发缺陷（均来自文档内容）。
> 
> ## 各模块对应论文
> 
> 1. **手/脸检测与人‑身份关联（COCO 风格人群场景）**
>    **PBADet**（ICLR 2024，doc `08b70b…`）：one‑stage、anchor‑free 的 part‑to‑body 关联检测，用单一 part‑to‑body 中心偏移把 hand/face 等部件关联到所属的人体，在 BodyHands、COCOHumanParts、CrowdHuman 上优于 BPJDet/HierR‑CNN 等。
> 
> 2. **4‑bit 优化器状态（Adam/AdamW + LoRA，受限 GPU 内存）**
>    **Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4‑bit States**（NeurIPS 2023，doc `8d5e14…`）：将 Adam/AdamW 一阶矩（B128/DE 分块量化）与二阶矩（zero‑exclusion 线性映射、Rank‑1 归一化、可因子化）压到 4‑bit，比 8‑bit 省更多内存；文中明确可与 LoRA 结合，并给出收敛证明。
> 
> 3. **时序 RNN + 兴奋/抑制（E/I）约束**
>    **Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly**（NeurIPS 2023，doc `e63a94…`）：分析 ColEI（Dale 律符号约束 RNN）与 DANN，结论是性能差距主要来自**初始循环权重的奇异值谱**而非符号约束。
> 
> 4. **谱引导以稳定 SGD/AdamW 训练**
>    **Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure**（ICML 2025，doc `582d13…`）：良训练的深度网络 Hessian 谱呈 power‑law，可用于预测泛化、指导 SGD/AdamW 下的稳定训练；专门讨论了 LoRA 微调不会像全量微调那样诱导出 power‑law 结构（与你的 LoRA 栈直接相关）。
> 
> 5. **JEPA 自蒸馏（cosine/MSE）为何学到鲁棒嵌入**
>    **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks**（NeurIPS 2024，doc `40fde0…`）：证明 JEPA 偏向学习高回归系数（高影响力）特征、对噪声特征学习更慢，深度越深抑制噪声越强，而 MAE 只按协方差 λ 排序。
> 
> 6. **自监督 RL + 随机特征 + MPC 快速迁移新操作奖励**
>    **RaMP / Self‑Supervised Reinforcement Learning that Transfers using Random Features**（doc `528b3e…`）：离线自监督预训练"随机 Q‑基函数"，新奖励只用线性回归拟合，再用 MPC 规划，在 Meta‑World/Hopper/D’Claw 上快速适应。
> 
> ## 各方法的开发缺陷
> 
> - **PBADet**：在单一部件（face‑body）任务上优势不如 BPJDet 明显；部件被遮挡时 part‑to‑body 中心偏移会失效；对小型/遮挡部件（手、脚）仍不够鲁棒，需要 task‑alignment 损失和多种多尺度技巧，复杂度随部件增加仍是隐患。
> - **4‑bit Optimizer**：最优量化设置是任务/数据集相关的，未覆盖所有场景；对小模型（RoBERTa‑L、GPT‑2）未经算子融合时**更慢**；总内存节省在 4‑bit 处饱和（激活、数据仍占大头）；同时量化一、二阶矩会带来轻微精度下降，4‑bit Factor 仅对维度>1 的张量适用。
> - **Dale 律 RNN**：ColEI 网络在四个基准上均学得更差且跨种子方差更大，必须依赖梯度裁剪；小网络或抑制神经元占比低时谱更差；该文是"归因性"研究，给出的是初始化/谱设计指导而非现成可训练的高性能 EI 网络。
> - **Hessian power‑law**：小宽度/深度、数据不足、噪声标签、大批量训练会破坏 power‑law；Hessian 计算代价高，SOTA LLM 被排除；**LoRA 微调不诱导 power‑law 结构**（对你的 LoRA 场景是个直接限制）；power‑law 与 sharpness 捕捉不同区间，并非通用稳定判据。
> - **JEPA 自蒸馏**：非对比式自蒸馏易发生表示坍缩，必须靠 stop‑gradient 等技巧；理论只在**深度线性网络**、特殊初始化与可同时对角化假设下严格成立，推广到非线性模型只是定性推断；JEPA 偏慢特征、且对 spurious 特征脆弱。
> - **RaMP**：采用蒙特卡洛价值估计，方差大；像素观测下能匹配 Dreamer 的部分任务（Pixel Reach/Faucet Open）但**打不过 Pixel Door Open**；多项式/高斯随机特征明显弱于 NN 随机特征；依赖共享动力学、仅换奖励的设定，MPC 规划仍受预测误差影响。
> 
> 整体上没有单一论文能端到端覆盖全部六块——它们分别由上述 6 篇（分属 ICLR/NeurIPS/ICML）对应，你需要按模块组合集成，且各自缺陷（LoRA 不诱导 power‑law、4‑bit 小模型慢、JEPA 坍缩、EI 谱病态等）需要在系统设计时单独缓解。

**community 最终答案**

> ## Papers covering your stack (all found in the collection)
> 
> 1. **Hands/face detection + person association in crowded scenes (COCO-style)** → **PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association Detection** (doc `08b70bc3…`). Detects hands/face as parts and associates them to parent bodies via a single part-to-body center offset; evaluated on COCO-HumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman (face-body association), vs BPJDet/HierR-CNN/ED-Pose.
> 2. **4-bit Adam/AdamW optimizer states under tight GPU memory** → **4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States** (doc `8d5e1455…`). Quantizes first/second moments (B128/DE, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer, factorized 4-bitFactor); works with LoRA-style fine-tuning, up to ~57.7% memory savings.
> 3. **LoRA fine-tuning + spectral guidance for stability (SGD/AdamW)** → **Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure** (doc `582d138d…`). Power-law Hessian spectra as spectral guidance, analyzed across optimizers (SGD, Adam, AdamW, etc.), including a dedicated LoRA fine-tuning analysis (TinyLlama, MathQA).
> 4. **Excitatory/inhibitory time-series RNNs** → **Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly** (doc `e63a94c4…`). Explains E/I (ColEI vs DANN) RNNs via spectral properties, normalised SVD entropy, gradient clipping.
> 5. **JEPA-style self-distillation (cosine/MSE) robustness** → **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks** (doc `40fde037…`).
> 6. **Self-supervised RL with random features + MPC for reward transfer** → **Self-Supervised Reinforcement Learning that Transfers using Random Features (RaMP)** (doc `528b3e89…`). Offline Q-basis on random-feature pseudo-rewards, linear regression to new rewards, MPC planning.
> 
> ## Development defects / limitations of these methods
> 
> **PBADet** – Part-to-body offsets become invalid when parts are occluded; the body-to-part alternative (BPJDet) degrades as the number of parts grows (longer representations, lower detection performance); on CrowdHuman its advantage over BPJDet for the single face-body task is less pronounced (comparable AP, leading MR-2 only); relies on association loss + multi-scale offsets + task-alignment to work.
> 
> **4-bit optimizers** – Optimal quantization settings are likely task-dependent (not fully in scope); validated only on language/vision tasks; unfused implementation is *slower* than 8-bit AdamW for small models; convergence proof covers quantized SGD(M) only; quantizing both moments brings a marginal accuracy drop (smaller block size and factorization needed to stay near-lossless).
> 
> **Hessian power-law spectral guidance** – Power-law structure is lost for small width/depth, limited data, noisy labels, and large-batch training; ~10 outlier eigenvalues deviate from the fit; LoRA-only fine-tuning does *not* induce the power-law that full fine-tuning shows, and d_ks can diverge from expected patterns (Hessian trace is a more reliable LoRA indicator); Hessian computation is too costly for SOTA LLMs, which were excluded.
> 
> **Dale's-law RNNs** – ColEI networks learn worse with much higher variance; their initial recurrent spectrum (column-mean rank-one structure) yields dispersed/multimodal singular values causing exploding/vanishing-gradient problems; smaller networks and fewer inhibitory units worsen spectra/performance; gradient clipping only mitigates, not fixes; DANN captures only fast PV+-type inhibition, and E/I ratio effects remain partly unexplained (normalised SVD entropy only correlates with error).
> 
> **JEPA** – The objective is collapse-prone without stop-gradient/architectural tricks; the theory is restricted to deep linear networks, balanced orthogonal initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable data, so nonlinear generalization is qualitative; JEPA prioritizes slow/low-variance (predictive) features, making it vulnerable to spurious or slow features and slower to learn genuinely noisy ones; only I-JEPA/MAE were compared on ImageNet.
> 
> **RaMP** – Suffers from Monte-Carlo value-estimation variance; on pixel observations it matches Dreamer only on Pixel Reach/Faucet Open but *not* Pixel Door Open; requires a sufficiently rich/universal random-feature set (NN features > polynomial/Gaussian); multi-step Q-functions only *reduce* compounding error, and transfer still assumes shared dynamics with changing rewards plus adequate offline coverage.

### paperscope:gap:319 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively tackle efficient and interpretable deep learning across perception and physical modeling, including: anchor-free part–body association in vision; training EI-constrained recurrent nets under Dale’s principle via spectral analysis; non-contrastive self-distillation (JEPA) that biases latent feature embeddings toward high-influence dimensions; memory-light optimizers that compress Adam/AdamW states to sub-byte levels for parameter-efficient Transformer fine-tuning (e.g., low-rank adapters end-to-end); and adaptive hierarchical graph simulators for time-series meshes. I’m looking for work that discusses squared-error metrics (MSE), cosine-similarity style objectives, cross-entropy loss, regularization trade-offs (quadratic penalties/Pareto), shallow predictors vs. feedforward classifiers, and reports Precision/F1/AUROC. Benchmarks can range from MNIST/ResNet-scale vision to large Transformers.Please analyze the development defects of these methods.
