> {'answer': 'Here are the development defects or limitations explicitly indicated in the provided works, organized by method:\n\nPBADet: One‑stage anchor‑free part‑to‑body detector (ICLR 2024)\n- Benefits shrink in single‑part settings: On CrowdHuman face‑body association (one part), the advantage over BPJDet is “not as pronounced” compared to multi‑part tasks (Appendix A.1).\n- Decoding requires the body to enclose the part: The inference step assigns a part only to bodies “that are unassigned and also enclose the part.” If the body box fails to include the part due to detection error or occlusion, association can fail (Section 3.4).\n- Gains rely on accurate detection/NMS/hyperparameters: The approach depends on correct body/part detections and tuned NMS thresholds (explicit NMS settings per dataset); mis‑tuning can degrade association (Section 4.1).\n- Training resources and scope: Experiments use 4×V100 GPUs, 100 epochs, and target specific datasets (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman). Animal results are qualitative only; broader generalization is not established (Appendix A.3).\n\nDale’s Law in recurrent nets: Column EI vs. Dale’s ANNs (NeurIPS 2023)\n- Column EI RNNs learn poorly and are unstable: They exhibit multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra, worse performance for small networks and with fewer inhibitory units, higher variance across seeds, and require gradient clipping; without clipping, they are “highly unstable” (Sections 3.1–3.4).\n- Dependence on network size/E:I ratio: Column EI performance improves only with larger networks and balanced E:I ratios; small networks or realistic low proportions of I units degrade learning (Figures 5–7).\n- Initialization assumptions are unrealistic: Key theoretical results rely on special, “somewhat unrealistic” balanced orthogonal initializations and simultaneously diagonalizable covariance matrices; generalization to practical settings is unproven (Section 6, Limitations).\n- Open theoretical questions: The origin of the unusual multi‑modal spectra and why large Column EI networks can learn despite large maximum singular values remain unresolved (Discussion).\n- Biological coverage limits in DANNs: Recurrent DANNs specifically model fast PV+ interneurons; they omit inhibitory‑to‑inhibitory connections and cell‑type‑specific time constants, limiting neurobiological fidelity (Discussion).\n\nJEPA self‑distillation: Implicit bias analysis in deep linear networks (NeurIPS 2024)\n- Requires deep encoders for the beneficial bias: JEPA’s priority for influential (predictive, low‑variance) features “takes hold only when the encoder is deep and diminishes substantially when the encoder is shallow” (Section 2, 3.2).\n- Vulnerability to spurious/slow features: The same bias toward low‑variance, slow‑changing features can make JEPA “vulnerable to spurious or slow features” (Discussion).\n- Theory restricted to simplified settings: Results depend on deep linear models, special initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable Σxx/Σyx; generalization to non‑linear models and non‑diagonalizable data is “yet remains unexplored” (Limitations).\n- No full practical validation: While toy generative processes are matched and some small‑scale empirical checks are shown, the paper acknowledges generalization to practical architectures/datasets is not rigorously established (Limitations).\n\n4‑bit Adam/AdamW optimizers for end‑to‑end fine‑tuning (NeurIPS 2023)\n- Second‑moment zero‑point failure mode: Dynamic‑exponent quantization with a zero point catastrophically pushes many second‑moment entries to zero, blowing up updates; removing zero (DE‑0) or using linear mapping is required (Section 4.1, Figure 3).\n- Rank‑1 normalization is not universally best: It improves approximation for long‑distance multimodal distributions but can be worse than block‑wise normalization on short‑distance multimodal/local structures (Appendix C.2; multiple cases where block‑wise wins).\n- Integration constraints with FSDP: Factorizing second moments was “difficult to apply” when parameters are packed into 1D arrays by FSDP (LLaMA‑7B), limiting memory gains (Appendix D.2).\n- Performance overhead without fused kernels: For smaller models, 4‑bit optimizers can be slower than 8‑bit baselines unless fused operators are used (Table 4), indicating implementation sensitivity.\n- Task coverage and tuning burden: Optimal quantization settings depend on task/data; evaluation is limited to language/vision and “applicability to reinforcement learning, audios, and graph learning tasks still needs further study” (Limitations).\n- Practical exclusions reduce savings: Small tensors (≤4096) and some layers (e.g., embeddings in 8‑bit baseline; normalization/bias for larger models) are not quantized, limiting total memory reduction (Appendix D.1).\n\nDifferentially Private RL with self‑play (DP‑Nash‑VI, NeurIPS 2024)\n- Sub‑optimal dependence of privacy cost: The additional regret due to DP has sub‑optimal dependence on H, S, A, B (acknowledged as inherent in model‑based algorithms with private transition estimation); improving it likely requires model‑free private Q‑learning (Section 5.4, Limitations).\n- Computational overhead: The algorithm requires solving O(HSABK) linear programs (CCE per state/time and post‑processing LPs for private counts), which is “computationally friendly” in theory but can be heavy in large spaces (Algorithm 1; Remark 5.7).\n- Requires cooperation to deploy correlated policies: CCE policies are potentially correlated and “require the cooperation of both players” at execution, which can be impractical in decentralized or independent-agent settings (Section 3, CCE and line 18 of Algorithm 1).\n- Strong modeling assumptions: Rewards are assumed deterministic and known; the analysis is limited to two‑player zero‑sum episodic games and tabular settings; extension to function approximation is left for future work (Section 2.1, Conclusion).\n- JDP relies on centralized access, LDP adds noise growth: JDP needs a central agent to see raw trajectories (privacy via output sharing), while LDP requires per‑trajectory Laplace noise with error scaling as O(H⋅√K/ϵ), which degrades regret as episodes grow (Section 5.1–5.2).\n- Post‑processing complexity and bias: The privatized counts require an LP post‑processing and constant offsets (Eϵ,β/2, Eϵ,β/(2S)), adding complexity and potential bias when counts are small (Section 5.3, Lemma 5.8).\n\nThese limitations are taken directly from the papers’ analyses, experiments, ablations, or stated limitations/remarks.'}

**naive 最终答案**

> Yes—the collection contains a matching paper for each component:
> 
> 1. **Anchor-free part-to-body detector**: **PBADet** (one-stage anchor-free, single part-to-body center offset; validated on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman).
> 2. **Spectral view of E/I-constrained RNNs**: **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (ColEI vs. DANN; NSE; singular-value spectrum analysis).
> 3. **JEPA-style SSL**: **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (latent-space prediction, self-distillation; also LDReg analyzes JEPA's dimensional collapse).
> 4. **4-bit Adam/AdamW**: **"4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States"** (Adam/AdamW with 4-bit first/second moments, up to 57.7% memory savings).
> 5. **DP RL with self-play + regret guarantees**: **"Differentially Private Reinforcement Learning with Self-Play"** (DP-Nash-VI under Joint DP and Local DP with regret bounds).
> 
> **Development defects / limitations (from context):**
> 
> **PBADet**: On CrowdHuman face-body association its advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced (single-part task); BodyHands only annotates "hand" without left/right distinction; it is a dense, per-pixel anchor-free head whose association depends on a single part-to-body offset and NMS thresholds; it does not address privacy at all, and is trained with plain SGD (no low-bit/DP integration).
> 
> **Spectral EI-RNN (Dale's Law)**: Constrained ColEI networks learn worse and with higher variance; sign constraints alone impair learning and gradient clipping is needed substantially (exploding-gradient tendencies); spectra are worse for small networks / fewer I units; the analysis focuses on initialization spectra and is qualitative — future work (I-to-I connections, cell-type time constants, hybridizing DANN/ColEI) is left unexplored; it studies *why* EI nets train poorly, not stability/regret guarantees.
> 
> **JEPA paper**: The latent objective is trivially collapsible (all inputs → same vector), so it relies on stop-gradient/architectural tricks; analysis is restricted to deep linear networks, special initialization, and simultaneous diagonalizability, so generalization is only qualitative; the noise-suppression bias holds only for deep encoders and fades when shallow; JEPA can over-prioritize "slow" or spurious features; it can suffer (local) dimensional collapse. It is a vision-only theoretical study — no audio/audiovisual JEPA is covered.
> 
> **4-bit optimizers**: Optimal quantization settings appear task-dependent (only language/vision tested); quantizing both moments causes a marginal accuracy drop; the second-moment zero-point problem requires dedicated quantizers; memory savings saturate as bitwidth drops; for smaller models (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2M) 4-bit AdamW is *slower* than 8-bit because of un-fused kernels. **LoRA is only cited as related work — it is not integrated into the 4-bit optimizer pipeline** (the paper explicitly notes LoRA freezes pretrained weights and applies only to LLM fine-tuning).
> 
> **DP-Nash-VI (self-play RL)**: Results are for finite-horizon two-player zero-sum tabular Markov games only; LDP regret is much worse (O~(S²AB√(H⁵T)/ε) vs. H³S²AB/ε for JDP); the additional DP cost is not yet reducible via model-free approaches; function approximation is left open (e.g., LDP under linear MDPs remains open); JDP requires a trusted central curator, and no privacy-preserving version of the audio/vision components above is provided.
> 
> **Cross-cutting gaps**: The five works are independent — none combines LoRA + 4-bit, none extends JEPA to audio, none gives privacy guarantees for the detector/representations, and the DP-RL work gives no guidance on the detection/SSL components. So they collectively cover your requirements only as a patchwork, with the noted integration and generalization defects.

**community 最终答案**

> Yes. Five works in the collection together cover all five capabilities:
> 
> 1. **Anchor-free part‑to‑body detector** → **PBADet** (one‑stage anchor‑free part‑body association, COCO‑WholeBody/HumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman).
> 2. **Spectral view of E/I‑constrained recurrent nets** → **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (ColEI vs DANN vs standard RNNs, singular‑value spectrum/NSE).
> 3. **JEPA‑style joint‑embedding SSL** → **"Why JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (latent‑space prediction vs MAE pixel reconstruction, implicit bias of self‑distillation).
> 4. **4‑bit Adam/AdamW for end‑to‑end fine‑tuning** → **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4‑bit States"** (4‑bit AdamW/factor, incl. LLaMA fine‑tuning; explicitly references LoRA).
> 5. **DP RL with self‑play + regret guarantees** → **"Differentially Private Reinforcement Learning with Self‑Play"** (DP‑Nash‑VI, JDP/LDP trajectory‑wise privacy, regret bounds).
> 
> **Development defects of each method:**
> 
> - **PBADet**: On the single‑part face‑body task (CrowdHuman) its advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced (better body MR‑2 but only competitive/occasionally lower face AP). Evaluation is limited to COCO‑style datasets, and hand/foot evaluation uses ground‑truth part boxes derived from COCO annotations while face/head parts are excluded due to inconsistent keypoints. The part‑to‑body offset depends on reliable bounding‑box supervision, and unseen/invisible parts still challenge association.
> 
> - **E/I‑RNN spectral study**: It is diagnostic, not a fix — no improved initialization is delivered. ColEI networks still train worse than standard/DANN RNNs on all four benchmarks, show high seed‑to‑seed variance, are unstable without gradient clipping, and small/low‑I networks learn poorly. NSE is only a correlational predictor. The models are simplified (DANN only models fast PV+ interneurons, no I‑to‑I connections), and the analysis is empirical on small benchmarks.
> 
> - **JEPA/SSL analysis**: Purely theoretical, restricted to deep linear networks with special initialization and (near‑)simultaneous diagonalizability; rigorous extension to nonlinear models is explicitly left open. JEPA still needs stop‑gradient/collapse‑prevention tricks and may be vulnerable to spurious or slow features; companion work (LDReg) shows joint‑embedding SSL still suffers local dimensional collapse, with LID estimation degrading in high dimensions.
> 
> - **4‑bit optimizers**: Optimal quantization settings are likely task/dataset‑dependent; small accuracy drops appear on some tasks (e.g., Swin‑T 80.8 vs 81.2; MT 26.28 vs 26.61). The zero‑point problem requires special linear mapping, and without fused operators the 4‑bit versions are *slower* on small models. Evaluations cover only language/vision; applicability to RL, audio, and graph learning is unverified, and the LoRA combination is only discussed for LM fine‑tuning.
> 
> - **DP‑RL with self‑play (DP‑Nash‑VI)**: Limited to tabular two‑player zero‑sum episodic Markov games with deterministic, known rewards. It is model‑based (private transition estimation), giving sub‑optimal DP‑cost dependence that the authors say requires new model‑free designs; function‑approximation settings (e.g., LDP under linear MDP) remain open. The work is purely theoretical with no experiments, and JDP requires the central agent to access raw user trajectories.

### paperscope:gap:355 — 评分与执行路径对照

Prefer works that also discuss fine‑tuning on benchmarks (e.g., MNIST, CIFAR‑100) and report practical considerations for evaluation and optimization.Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Development defects and limitations synthesized across the five methods
> 
> 1) PBADet (one‑stage anchor‑free part‑to‑body association, ICLR 2024)
> - Advantage diminishes in single‑part settings: On CrowdHuman (face–body association, only one part per body), “the advantages of our method over BPJDet are not as pronounced” as in multi‑part scenarios. This indicates reduced payoff when only one part type is annotated/required (Appendix A.1).
> - Sensitivity to task design and hyperparameters: Training relies on multiple loss weights (λiou, λdfl, λcls, λassoc), a scaling factor λ, and anchor‑alignment parameters (K, α, β); ablations show performance drops without multi‑scale features or task‑alignment learning, highlighting dependence on these design choices (Ablation Table 4).
> - Data/annotation dependence: Supervision needs both part boxes and corresponding body centers; the approach presumes a one‑to‑one part‑to‑body assignment, which may not capture edge cases with ambiguous ownership under extreme occlusion (the method enforces one‑to‑one, Section 3.1), and relies on datasets providing reliable body–part pairs.
> 
> 2) Learning with Dale’s Law in RNNs (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Poor learning of simple EI partitions (ColEI): Constraining columns to excitatory/inhibitory (sign‑constrained ColEI) leads to multi‑modal and dispersed singular value spectra (with large modes), which harms optimization, causes higher variance across seeds, and makes training unstable without gradient clipping (Sections 3.1–3.3; Fig. 2–4).
> - Sensitivity to network size and E/I ratio: Performance and spectra deteriorate for small networks and for biologically realistic low fractions of inhibitory units; learning improves mainly for larger models and more balanced E/I ratios (Sections 3.4; Fig. 5–7).
> - Heavy dependence on spectral properties and initialization: Even when sign constraints are relaxed, spectra dominate performance; ColEI requires careful spectral radius and often gradient clipping for stability (Sections 3.1–3.3). Open questions remain about the origin of ColEI spectrum pathologies and why some large ColEI networks learn despite large maximum singular values (Discussion).
> 
> 3) JEPA vs. MAE (deep linear self‑distillation analysis, NeurIPS 2024)
> - Depth‑dependent bias: JEPA’s favorable bias toward “influential” features (high regression coefficients) emerges only with deep encoders; with shallow encoders, its advantage diminishes and dynamics resemble MAE (Corollary 3.3; Sections 3.2–3.3).
> - Potential vulnerability to spurious/slow signals: The same bias that helps avoid pixel noise can make JEPAs “focus on ‘slow features’” and be vulnerable to spurious/low‑variance signals (Discussion), implying risk if such signals are not predictive for downstream tasks.
> - Theoretical scope limitations: Results are derived for deep linear networks under special initializations and simultaneously diagonalizable Σxx and Σyx; generalization to nonlinear encoders and non‑diagonalizable real data is not established (Limitations, Section 6). This constrains immediate practical guarantees.
> 
> 4) 4‑bit optimizers with quantized states (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Zero‑point failure in second moment quantization: Naïve 4‑bit designs (e.g., DE mapping including 0) push many v entries to zero, exploding the update 1/sqrt(v) and destabilizing training (“zero‑point problem,” Fig. 3; Table 1). Robustness requires excluding zero or switching to linear mapping and new normalization.
> - Sensitivity to outliers and block size: Large block quantization (e.g., B2048/DE) can fail to approximate moments with complicated outlier patterns; smaller blocks (B128) and rank‑1 normalization are needed to recover accuracy (Sections 3–4; Figs. 1–2, 23–31).
> - Task‑dependent quantization settings: Authors note “optimal quantization setting probably depends on task, datasets, and training details,” so hyperparameter/format choices may need per‑task tuning (Limitations, Section 7).
> - Throughput limitations without fusion: For some smaller models (e.g., RoBERTa‑L, GPT‑2 M), the unfused 4‑bit implementation is slower than 8‑bit; matching or exceeding 8‑bit speed requires operator fusion (Table 4).
> - Scope limits: Evaluation focuses on NLP/Vision; applicability to RL, audio, graphs is untested (Limitations, Section 7).
> 
> 5) RLCD (rank‑based latent causal discovery allowing causally‑related hidden variables, ICLR 2024)
> - Model and faithfulness assumptions: Identifiability relies on linearity and rank‑faithfulness; like CI‑based PC/FCI, violations (e.g., special parameter couplings/path cancellations) break guarantees (Assumption 1; Sec. 3.1; Appx. B.2).
> - Graphical preconditions for full identifiability: Correct recovery of the Markov Equivalence Class is proved under graphical Conditions 1–2 (e.g., atomic cover availability and collider size bounds). When conditions fail, outputs may be uninformative or partially incorrect, requiring additional checks/refinements (Sec. 4–5; Appx. D.2), and cycles are not handled.
> - Finite‑sample sensitivity of rank tests: The method uses canonical correlation‑based rank testing; with limited data, test errors can lead to self‑contradictions and spurious clusters that require post‑hoc refinement (Sec. 6; Appx. A.19, B.6, D.2).
> - Algorithmic complexity vs. exhaustive search: While RLCD avoids intractable exhaustive enumeration, its search still scales with cluster size levels and combinatorics (Appx. B.16), requiring careful engineering (e.g., collider checks, refinement phase) to remain practical.
> 
> Cross‑cutting observations
> - Several methods are highly sensitive to their implicit or explicit biases: spectral initialization/constraints for ColEI RNNs; depth‑induced feature bias for JEPA; zero‑point mapping and block granularity for 4‑bit optimizers; and rank‑faithfulness/graphical covers for RLCD.
> - Robustness depends on satisfying problem‑specific conditions: PBADet’s gains rely on multi‑part association settings; ColEI needs favorable spectra and adequate inhibitory units; JEPA gains require deep encoders; 4‑bit optimizers need zero‑free second‑moment mappings and outlier‑aware normalization; RLCD needs linearity, rank‑faithfulness, and atomic‑cover preconditions.
> - Practical deployment often requires nontrivial hyperparameter choices and engineering: loss/task‑alignment and thresholds for PBADet; gradient clipping and spectral radius for ColEI; quantizer design (mapping, block size, normalization) and fused kernels for 4‑bit optimizers; robust rank testing and collider handling/refinement for RLCD; and encoder depth decisions for JEPA.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the document collection, here are the papers matching each requirement and their development defects.
> 
> ## (1) Joint-embedding SSL biased to informative signals
> **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks"** — analyzes why JEPA (joint-embedding predictive architecture) biases features toward high-influence/informative signals rather than pixel noise, contrasting squared-error prediction in latent space vs. MAE pixel reconstruction. (LDReg is a related joint-embedding work regularizing local dimensionality to avoid collapse.)
> 
> **Defects:** Analysis is limited to deep *linear* networks with balanced-orthogonal initialization and simultaneous diagonalizability; the bias vanishes for shallow encoders; JEPA is vulnerable to spurious/slow features; generalization to real nonlinear settings is only empirical. (LDReg: LID estimation degrades in high dimension and relies on minibatch nearest neighbors; forcing very low LID triggers total collapse.) Note: no paper in this collection explicitly dissects squared-error vs. entropy-based *classification* losses; the closest is this squared-error-vs-reconstruction analysis.
> 
> ## (2) Memory-lean training with ~4-bit optimizer states
> **"4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States"** — pushes optimizer states to 4 bits for Adam/AdamW-style (framework also supports SGD(M)), for end-to-end Transformer fine-tuning (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2, Swin-T, LLaMA-7B/13B/33B) and is combinable with LoRA-style low-rank updates.
> 
> **Defects:** Optimal quantization settings are task/dataset-dependent (task-specific schemes might be lossless); only language and vision tasks were tested (no RL/audio/graph); on small models 4-bit is slower than 8-bit unless fused kernels are used; quantizing both moments causes a marginal accuracy drop; total memory savings saturate because activations/data dominate. Also, this paper uses ImageNet/GLUE/LLaMA — not MNIST/CIFAR-100; the only document in the collection running MNIST/CIFAR-100 fine-tuning with practical optimization detail is the **Hessian-structure paper** (many optimizers, batch-size/evaluation analysis), which is not a memory-lean method.
> 
> ## (3) Anchor-free one-stage part-body association
> **"PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association"** — reports Precision/Recall/F1 (vs. ED-Pose) and AP; uses standard objectives: IoU/DFL regression, cross-entropy classification, and an L1 (squared-error-like) association loss.
> 
> **Defects:** Its advantage over BPJDet is much less pronounced on the single-part CrowdHuman face-body task; performance degrades without the task-alignment supervision, multi-scale center offsets, or the dedicated association loss (shown in ablations); relies on the anchor-free dense prediction scheme whose recall is inherently lower than anchor-based counterparts.
> 
> ## (4) Rank-based causal discovery with causally-related hidden variables
> **"A Versatile Causal Discovery Framework to Allow Causally-Related Hidden Variables (RLCD)"** — rank-deficiency-based latent causal discovery where hidden variables can be confounders, mediators, effects, or hierarchical, with identifiability (Markov equivalence class) guarantees.
> 
> **Defects:** Assumes linear latent causal models and rank faithfulness; asymptotic correctness holds only under specific graphical conditions that can be violated (explicit failure modes when conditions break); requires pure children/covers; finite-sample rank tests degrade; with no latents it degenerates to PC.
> 
> **Bottom line:** The four best matches are (1) the JEPA implicit-bias paper, (2) the 4-bit optimizer paper, (3) PBADet, and (4) RLCD. Their main development defects are theoretical-restriction (JEPA linear-only), limited-task-coverage and task-dependent quantization (4-bit optimizer), weakened gains on single-part tasks and reliance on task-alignment (PBADet), and linearity/faithfulness/graphical-condition assumptions (RLCD). The requested MNIST/CIFAR-100 fine-tuning optimization analysis is only present in the Hessian paper, which is not a sub-byte-training method.

**community 最终答案**

> ## Papers Found
> 
> **1. Joint-embedding SSL vs. pixel noise (squared-error vs. entropy-based objectives)**
> - **"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features: A Deep Linear Network Analysis"** (NeurIPS 2024, doc `40fde037…`). It analyzes why JEPA-style squared-error latent prediction biases embeddings toward *informative* signals (high regression coefficient ρ) rather than high-variance pixel noise, whereas MAE-style squared-error reconstruction prioritizes only covariance λ. It notes MAE-like generative losses learn subspaces that "explain the bulk of observed variance and can include unhelpful information for perception," while JEPA steers to the low-variance, semantically rich subspace (validated on ImageNet via CCA).
> 
> **2. Memory-lean training with ~4-bit optimizer states**
> - **"4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States"** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `8d5e1455…`). Compresses Adam/AdamW (and SGDM-compatible framework) first/second moments to 4 bits via smaller block size (B128), rank-1 normalization, and zero-point-excluding linear mapping; supports end-to-end fine-tuning of Transformers (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2, LLaMA-7B/13B/33B, Swin-T) and is compatible with LoRA-style low-rank/parameter-efficient tuning, with up to 57.7% memory savings and convergence proofs for quantized SGD(M).
> 
> **3. Anchor-free one-stage part–body association**
> - **"PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association"** (ICLR 2024, doc `08b70bc3…`). One-stage anchor-free detector linking human parts (hands, face, feet) to bodies via a single part-to-body center offset, using standard classification, IoU/DFL and association (L1) losses; reports Precision/Recall/F1 (e.g., F1 48.52 all-parts vs. ED-Pose 31.51), conditional accuracy, joint AP, and mMR−2 on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman.
> 
> **4. Rank-based causal discovery with hidden variables**
> - **"RLCD: A Flexible Rank-Based Method for Latent Causal Discovery"** (ICLR 2024, doc `f8eb4c37…`). Uses rank deficiency of sub-covariance matrices (canonical-correlation rank tests) to locate causally related latent variables (confounders, mediators, effects, hierarchical structures), with identifiability conditions and Markov-equivalence-class recovery, validated on synthetic and Big Five personality data.
> 
> **Note on the MNIST/CIFAR-100 preference:** none of these four works fine-tune on MNIST/CIFAR-100; the 4-bit optimizer paper reports fine-tuning on GLUE/SQuAD/E2E-NLG/ImageNet/Alpaca and practical memory/time considerations. (In the collection, a separate Hessian-spectrum paper uses MNIST/CIFAR-100 ViT fine-tuning, but it does not match these four topics.)
> 
> ## Development Defects of These Methods
> 
> **1. JEPA/MAE analysis:**
> - Theory restricted to *deep linear* networks with balanced orthogonal initialization and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances; nonlinearities and realistic initialization only covered by qualitative experiments.
> - The JEPA objective is inherently collapse-prone; it needs stop-gradient/architectural tricks, and the "informative feature" bias weakens substantially with shallow encoders.
> - MAE's defect is that reconstruction targets unpredictable pixels, so encoder quality depends critically on how x,y are sampled.
> 
> **2. 4-bit optimizers:**
> - Optimal quantization settings likely depend on task/dataset/training details; only language and vision were tested (RL/audio/graph open).
> - Without fused operators, 4-bit versions are *slower* than 8-bit on small models (throughput regression), and total-memory savings saturate once activations/data are counted.
> - Sublinear baselines (Adafactor β1=0, SM3) still degrade accuracy, and small accuracy drops persist on some tasks (e.g., Swin-T 81.2→80.8).
> 
> **3. PBADet:**
> - On single-part CrowdHuman face–body association, its advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced; per-category results vary.
> - Decoding relies on NMS thresholds and Euclidean nearest-body matching (heuristic), and the association loss/hyperparameters (K, α, β, λ) need tuning; occlusion handling inherits ambiguity from anchor-free dense prediction.
> 
> **4. RLCD:**
> - Identifiability holds only under rank faithfulness plus specific graphical conditions (Conditions 1–2, atomic covers); when violated, failure modes occur.
> - Latent variables sharing identical neighbor sets are indistinguishable (atomic-cover limitation), and some structures (e.g., latent without enough pure children) are unidentifiable.
> - Rank estimation via canonical correlations is approximate on finite samples, and the model is limited to linear causal models.

### paperscope:gap:364 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building a resource‑constrained, multi‑modal pipeline: (1) on‑device hand/face association for HCI evaluated on COCO, (2) a chemistry assistant that proposes synthesizable molecules with interpretable substructures, and (3) LoRA end‑to‑end fine‑tuning of Transformers under tight GPU memory. I need research that shows how to use anchor‑free detection, avoid spurious high‑variance pixels via self‑supervised latent‑space prediction, understand how E/I constraints impact RNNs on sequential data, and shrink optimizer memory with 4‑bit Adam/AdamW while maintaining accuracy on MNIST/CIFAR‑100/SVHN and business metrics like Precision/F1. Practical guidance on losses (MSE, cross‑entropy), feature embeddings, and online implementation/diagrams would be ideal.Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Development defects by method:
> 
> PBADet (one-stage anchor-free part–body association)
> - Gains are not pronounced when there is only a single part to associate (e.g., CrowdHuman); the method’s advantages over baselines diminish in that setting.
> - Association accuracy remains limited in crowded scenes (reported mMR−2 around ~50), indicating non-trivial mismatches persist.
> - Decoding relies on selecting the body with the smallest Euclidean distance to the predicted center; this simple rule can be error-prone under occlusion and crowding.
> - Strong sensitivity to training/decoding hyperparameters (top-K anchor assignment, α/β, scaling factor λ, dataset-specific NMS thresholds); performance degrades without multi-scale prediction or task-alignment learning.
> - Heavy training setup (large input resolution, multi-GPU training) and per-dataset threshold tuning increase deployment complexity.
> 
> EI RNNs with Dale’s Law (ColEI and DANN recurrent architectures)
> - ColEI networks (column-wise excitatory/inhibitory partition):
>   - Learn poorly and show high variance across seeds; training is unstable without gradient clipping.
>   - Pathological spectral properties at initialization (multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra, large singular values) lead to exploding/vanishing activations and impaired learning.
>   - Performance is strongly sensitive to the E/I ratio and network size; small networks or fewer inhibitory units worsen spectra and learning.
>   - Tuning spectral radius alone does not fix learning issues; sign constraints explain only part of the degradation.
> - DANN recurrent networks:
>   - While robust and closer to standard RNNs, results depend on specific initializations/parametrizations; broader applicability beyond the studied settings is not established.
> - Theory/analysis limitations:
>   - Results rely on deep linear models and simultaneously diagonalizable data covariances; generalization to non-linear networks and non-diagonalizable settings remains unproven.
> 
> JEPA (deep linear self-distillation analysis)
> - Implicit bias requires deep encoders; with shallow encoders the beneficial bias (toward influential features) diminishes substantially.
> - JEPA can be slower to learn noisy features and converges to lower-amplitude weights for them, potentially making such features less useful downstream.
> - Vulnerability to “slow” or spurious features is acknowledged; the bias away from high-variance pixels can miss useful highly covarying signals under some conditions.
> - Theoretical setting is restricted (deep linear encoders, simultaneously diagonalizable covariances), so practical generalization to non-linear, real-world distributions is not validated.
> 
> 4-bit Adam/AdamW optimizers
> - Second-moment quantization suffers a critical zero-point problem: mapping non-zero values to zero causes large update-direction errors and instability unless the zero level is excluded.
> - Stability and accuracy depend on specialized quantization choices (small block size, rank-1 normalization, linear mapping without zero); these are task/data dependent and sometimes rank-1 normalization underperforms block-wise normalization for certain distributions.
> - Without fused kernels, 4-bit training can be slower than 8-bit baselines; overall memory savings may saturate when total training memory (activations, fragments) is considered.
> - Factorization helps only the second moment; first moment still needs quantization. Small tensors and embedding layers are excluded from quantization, reducing uniformity.
> - Reported evaluation focuses on vision/NLP; applicability to RL, audio, and graph tasks remains untested.
> 
> Foundation Molecular Grammar (FMG) with multi-modal foundation models
> - Coverage limitations on very small datasets: diversity and broader coverage lag, even when synthesizability and class membership are strong.
> - Trade-off controlled by tournament ranking (Top-k vs 1-k): increasing k improves diversity and synthesizability but degrades class membership; performance is sensitive to the choice of k.
> - Distributional match is weak on large, general benchmarks (e.g., MOSES subset shows poor FCD/SNN despite strong uniqueness/diversity), indicating grammar may not capture broader data distributions.
> - Dependence on MMFMs and prompt design: results are sensitive to image vs text inputs, dynamic descriptions, and rendering choices; text-only variants can lose global substructure reasoning.
> - LLM-as-judge resolves discrepancies without human experts but may select suboptimal grammars; expert reviews note that high-complexity decisions can miss nuanced, experience-driven chemistry interpretations.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based only on the retrieved context, here is the analysis of the development defects of the methods you listed.
> 
> ## 1. Anchor-free part-body detection (PBADet, COCO-based HCI)
> - **Two-stage/heuristic predecessors are criticized** (Zhou et al. 2018 heuristics; BodyHands two-stage association; BPJDet's body-to-part offsets): complexity grows with #parts, invalid offsets when parts are obscured, degraded detection performance.
> - **PBADet's own defects**: its advantage over BPJDet is *less pronounced for the single-part (face-body) task* on CrowdHuman; on BodyHands, removing the association loss, multi-scale offsets, or task-alignment each degrades metrics (e.g., joint AP 78.07 → 85.98 with all components); the approach is a per-pixel dense prediction that needs task-alignment (top-K anchor selection) to be stable.
> - Qualitative comparisons (vs ED-Pose) show unreliable predictions for limbs (legs/arms), which can cloud body–part association.
> 
> ## 2. Chemistry assistant with interpretable substructures (FMG)
> - **Weak distributional fidelity**: on MOSES it produces valid/unique/novel/diverse molecules but poor FCD (26.30) and SNN (0.29).
> - **Interpretability is not guaranteed**: learned graph-grammar production rules are rarely guaranteed to be interpretable (functional groups), and interpretable vocabularies typically require expensive expert annotation.
> - **Reasoning defects**: in GPT-4o case studies, medium/hard tasks occasionally miss empirical nuance — unnecessary motif combinations or overlooked groups (e.g., cyanoformamide).
> - **Data efficiency trade-off**: ablated MST heuristic lowers quality; text inputs are a competitive alternative but images perform best for diversity/synthesizability — the method depends heavily on the chosen modality.
> 
> ## 3. LoRA end-to-end fine-tuning of Transformers (Hessian/LoRA analysis)
> - **LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the power-law Hessian structure that full fine-tuning does** (the Hessian spectrum of adapters diverges from expected patterns; the trace is a more reliable generalization indicator).
> - **Applicability**: LoRA freezes pretrained weights and tunes only low-rank parameters, which "greatly reduces the size of the computation graph but is only applicable to language model fine-tuning" (per the 4-bit optimizer paper).
> - Hessian analyses are limited to small models/datasets (TinyLlama, MathQA; GPT-2, Shakespeare) due to computational cost; SOTA LLMs are excluded.
> 
> ## 4. Avoiding spurious high-variance pixels via self-supervised latent-space prediction (JEPA-style)
> - **Theoretical scope is limited**: results are derived for *deep linear* networks, special (balanced/orthogonal) initialization, and simultaneous diagonalizability; generalization to real networks is only qualitative.
> - **Noise suppression has limits**: in the Block-MDP analysis, forward modeling and temporal contrastive learning both *fail when exogenous (pixel) noise is too large*; video-only methods degrade with exogenous noise.
> - Related SSL regularization (LDReg) has its own defects: **LID estimation accuracy degrades in high dimensions**, uses minibatch nearest neighbors, and forcing very low LID can trigger complete collapse.
> 
> ## 5. E/I constraints in RNNs on sequential data (Dale's Law)
> - **ColEI (simple E/I column partitioning) learns worse and with higher variance across all four tasks** (adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition).
> - **Cause**: multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra at initialization (column-mean rank-one nilpotent structure), not the sign constraints themselves; performance degrades for *smaller networks and fewer inhibitory units*.
> - Needs substantially more gradient clipping; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) is only a proxy — anti-correlated with final error, not a fix.
> 
> ## 6. 4-bit Adam/AdamW memory reduction
> - **Coverage defect relative to your ask**: the context reports ImageNet (Swin-T), GLUE, SQuAD, E2E-NLG, WMT, Alpaca — **no MNIST/CIFAR-100/SVHN experiments**, and Precision/F1 only appear as QA (SQuAD F1) metrics, not as business metrics on those datasets. So accuracy retention on MNIST/CIFAR-100/SVHN is unverified here.
> - **Explicit limitations stated**: the optimal quantization setting probably depends on task/datasets/training details; evaluation limited to language and vision (RL, audio, graph untested).
> - **Accuracy/memory trade-offs**: quantizing both first and second moments gives a marginal accuracy drop; memory savings saturate (reported total memory, not just optimizer states); zero-point problem in second-moment quantization can cause catastrophic update-direction deviation if not excluded.
> - **Speed defect**: on smaller models (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2 Medium) 4-bit is *slower* than 8-bit AdamW without fused operators; the authors note fused operators are needed to match/exceed 8-bit speed.
> 
> ## 7. Losses, embeddings, and online implementation
> - PBADet uses IoU + DFL + classification losses with task-alignment and an ℓ1-style association loss (MSE-like center-offset regression); removing task-alignment or multi-scale offsets hurts accuracy — i.e., naive loss/embedding choices are a defect source.
> - The 4-bit optimizer provides Algorithm 1 (compress/decompress framework) and quantization pseudocode, but un-fused implementation is a documented practical defect; online/diagrammatic guidance (pipeline diagram) is present only for PBADet.
> 
> **Bottom line**: the methods individually carry clear development defects — PBADet needs task alignment and multi-scale offsets and loses its edge on single-part tasks; FMG has weak distributional fidelity and imperfect expert-level reasoning; LoRA changes the loss landscape and is limited to LM fine-tuning; JEPA's noise-avoidance is only proven in idealized linear settings; E/I RNNs suffer spectral pathology (worse with small nets/few I units); and 4-bit Adam/AdamW is task-dependent, untested on MNIST/CIFAR-100/SVHN, and slower without fused kernels. Claims about Precision/F1 business metrics on those specific datasets cannot be established from this context.

**community 最终答案**

> Based only on the retrieved context, here are the development defects of each method:
> 
> **1. Anchor-free hand/face association (PBADet)**
> - On the single-part CrowdHuman face–body task its advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced: leading body MR-2 but only *competitive* AP, not clearly better.
> - Ablations show every component is load-bearing: removing the association loss, using non-multi-scale center offsets (normalized absolute distance), or dropping task-alignment learning each degrades hand accuracy, conditional accuracy, and joint AP.
> - Multi-scale feature maps and dense per-pixel prediction are required, adding complexity; the framework is benchmarked on COCO/WholeBody/CrowdHuman-style data and its universality beyond parts-to-body is only argued, not fully validated.
> 
> **2. Chemistry assistant / molecular grammar (FMG)**
> - On MOSES it achieves good validity/novelty/diversity but **weak distributional fidelity**: FCD 26.30, SNN 0.29, and it trains on only 0.05% of ZINC.
> - Interpretability is fragile: graph-grammar production rules are "rarely guaranteed" to be interpretable, and building an interpretable substructure vocabulary typically requires time- and resource-intensive expert annotation.
> - GPT-4o expert review: 18 correct / 2 partially correct, none wrong, but medium/hard tasks show missing nuance (unnecessary motif combinations, overlooked cyanoformamide groups).
> - Image-vs-text trade-off: images drive global substructure reasoning/synthesizability, while text is more robust for small motifs; CoBO-style molecular optimization also carries risk of generating toxic/harmful substances.
> 
> **3. LoRA end-to-end fine-tuning**
> - LoRA-only fine-tuning does **not** induce the power-law Hessian structure that full fine-tuning produces; power-law/KS-distance behavior can diverge, making Hessian trace the more reliable generalization indicator.
> - In the 4-bit optimizer work, LoRA is described as "only applicable to language model fine-tuning," limiting generality to your multimodal pipeline.
> - Random LoRA initialization matters for fine-tuned-model agreement lines (PEFT); performance/quality depends on initialization choices.
> 
> **4. 4-bit Adam/AdamW optimizers**
> - The paper's own stated limitations: the optimal quantization setting probably depends on task, dataset, and training details; task-specific quantization schemes (not studied) might beat the proposed ones.
> - Evaluation is limited to language and vision; applicability to RL, audio, and graph learning "still needs further study."
> - Quantizing both first and second moments causes a marginal accuracy drop; smaller models can be *slower* than 8-bit AdamW because fused operators are not yet implemented.
> - Memory savings saturate when total memory (data, activations, fragments) is counted; 8-bit baselines don't quantize embedding-layer states.
> - Notably, the context reports only GLUE/SQuAD/ImageNet/E2E-NLG/WMT/MMLU metrics (accuracy, BLEU, F1 for QA) — it does **not** establish results on MNIST/CIFAR-100/SVHN or Precision/F1 business metrics.
> 
> **5. E/I-constrained RNNs (Dale's law)**
> - Simple column-wise E/I partitioning (ColEI) learns worse and with higher variance on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and object recognition; it is highly unstable without gradient clipping.
> - Root cause is the initial recurrent-weight spectrum (multimodal, dispersed singular values from a rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure), not the sign constraints per se; sign constraints account for only part of the gap.
> - Smaller networks or fewer inhibitory units worsen the spectrum and performance; normalized SVD entropy at initialization anti-correlates with final test error.
> 
> **6. Self-supervised latent-space prediction (JEPA vs MAE)**
> - JEPA suppresses noisy/high-variance pixels by biasing toward high-influence features, while MAE predicts in pixel space and can fit spurious noise (feature ordering depends on eigenvalues).
> - The analysis is limited to deep linear networks, special balanced-orthogonal initialization, and simultaneous diagonalizability; a temporal flickering model reveals a noise-vs-temporal-correlation trade-off.
> - Related SSL defects: the proposed variance-reduction loss in contrastive learning can suppress meaningful semantic variance, and forcing very low local intrinsic dimensionality (LDReg) triggers complete dimensional collapse.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Development defects and limitations across the five methods:
> 
> 1) Spectral and regularization effects in EI-constrained RNNs trained with SGD (Dale’s Law)
> - Instability without gradient clipping: Column EI (ColEI) networks were highly unstable without gradient clipping; clipping benefited ColEI substantially more than standard RNNs and DANNs (Fig. 2A and Appendix Fig. 10), indicating training fragility.
> - Sensitivity to spectral initialization: ColEI performance varied strongly with spectral radius (ρ); no setting of ρ matched the best standard RNNs/DANNs, and ColEI performed worse at smaller ρ (Appendix Fig. 9).
> - Poor performance in small networks and with realistic E/I ratios: ColEI learned poorly for small networks or when inhibitory units were few (biologically realistic E>I ratios), correlating with pathological singular-value spectra (Figs. 5–6).
> - High variance across seeds: ColEI showed more variance during training and across initializations than DANNs & standard RNNs, attributed to fewer well-conditioned activity modes (Discussion).
> - Pathological singular-value spectra at initialization: ColEI’s multimodal, dispersed singular-value distributions (with large modes) caused deformed activations/gradients and poor learning; improvements in large networks were not due to removing this pathology but to rotations avoiding large singular-value directions (Figs. 3, 5–6; Discussion).
> - Limited theoretical guarantees/generalization: While spectra were shown to matter more than sign constraints (Fig. 4), open questions remain on origins of ColEI spectra (nilpotent column-mean matrix) and why large max singular values coexist with good learning in large ColEI networks (Discussion). DANNs performed well, but extensions (e.g., I→I connections, cell-type specific time constants) were not explored (Discussion).
> 
> 2) Implicit bias of self-supervised learning: JEPA vs MAE (deep linear analysis)
> - Restricted theory scope: Results rely on deep linear encoders with special initializations and the assumption that Σxx and Σyx are simultaneously diagonalizable; generalization to non-linear models or generic data is unproven (Limitations, Assumption 3.1).
> - Depth dependence: The influential-feature bias (toward large regression coefficients ρ) emerges only for deep encoders; it diminishes with shallow encoders (Theorem 3.2, Corollary 3.3), limiting applicability when encoders are not deep.
> - Potential vulnerability to spurious/slow features: Authors note the same mechanism that favors influential, low-variance features may also bias JEPA toward “slow” or spurious features (Discussion), implying a possible failure mode.
> - Practical reach not fully established: While some empirical support is shown (e.g., ImageNet/ViT feature-similarity trends in Appendix D), the paper states the generalizability to practical, non-diagonalizable data and non-linear architectures remains unexplored (Limitations).
> 
> 3) Memory-efficient fine-tuning with 4-bit Adam states (row/column quantization, rank-1 normalization)
> - Zero-point failure in second-moment quantization: Quantizing the second moment with mappings that include zero (e.g., standard DE) caused severe distortion of update directions and high instability (e.g., 33–66% unstable runs on E2E-NLG), necessitating zero-excluding mappings (DE-0) or linear mapping (Sec. 4.1, Tab. 1, Fig. 3).
> - Sensitivity to quantization design: Performance depends critically on block size, mapping (DE-0/Linear), and normalization (rank-1 vs block-wise); suboptimal choices led to noticeable degradation or instability (Tabs. 1, 6; Secs. 3–4.2; Figs. 20–28).
> - Not universally lossless in pretraining: Small but consistent drops were observed on some pretraining tasks (e.g., Swin-T ImageNet top-1: 81.2 32-bit vs 80.8 4-bit; Transformer WMT14: 26.61 vs 26.28, Tab. 2), indicating a residual accuracy gap in certain regimes.
> - Implementation-dependent speed: The 4-bit optimizer was slower than 8-bit for smaller models without fused kernels; only with fused implementation did speed match/surpass 8-bit (Tab. 4), highlighting engineering dependencies for throughput gains.
> - Partial coverage of parameters: For stability/overhead, small tensors (≤4096) are not quantized; factorization is applied only to ≥2D second-moment tensors, leaving 1D second moments to be quantized, which can limit maximal memory savings (App. D.1, Sec. 4.3).
> - Task coverage and tuning: Authors note optimal quantization settings can be task-dependent and their evaluation is limited to vision/NLP; broader domains (RL, audio, graphs) are not validated (Limitations).
> 
> 4) Anchor-free part–body association (PBADet with task-alignment regularization)
> - Gains depend on problem structure: On CrowdHuman (single-part face–body association), PBADet’s advantages over BPJDet were “not as pronounced” as in multi-part settings (Appendix A.1, Tab. 5–6), indicating reduced benefit when only one part type is annotated.
> - Dependence on task-alignment and multi-scale design: Removing task-alignment learning or multi-scale formulation degraded conditional accuracy and joint AP (Table 4), revealing sensitivity to these training components.
> - Association vs detection trade-offs: On COCOHumanParts, PBADet’s detection APs were only “on par” with BPJDet while association metrics improved (Table 2–3), suggesting that improvements concentrate on association rather than uniformly boosting detection.
> - Hyperparameter and post-processing sensitivity: The method relies on top-K task-aligned anchor assignment and multiple NMS thresholds for bodies/parts (Sec. 3.3–3.4), implying practical sensitivity to these settings (the paper fixes K, α, β, λ and NMS thresholds for datasets; Sec. 4.1 and inference settings).
> 
> 5) Time-resolved NeRFs for lidar transients (Transient NeRF)
> - Limited light transport modeling: The reconstruction models single-bounce, time-resolved volume rendering and requires convolution with a calibrated system impulse response; without it, density “thickens” around surfaces (Sec. 3.2), and multiple scattering present in the dataset is not modeled (Discussion).
> - Calibration sensitivity on real data: Captured results showed smaller gains and depth degradation attributed to ≈1 mm extrinsic misalignment; precise multiview calibration was noted as non-trivial and impactful (Sec. 5.2, Fig. 6–7; Calibration section).
> - Regularization needed to avoid spurious density: Without the proposed space-carving regularizer (Lsc), the network places spurious density in front of dark surfaces while still matching histograms (Sec. 3.3), indicating a reliance on this prior to get correct geometry.
> - Assumptions on acquisition regime: The transient image-formation model assumes low-flux Poisson statistics and uses a pixel-footprint Gaussian; performance at high-flux/pileup or non-coaxial lidar/SPAD setups is not addressed (Sec. 3.1, 3.4; Discussion).
> - Data acquisition burden: Real scans required long exposures (~20 minutes per viewpoint) to reduce noise (Sec. 4, Captured dataset), which may limit applicability where capture time is constrained.
> 
> Note: All points above are drawn from the papers’ empirical findings, ablations, discussions, or explicitly stated limitations in the provided texts, without adding external claims.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on my searches of the available context, I can identify the following papers, each matching one of the five requested topics. I'll analyze them collectively and point out development defects where the context supports them.
> 
> ## Identified papers
> 
> **1. Spectral/regularization effects with SGD, E/I constraints, MNIST**
> - **"Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly"** (NeurIPS 2023) — studies E/I (Dale's Law) constraints in RNNs, spectral properties of recurrent weights, sequential MNIST tests, NSE as spectral pathology measure, gradient clipping as mitigation.
> - **"Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure: From CNNs to LLMs"** (ICML 2025) — power-law Hessian spectra of well-trained networks (LeNet on MNIST/CIFAR, ResNet-18, ViT), across SGD/Adam; slope predicts generalization; power-law lost with small width/depth, limited data, noisy labels, large-batch training; LoRA-only fine-tuning doesn't induce it.
> 
> **2. Implicit bias of SSL: joint-embedding predictor vs masked reconstruction**
> - **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks"** (NeurIPS 2024) — deep linear networks, JEPA vs MAE ordering, influential features vs variance, critical times, ImageNet-1K I-JEPA CCA experiments.
> 
> **3. Memory-efficient fine-tuning, 4-bit Adam, row/column quantization**
> - **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023) — 4-bit Adam/AdamW with B128 block + rank-1 (row/column) normalization for second moment, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer, factorization; evaluated on Swin-T (ImageNet), RoBERTa-L, GPT-2, Transformer-base, LLaMA. **Important caveat:** the context does NOT contain results on CIFAR-100, ResNet-50, or F1/Precision metrics — its vision benchmark is Swin-T on ImageNet (Accuracy) and QA F1 is for RoBERTa-L on SQuAD. So that specific combination is not substantiated by the available context.
> 
> **4. Anchor-free part–body association with task alignment**
> - **"PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association"** (ICLR 2024) — single part-to-body center offset, task-alignment learning (TOOD-style anchor metric), ablation shows task-align removal degrades performance.
> 
> **5. Time-resolved NeRFs for lidar transients**
> - **"Transient Neural Radiance Fields for Lidar View Synthesis and 3D Reconstruction"** (NeurIPS 2023) — time-resolved volume rendering of single-photon lidar histograms, novel-view transient synthesis, improved geometry from few (2–5) views.
> 
> ## Development defects (from the context)
> 
> **Paper 1 (Dale's Law RNN):**
> - ColEI networks learn worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs; simple sign-constraint partitioning inherently impairs learning.
> - Small networks or few inhibitory units have pathological spectra and perform worse.
> - Only mitigates via gradient clipping; no principled fix for the pathological spectrum.
> - Analysis limited to RNN settings; no resolution for exploding/vanishing gradient issues under E/I constraints.
> 
> **Hessian paper:**
> - Power-law structure disappears in underparameterized models, with limited data, noisy labels, and large-batch training — so its diagnostic value is restricted to well-trained, overparameterized regimes.
> - SOTA LLMs excluded due to Hessian computation cost.
> - LoRA/parameter-efficient fine-tuning does not induce the power-law, limiting its usefulness for common fine-tuning workflows.
> - A small number of outlier eigenvalues (~10) deviate from the fitted power law.
> 
> **Paper 2 (JEPA implicit bias):**
> - Analysis restricted to deep linear networks, special balanced orthogonal initialization, and simultaneous diagonalizability assumptions; qualitative generalization only.
> - The JEPA bias toward influential features only holds when the encoder is deep; it diminishes for shallow encoders.
> - Susceptibility to representation collapse (objective can be trivially minimized) is a known weakness acknowledged in context; MAE suffers dimensional collapse.
> 
> **Paper 3 (4-bit optimizers):**
> - Quantizing both first and second moments causes a marginal accuracy drop; lossless performance is not always achieved.
> - Optimal quantization settings are task/dataset-dependent; results only validated on language and vision tasks (RL, audio, graph untested).
> - Slower than 8-bit optimizers on smaller models without fused operators.
> - Swin-T ImageNet classification (81.2→80.8) shows a slight accuracy drop vs 32-bit.
> 
> **Paper 4 (PBADet):**
> - Without the association loss, part-body association degrades (uses Euclidean distance heuristic).
> - Removing task-alignment (training on all positive samples) decreases all metrics.
> - Multi-scale center offsets interpreted as normalized absolute distance decline in performance.
> - Advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced on the single-part CrowdHuman face-body task.
> 
> **Paper 5 (Transient NeRF):**
> - Limited to modeling single-bounce (direct) reflections of laser light; captured dataset contains multi-bounce effects it cannot render.
> - Requires coaxial setup; small calibration errors in estimated extrinsics reduce accuracy on captured data (sub-mm registration is non-trivial and out of scope).
> - Raw lidar transient data was not widely available; needed a first-of-its-kind dataset.
> 
> **Missing/unsupported claims:** The context does not support the exact combination of CIFAR-100 + ResNet-50/Swin/Transformer + F1/Precision metrics for the 4-bit Adam method (that paper uses Swin-T/ImageNet accuracy, GLUE/SQuAD F1), and does not contain a paper explicitly contrasting cosine-similarity predictor heads vs MSE losses in Transformers for SSL (the closest is the JEPA-vs-MAE deep linear analysis).

**community 最终答案**

> Based on my searches across the document collection, I can identify the following five papers matching your five topics. Note: the collection contains the JEPA paper (deep linear analysis, joint-embedding vs. masked reconstruction) and the "4-bit Optimizers" paper (Adam with 4-bit states, row/column quantization, Swin-T/Transformer backbones), but the exact variants you describe (cosine-similarity heads vs MSE in Transformers; CIFAR-100/ResNet-50 F1/Precision) are not present in the collection. Below are the development defects of each matched method:
> 
> **1. "Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly" (NeurIPS 2023)** — spectral/regularization effects, E/I constraints, MNIST.
> - ColEI networks learn worse and with high variance; performance degrades for small networks with few inhibitory units.
> - Pathological multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra at initialization (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure); needs heavy gradient clipping to stabilize, otherwise unstable.
> - Sign constraints alone do not explain the gap; NSE-based diagnosis only predicts, doesn't fix, and the paper offers no improved initialization.
> - Limited to direct-gradient training; biological fidelity is incomplete (e.g., no inhibitory-to-inhibitory connections).
> 
> **2. "Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024)** — implicit bias of SSL, JEPA vs MAE, deep linear networks.
> - Analysis restricted to deep linear MLPs, balanced orthogonal initialization, and simultaneous diagonalizability; qualitative only for Transformers (the collection does not include the cosine-head vs MSE Transformer study you describe).
> - JEPA objective is susceptible to representation collapse (mitigated only by stop-gradient), and its bias toward "influential/slow features" means it can ignore high-variance but semantically relevant directions.
> - Differences vanish with shallow encoders; the step-wise greedy order differs but final feature sets can be the same.
> 
> **3. "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (NeurIPS 2023)** — Adam with 4-bit state approximation, row/column (rank-1) quantization.
> - Quantizing both first and second moments causes a marginal accuracy drop; quantization settings are task/dataset-dependent (no universal optimal scheme).
> - Smaller models (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2) run *slower* than 8-bit Adam because fused operators aren't implemented; the zero-point problem of the second moment needs a special linear/exclusion quantizer.
> - Not validated on RL, audio, graph learning; memory savings saturate at 4-bit since total memory includes activations/data.
> 
> **4. "PBADet" (ICLR 2024)** — anchor-free part–body association with task-alignment regularization.
> - Its advantage over BPJDet shrinks for single-part (face-body) tasks on CrowdHuman; relies on TOOD-style task-alignment and top-K anchor selection, so performance is sensitive to α/β hyperparameters and multi-scale feature choices.
> - Dense anchor-free representation can degrade without multi-scale center offsets; limited generalization to heterogeneous part sets or overlapping/occluded parts.
> 
> **5. "Transient Neural Radiance Fields" (NeurIPS 2023)** — time-resolved NeRFs rendering lidar transients over t.
> - Models only single-bounce/direct reflection; multiple light bounces and surface reflectance effects present in the dataset are not captured.
> - Requires coaxial setup; sensitive to imperfect extrinsics (sub-mm registration needed), and relies on first-of-its-kind hardware/dataset.
> 
> **Not established from the collection:** the specific papers reporting cosine-similarity-head vs MSE comparisons in Transformers, and 4-bit fine-tuning with CIFAR-100/ResNet-50 F1/Precision metrics.

</details>

<summary>展开完整 gold 与两份最终答案</summary>

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Development defects and limitations reported by the cited works
> 
> PBADet (one‑stage anchor‑free part–body association)
> - Limited advantage on single‑part association: On CrowdHuman (face–body only), the authors note the gains over BPJDet are “not as pronounced” because the task involves just one part, so the proposed design’s multi‑part scalability brings little benefit in that setting (Appendix A.1).
> - Sensitivity to key components: Ablations show performance drops when either multi‑scale formulation or task‑alignment learning is removed; w/o Multi‑scale and w/o Task‑align both degrade hand detection, conditional accuracy, and joint AP (Table 4), indicating reliance on these choices.
> - Hyperparameter dependence across datasets: Inference required dataset‑specific NMS/confidence/IoU thresholds (Section 4.1), and loss/assignment hyperparameters (λ, K, α, β), suggesting tuning burden.
> - Only moderate detection parity in some metrics: On COCOHumanParts, original/subordinate APs are only “on par” with BPJDet for some categories and sizes (Table 2), showing benefits are dataset/metric‑dependent.
> 
> Dale’s Law in RNNs (ColEI vs DANN; spectral perspective)
> - ColEI networks learn poorly and are unstable: They exhibit multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra with large modes, causing exploding/vanishing behaviors and worse learning than standard RNNs/DANNs; training variance is higher and they are highly unstable without gradient clipping (Sections 3.1–3.3; Discussion).
> - Performance degrades in small networks and with few inhibitory units: Small ColEI models and realistic E:I ratios (few I cells) learn less effectively; NSE (normalized SVD entropy) diagnoses more pathological spectra and correlates with poorer test error (Sections 3.4, Figs. 5–7).
> - Heavy dependence on spectral initialization: ColEI requires careful spectral radius tuning (ρ) and still underperforms; spectrum “transplants” show spectra matter more than sign constraints for performance (Section 3.3).
> - DANN scope limitation: While DANN RNNs learn well, the authors note DANNs specifically model fast PV+ interneurons, whereas ColEI is a more general inhibitory abstraction; modeling other interneuron types may require hybrid/extended architectures (Discussion).
> 
> JEPA vs MAE (deep linear self‑distillation; implicit bias)
> - Theoretical scope limits: Results rely on deep linear networks, special balanced initializations, and simultaneously diagonalizable Σxx and Σyx; generalization to non‑linear models and non‑diagonalizable data is not established (Limitations, Section 6).
> - Depth dependence and diminished benefits for shallow encoders: The JEPA bias toward influential features (high regression coefficient) strengthens with depth and diminishes substantially for shallow encoders (Sections 3.2–3.4).
> - Potential vulnerability to slow/spurious features: The authors discuss that JEPA’s bias toward predictive low‑variance (slow) features may make it vulnerable to spurious/slow signals (Discussion, Section 7).
> - Empirical setting constraints: Experiments center on synthetic linear‑Gaussian data and toy temporal/masking models; broader practical validation remains to be shown (Sections 4, 6).
> 
> Memory‑Efficient 4‑bit Optimizers (quantized Adam states)
> - Critical zero‑point failure mode for second moment: Quantizing v with mappings that include zero collapses many bins to zero, catastrophically distorting update directions (Fig. 3; Table 1). The method must exclude zero (DE‑0) or use linear mapping to avoid this defect, indicating fragility to quantizer design.
> - Task- and setting‑dependent quantization: Authors state optimal quantization settings can be task‑dependent; rank‑1/linear works well in their tests but other tasks may need different settings (Limitations, Section 7).
> - Domain coverage limits: Evaluation is limited to language and vision; applicability to RL, audio, graphs remains untested (Limitations, Section 7).
> - Throughput caveat without fused ops: 4‑bit implementations can be slower than 8‑bit without kernel fusion; only after fused operators do speeds match/surpass baselines (Table 4), revealing an engineering dependency.
> - Not strictly lossless in all regimes: While fine‑tuning is “lossless,” pretraining results are reported as “comparable” rather than strictly equal; some vision tasks show parity instead of clear wins (Table 2).
> 
> Transient NeRFs for single‑photon lidar view synthesis
> - Restricted physical modeling: The method models single‑bounce (direct) returns; the dataset contains richer multipath transport that is not captured by the current rendering model (Discussion, Section 6).
> - Sensitivity to calibration and alignment: On captured data, improvements are smaller than in simulation due to ≈1 mm extrinsic misalignment; the method’s depth accuracy degrades relative to simulation (Section 5.2), indicating reliance on precise calibration.
> - Need for lidar impulse response handling: Without convolving with the calibrated temporal impulse response, optimization yields thick density clouds around surfaces (Section 3.2), revealing sensitivity to accurate system response modeling.
> - Regularization dependence: Captured data required stronger space‑carving regularization (λsc increased from 1e‑3 to 1e‑2) to suppress spurious density (Section 3.4), indicating tuning sensitivity.
> - Capture practicality constraints: Building the dataset required 20‑minute exposures per scan to minimize noise (Section 4), which is a practical limitation for real‑time scenarios.
> - Configuration generality: The work does not explore non‑coaxial lidar/SPAD setups; extending to more general active single‑photon configurations remains future work (Discussion, Section 6).

**naive 最终答案**

> **Yes — collectively, the collection covers all of these, but as separate papers, not one unified work:**
> 
> 1. **Part–body linking in crowded scenes**: *PBADet* (one-stage anchor-free part-body association with a single part-to-body center offset; reports precision/recall/F1 vs ED-Pose).
> 2. **Raw single-photon lidar simulation/reconstruction along time t**: *Transient NeRFs for Lidar View Synthesis and 3D Reconstruction* (time-resolved volume rendering of photon-count histograms, transient rendering along t).
> 3. **4-bit optimizer states for memory-lean Transformer fine-tuning**: *Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States* (4-bit Adam/AdamW, QA F1 metric, LLaMA fine-tuning, ~57.7% memory savings).
> 4. **JEPA-style self-supervised pretraining vs pixel reconstruction**: *How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features* (JEPA vs MAE implicit-bias analysis).
> 5. **Excitatory/inhibitory constraints**: *Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective*.
> 6. **Cosine-similarity vs squared-error objectives on MNIST/CIFAR**: closest are *On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning* (cosine-similarity analysis, CIFAR-10/100 with SGD) and *Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure* (MNIST/CIFAR-100/10 across SGD/Adam). No single paper directly compares cosine-similarity vs squared-error objectives on MNIST/CIFAR-100.
> 
> **Development defects of these methods (from the context):**
> 
> - **PBADet**: On the single-part CrowdHuman face-body task its advantage over BPJDet shrinks; removing the association loss, multi-scale offsets, or task-alignment degrades all metrics; multi-stage predecessors were inefficient and BPJDet-style body-to-part offsets degrade detection as part count grows.
> - **Transient NeRFs**: Assumes single-bounce (direct reflections only, no multipath), coaxial setup only, sensitive to small calibration errors; Poisson noise model assumes low flux (<5% detection probability) so pileup distortion isn't handled; raw transient data was previously unavailable and training still requires a large GPU (single A40).
> - **4-bit optimizers**: Optimal quantization settings may be task-dependent and weren't searched; only language/vision tasks tested (not RL/audio/graph); smaller models (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2M) run *slower* than 8-bit AdamW without fused operators; quantizing both moments causes a marginal accuracy drop.
> - **JEPA analysis**: Theory restricted to deep *linear* MLPs, special balanced orthogonal initialization, and simultaneous diagonalizability; non-contrastive JEPA is inherently collapse-prone without stop-grad; noise suppression is only qualitative/generalized, and JEPA still learns noisy features, just at lower weight amplitude.
> - **Dale's Law EI networks**: Column-constrained (ColEI) networks learn markedly worse with higher variance — multimodal/dispersed singular spectra; performance degrades further with fewer inhibitory units or smaller networks; gradient clipping is needed to compensate; sign constraints limit the solution space.
> - **Cosine-similarity contrastive analysis**: The auxiliary variance-reduction loss adds a tunable hyperparameter λ and may suppress meaningful semantic variance; analysis assumes normalized encoders, and full-batch optimality (perfect positive alignment) doesn't hold in mini-batch settings.
> - **Hessian power-law analysis**: Power-law structure disappears with small width/depth, limited data, noisy labels, and large-batch training; conventional sharpness measures become nearly useless as LLM generalization predictors; largest models excluded due to Hessian computation cost.
> 
> In sum: each method is validated on a narrow domain (one-stage detection, single-bounce coaxial lidar, language/vision fine-tuning, deep-linear theory, small RNNs, contrastive/CIFAR), so assembling them into one robotics stack would require bridging gaps none of them individually closes (e.g., transient lidar's single-bounce limit, EI networks' poor small-scale learning, and the absence of a direct cosine-vs-MSE benchmark study).

**community 最终答案**

> Yes — the collection collectively covers all four requested areas:
> 
> 1. **Part–body linking detection** — PBADet (one-stage anchor-free part-body association, e.g., hand/body in crowded scenes; reports F1/Precision).
> 2. **Transient NeRF along time t** — Transient NeRFs render raw single-photon lidar time-resolved histograms and reconstruct 3D geometry.
> 3. **4-bit optimizer states** — 4-bit Adam/AdamW quantized states for memory-lean fine-tuning of large Transformers (QA F1 reported).
> 4. **Cosine-similarity vs squared-error analyses on MNIST/CIFAR** — "On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning" (CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100), "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (JEPA vs MAE squared-error objective), plus LDReg.
> 5. **Excitatory/inhibitory constraints** — "Learning better with Dale's Law" (spectral analysis of E/I RNNs).
> 
> **Development defects of these methods:**
> 
> - **PBADet & prior association work:** two-stage approaches (Zhou et al., BodyHands) rely on heuristic/learned association networks, adding complexity and compromising efficiency. BPJDet's body-to-part offsets grow with the number of parts, degrading detection performance, and its offsets become invalid when parts are occluded. PBADet itself shows only a marginal advantage over BPJDet on the single-part CrowdHuman face-body task.
> - **Transient NeRFs:** handle only direct reflections, assume a coaxial setup, tolerate only small calibration errors, and rely on a low-flux Poisson measurement model; validated mainly on simulated and prototype-captured datasets.
> - **4-bit optimizers:** optimal quantization appears task-dependent and only language/vision tasks were tested; without operator fusion they are slower than 8-bit optimizers; total memory savings saturate because activations/data dominate; quantizing both moments causes a marginal accuracy drop; sublinear-memory alternatives (Adafactor, SM3) save more memory but degrade accuracy, especially on classification.
> - **Cosine-similarity vs squared-error analyses:** mini-batch training increases negative-pair similarity variance (worse with smaller batches), degrading representations; perfect positive alignment is unattainable when negative similarities fall below a threshold; the proposed variance-reduction loss adds a tunable hyperparameter and may suppress meaningful semantic variance. The JEPA analysis is restricted to deep linear networks with special initialization and simultaneous diagonalizability, and the JEPA objective itself is collapse-prone (needs stop-grad), while MAE-style squared-error reconstruction prioritizes high-variance, often uninformative pixel subspaces.
> - **E/I architectural constraints:** simple ColEI partitioning learns worse and with higher variance (gradient clipping only mitigates it); smaller networks with fewer inhibitory units further worsen spectra and performance; the deficit stems mainly from a pathological multimodal, dispersed initial singular-value spectrum rather than sign constraints alone (though sign constraints also contribute).
> 
> Additionally, the Hessian-spectrum analysis (MNIST/CIFAR-10/100, SGD/Adam) notes its power-law findings break down with small width/depth, limited data, noisy labels, and large-batch training, and SOTA LLMs were excluded due to Hessian computation cost.

</details>

### paperscope:gap:373 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively cover: (1) selecting a small subset of open, unlabeled text to warm‑start fine‑tuning large language models using feature embeddings and distributional matching (rather than full continued pretraining), compatible with SFT/LoRA workflows and reported with F1/Precision style metrics; (2) memory‑lean training via compressing optimizer states to very low bitwidth while keeping Adam/AdamW/SGD behavior for Transformer backbones; (3) analyses of non‑contrastive self‑supervised objectives that predict in latent space (vs reconstruction losses like MSE) and their implicit bias in deep networks; (4) a spectral perspective on recurrent models with separate excitatory/inhibitory units (Dale‑style constraints) for stability/interpretability; and (5) an anchor‑free, one‑stage detector that associates parts to their parent instances on whole‑body benchmarks (e.g., COCO‑like), with attention backbones and standard detection metrics. Prefer works that discuss fine‑tuning, self‑supervised learning, cosine‑style similarity/embeddings, and common optimizers (Adam/AdamW).Please analyze the development defects of these methods.
