**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below are the key development defects and practical limitations explicitly documented in the five methods that together span the requested areas. Each item ties to the paper’s own statements (or procedures/apparatus they relied on) and is kept within the evidence provided.
> 
> 1) GOT-D: OT‑gradient data selection for pre‑fine‑tuning LLMs (ICLR’24)
> - Dependence on pretraining‑candidate match: Assumes the candidate pool DS approximately matches the (often undisclosed) pretraining distribution DP (OT(DP, DS) ≤ ε). Authors note their approach is not intended for tasks whose domain knowledge is very different from pretraining (e.g., programming if the model was trained only on English literature). This narrows applicability outside domains covered by common pretraining sources.
> - Low‑data and light fine‑tuning regime assumptions: The theoretical optimality is derived under small selection budgets and light fine‑tuning (few epochs, small learning rates). Performance guarantees do not cover heavy continued pretraining or regimes where λ (fine‑tuning weight) is not small.
> - Proxy and embedding sensitivity: Uses target training data as a proxy for test distribution and relies on text embeddings (e.g., distil‑BERT) to compute OT; while fast, selection quality depends on the chosen embedding and the re‑sampling heuristic that pre‑filters domains by OT relevance.
> - Practical compute still needed upstream: Although the OT solve is minutes on a single GPU, the pipeline requires embedding millions of samples (e.g., ~1 hour on an A100 for ~2M samples), so end‑to‑end runtime depends on embedding throughput.
> - Metric dependence in detoxification: Toxicity reductions were validated with Perspective and Moderation APIs, but these APIs can disagree and change over time (Appendix shows distributional shifts and imperfect correlation). Gains in “toxicity” rely on these specific automated detectors; measured benefits can vary with the metric provider.
> - Small utility dips in some settings: In detoxification, reductions in toxicity came with small drops in downstream zero‑shot utility (e.g., average accuracy from 0.422 to ~0.408 in one 20k subset), highlighting a trade‑off in some use cases.
> 
> 2) Memory‑lean 4‑bit optimizers for Adam/AdamW/SGD (NeurIPS’23)
> - Second‑moment zero‑point failure mode: Quantizing the second moment with mappings that include zero collapses many entries to zero, catastrophically distorting update magnitudes (large 1/√v effect). The remedy (exclude zero via linear mapping or DE‑0 and use rank‑1 normalization) is necessary; without it, 4‑bit fails or becomes unstable.
> - Task‑dependent settings: Authors explicitly state optimal quantization settings can be task/dataset dependent. The proposed B128 + rank‑1 normalization + linear mapping works broadly in their tests, but other tasks may require retuning, limiting plug‑and‑play use.
> - Coverage limited to language/vision: Evaluation spans NLU/QA/NLG/CLS/MT and instruction tuning; applicability to RL, speech/audio, graphs is untested and left for future work.
> - Throughput depends on fused kernels: On smaller models, the unfused 4‑bit optimizer can be slower than 8‑bit/FP32; speed matched or exceeded baselines only after operator fusion, so production gains depend on engineering support (fused ops).
> - Total memory savings can saturate: While optimizer state memory drops sharply (4‑bit or factorized), total footprint is also dominated by activations, data, and fragmentation; measured end‑to‑end savings sometimes plateau, tempering overall gains.
> - Factorization only for ≥2D tensors: Second‑moment factorization is not applied to 1D tensors (those are still quantized), so extreme memory reductions depend on parameter shapes in the backbone.
> 
> 3) JEPA implicit bias in deep linear self‑distillation (NeurIPS’24)
> - Strong assumptions limit generality: Theory assumes deep linear encoders/decoders, special balanced/orthogonal initializations, small initialization scale, and simultaneously diagonalizable Σxx and Σyx; authors explicitly mark this as a limitation and an open question for nonlinear and realistic data.
> - Depth dependence of the bias: The “influential‑feature” prioritization in JEPA emerges with depth; for shallow encoders the effect diminishes, so desired bias may not arise in shallow/parameter‑efficient variants.
> - Potential vulnerability to slow/spurious features: Authors note JEPA’s bias toward predictive low‑variance directions can lead to a focus on slowly varying or spurious features, which can be undesirable in some real‑world settings.
> - Empirical scope: Results validating theory largely use solvable linear models and controlled generative processes; extension to modern nonlinear architectures/backbones remains future work.
> 
> 4) Spectral perspective on Dale’s‑law RNNs (NeurIPS’23)
> - ColEI (column‑constrained EI) pathology: Simple “column” Dale’s‑law RNNs exhibit multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra that correlate with poor, unstable learning—especially in small networks or with few inhibitory units. They also require gradient clipping to avoid instability.
> - Sensitivity to EI ratio and network size: Performance of ColEI networks degrades when inhibitory units are scarce and improves with larger networks; thus, small ColEI models are weak, and good behavior depends on network width and E/I balance.
> - Initialization dependence and variance: Results hinge on particular orthogonal/balanced initializations and show high variance across seeds for ColEI. Generalization of the spectral cures beyond studied inits remains open.
> - Open theoretical gaps: The origin of ColEI’s multimodal spectra and why large ColEI networks learn despite large maximum singular values are noted as open questions. NSE (normalized SVD entropy) is proposed as a predictor but adds analysis overhead.
> - Biological fidelity trade‑offs: DANN RNNs (which perform well) are tailored to fast PV+ interneurons; they omit some biologically plausible features (e.g., I‑to‑I connections, time‑constant heterogeneity), limiting direct neurobiological interpretability in some settings.
> - Benchmark scope: Empirics cover adding problem, sMNIST, Penn Treebank language modeling, and a naturalistic object recognition task; broader tasks/backbones (e.g., Transformers) aren’t assessed.
> 
> 5) PBADet: One‑stage anchor‑free part‑to‑body association detector (ICLR’24)
> - Gains depend on multi‑part settings: Authors show advantages are modest on single‑part association (e.g., face‑body in CrowdHuman), where PBADet is only comparable to prior art; the benefits are pronounced mainly when many parts must be associated.
> - Heavy training/inference configuration: Reported training uses large inputs (1024–1536 px), multi‑scale heads, and 4× V100 GPUs over 100 epochs, and relies on several loss/assignment hyperparameters (K, α, β, λiou, λdfl, λcls, λassoc). Practical deployment must budget compute and tuning effort.
> - Decoding assumption (enclosure): Inference assigns a part to the nearest body center among bodies that also enclose the part. This assumes a valid body box exists that contains the part; corner cases (annotation noise or extreme poses where the part isn’t enclosed) can violate the assumption and complicate assignment.
> - Mixed metric improvements: On COCO‑HumanParts, detection AP is “on par” with the best baseline and better on some scales/categories, but not uniformly superior; hence the method is not strictly state‑of‑the‑art across all metrics.
> - Dataset dependence: The approach requires datasets with explicit part boxes and body boxes (e.g., COCO‑WholeBody/COCO‑HumanParts/BodyHands). Outside such settings (e.g., pure keypoint‑only pose datasets), PBADet’s formulation does not directly apply without additional box supervision.
> 
> Notes on shared implementation/optimizer aspects
> - Optimizers and training stability: Several methods rely on standard optimizers (SGD/Adam/AdamW) but report instability without auxiliary tricks (e.g., ColEI needs gradient clipping; 4‑bit optimizers need zero‑point‑free mapping and rank‑1 normalization to avoid divergence). These are non‑optional engineering constraints for robust training.
> - Metrics and evaluation sensitivity: Reported gains often depend on particular metrics (e.g., AP flavors in COCO, GLUE F1/accuracy, toxicity APIs). Reproducibility across alternative but reasonable metrics can vary (explicitly acknowledged in the detoxification study).
> 
> Overall, each method delivers its promised contribution but comes with clearly stated boundaries: assumptions (distributional proximity, low‑data fine‑tuning), data/compute prerequisites (embedding millions of samples, high‑res detection pipelines, fused kernels for 4‑bit speed), and task‑regime sensitivities (single‑part detection, JEPA depth, ColEI small‑network weakness). These are the concrete development defects/limitations to account for when adopting or extending the methods.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the document collection, the five papers that collectively cover the requested topics are:
> 
> 1. **GOT-D ("Get More for Less: Principled Data Selection for Warming Up Fine-Tuning in LLMs")** — selects a small subset of open, unlabeled data for pre-fine-tuning LLMs via gradient of optimal-transport distributional matching (a form of distributional matching), using feature embeddings (sentence-transformer/distilled-BERT), is compatible with a two-stage SFT-style fine-tuning, and is evaluated with F1/accuracy (GLUE, AG News, BoolQ).
> 2. **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** — compresses Adam/AdamW optimizer states to 4-bit (very low bitwidth), preserving Adam/AdamW/SGD behavior, validated on Transformer backbones (RoBERTa, GPT-2, Transformer, LLaMA-7B/13B/33B, Swin-T).
> 3. **"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features"** — analyzes non-contrastive JEPA self-distillation that predicts in latent space vs. MAE-style reconstruction (MSE in data space), and characterizes the implicit bias (influential/high-regression-coefficient features) in deep linear networks.
> 4. **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** — spectral analysis of recurrent models with separate excitatory/inhibitory units (ColEI/DANN, Dale-style constraints), linking the singular-value spectrum at initialization to learning stability/performance.
> 5. **PBADet ("One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association")** — anchor-free, one-stage detector associating parts to parent bodies via a single part-to-body center offset, evaluated on whole-body/COCO-like benchmarks (COCOHumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman) with standard detection metrics (AP, MR, F1).
> 
> ---
> 
> ## Analysis of development defects
> 
> **1. GOT-D (data selection for warm-start fine-tuning)**
> - Assumes the selected data overlaps with the pre-training scope/distribution; its optimality is derived only under certain conditions, so results may not hold when open data and target distribution diverge.
> - The target-domain metric used (Perspective API scores) drifts over time, weakening the reliability of the detoxification evaluation.
> - The effectiveness is budget-sensitive: gains in the low-selection-budget regime are marginal, and performance depends on the quality of the embeddings used for distributional matching.
> 
> **2. 4-bit optimizers**
> - The optimal quantization setting is likely task-, dataset-, and training-detail-dependent; the proposed fixed schemes (rank-1 normalization, linear zero-excluded mapping) may not be optimal everywhere.
> - Evaluation is limited to language and vision tasks; applicability to RL, audio, and graph learning is unverified.
> - On small models (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2) the 4-bit optimizer is actually *slower* than 8-bit because operators are not fused yet — efficiency gains only materialize after fusion or at larger scale (e.g., reduced communication in FSDP).
> - Quantizing both moments causes a marginal accuracy drop, requiring careful choices (smaller block size, factorization) to stay lossless.
> 
> **3. JEPA analysis (non-contrastive latent-space prediction)**
> - The theory is confined to a tractable setting: deep *linear* networks, balanced orthogonal initialization, and simultaneous diagonalizability — limiting direct generalization to practical nonlinear encoders.
> - Non-contrastive JEPA objectives are inherently susceptible to representation collapse (must rely on StopGrad-type bias), and the analysis of the implicit bias only "qualitatively" transfers; the paper acknowledges it doesn't fully characterize the collapse problem.
> - It explains a bias (prioritizing influential features) but not the safety/generalization boundary: the same mechanism that avoids noise could also over-prioritize a specific low-variance subspace.
> 
> **4. Dale's Law spectral RNNs**
> - The most direct implementation (ColEI, column-sign-constrained) learns poorly: multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectrum, high variance across initializations, and highly unstable without gradient clipping.
> - Performance degrades sharply for small networks and for skewed E:I ratios (fewer inhibitory units), making the method sensitive to architectural hyperparameters.
> - Open theoretical questions remain (origin of the multimodal spectrum; why large ColEI networks learn well despite large max singular value), so design guidance is empirical rather than fully principled; interpretability/stability gains come at the cost of extra initialization/spectral tuning.
> 
> **5. PBADet (anchor-free part-body association)**
> - The advantage over prior art (e.g., BPJDet) is less pronounced on the single-part (face–body) task on CrowdHuman — the benefit is mainly in multi-part settings.
> - Ablations show it depends on all three components: the association loss, multi-scale part-to-body center offsets, and task-alignment learning; removing any of them degrades performance.
> - The paper's backbones are YOLOv5/YOLOv7 (CNN) rather than attention backbones, so the "attention backbone" requirement is only partially satisfied; association accuracy relies on anchor-free positive-sample geometry, which can be sensitive to how many anchor points fall inside part boxes.
> 
> **Overall pattern of defects across the set:** All five methods are validated under narrow conditions — GOT-D on tasks assumed to overlap with pre-training, 4-bit optimizers on language/vision only and with un-fused slow implementations, the JEPA analysis in idealized linear settings, the Dale's-Law RNNs on small/balanced EI architectures that are unstable without clipping, and PBADet on CNN backbones with gains concentrated in multi-part rather than single-part association. Consequently, their reported gains may not transfer to out-of-scope tasks, scales, or architectures without additional tuning.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved documents, the five papers that collectively cover your topics are:
> 
> 1. **GOT-D** ("Get More for Less: Principled Data Selection for Warming Up Fine-Tuning in LLMs", ICLR 2024) — selects a small subset of open, unlabeled text to pre-fine-tune LLMs by matching pre-training to target distributions (optimal-transport gradient), using feature embeddings (sentence-transformer), reported with F1/accuracy metrics on GLUE/AG News/BoolQ.
> 2. **4-bit Optimizers** ("Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States", NeurIPS 2023) — compresses Adam/AdamW optimizer states to 4-bit (B128 block, zero-point-excluded linear/rank-1 normalization), evaluated on Transformer/LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning and instruction tuning, up to 57.7% memory savings.
> 3. **JEPA/MAE implicit bias** ("How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks", NeurIPS 2024) — analyzes non-contrastive self-distillation objectives that predict in latent space vs. MSE-style reconstruction, showing JEPA biases toward high-influence features.
> 4. **Dale's Law spectral perspective** ("Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective", NeurIPS 2023) — spectral analysis of RNNs with excitatory/inhibitory (ColEI vs DANN) units, showing initialization singular-value spectra matter more than sign constraints for learning/stability.
> 5. **PBADet** (ICLR 2024) — one-stage anchor-free part-body association detector (single part-to-body center offset), evaluated on COCO-HumanParts, COCO-WholeBody, BodyHands, CrowdHuman with AP/F1 metrics (YOLOv5/v7 backbones).
> 
> ## Development defects (as reported in the papers)
> 
> - **GOT-D**: Perspective API toxicity scores drift over time; method assumes overlap with the pre-training scope (performance relies on candidate data containing relevant content); conclusions are conditional on that assumption.
> - **4-bit Optimizers**: optimal quantization settings are likely task/dataset-dependent (rank-1 + linear mapping worked well empirically but task-specific settings might be better); validation limited to language and vision—RL, audio, graph tasks unstudied; on small models it is *slower* than 8-bit AdamW because the implementation lacks fused operators.
> - **JEPA implicit-bias analysis**: theoretical results hold only for deep *linear* MLPs with special (balanced orthogonal) initialization and simultaneous diagonalizability; generalization to nonlinear networks is only qualitative/empirical; findings show JEPA's bias manifests only when the encoder is deep.
> - **Dale's Law spectral study**: ColEI networks are inherently unstable without gradient clipping, have higher variance across seeds, and learn poorly especially when small or with few inhibitory units; the paper explicitly does not explore I-to-I connections, cell-type time constants, or hybrid ColEI/DANN models, so those remain open.
> - **PBADet**: on the CrowdHuman single-part (face-body) task its advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced; the method is built on YOLO backbones (not the attention backbones you preferred, though it compares against DETR-type methods); ablations show performance degrades if the center offset is treated as normalized absolute distance (multi-scale anchoring is required) and without task-alignment learning; association relies on one-to-one part-to-body correspondence, which is less flexible in complex occlusion scenarios than body-to-part offsets in some prior work.
> 
> Note: no paper in the collection matches your exact preference of an *attention-backbone* anchor-free part-body detector — PBADet uses CNN (YOLO) backbones.

### paperscope:gap:376 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building a resource‑constrained assistant for hospitals: it must reliably link hands/faces to the right person in crowded scenes, run on a single GPU, and be adapted safely and cheaply to our domain. I need: a compact one‑stage approach to associate human parts to bodies on whole‑body datasets; a way to pre‑select a tiny slice of open text to ‘warm up’ our model before a short supervised fine‑tune; memory‑efficient optimizers that shrink training states to fit into limited VRAM; theory to understand biases of the self‑distillation objective we plan to use for representation learning; and guidance on stable recurrent controllers that respect excitatory/inhibitory sign constraints. Are there papers that, together, address these needs for Transformers and related deep models without requiring massive labeled data?Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

**score：3→3（Δ+0）；rounds：4→2（Δ-2）。**

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> {'answer': 'Development defects and limitations per method, as stated or evidenced in the papers:\n\nPBADet (one-stage, anchor-free part-to-body association for whole-body datasets)\n- Gains diminish in single-part settings: On CrowdHuman, where the association task involves just one part (face-body), PBADet’s advantage over BPJDet is “not as pronounced” as on multi-part datasets (BodyHands, COCO-HumanParts). This indicates limited improvement when only one part category is present.\n- Heavy training requirements: Reported training uses 4 Tesla V100 GPUs for 100 epochs with AMP and large input sizes (e.g., 1024–1536), which may not align with strict resource constraints even if inference is one-stage.\n- Dependence on careful hyperparametering: Anchor alignment (top-K), scaling factor λ, and multiple NMS thresholds are important; performance is sensitive to these choices (evident in ablation results where removing multi-scale or task-align components reduces accuracy). While common in detection papers, this reduces robustness without careful tuning.\n\nGOT-D (Gradients of Optimal Transport for Data Selection to warm up fine-tuning)\n- Assumption dependence: Effectiveness relies on the candidate pool DS approximately matching the pretraining distribution DP (OT(DP, DS) ≤ ε). The authors explicitly note the method “is not intended” for tasks whose domain is very different from pretraining (e.g., adapting English-only LLMs to programming-language expertise), where small-scale unsupervised fine-tuning is generally ineffective.\n- Low-data approximation: The selection optimality relies on a first-order Taylor approximation in the low-data regime (λ ≪ 1); if fine-tuning is not “light,” the approximation and gradient-based selection may be suboptimal.\n- Possible utility trade-offs: In detoxification, while toxicity decreases substantially, average downstream zero-shot utility sometimes drops slightly (e.g., minor accuracy declines reported), reflecting a trade-off when shifting distributions toward the target.\n- Evaluation tool variability: Toxicity evaluation via Perspective API and Moderation API can diverge; while the method is robust across both, the paper highlights evolving/bias concerns in the tools, complicating consistent assessment (this affects evaluation, not the core algorithm, but still limits definitive comparisons).\n\nMemory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States (4-bit AdamW, 4-bit Factor)\n- Zero-point pathology for second moment: Using standard DE mapping quantizes many small second-moment values to zero, catastrophically distorting update directions (since updates scale with 1/sqrt(v)). The paper explicitly identifies and fixes this with zero-excluding mappings (DE-0, Linear), but this underscores a core sensitivity in 4-bit designs.\n- Rank-1 normalization is not universally superior: The authors show cases where block-wise normalization (e.g., B128) approximates certain second-moment distributions better than rank-1; normalization choice is data-dependent and not one-size-fits-all.\n- Task-dependence and scope limitations: They note “optimal quantization setting probably depends on task, datasets, and training details,” and their evaluation is limited to language and vision; applicability to RL, audio, and graph learning remains unstudied.\n- Speed and memory caveats: For smaller models, 4-bit optimizers can be slower than 8-bit baselines without fused kernels; total memory savings “saturate” at whole-training level because activations and other components dominate. Also, embeddings are not quantized in some baselines (consistent with standard practice), reducing end-to-end savings.\n\nDale’s-law-constrained RNNs (ColEI and DANN variants)\n- ColEI defects (explicitly documented by the authors):\n  - Poor learning and instability: Column-signed EI constraints yield multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra with large modes that lead to unstable training (high sensitivity and need for gradient clipping), worse convergence, and higher variance across seeds.\n  - Sensitivity to EI ratio and size: Small networks and biologically realistic low fractions of inhibitory units degrade spectral properties and performance (lower normalized SVD entropy), making learning unreliable.\n  - Sign constraints reduce solution space: The paper shows sign constraints contribute to performance gaps beyond spectral effects.\n- DANN limitations (the authors’ scope and biological faithfulness):\n  - Reduced biological completeness: The recurrent DANNs model fast PV+ interneurons; they lack inhibitory-to-inhibitory connections and cell-type specific time constants. The authors note future work to hybridize models (DANN + ColEI) for broader biological fidelity.\n  - Initialization/specs matter: Performance analyses rely on particular initializations and settings; although DANNs are robust in the paper’s tests, broader generality across architectures and constraints is not fully established.\n\nJEPA (self-distillation, deep linear analysis of implicit bias)\n- Theoretical scope limitations: Results are restricted to deep linear encoders under a special initialization and simultaneously diagonalizable covariance assumptions (Σxx and Σyx). The authors explicitly state generalization to non-linear models and non-diagonalizable settings is unproven and remains future work.\n- Depth-dependent bias: The main benefit (prioritizing “influential features” with high regression coefficients ρ) emerges strongly only for deep encoders; shallow encoders do not exhibit the same JEPA bias advantage.\n- Potential vulnerability to slow/spurious features: The authors discuss that JEPA’s bias toward predictive, low-variance (“slow”) features may make it vulnerable to spurious or overly slow signals, which can be a drawback depending on task.\n- Assumption-driven analysis: Dependence on particular data models (static/temporal linear generative processes) and StopGrad self-distillation setup; real data often violate these simplifications, limiting immediate practical guarantees.\n\nIn sum: PBADet’s advantage narrows for single-part tasks; GOT-D requires candidate data close to the pretraining distribution and relies on low-data approximations; the 4-bit optimizer design is sensitive to zero-point handling and normalization choices and shows task-dependent speed/memory trade-offs; EI-constrained RNNs (ColEI) suffer spectral pathologies and instability, while DANNs are biologically narrower; JEPA’s theoretical insights hinge on linear, specialized assumptions and reveal a depth-dependent bias that can be a liability in some settings.'}

**naive 最终答案**

> Yes — five papers in the collection jointly cover your needs, though not as one unified framework and not entirely label-free.
> 
> **1. Part‑body association — PBADet (ICLR 2024).** One‑stage, anchor‑free detector (YOLOv5/v7) that links parts (hands, face, feet) to bodies via a single part‑to‑body center offset; evaluated on COCO‑WholeBody, COCO‑HumanParts, CrowdHuman, BodyHands. *Defects:* it is **supervised**, needing part/body box labels (not "without massive labeled data"); the backbone is CNN‑based (no native Transformer adaptation shown); decoding relies on NMS + Euclidean body‑center matching, which can misfire in heavy crowds; small/occluded parts (limbs) still produce unreliable associations; performance is sensitive to components (association loss, multi‑scale offsets, task alignment) and scaling hyperparameter λ; on the single‑part CrowdHuman face task its gain over BPJDet is marginal.
> 
> **2. Data warm‑up — GOT‑D (ICLR 2024).** Selects a tiny slice of unlabeled open text (gradient of OT distance) to pre‑fine‑tune before a short supervised fine‑tune; scales to millions of samples on one GPU in about an hour. *Defects:* optimality holds only under assumptions (k‑Lipschitz loss, low‑data regime, 1–few epochs, candidate ≈ pretraining distribution, target train ≈ test); fails when the task is entirely outside pretraining scope (e.g., medical expertise absent from pretraining data); validated only on LLM/NLU‑style tasks (up to 2.7B), not vision/medical; gains are small for tasks where the vanilla model is already strong; toxicity evaluation depends on the Perspective API, which drifts over time.
> 
> **3. Memory‑efficient optimizers — 4‑bit optimizers (NeurIPS 2023).** 4‑bit Adam/AdamW states (smaller blocks for 1st moment, rank‑1 normalization and zero‑point‑excluded linear quantizer for 2nd, optional factorized 2nd moment); works for Transformers (RoBERTa, LLaMA‑7B/13B/33B) with ~57.7% memory savings. *Defects:* optimal quantization is task/dataset‑dependent; tested only on language and vision (not RL, audio, graph); slower than 8‑bit for small models without fused operators; total memory savings saturate because data/activations/fragmentation dominate; the convergence proof covers quantized SGD(M), not the full 4‑bit Adam; quantizing both moments yields a marginal accuracy drop; 4‑bitFactor's factorization is only applicable to matrix‑shaped 2nd moments.
> 
> **4. Self‑distillation bias theory — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024).** Shows JEPA/self‑distillation implicitly biases toward high‑influence, low‑variance ("slow") features, explaining noise suppression vs. MAE. *Defects:* analysis is restricted to **deep linear networks**, balanced orthogonal initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable data; no nonlinear guarantees; implies vulnerability to spurious/slow features; extension to practice is qualitative; trade‑offs appear in the noise/temporal‑correlation model, so behavior under real medical video noise is untested.
> 
> **5. Recurrent controllers with E/I sign constraints — "Learning better with Dale's Law" (NeurIPS 2023).** Explains why Dale's‑law (excitatory/inhibitory) RNNs fail: the culprit is the multimodal, dispersed singular‑value spectrum at initialization, not the sign constraints per se; DANN‑style architectures learn well, and normalised SVD entropy predicts performance. *Defects:* naive column‑partitioned (ColEI) RNNs remain unstable without gradient clipping and train poorly with high variance, especially small networks with few inhibitory units; sign enforcement via projecting violated weights to 0 is crude; sign constraints alone still measurably impair learning; DANN models only fast PV+ interneurons (no I→I connections); conclusions are largely empirical/heuristic (rank‑one nilpotent decomposition intuition), not formal stability guarantees.
> 
> **Bottom line:** Together they address detection, warm‑up, VRAM‑saving optimization, self‑distillation theory, and E/I‑constrained recurrence, but each has development defects — supervision requirements (PBADet), domain/scope assumptions (GOT‑D, JEPA), task‑dependence and incomplete theory (4‑bit optimizers), and instability/simplification issues (Dale's‑law RNNs) — so a production pipeline would need additional validation for medical imaging and Transformers specifically.

**community 最终答案**

> Yes. Five papers in the collection together cover your needs. Their development defects:
> 
> **1. PBADet (one-stage part-body association)** — One-stage, anchor-free, single part-to-body center offset; outperforms BPJDet/HierR-CNN on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman. Defects:
> - Ablations show it degrades without each component: association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and task-alignment learning are all needed.
> - On the single-part CrowdHuman face-body task, its advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced (body MR-2 36.5 vs 39.7–41.3, but face MR-2 44.7 vs 45.0–46.3; mMR-2 50.8 vs 50.1–51.4).
> - Relies on supervised whole-body ground truth (part-to-body offset requires a well-defined body center); no mechanism to avoid labeled data.
> - Offsets need post-processing for association.
> 
> **2. GOT-D (data selection to warm up fine-tuning)** — Selects a tiny slice (0.01%–0.7%) of open unlabeled text to pre-fine-tune before targeted fine-tuning; ~1 GPU hour for millions of samples. Defects:
> - Theory holds only under assumptions: k-Lipschitz loss, low-data regime, candidate set approximately matching pretraining distribution (OT distance ≤ ε), target data i.i.d. — it "assumes overlap with pretraining scope."
> - Embedding choice affects results (token space clearly worse: 50.3 vs 53.5/52.7 at 5k).
> - Evaluation metrics drift (e.g., Perspective API scores) and it was only tested on language/zero-shot tasks.
> 
> **3. 4-bit optimizer states (memory-efficient training)** — 4-bit AdamW/Adam reduces memory up to 57.7%, enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU. Defects:
> - "Optimal quantization setting probably depends on task, datasets, and training details"; task-specific settings outside scope might outperform.
> - Quantizing both moments causes a marginal accuracy drop; only language/vision tasks were tested.
> - Slower than 8-bit AdamW on small models (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2 Medium) without fused operators.
> - Reported savings saturate because total memory includes data, activations, and memory fragments.
> 
> **4. JEPA self-distillation bias theory** — Shows JEPA/self-distillation implicitly biases toward high-influence ("slow," low-variance) features vs MAE. Defects:
> - Analysis is restricted to deep linear networks, balanced orthogonal initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable data — "a less than rigorous leap to practical settings."
> - The objective is inherently collapse-prone and requires StopGrad; the bias may make JEPA "vulnerable to spurious or slow features."
> - Nonlinear models and non-simultaneously-diagonalizable distributions remain unproven.
> 
> **5. Dale's-Law (E/I sign-constrained) recurrent networks** — Guidance: spectral properties at initialization matter more than sign constraints; DANN-style E/I RNNs learn as well as standard RNNs. Defects:
> - Naive ColEI networks learn worse with higher variance, are highly unstable without gradient clipping, and have multimodal/dispersed singular spectra (worse for small networks and few inhibitory units).
> - Sign constraints still impair learning (≈0.7–1% error increase) even though spectra explain the larger gap.
> - Origin of the multimodal ColEI spectrum and why large ColEI networks learn well remain open theoretical questions.
> 
> Caveat on the "without massive labeled data" requirement: only the self-distillation theory (JEPA) and, partly, GOT-D (unlabeled open text) address label-free learning; PBADet, the 4-bit optimizers, and the RNN analysis assume supervised training and do not by themselves remove the need for labeled domain data.

</details>

### paperscope:gap:379 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find research that together spans: (a) one‑stage anchor‑free human part–body association detectors with precise metrics (AP, F1, Precision) and streamlined post‑processing; (b) spectral analyses of biologically‑constrained recurrent nets (excitatory/inhibitory) showing how initialization and stochastic gradient methods shape deep network training under squared‑error or log‑loss; (c) joint‑embedding self‑supervision that predicts latent targets (vs. masked reconstruction) to avoid noisy features, with experiments on classic vision datasets like MNIST, SVHN, and CIFAR‑100; (d) anytime‑valid risk‑controlling prediction sets for low‑risk deployment, including active labeling budgets and e‑process/betting formulations; and (e) instruction tuning of permissively‑licensed code LLMs (using low‑rank adapters or end‑to‑end finetuning) evaluated on HumanEval‑style tasks with feature embeddings, angular similarity, and practical diagrams. I’m also interested in near‑linear runtime discussions, SFT backbones, ResNet‑50 baselines, and clean‑label subsets used for calibration.Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

Gold 1：

> {'answer': 'Below are the main development defects and limitations reported or implied by each method in the provided papers (restricted strictly to the contents you supplied). 1) PBADet (one‑stage anchor‑free human part–body association) • Benefits are muted for single-part association tasks: On CrowdHuman, where association is only face↔body, the authors note their advantages over BPJDet are “not as pronounced” compared to multi-part settings (appendix A.1). • Improvements are not uniform across metrics/categories: On COCOHumanParts, gains over strong baselines are competitive rather than dominant; some categories/metrics are only on par with BPJDet (Tables 2–3). • Sensitivity to design choices: Ablations show notable degradation without multi‑scale anchors or task-alignment learning, indicating dependence on these components (Table 4). • Heavy hyperparameter and threshold tuning: Method relies on multiple loss weights, alignment parameters K, α, β, a scaling factor λ for offsets, and different NMS/confidence/IoU thresholds per dataset (Sec. 4.1), suggesting nontrivial tuning burden. • Resource‑intensive training/inference setup: Trained for 100 epochs on 4×V100 GPUs with large input resolutions (1024–1536), and requires pretrained YOLO backbones (Sec. 4.1, A.1). • Assumption that valid assignments exist inside enclosing body boxes: Decoding assigns the part to the nearest unassigned body that “encloses the part” (Sec. 3.4). When body/part boxes fail to mutually enclose in clutter/occlusion, assignment can be brittle (the paper’s rule requires enclosure). 2) Learning better with Dale’s Law (EI RNNs; ColEI vs recurrent DANNs) • ColEI networks learn poorly without careful spectral control: They exhibit multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra with large modes (Fig. 3), causing gradient/activation deformation and unstable learning; require gradient clipping to avoid instability (Fig. 2, App. Fig. 10). • Strong dependence on network size and E/I ratio: Performance and spectra degrade for smaller networks or biologically realistic lower fractions of inhibitory units; fewer I units increase the largest singular value and reduce NSE, harming learning (Figs. 5–6). • High variance across seeds and sensitivity to spectral radius: Performance varies more across initializations; tuning the spectral radius (ρ) is required and differs in optimal range vs standard/DANN RNNs (App. Fig. 9). • Projected sign constraints can impede optimization: Enforcing Dale’s Law by projection sets sign-violating weights to zero each step (Sec. 2.1), which can slow or hamper learning in ColEI. • DANN recurrent architecture still simplifies biology: It targets fast feedforward inhibition (PV+‑like) and omits some biological features (e.g., I→I connections; cell-type specific time constants), limiting biological fidelity (Sec. 4 Discussion). • Limited task scope: Empirically validated on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Treebank, and a small naturalistic vision task; generalization to broader tasks not demonstrated (Sec. 3.1). 3) How JEPA avoids noisy features (deep linear self‑distillation) • Strong theoretical assumptions: Results rely on deep linear networks, special balanced/orthogonal-like initializations, and simultaneous diagonalizability of Σxx and Σyx (Assumption 3.1; Sec. 6 Limitations), which are rarely met in practice. • Unknown generality to nonlinear/realistic data: Authors explicitly state generalizability to practical nonlinear models and non‑diagonalizable data remains unexplored (Sec. 6). • Depth dependence: The favorable JEPA bias (prioritizing high regression‑coefficient “influential” features) only manifests with deep encoders; with shallow encoders the advantage diminishes (Corollary 3.3, Sec. 3.2). • Potential vulnerability to “slow/spurious” features: The mechanism steering JEPA toward low‑variance, highly predictive features may also bias it toward “slow” or spurious features (Discussion), which can be undesirable depending on the downstream task. 4) Active, anytime-valid risk‑controlling prediction sets (sequential/active RCPS) • i.i.d. requirement: Guarantees are developed for i.i.d. data; handling of distribution shift is left to future work (Sec. 6). • Lower‑bounded label policy: Theory requires the labeling probability to be bounded away from zero (qt(x) ≥ ε), plus existence of an optimal policy; authors acknowledge this boundedness/existence assumption and note it may be relaxable with more analysis (Sec. 3, Assumption 2; Sec. 6). • Variance and efficiency depend on prediction quality: Using predictors (risk estimates conditioned on X) improves label efficiency; poor predictors can increase variance and slow e‑process growth (Sec. 2.2, Theorem 3). • Practitioner burden in betting design: Performance depends on choosing/controlling betting parameters (λt), valid ranges tied to the minimum labeling probability, and adopting online learning (e.g., ONS) to reduce regret—adding implementation complexity (Sec. 2–3). • Utility constrained by label budget: The need to respect an expected label budget B can limit how quickly unsafe β are eliminated (Sec. 3). 5) OCTOPACK (CommitPack, HumanEvalPack; OCTOCODER/OCTOGEEX) • Still behind closed models: OCTOCODER/OCTOGEEX, though best among permissive models, are substantially outperformed by GPT‑4 across tasks and languages (Table 2). • Language performance mirrors pretraining skew: Performance correlates with pretraining language proportions; Rust (lowest resource) lags notably (Sec. 4.2), indicating limited cross‑language robustness when pretraining data are imbalanced. • Models struggle with small, targeted edits and code↔text switching: Even strong models often regenerate buggy code unchanged or introduce new bugs (HUMANEVALFIX), and some generate code instead of explanations (HUMANEVALEXPLAIN) (Sec. 4.2; Figs. 33–38). • Poor adherence to output-length constraints for explanations: Models frequently under‑ or overshoot character limits, harming explanation‑then‑synthesis evaluation (Sec. 4.2). • Evaluation near saturation on standard synthesis: Python HumanEval synthesis is close to saturated (GPT‑4 pass@1 ≈ 86.6%), limiting headroom and possibly masking weaknesses; necessitates harder variants (Sec. 4.2). • CommitPack construction constraints: For data quality, they discard multi‑file commits and apply strict filtering; while simplifying supervision, this limits representativeness of real‑world multi‑file changes (Sec. 2). • Dependence on mixed NL targets for steerability: Without NL‑target data (e.g., OASST), instruction‑tuned code models tend to output code even when NL is required (Sec. 4.1), reducing general usability unless such data are included. • Contamination caveat in benchmarking: HumanEval decontamination is discussed for many open models, but cannot be guaranteed for closed ones (e.g., GPT‑4); cross‑model comparisons should be interpreted with care (Sec. 3).'}

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Matching research (from the collection)
> 
> **(a)** PBADet — one-stage anchor-free part–body association (ICLR 2024). Metrics: Hand AP, Conditional Accuracy, Joint AP (BodyHands), Precision/Recall/F1 vs ED-Pose, AP on COCO-HumanParts/CrowdHuman. One-to-one part-to-body center offset gives streamlined post-processing.
> 
> **(b)** "Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly" (NeurIPS 2023) — spectral analysis of E/I (ColEI vs DANN) RNNs: initialization spectrum (eigenvalues, singular values, normalised SVD entropy), gradient clipping/stochastic training effects on benchmarks. Relatedly, "Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure" (ICML 2025) covers initialization (random vs SGD) and optimizer shaping of spectra on MNIST/CIFAR.
> 
> **(c)** "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks" (NeurIPS 2024) — joint-embedding predictive architecture predicts latent targets vs MAE masked reconstruction, showing JEPA suppresses noisy features (ImageNet-1K, CCA). Classic-dataset experiments (CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100, ResNet-50) appear in "On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning".
> 
> **(d)** "Anytime-Valid Risk-Controlling Active Labeling" — anytime-valid RCPS with e-processes, testing-by-betting wealth processes, active labeling with label budgets, inverse propensity weighting, regret bounds, ImageNet experiments (θ=0.1, α=0.05).
> 
> **(e)** OctoPack (instruction tuning of permissively-licensed StarCoder; HumanEvalPack synthesis/repair/explanation in 6 languages, pass@k; end-to-end finetuning) and NEFTune (noisy-embedding instruction finetuning; LoRA/QLoRA-compatible; AlpacaEval). Astraios (LoRA instruction tuning of code LLMs) is cited but not detailed in the collection.
> 
> ## Development defects (as stated in the papers)
> 
> - **PBADet**: advantage over BPJDet is far less pronounced on the single-part CrowdHuman face–body task (competitive AP, only body MR-2 leading); removing the association loss, multi-scale center offsets, or task-alignment learning degrades all metrics; still depends on YOLO backbones and multi-scale feature engineering.
> - **Dale's Law RNNs**: ColEI nets learn worse and with higher seed variance; sign constraints hurt learning (~1–2.3%); constrained spectral radius still leaves unconstrained large singular values causing exploding/vanishing gradients; no inhibitory-to-inhibitory connections or cell-type time constants; only limited tasks tested; results need hybridizing ColEI/DANN models.
> - **JEPA analysis**: theory restricted to deep linear MLPs, balanced-orthogonal initialization and simultaneously-diagonalizable data; needs extension to non-linear/non-diagonalizable settings; JEPA may be vulnerable to spurious or slow features; mechanism may not transfer to other joint-embedding architectures.
> - **Anytime-valid RCPS**: i.i.d. data assumption; bounded-label-policy (Assumption 2) and existence assumptions (Prop. 5) that need relaxing; poor risk predictors increase variance and slow e-process growth (guarantee itself is preserved); results rely on log-optimal betting and specific regret analysis.
> - **OctoPack**: open models remain far behind GPT-4 (86.6% pass@1 vs 46.2% Python); HumanEval synthesis near saturation; possible contamination/evaluation differences; models struggle with length constraints, small bug fixes, and code/text switching; filtering Git commits is heuristic (imperative-message, single-file filters).
> - **NEFTune**: evaluation relies on GPT-4 judging; 30B/70B validation limited; no conclusive mechanism and no safety evaluation; gains appear only on conversational quality, not on OpenLLM-style factual tasks.
> - **Supporting interest points**: near-linear/stable runtime (MNL-VQL keeps stable runtime; GOT-D ≈1h on one GPU); SFT backbones (CodeSteer uses 12k SFT trajectories); ResNet-50 baselines (contrastive-embeddings paper, LDReg); clean-label vs noisy-label subsets used for calibration/spectral analysis (Hessian power-law paper uses clean labels vs 40/80% label noise; GOT-D selects clean data subsets).

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved collection, here is how the requested research spans map to documents, followed by an analysis of each method's development defects.
> 
> ## (a) One-stage anchor-free part–body association
> **Match: PBADet (ICLR 2024).** One-stage anchor-free detector with a single part-to-body center offset, task-alignment learning, multi-scale features; reports Hand AP, conditional accuracy, Joint AP, and vs ED-Pose gives higher Precision/Recall/F1; one-to-one correspondence "simplifies post-processing."
> **Development defects:** performance drops without the association loss, multi-scale offsets, or task-alignment (ablations show declines in all metrics); on the single-part CrowdHuman face-body task the advantage over BPJDet is "less pronounced"; anchor-based body-to-part variants underperform the anchor-free part-to-body formulation.
> 
> ## (b) Spectral analyses of biologically constrained recurrent nets + optimization
> **Match: "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023).** E/I (excitatory/inhibitory) RNNs under Dale's Law; shows the initial recurrent-weight spectrum (not sign constraints) governs learning; ColEI networks have multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final error; tasks include sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition.
> **Development defects:** ColEI networks learn poorly, with high variance across initialisations and instability without gradient clipping; small networks with few inhibitory units are worst; analysis is empirical with deep-linear/random-matrix idealizations; DANN requires reparameterisation and post-update clipping of illegal weights.
> **Related:** "Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure" (ICML 2025) shows how SGD vs random initialization, batch size, optimizers, and clean vs noisy labels shape the power-law Hessian spectrum of deep nets (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10/100, LeNet/ResNet18/LLMs). **Defects:** power-law is lost with small width/depth, limited data, noisy labels, and large-batch training; LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce it; SOTA LLMs excluded due to Hessian cost; power-law goodness and sharpness capture different regimes.
> 
> ## (c) Joint-embedding self-supervision predicting latent targets
> **Match: "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024).** JEPA (predict latent targets of a target encoder) vs MAE (masked input-space reconstruction); proves JEPA is biased to high-influence features and avoids noisy, high-variance features.
> **Development defects:** JEPA objective is susceptible to collapse (needs stop-grad); may be vulnerable to spurious or slow features; theory is limited to deep linear MLPs, balanced orthogonal initialization, and simultaneous diagonalizability; ImageNet validation only at 64×64 resolution; the claimed experiments on MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR-100 are **not established** in this collection (SVHN appears nowhere; CIFAR-10/100 appear in LDReg/contrastive/BSO papers, not JEPA). **LDReg (ICLR 2024)** — ResNet-50 ImageNet baselines with CIFAR-10/100 linear eval — has defects: LID estimation degrades in high dimensions, uses minibatch nearest neighbors, and forcing very low LID can trigger complete collapse.
> 
> ## (d) Anytime-valid risk-controlling prediction sets
> **Match: "Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets" (Xu et al.).** Extends RCPS to sequential/adaptive data with anytime-valid guarantees via e-processes and betting, active labeling with IPW, label budgets, risk predictors as control variates, log-optimal policies, regret bounds; ImageNet experiments (θ=0.1, α=0.05).
> **Development defects:** assumes i.i.d. data; requires bounded label policies (Assumption 2) and an existence assumption in Proposition 5; no covariate/label-shift handling; bad risk predictors only slow e-process growth (guarantee preserved but utility suffers); empirical-Bernstein extensions for average-risk control are left as future work.
> 
> ## (e) Instruction tuning of permissively licensed code LLMs
> **Match: OctoPack (ICLR 2024).** End-to-end instruction tuning of StarCoder (16B) on permissively licensed CommitPack/CommitPackFT + OASST; OctoCoder best permissively licensed model on HumanEvalPack (synthesis/repair/explanation, 6 languages), 46.2% pass@1 Python; includes practical diagrams (pipeline, data distributions, ablation figures).
> **Development defects:** falls short of GPT-4 (86.6% pass@1); struggles with length constraints, small fixes, and code/text switching; decontamination may not hold for all models; results should be interpreted carefully; gains depend on mixing natural-language targets (OASST) and commit-fix data. **NEFTune (ICLR 2024)** adds noisy embeddings to instruction finetuning (works with QLoRA): defects — relies on GPT-4 judging, limited 30B/70B validation, no conclusive mechanism or safety evaluation, gains only on conversational tasks (OpenLLM scores unchanged). **Not established:** low-rank-adapter (LoRA) instruction tuning of code LLMs (Astraios is only cited, not present) and feature-embedding/angular-similarity analyses of code LLMs (cosine/angular similarity appears in contrastive-learning and causal-agent papers, not code models).
> 
> ## Cross-cutting interests
> - **Near-linear runtime:** linear-time HSIC independence testing (seconds on 100k samples vs quadratic baselines; no single test dominates; power–runtime trade-offs).
> - **SFT backbones:** OctoPack (StarCoder), NFTS (ResNet-18/34 backbones with per-layer freeze/fine-tune + adapters; defects: hyperparameter/cost sensitivity).
> - **ResNet-50 baselines:** LDReg, contrastive-learning similarity analysis (ImageNet-100, CIFAR; variance-reduction loss adds a tuning hyperparameter and may suppress meaningful semantic variance).
> - **Clean-label subsets for calibration:** Hessian paper contrasts clean labels vs 40%/80% label noise (noise breaks power-law spectra); GOT-D "clean" vs "contrast" data subsets (Perspective API score drift; assumes overlap with pretraining scope); Agreement-on-the-Line uses data subsetting/ordering for OOD performance prediction (only random head initialization reliably induces AGL in lightly fine-tuned foundation models).
> 
> **Overall:** every matched method has stated limitations — PBADet's gains shrink on single-part tasks and depend on task-alignment; the EI-RNN analysis is confined to linear/idealized settings and ColEI trains poorly; JEPA's noise-avoidance theory is linear-only and its classic-dataset experiments (MNIST/SVHN) are not present in the collection; RCPS active labeling relies on i.i.d. and bounded-policy assumptions; and OctoPack/NEFTune underperform GPT-4, rely on judge-based evaluation, and lack conclusive mechanistic or safety validation.

</details>

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below are the development defects reported or evidenced in the five works, grouped by method and grounded only in the papers’ own text.
> 
> PBADet (ICLR 2024: One‑stage anchor‑free part‑to‑body association)
> - Limited advantage in single‑part tasks: On CrowdHuman’s face‑body association (a single‑part setting), the authors note their advantages over BPJDet “are not as pronounced,” with mMR−2 still ~50 (Appendix A.1; Tables 5–6).
> - Sensitivity to training design: Ablations show performance drops without multi‑scale supervision (w/o Multi‑scale) and without task‑alignment learning (w/o Task‑align) (Table 4), indicating reliance on these components.
> - Heavy hyperparameter/threshold dependence: The method requires dataset‑specific NMS thresholds and multiple tuned loss/assignment parameters (e.g., λiou, λdf l, λcls, λassoc, K, α, β; Section 4.1), suggesting nontrivial tuning burden across datasets.
> - Residual mismatches and non‑perfect association: Despite improvements, average mismatching rates (mMR−2) across parts remain in the 27–52% range (Tables 2–3), evidencing remaining association errors in crowded or occluded scenes.
> 
> EI Recurrent Networks under Dale’s Law (NeurIPS 2023: ColEI vs recurrent DANNs)
> - ColEI learning instability and poor performance: Column‑wise EI sign‑constrained RNNs (ColEI) learn poorly, with higher variance across seeds and strong need for gradient clipping; they exhibit multimodal, dispersed singular‑value spectra (Figure 3; Section 3.1–3.3) leading to exploding/vanishing dynamics and unstable training.
> - Fragility to EI ratio and network size: Small networks and few inhibitory units (realistic E:I ratios) degrade spectra (lower NSE) and impair learning; ColEI needs larger, more balanced EI ratios for acceptable training (Figures 5–6, 7).
> - Spectral‑radius tuning alone insufficient: Even with spectral radius constrained (ρ), ColEI retains large singular values and pathological spectra; performance depends more on the singular‑value distribution than sign constraints (Section 3.3; Figure 4).
> - Restricted theoretical scope: Results rely on deep linear networks, special “balanced” initializations, and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances; generalization to nonlinear models and broader data distributions remains open (Section 4 Discussion; assumptions in Section 2; Limitations embedded in Discussion).
> 
> JEPA vs. MAE (NeurIPS 2024: Deep linear self‑distillation analysis)
> - Depth‑dependent bias: JEPA’s favorable bias toward “influential” (high‑regression‑coefficient) features holds strongly only with deep encoders and “diminishes substantially” for shallow encoders (Sections 2–3.2; Corollary 3.6).
> - Potential vulnerability to spurious/slow features: The authors note this implicit bias “may shed light on…drawbacks,” including a tendency to focus on predictive yet low‑variance “slow” features, making JEPA susceptible to spurious slow signals (Section 7 Discussion).
> - MAE bias toward high covariance—even if noisy: MAE prioritizes highly covarying features (Section 3.2), which can be uninformative or noisy for perception (linked to [20] in the paper).
> - Strong modeling assumptions: Analysis requires deep linear models, special initializations, and simultaneously diagonalizable Σxx and Σyx; the authors explicitly state generalizability to practical nonlinear settings and non‑simultaneously‑diagonalizable data “remains unexplored” (Section 6 Limitations).
> 
> Active, Anytime‑Valid RCPS (NeurIPS 2024)
> - i.i.d. requirement and distribution‑shift gap: Guarantees are proven under i.i.d. (Xt, Yt) ~ P*; extending to test‑time distribution shift is listed as future work (Section 6).
> - Label‑policy constraints: The e‑process requires a bounded labeling probability (qt(x) ≥ q_min) for nonnegativity and validity; Assumption 2 (ε lower bound) and existence of the optimal policy in Proposition 5 are called out as limitations (Sections 2.1–2.2; 3; 6).
> - Sensitivity to predictor quality: Using predictors (risk estimates conditioned on X) reduces variance, but inaccurate predictors increase variance and slow growth of the wealth process; regret and growth depend directly on predictor and policy estimation errors (Proposition 3; Theorem 3).
> - Operational cost and complexity: Active labeling still requires querying labels under a budget and tuning λ within bounds for e‑process admissibility; dataset‑specific choices are needed (Sections 2–3; Figure 1 workflow).
> 
> OctoPack (COMMITPACK/COMMITPACKFT; HUMANEVALPACK; OCTOCODER/OCTOGEEX)
> - Performance gap to closed models: OCTOCODER (permissive) “falls short” of GPT‑4 across HUMANEVALPACK; GPT‑4 achieves near‑saturation on Python HumanEval synthesis (86.6% pass@1) while instruction‑tuned permissive models lag (Sections 1, 4.2; Table 2).
> - Struggles with small targeted edits: Multiple models often regenerate buggy code unchanged or introduce new bugs on HUMANEVALFIX; removing excess code is particularly challenging (Appendix M; Figures 33–34; Table 2).
> - Difficulty switching between code and text: Base code LLMs and some instruction‑tuned variants fail to produce natural‑language explanations for HUMANEVALEXPLAIN, instead outputting code (manual inspection; Section 4.2).
> - Poor adherence to specified output length: Models lack awareness of character limits, producing either too short (underspecified) or excessively long (truncated) explanations (Section 4.2; Figures 35, 38).
> - Data design trade‑offs: COMMITPACKFT is built via strict filtering (e.g., single‑file commits, imperative message heuristics) to ensure instruction quality; while effective, this narrows data scope and requires careful curation (Section 2; Appendix D).
> - Benchmarking caveats: HumanEval Python is likely close to saturation; contamination concerns and differing prompts/evaluation pipelines can affect cross‑paper comparability (Section 4.2).
> 
> These defects reflect each paper’s own findings, ablations, limitations sections, and empirical observations, without adding external assumptions.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Recommended works per need
> 
> 1. **Hands/faces → person association (crowded rooms):** **PBADet** (one-stage anchor-free part-body association) — links hands/face/feet to parent bodies via a part-to-body center offset on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman; reports Precision/Recall/F1.
> 2. **EI-constrained forecasting that trains stably:** **"Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly"** (EI spectral analysis, gradient clipping, NSE) plus **DAML** (decision-aware spatiotemporal forecasting that maximizes likelihood subject to a top-K constraint).
> 3. **Self-supervised backbone robust to pixel noise:** **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (latent-space prediction suppresses pixel noise; deep-linear analysis) and **LDReg** (local-dimension regularization against SSL dimensional collapse).
> 4. **Low-risk deployment querying a fraction of labels:** **"Anytime-Valid Risk-Controlling Active Labeling"** (sequential risk control with a label-budget policy).
> 5. **Code copilot from open Git commits via low-rank adapters:** **OctoPack** (4TB CommitPack of Git commits → instruction-tuned OctoCoder/OctoGeeX) with **LoRA**-style low-rank fine-tuning and **4-bit optimizers** for memory-efficient finetuning.
> 
> ## Supporting topics found in the collection
> - **Stochastic gradient training:** Hessian-spectrum paper (SGD/adaptive optimizers on MNIST, CIFAR-10/100, LeNet/ResNet18) and PPO-Clip two-timescale convergence analysis.
> - **Angular similarity in embeddings:** "On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning" (cosine/negative-pair similarity analysis, batch-size variance, auxiliary variance-reduction loss).
> - **F1/Precision evaluation:** PBADet (per-part Precision/Recall/F1 vs ED-Pose), CEGA (fidelity/F1), CMA (F1).
> - **Finetuning on backbones with adapters:** NFTS (per-layer freeze/adapter search on ResNet/ViT), LoRA, 4-bit AdamW finetuning (RoBERTa/Swin/LLaMA).
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods (from the context)
> 
> **PBADet (vision):**
> - On the *single-part* face-body task its advantage over BPJDet is not as pronounced as for multi-part tasks.
> - Requires hand-tuned NMS thresholds (τ_body, τ_part); the body-to-part representation (BPJDet-style) wastes unused positions, and the method needs careful task-alignment/offset-loss design.
> 
> **EI forecasting:**
> - Naive ColEI partitioning gives multimodal, dispersed spectra → poor, high-variance training, unstable *without gradient clipping*; small networks / few I-units learn markedly worse. Even DANN/RNN approaches are impaired somewhat by sign constraints.
> - DAML: direct BPR optimization degrades likelihood badly; the constrained objective needs a nuisance λ; Monte-Carlo gradient estimation needs large M/J (cost vs. variance); evaluation is fixed-K and BPR-centric.
> 
> **Self-supervised backbone:**
> - JEPA analysis restricted to deep linear nets with special initialization and simultaneous diagonalizability; forward-modeling/pixel-reconstruction methods degrade quickly as exogenous/pixel noise grows (empirical performance "unpredictable").
> - LDReg: LID estimation degrades in high dimensions and uses minibatch nearest neighbors; over-penalizing LID can trigger full mode collapse.
> 
> **Deployment layer:**
> - Anytime-valid active labeling assumes i.i.d. data and bounded label policies; optimal policy needs conditional-risk estimation (a predictor), otherwise risk control is looser.
> 
> **Code copilot / low-rank adaptation:**
> - OctoPack models still fail on length constraints, small fixes, and code/text switching; lag GPT-4; HumanEval nears saturation so gains are diluted; contamination/eval differences may inflate scores.
> - LoRA-only fine-tuning does **not** induce the power-law Hessian structure that full fine-tuning does (per the Hessian paper) — a known structural limitation of low-rank adaptation.
> - 4-bit optimizers: the optimal quantization scheme is task/dataset-dependent.
> 
> **Not established in this collection:** a direct **squared-error vs. log-loss** comparison, **SVHN** experiments, and explicit **near-linear-time finetuning on ResNet-50/SFT backbones**. The collection covers MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10/100 (SGD/Hessian studies) but not SVHN; "linear-time" appears only for HSIC independence testing, and efficient finetuning is addressed via parameter-efficient adapters/LoRA/quantization rather than a stated near-linear-time ResNet-50/SFT method. These specific claims cannot be confirmed from the context.

**community 最终答案**

> ## Pointers (works in the collection)
> 
> **1. Vision – hands/faces ↔ person in crowds**
> - **PBADet** (one-stage anchor-free part-body association detection): detects human parts (hands, faces, feet) as objects and links each to a parent body via a single part-to-body center offset. Evaluated on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman (face–body association) with **Precision/Recall/F1** vs ED-Pose and MR-2/AP tables. Its references also cover BFJDet (body–face joint detection via embedding matching + head hook) and "Whose hands are these?" (hand detection + hand–body association).
> 
> **2. Forecasting block respecting EI constraints + stable training**
> - **Decision-Aware Training of Spatiotemporal Forecasting Models (DAML)**: maximizes likelihood subject to a top-K decision (BPR) constraint; uses score-function/perturbed optimizers to get non-zero gradients (discrete top-K otherwise gives all-zero gradients) — i.e., constrained forecasting that still trains via SGD. It explicitly contrasts **squared/absolute error vs likelihood/log-loss** (square error is "not well matched" to top-K decisions; pure BPR training degrades likelihood; DAML walks the Pareto frontier).
> - For **EI (excitatory–inhibitory) constraints**: "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" — EI RNNs whose stability/learnability depends on the initial recurrent-weight spectrum; simple EI partitioning (ColEI) trains poorly/unstably and needs gradient clipping; DANN-style EI networks match standard RNNs.
> - Optionally **ChaosBench** for physics-based constraints, error-propagation control, and ensembles in forecasting.
> 
> **3. Self-supervised backbone robust to pixel noise**
> - **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"**: JEPA self-distillation implicitly prioritizes high-influence features and suppresses pixel noise vs MAE (deep-linear analysis; I-JEPA aligns faster with the perceptual low-variance PCA subspace).
> - **LDReg**: local-dimensionality regularization against local dimensional collapse (ResNet-50, ViT-B, ImageNet; improves SimCLR/BYOL/MAE linear eval and transfer).
> 
> **4. Deployment layer: low-risk outputs, fraction of labels queried**
> - **"Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets"**: guarantees risk ≤ θ at all times (anytime-valid) while an active labeling policy keeps the expected proportion of queried labels under a budget; e-processes/testing-by-betting; applied to image classification, medical imaging, LLM safety outputs.
> - Complementary: **Design-Based Supervised Learning (DSL)** — uses imperfect LLM surrogate labels on all data plus a small gold-labeled subset (≈100 labels) with bias-corrected doubly robust estimation.
> 
> **5. Code copilot from open Git commits, via LoRA**
> - **OctoPack**: CommitPack (~4TB of permissively licensed **Git commits**, 350 languages) + CommitPackFT; instruction-tuning StarCoder gives OctoCoder, best permissively-licensed model on HumanEvalPack (46.2% pass@1 Python), explicitly **not trained on OpenAI outputs**. LoRA appears in this corpus as the adaptation route (e.g., 4-bit optimizer paper fine-tunes LLaMA-7B/13B/33B with LoRA on Alpaca SFT data).
> 
> **Cross-cutting topics**
> - **Stochastic gradient training**: Hessian-structure paper trains LeNet/FCN/ResNet18/ViT with SGD/Adam on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10/100; contrastive-embedding paper uses SGD (200 epochs, linear LR scaling, cosine decay) on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet-100.
> - **Angular similarity in embeddings**: "On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning" — cosine similarity, positive pairs aligned, negatives uniformly separated at −1/(n−1), equiangular tight frame, mini-batch-induced variance and an auxiliary variance-reduction loss.
> - **Benchmarks**: MNIST, CIFAR-10/100 appear (Hessian paper; LDReg; embedding paper; VectorGrimoire uses MNIST). **SVHN does not appear anywhere in the collection** — I cannot cover it from context.
> - **F1/Precision**: PBADet (hands/feet F1 vs ED-Pose); RLCD and CMA report F1.
> - **ResNet-50/SFT fine-tuning**: LDReg and the embedding paper use ResNet-50; NFTS searches per-layer freeze/fine-tune + adapters on ResNet/ViT backbones; 4-bit optimizers do LoRA/SFT of LLaMA. **"Near-linear time complexity" is not claimed by any retrieved document** — closest efficiency results are HASSOD (1/5 images, 1/12 iterations vs CutLER), GOT-D (~1 h on one GPU), and linear-time HSIC testing.
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods (from the context)
> 
> - **PBADet**: its CrowdHuman face–body advantage over BPJDet is *less pronounced* for this single-part task; single center-offset association may degrade in dense/occluded crowds; multi-part scalability is a stated goal, and association quality depends on task-alignment learning.
> - **DAML**: fixed K, BPR-centric evaluation, no sensitivity analysis; pure BPR objectives can yield forecasts with low likelihood/utility; Monte-Carlo gradient estimates (M, J) trade variance vs runtime; λ must be tuned; constraint not satisfied → gradient pushes toward constraint directions.
> - **Dale's-law/EI RNNs**: ColEI-style constraints give multi-modal, dispersed singular-value spectra, higher training variance, and instability without gradient clipping; small networks with few inhibitory units are worst; spectral diagnosis (NSE) only predicts, doesn't fix.
> - **JEPA analysis**: proven only for deep linear MLPs with special initialization/simultaneous diagonalizability; generalizability to real networks is supported only empirically.
> - **LDReg**: LID estimation degrades in high dimensions and relies on minibatch nearest neighbors; pushing LID too low can trigger complete collapse; extra hyperparameters; global covariance/variance regularizers barely helped.
> - **Contrastive-embedding work**: the variance-reduction loss adds a tuning hyperparameter and may suppress meaningful semantic variance; small batches inherently raise negative-pair similarity variance; temperature sensitivity remains.
> - **Risk-controlling active labeling**: assumes i.i.d. data and bounded label policies (plus an existence assumption); covariate/label shift not handled; control is in the average sense unless stronger assumptions are made.
> - **OctoPack**: open models still struggle with length constraints, small fixes, and code/text switching; remain behind GPT-4; HumanEval synthesis is nearing saturation with possible contamination/evaluation confounds; 4TB commit data needs heavy filtering.
> - **DSL**: requires gold-standard annotation and design-based sampling, excludes domain shift, and optimizes bias/coverage at the expense of RMSE.
> - **Hessian-structure work**: power-law structure breaks with small width/depth, limited data, noisy labels, and large batch sizes; LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the power law that full fine-tuning does; Hessian computation is too costly for SOTA LLMs.
> - **4-bit optimizers**: optimal quantization appears task-dependent; tested only on language/vision (RL/audio/graphs unstudied).
> - **NFTS**: per-episode architecture selection is expensive; N=3 is a sweet spot; adapter placement is data-dependent (early/late layers, not middle).
> 
> **Gaps in the collection for your spec**: SVHN results and an explicit "near-linear time complexity" fine-tuning method are not present in the retrieved context.

</details>

### paperscope:gap:388 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building an end‑to‑end AI stack where: a vision module must associate hands/faces to the right person in crowded scenes (COCO‑style data) with high precision; training must fit tight GPU memory, so I need 4‑bit AdamW/SGD states; pretraining should be self‑supervised but avoid noisy pixel features (favoring latent prediction over pure reconstruction with MSE/cosine alignment); a reasoning agent should decide when to write Python vs natural language, guided by SFT/DPO; and a small RNN for physiological time‑series should respect excitatory/inhibitory constraints with stable spectra. Are there papers that together cover anchor‑free detection, low‑bit optimizers, JEPA‑style implicit bias, Transformer‑based conditional guidance for code/text, and EI RNN spectral analyses, along with practical fine‑tuning (e.g., End‑to‑end LoRA), regularization, and CE vs MSE trade‑offs?Please analyze the development defects of these methods.
