> | Your requirement | Paper in collection |
> |---|---|
> | (a) Anchor-free part-body association, COCO-like | **PBADet** (ICLR 2024) – one-stage anchor-free detector, single part-to-body center offset; evaluated on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman with AP, mMR-2, and Precision/Recall/F1 vs ED-Pose |
> | (b) 4-bit memory-efficient optimizer (AdamW) | **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023) – 4-bit AdamW/4-bit Factor, LLaMA fine-tuning, up to 57.7% memory savings (mentions LoRA only as related work; no combined LoRA+4-bit experiment) |
> | (c) JEPA-style self-distillation (MSE, not CE) | **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024) – analyzes MSE self-distillation in deep linear nets; related **LDReg** for SSL representation quality |
> | (d) EI RNN spectral constraints | **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023) – E/I RNNs, singular-value spectra, normalized SVD entropy (NSE) on sequential MNIST |
> | (e) Unsupervised TSP routing | **UTSP** (NeurIPS 2023) – unsupervised surrogate loss + heatmap-guided local search for Euclidean TSP |
> 
> None evaluates on MNIST and COCO together, and none combines these methods into one pipeline.
> 
> ## Development defects
> 
> **(a) PBADet**
> - Still relies on NMS post-processing and a final Euclidean-distance greedy match between parts and unassigned bodies — not truly end-to-end.
> - Requires heavy training (YOLOv7, 4×V100, 100 epochs, AMP); no VRAM-efficiency evidence for edge deployment.
> - Unreliable predictions for limbs (legs/arms) cloud body–part association; occluded/invisible parts degrade detection even though the offset itself stays valid.
> - Advantage over BPJDet shrinks on the single-part CrowdHuman task; subordinate (association) APs are consistently lower than original APs.
> 
> **(b) 4-bit optimizers**
> - Optimal quantization setting is task/dataset-dependent; rank-1/linear schemes are not guaranteed lossless elsewhere.
> - Tested only on language and vision tasks — applicability to RL, audio, graph learning unverified.
> - Slower than 8-bit AdamW for small models due to missing fused operators; memory savings saturate as bitwidth drops (total memory includes data/activations/fragments).
> - Second-moment quantization suffers a zero-point problem requiring dedicated linear/rank-1 quantizers; only optimizer states are compressed, so benefits are limited.
> 
> **(c) JEPA analysis (and LDReg)**
> - JEPA theory is restricted to deep linear MLPs, special initializations, and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances; generalizability to practical nonlinear settings is unexplored.
> - JEPA objectives are collapse-prone (needs stop-grad); implicit bias toward "slow"/low-variance features makes it vulnerable to spurious features.
> - LDReg's LID estimation degrades in high dimensions and uses minibatch nearest neighbors; forcing very low LID can trigger complete collapse.
> 
> **(d) EI RNN spectral work**
> - The paper only *diagnoses* spectra (NSE as a predictor); it does not propose a training-time spectral constraint — the user's "enforcing" step is not implemented.
> - ColEI networks learn worse, with higher variance across seeds and instability without gradient clipping; small networks with few inhibitory units fail badly.
> - Eigenvalue-radius constraints alone don't control the singular-value spectrum (rank-one nilpotent column-mean term), so stability is hard to guarantee.
> 
> **(e) UTSP**
> - No theoretical guarantee that the surrogate loss measures solution quality — the claim is purely empirical.
> - Search quality depends heavily on local-search hyperparameters (candidate size M, edge-removal K, expansion budget T) and search time grows with instance size.
> - Low-pass GNNs cause oversmoothing → indistinguishable heatmaps; the method's success hinges on band-pass (scattering) representations.
> - Gap to optimality grows on larger instances (0.09% at TSP200 → 1.18% at TSP1000).
> 
> **Conclusion:** the requested combined pipeline does not exist in this collection; each component exists only as an isolated method with the defects above, so any integration (e.g., 4-bit LoRA fine-tuning of a frozen LLM with JEPA-style MSE, EI-RNN spectral enforcement, TSP local-search learning) would be a novel, unvalidated combination.

**community 最终答案**

> ## Answer
> 
> **No paper in this collection combines all five components.** The corpus contains separate works, each covering one requirement:
> 
> - **(a) Anchor-free part-body detection:** PBADet (one-stage anchor-free, part-to-body center offset; COCO-HumanParts/BodyHands/CrowdHuman; AP, Precision/Recall/F1 vs ED-Pose).
> - **(b) 4-bit optimizer + LoRA/AdamW fine-tuning:** "4-bit Optimizers" (4-bit AdamW states, LLaMA fine-tuning, up to 57.7% memory savings).
> - **(c) JEPA-style self-distillation with MSE/cosine objectives:** JEPA deep-linear analysis (self-distillation, latent-space prediction) and LDReg (dimensional-collapse regularization).
> - **(d) EI RNN spectral constraints:** "Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly" (ColEI vs DANN, singular-value spectra, NSE; sequential MNIST).
> - **(e) Unsupervised TSP with local search:** UTSP (GNN surrogate loss, heatmap-guided best-first local search, TSP20–1000).
> 
> Evaluations are split: MNIST only for EI RNNs; COCO for PBADet; ImageNet for JEPA; TSP for UTSP. No unified MNIST/COCO evaluation exists across these methods.
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods
> 
> **PBADet:** Supervised only (needs well-defined part/body ground truth, which breaks for invisible parts in body-to-part variants); advantage over BPJDet shrinks on single-part (face-body) tasks; performance degrades without multi-scale offsets or task-alignment learning; absolute F1 on small parts (hands/feet ~46–51) remains limited; requires a scaling factor λ and post-processing.
> 
> **4-bit optimizers:** Optimal quantization is task/dataset-dependent (no lossless guarantee outside tested settings); slower than 8-bit on small models without fused operators; memory savings saturate (total memory includes activations/data/fragments); quantizing both moments causes a marginal accuracy drop; factorization only applies to the second moment; only language/vision tasks tested — no detection/edge-AI validation.
> 
> **JEPA self-distillation:** The MSE objective is inherently susceptible to collapse (trivial all-same-vector solution), requiring stop-gradient and architectural tricks; the theoretical analysis holds only for deep linear networks, special balanced orthogonal initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable data; bias vanishes for shallow encoders; JEPA is vulnerable to spurious/slow features and converges to lower-amplitude weights on noisy features; LDReg's LID estimation degrades in high dimensions and forcing very low LID can cause full collapse.
> 
> **EI RNN spectral constraints:** Traditional ColEI partitioning yields multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra with a rank-one nilpotent component — learning is worse, more variable, and unstable without gradient clipping; small networks with skewed E/I ratios fail; sign constraints alone cost ~0.7–1% accuracy, but spectral properties matter more; only the DANN-style architecture (which mimics standard RNN spectra) trains well, so the "biologically inspired" constraint itself is the defect.
> 
> **UTSP:** The surrogate loss has no theoretical guarantee of correlating with solution quality (empirically only); requires expensive heatmap-guided local search with many search hyperparameters (α, β, M, K, T); low-pass GNNs (GCN) fail via oversmoothing, so expressive band-pass SAG is mandatory; small-instance "negative" gaps stem from rounding; search space reduction is large but still leaves hundreds of candidate edges; validated only on Euclidean TSP, not COCO/MNIST-style perception tasks.

</details>

<summary>展开完整 gold 与两份最终答案</summary>

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below are the main development defects and limitations explicitly evidenced in the provided papers, organized by method.
> 
> 1) PBADet (one-stage, anchor-free part–body association)
> - Benefit depends on task structure: The advantage over body-to-part designs is small on single-part association (e.g., face–body on CrowdHuman) where the paper notes the gains are “not as pronounced” as in multi-part settings; this limits expected lift in tasks with only one part class.
> - Dependence on enclosure-based decoding: Association decoding requires selecting among bodies that both remain unassigned and enclose the detected part; the paper does not specify a fallback when a part is not enclosed by any detected body, making the post-processing reliant on correct body detections and enclosure relations.
> - Sensitivity to training/inference hyperparameters: Ablations show notable drops without task-alignment learning and multi-scale supervision, indicating sensitivity to K, α, β (anchor selection), the scaling λ, and dataset-specific NMS thresholds.
> - External validation scope: Non-human (animal) experiments are qualitative only; generalization to non-human domains (e.g., wheel–car) is argued but not quantitatively established.
> 
> 2) Learning with Dale’s Law (EI RNNs; DANN vs. column EI) and the SVD entropy perspective
> - ColEI RNNs train poorly and unstably: The paper shows ColEI networks often require gradient clipping and still learn less effectively, with worse and more variable performance than standard RNNs/DANNs; they are especially fragile for small networks and when the fraction of inhibitory units is small (high E:I ratio), reflecting multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra.
> - Dependence on spectrum, not just signs: Results highlight that the spectral properties at initialization, not only sign constraints, govern performance; without suitable spectra, training is unstable (exploding/vanishing gradients), which is a practical limitation for straightforward “Dale’s Law by column sign” implementations.
> - Architectural biological coverage limits: The recurrent DANN implementation models fast PV+ interneurons and (as noted) omits inhibitory-to-inhibitory connections and cell-type-specific time constants, limiting physiological fidelity to other interneuron subtypes.
> - Scope and open questions: Analyses rely on specific initializations (balanced, ReLU) and gradient-flow arguments, and are evaluated on a narrow task set (adding problem, sMNIST, Penn Treebank, a small object recognition task). The origin of the unusual multi-modal spectra and why large max singular values are tolerated in wide ColEI networks remain unresolved.
> 
> 3) How JEPA avoids noisy features (deep linear self-distillation vs. masked reconstruction)
> - Restricted theoretical setting: All guarantees are for deep linear encoders under special, “balanced” initializations and simultaneous diagonalizability of Σxx and Σxy; the authors explicitly note generalization to non-linear networks (e.g., Transformers) and real data distributions is unproven.
> - Depth dependence: The beneficial JEPA bias toward “high-influence” (high regression-coefficient) features fades with shallow encoders; thus, the predicted advantage is contingent on sufficient encoder depth.
> - Potential bias risks: The paper notes JEPA focuses on “influential/slow” (often low-variance) features; while helpful for avoiding noisy pixels, this implicit bias can leave JEPA vulnerable to spurious/slow features and may slow learning of truly predictive but noisy signals.
> - Collapse handling limited to the setup: Collapse prevention (e.g., StopGrad) is assumed; broader stability behaviors in non-linear or larger models are not addressed.
> 
> 4) Memory-Efficient 4-bit Optimizers (quantized first/second moments with rank-1 normalization)
> - Zero-point sensitivity in 2nd moment: Naïvely quantizing the second moment with 4-bit dynamic exponent mapping leads to many values quantized to zero and catastrophic update deviations (via 1/√v); the fix (DE-0 or linear mapping without zero) and rank-1 normalization are necessary, and settings may require per-task tuning.
> - Implementation trade-offs and overhead: Without fused kernels, 4-bit training can be slower than 8-bit on smaller models; overall memory savings saturate in end-to-end training because activations and other states dominate total memory; small tensors (≤4096) and specific layers (e.g., embeddings in some baselines) are left unquantized.
> - Factorization coverage: Factorization is applied only to ≥2D tensors; 1D moments are still quantized; with certain sharding/packing (e.g., FSDP on LLaMA-7B), the factorized variant was not applied due to engineering constraints.
> - Evaluation scope and theory: Experiments focus on vision and language tasks; reinforcement learning, audio, and graph domains are not evaluated. Convergence is shown for a quantized SGDM case; Adam/AdamW convergence is not theoretically established in this work.
> 
> 5) Prompt-based Continued Pretraining (PCP)
> - Dependence on pseudo-label quality and templates: PCP requires an initial prompt-based fine-tuning pass to produce pseudo-labels; the paper shows that incorrect pseudo-labels degrade performance and that gains depend on template/verbalizer choices.
> - Scope and scalability limits (as stated by the authors): Evaluations use encoder-only models and classification/regression tasks; generative and multi-modal tasks are not covered. Scaling PCP with full parameter updates to very large LMs may be computationally expensive; the authors suggest multi-task or parameter-efficient variants as future work.
> - Not always superior to SOTA semi-supervised methods: While PCP often outperforms iterative self-training methods, there are cases (e.g., IMDB with 20 labels) where FixMatch performs better. PCP still incurs an extra continued pretraining step.
> - TAPT instability remains a risk factor: The paper documents that conventional TAPT can hurt sentence-pair tasks and prompt-based fine-tuning; while PCP alleviates this, the outcome still hinges on unlabeled corpus choice/size and the instruction/prompt design.
> 
> Note: All points above are drawn directly from the limitations, ablations, or empirical findings reported in the respective papers; no external claims are added.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Matched papers and their development defects
> 
> **1. "4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States"** (memory-lean optimizer; keeps accuracy/F1 on GLUE, SQuAD QA-F1, ImageNet/Swin-T, MT, instruction tuning; Fig. 4 training-loss curve)
> Defects:
> - On small models (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2M) it is *slower* than 8-bit AdamW because fused operators are not yet implemented; speed parity is only promised "after operator fusion" — the efficiency claim is not fully realized in the current code.
> - Quantizing both first and second moments causes a "marginal drop in accuracy"; lossless behavior partly comes from factorizing the second moment.
> - Optimal quantization appears task-dependent; experiments cover only language/vision tasks, and image classification uses Swin-T (not MNIST/CIFAR-100 + ResNet-50 with F1/Precision as the question mentions).
> 
> **2. "Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features"** (implicit bias of JEPA vs MAE; MSE-based, deep linear analysis)
> Defects:
> - Analysis is confined to deep *linear* MLPs, special balanced-orthogonal initialization, and simultaneously-diagonalizable data; non-linear models remain an open challenge.
> - The bias toward "influential" (high-regression-coefficient) features only holds when the encoder is deep and "diminishes substantially" for shallow encoders.
> - It may also explain vulnerability to spurious/slow features, and generalization to joint-embedding architectures not relying on self-distillation is unverified.
> 
> **3. "Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (EI constraints, normalized SVD entropy as guidance)
> Defects:
> - ColEI networks learn worse with higher variance and are "highly unstable without gradient clipping."
> - The cause is a pathological (multimodal, dispersed) initial singular-value spectrum; small networks with fewer inhibitory units learn especially poorly — so respecting Dale's Law naively is a genuine limitation.
> - NSE is only a correlational diagnostic; the origin of the multi-modal spectrum and why large ColEI networks learn well despite a large max singular value remain open theoretical questions.
> 
> **4. "Don't Stop Pretraining? Make Prompt-based Fine-tuning Powerful Learner (PCP)"** (prompt-based continued pretraining with templates + golden/pseudo labels; Fig. 2 pipeline diagram)
> Defects:
> - Conventional continued pretraining (TAPT) is itself shown to be *detrimental* on sentence-pair tasks and for prompt-based FT (up to ~10% drops), motivating PCP.
> - Ablations: using labels *or* templates alone hurts performance — both must be combined.
> - Only modest encoder-only models (RoBERTa) tested; scaling to LLMs (Llama-2/GPT-4) is open, and full-parameter continued pretraining is deemed hard to justify computationally there.
> - Compatibility with parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA is explicitly left as future work — so the claimed "including LoRA / end-to-end fine-tuning" is not actually demonstrated.
> 
> **5. "PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association Detection"** (reports Precision/Recall/F1 vs ED-Pose; Fig. 2 pipeline)
> Defects:
> - Its advantage over BPJDet is "less pronounced" for the single-part CrowdHuman face-body task, and body-detection AP is only comparable (not better) than cumbersome DETR-based detectors.
> - The one-to-one part-to-body offset trade-off: anchor-based variants and non-task-aligned variants degrade all metrics; multi-scale absolute-offset interpretation hurts performance.
> 
> **Bonus:** Pipeline diagrams are provided (PCP Fig. 2 overview; PBADet Fig. 2; Dale's Law spectrum-transplant figures; JEPA ODE/feature-ordering figures). No work in the collection makes an explicit *near-linear time-complexity* claim; the 4-bit optimizer instead reports wall-clock/memory trade-offs and notes a throughput deficit on small models pending operator fusion — which is itself one of its development defects.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved documents, the matching papers and their development defects are:
> 
> **1. 4-bit Optimizers ("4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States", doc 8d5e1455)**
> - Optimal quantization settings are likely task-, dataset-, and training-detail-dependent; task-specific settings outside the study might do better.
> - Evaluation limited to language and vision tasks (RL, audio, graph learning untested).
> - For small models (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2 Medium) it is *slower* than 8-bit AdamW because fused operators are not implemented (speed should match after fusion).
> - Quantizing both first and second moments causes a marginal accuracy drop; it needs factorization/rank-1/linear schemes (with zero-point exclusion) to stay lossless. QA F1 and NLU accuracy are preserved, but only marginal—not guaranteed across all settings.
> 
> **2. JEPA implicit bias ("How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features", doc 40fde037)**
> - Theory restricted to deep *linear* MLPs, specific initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances Σyx/Σxx—real data deviates from this.
> - Generalization to nonlinear models and fully practical scenarios remains unexplored.
> - The plain JEPA objective is susceptible to representation collapse (trivial solution), avoided only via StopGrad; the bias (priority to high-regression-coefficient "influential" features, increasingly with depth) also implies vulnerability to spurious/slow features.
> 
> **3. Dale's Law spectral analysis ("Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective", doc e63a94c4)**
> - ColEI (column-constrained E/I) RNNs learn worse with higher variance across seeds on all four benchmarks; without gradient clipping they are highly unstable.
> - Small networks and skewed E:I ratios worsen both spectra (multimodal, dispersed singular values; lower NSE) and performance.
> - Open theoretical questions remain: origin of the multi-modal spectrum and why large ColEI networks learn well despite a large max singular value.
> 
> **4. PCP ("Don't Stop Pretraining? Make Prompt-based Fine-tuning Powerful Learner", doc af1b1cf8)**
> - Limited to relatively modest encoder-only models (RoBERTa-base/large); scaling to LLMs (e.g., Llama-2, GPT-4) is an open question, and full-parameter updates for a specific task may be computationally unjustifiable at that scale.
> - Not tested on encoder-decoder/decoder-only architectures, nor on generative/multimodal tasks.
> - Incorrect pseudo-labels typically hurt performance (random labels help in only ~19/32 scenarios), so pseudo-label quality matters; TAPT is shown to be detrimental for sentence-pair tasks, and PCP's benefits rely on combining both templates and pseudo-labels (each alone hurts).
> 
> **5. PBADet (doc 08b70bc3)**
> - Advantage over BPJDet is far less pronounced for the single-part (face-body, CrowdHuman) task; it mainly shines with multi-part associations (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts).
> - It reports practical metrics (Precision/Recall/F1 vs ED-Pose, AP, Cond. Accuracy, Joint AP, mMR-2), but no explicit runtime/latency or near-linear time-complexity analysis is given in the retrieved material; "efficiency" is argued qualitatively (concise part-to-body representation, one-stage).
> 
> **Bonus notes:** No retrieved paper explicitly discusses near-linear time complexity patterns; PBADet (Fig. 2), PCP (Fig. 2g), and the Dale's Law paper (Fig. 1) do provide pipeline/architecture diagrams clarifying their designs.

</details>

### paperscope:gap:412 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building a resource‑constrained pipeline that: (1) fine‑tunes Transformer models with attention for both vision and NLP; (2) runs real‑time part–body association (hands/face) in a multi‑person setting; and (3) updates text models via prompt templates and pseudo labels without heavy iterative loops. I need guidance on: compressing optimizer states to ~4‑bit while keeping CE/F1/Precision stable; avoiding noisy features in representation learning with a JEPA‑style approach; improving prompt‑based fine‑tuning via continued pretraining on task‑related text; and understanding spectral pitfalls when enforcing EI (Dale’s Law) in recurrent controllers. End‑to‑end LoRA fine‑tuning or an SFT backbone is preferred, and I’ll validate on small/standard datasets (e.g., MNIST/CIFAR‑100) before deployment. Can you point me to works that cover these needs together?Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Development defects and limitations identified in the five methods:
> 
> 1) PBADet: A one-stage anchor-free approach for part–body association (ICLR 2024)
> - Advantage depends on multi-part settings: On single-part association tasks (e.g., face–body on CrowdHuman), the paper notes that PBADet’s benefits over BPJDet are “not as pronounced” as in multi-part scenarios, so gains may be small when only one part is annotated.
> - Detection AP not consistently higher: On COCOHumanParts, the paper reports APs “on par” with BPJDet, with most wins appearing in association metrics (e.g., lower mMR−2) rather than per-category detection AP; thus, pure detection accuracy is not uniformly improved.
> - Sensitivity to training design: Ablations show noticeable drops if multi-scale supervision or task-alignment learning are removed; performance relies on these components and on several hyperparameters (e.g., K=13, α=1.0, β=6.0, λ=2.0 and NMS thresholds), indicating tuning sensitivity.
> - Limited evidence beyond humans: Although an animal qualitative demo is provided, broader cross-domain validation is limited; the strongest empirical evidence is on human datasets.
> 
> 2) Learning better with Dale’s Law: A Spectral Perspective (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Naive Dale’s Law implementation (ColEI) often learns poorly: Simply constraining columns by sign (excitatory/inhibitory) yields a multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectrum at initialization, causing unstable/poor learning, high variance across seeds, and stronger need for gradient clipping.
> - Strong sensitivity to EI ratio and network size: With fewer inhibitory units or smaller networks, ColEI spectra worsen (lower normalized SVD entropy), and performance degrades; this dependence makes small or biologically realistic E:I ratios hard to train.
> - Spectrum/initialization dependence: Performance hinges more on the weight spectrum than on sign constraints, and requires careful spectral initialization (e.g., spectral radius); despite tuning, ColEI remains inferior to standard RNNs/DANNs in many settings.
> - Biological and modeling simplifications: The recurrent DANNs used to satisfy Dale’s Law omit several biological details (e.g., inhibitory–inhibitory connections, cell-type-specific time constants), and primarily model fast feedforward inhibition (PV+). The authors note future work is needed for more faithful models and hybrids; current conclusions derive from specific initializations and tasks.
> 
> 3) How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self‑Distillation Networks (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Strong assumptions in theory: Results rely on deep linear encoders, special “balanced” initializations, and simultaneously diagonalizable data covariances. The authors explicitly note generalization to non-linear models and generic data (non-simultaneously diagonalizable) is unproven.
> - Depth dependence: The beneficial JEPA bias toward influential (high-regression-coefficient) features emerges only when the encoder is deep; with shallow encoders, this advantage largely disappears.
> - Possible vulnerability to spurious/slow features: While JEPA avoids noisy high-variance features, the paper cautions that JEPA’s bias toward slowly varying, high-influence features may expose it to spurious or slow features in practice (an open risk flagged by the authors).
> 
> 4) Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4‑bit States (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Severe instability if zero-point is mishandled: The authors identify a “zero-point problem” for the second moment; naive 4‑bit quantization that permits zero massively distorts 1/√v and can cause divergence or training instability. Their fixes (zero‑excluding mapping, rank‑1 normalization) are necessary; misconfiguration is brittle.
> - Performance/settings are task dependent: The paper notes optimal quantization settings likely depend on task/data/training details; rank‑1 normalization + linear mapping works across their tests but may not be universally best.
> - Limited scope of evaluation: Experiments cover language and vision; applicability to reinforcement learning, audio, or graph tasks is untested.
> - Throughput depends on engineering: Without fused kernels, their 4‑bit optimizers can be slower than 8‑bit; speed parity requires operator fusion. Also, overall memory savings saturate because activations and other buffers dominate total memory on some setups.
> - Theory gap: They provide a convergence guarantee for quantized SGDM but not for Adam/AdamW (stating only a belief that AdamW convergence would follow), leaving a theoretical gap for the main target optimizer.
> 
> 5) Don’t Stop Pretraining? Prompt‑based Continued Pre‑training (PCP) (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Model/architecture scope: Results are on encoder‑only, modest‑sized models (RoBERTa BASE/LARGE) and classification/regression; the method is untested on encoder–decoder or decoder‑only LMs, generative or multimodal tasks, or very large LLMs where full‑parameter PCP may be too costly (authors suggest PEFT or multi‑task strategies for future work).
> - Not universally superior to SSL baselines: Although PCP outperforms state‑of‑the‑art semi‑supervised methods on most datasets, there are cases (e.g., IMDB with 20 labels) where SSL wins; thus PCP is not strictly dominant across all settings.
> - Sensitivity to pseudo‑label quality: PCP requires pseudo labels for unlabelled texts; the paper shows that using incorrect labels hurts performance, and random labels only help in a subset of cases. Benefit depends on reasonable pseudo‑label quality.
> - Template specificity: PCP conditions continued pre‑training on specific task templates; while effective, this may entrench a task‑specific prompt and does not directly address cross‑task generalization (unlike instruction‑tuning works).
> - Data/compute considerations: PCP works with as few as hundreds of unlabelled examples and <10 minutes for 1k samples on 2×3090 GPUs, but scaling to much larger LMs or tasks could make full‑parameter continued pre‑training less practical without parameter‑efficient variants.
> 
> Overall cross‑paper takeaways
> - Practical sensitivity: PBADet and 4‑bit optimizers both rely on critical implementation choices (anchor‑free task alignment, multi‑scale supervision; zero‑point‑free mapping, rank‑1 normalization). Missteps can negate gains.
> - Spectrum matters for EI RNNs: Enforcing Dale’s Law by naive sign constraints leads to spectral pathologies that harm learning—performance is controlled more by the weight spectrum than constraints alone.
> - Theory–practice gap: The JEPA analysis explains an implicit bias in an idealized linear regime; benefits depend on depth and may not directly carry to non‑linear, non‑diagonalizable real‑world settings.
> - Scope limits: PCP and 4‑bit optimizers demonstrate strong results within tested domains (NLP/vision) but do not yet establish robustness across broader modalities and problem families.

**naive 最终答案**

> **Works matching your pipeline:**
> 
> 1. **~4-bit optimizer states with stable CE/F1/Precision** → *"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"* (NeurIPS 2023): 4-bit AdamW/AdamW-Factor with smaller blocks (B128), rank-1 normalization and zero-point-excluded linear quantization of the second moment. It covers both vision (Swin-T on ImageNet) and NLP Transformers (GLUE, SQuAD QA F1, GPT-2 NLG, WMT, LLaMA instruction tuning) and notes it can be combined with LoRA.
> 2. **Real-time multi-person part–body association (hands/face)** → *PBADet* (ICLR 2024): one-stage anchor-free part-to-body center offset on YOLO backbones; outperforms BPJDet/ED-Pose on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts (head, face, hands, feet), CrowdHuman.
> 3. **Prompt-based fine-tuning via continued pretraining with templates + pseudo labels, no iterative loops** → *"Don't Stop Pretraining? Make Prompt-based Fine-tuning Powerful Learner"* (PCP): integrates prompt templates into task-related texts with golden/pseudo labels; eliminates iterative self-training and data augmentation (up to 20.1% absolute gains).
> 4. **JEPA-style avoidance of noisy features** → *"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"* (deep-linear analysis: JEPA prioritizes high-influence/ρ features and suppresses noisy ones; depth strengthens this) and *LDReg* (local-dimensionality regularization against dimensional collapse).
> 5. **Spectral pitfalls of EI/Dale's Law in recurrent controllers** → *"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"*: ColEI nets have multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure); normalized SVD entropy (NSE) predicts performance; DANN recurrent variants retain standard-RNN-like spectra.
> 6. **LoRA vs SFT backbone** → the 4-bit optimizer paper (LoRA compatibility), plus *"Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure"*: LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the power-law Hessian structure that full fine-tuning does, implying different generalization.
> 
> **Development defects of these methods:**
> 
> - **4-bit optimizers**: optimal quantization settings are likely task/dataset-dependent (task-specific settings out of scope); validated only on language/vision tasks (RL, audio, graphs untested); quantizing both moments yields a marginal accuracy drop; unfused 4-bit is slower than 8-bit on small models; embedding layers are typically left unquantized.
> - **PBADet**: on the single-part CrowdHuman face–body task its advantage over BPJDet shrinks; part-object representations degrade when parts are occluded/invisible; pose-estimation comparisons were limited to four parts (hands/feet) with inconsistent face/head keypoints.
> - **PCP**: limited to modest encoder-only models (RoBERTa); full-parameter updates may be unjustifiable for LLMs (Llama-2/GPT-4 scaling is open); encoder–decoder generalization unverified; conventional TAPT can be *detrimental* for sentence-pair tasks and prompt-based FT, so it must be replaced by PCP rather than naively combined.
> - **JEPA analysis**: theory assumes deep linear MLPs, special (balanced orthogonal) initialization, and simultaneous diagonalizability; the noise-avoidance bias diminishes for shallow encoders; JEPA can still learn noisy features (at lower weight amplitude) and is susceptible to representation collapse without stop-gradient tricks. LDReg's LID estimation degrades in high dimensions (minibatch neighbors) and forcing very low LID can cause complete collapse.
> - **Dale's Law / ColEI**: sign constraints impair learning (small but non-zero), and ColEI nets show high variance across initializations and are highly unstable without gradient clipping; small networks with few inhibitory units have pathological spectra and learn poorly; constraining the eigenvalue radius does not fix the nilpotent-mode singular values.
> - **LoRA (Hessian view)**: LoRA cannot significantly change the Hessian/power-law structure of the base model, so its generalization behavior differs from full SFT; LoRA is noted in the 4-bit paper as applicable mainly to language-model fine-tuning.
> - **Related**: GOT-D (pre-fine-tuning data selection) assumes overlap with pretraining scope and its toxicity metrics drift; video-based representation learning (forward modeling/temporal contrastive) provably fails when exogenous noise is too large—only trajectory-based methods (ACRO) stay robust.
> 
> Note: no single work covers all six needs jointly; the set above must be combined, and none of the retrieved works validates on CIFAR-100 specifically (MNIST/sequential-MNIST and CIFAR-10 appear only).

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the relevant works from the context for each need, followed by an analysis of their development defects.
> 
> ## Relevant works
> 
> 1. **4-bit optimizer states (CE/F1/Precision stable)** — *Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States* (4-bit AdamW/4-bit Factor). Compresses Adam/AdamW first/second moments to 4-bit (smaller blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluding linear quantizer). Matches 32-bit AdamW on GLUE (NLU accuracy/correlation), SQuAD (F1), ImageNet/Swin-T (accuracy), E2E-NLG (BLEU), WMT (BLEU), and LLaMA instruction tuning, with ~57.7% memory savings.
> 
> 2. **Real-time multi-person part–body association (hands/face)** — *PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association*. Single part-to-body center offset; SOTA on BodyHands (hand-body) and COCOHumanParts (multi-part incl. face/hands/feet), leading body MR-2/AP on CrowdHuman face-body association.
> 
> 3. **JEPA-style representation learning avoiding noisy features** — *Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features: A Deep Linear Network Analysis*. Shows JEPA implicitly prioritizes high-influence (high regression coefficient) features and suppresses noisy, high-variance directions with depth, unlike MAE which learns highly covarying but noisy features.
> 
> 4. **Prompt-based fine-tuning via continued pretraining with pseudo labels** — *Don't Stop Pretraining? Make Prompt-based Fine-tuning Powerful Learner* (PCP). Presents task-related text + prompt templates with golden/pseudo labels through MLM before prompt-based FT; consistently improves prompt-based FT (up to 20.1% absolute) without iterative loops, outperforming TAPT and semi-supervised baselines.
> 
> 5. **Spectral pitfalls in EI (Dale's Law) recurrent controllers** — *Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective*. Diagnoses why ColEI RNNs learn poorly: the issue is not sign constraints but the multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectrum from the rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure; proposes normalized SVD entropy (NSE) as a predictive diagnostic.
> 
> 6. **LoRA/SFT preference** — *Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure*: LoRA fine-tuning does not induce the power-law Hessian structure that full fine-tuning does; *4-bit Optimizers* notes LoRA freezes pretrained weights and is only applicable to LM fine-tuning.
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods
> 
> **4-bit optimizers:** optimal quantization settings are task/dataset/training-detail dependent (no single lossless setting); second moment suffers a zero-point problem (quantizing near-zero values to zero catastrophically changes update direction) — handled only by zero-exclusion/rank-1 normalization; without operator fusion, 4-bit variants are slower than 8-bit on smaller models; only language/vision tasks tested; 4-bit Factor's sublinear-memory schemes (Adafactor, SM3) degrade on classification.
> 
> **PBADet:** its advantage over BPJDet shrinks for single-part face-body association (CrowdHuman) since the design targets multi-part scalability; face/body detection remains only comparable to cumbersome DETR-based detectors; failures on overlapping similar objects and heterogeneous parts; requires NMS threshold tuning.
> 
> **JEPA analysis:** theory is limited to deep *linear* networks, balanced orthogonal initialization, and simultaneous diagonalizability — generalization to nonlinear models is not rigorous; JEPA is susceptible to representation collapse (needs stop-grad/architectural tricks); the implicit bias toward influential features can make JEPA vulnerable to spurious/slow features and slower to learn genuinely informative low-variance features; bias diminishes for shallow encoders.
> 
> **PCP:** conventional continued pretraining (TAPT) can actively hurt sentence-pair and prompt-based FT; using templates alone or pseudo labels alone degrades performance (both must be integrated); relies on pseudo-labels that may be noisy; only studied with MLM-objective models (RoBERTa); larger continued-pretraining corpora don't fix TAPT's shortcomings.
> 
> **Dale's Law spectral study:** ColEI networks learn worse with higher variance across seeds and are highly unstable without gradient clipping; smaller networks with fewer inhibitory units have worse spectra and performance; spectral constraints don't fix the nilpotent column-mean contribution; only mitigates (not eliminates) the defect — design guidance for alternative initializations remains open.
> 
> **LoRA (Hessian finding):** power-law Hessian structure does not emerge with LoRA-only fine-tuning (unlike full FT), implying potentially different/weaker generalization; LoRA's applicability is limited to language model fine-tuning (freezes pretrained weights), not general vision training.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> {'answer': 'Development defects and limitations for each method, based strictly on the provided papers:\n\n1) PBADet (ICLR 2024; one-stage anchor-free part–body association)\n- Benefit diminishes in single-part settings: The authors report that advantages over BPJDet are “not as pronounced” on the face–body association task in CrowdHuman, where only one part is involved (Appendix A.1). This indicates limited gains when multi-part association is not required.\n- Slightly higher mismatching in CrowdHuman in some metrics: While overall detection is strong, the mismatched body–face rate (mMR−2) is comparable to or slightly worse than BPJDet in CrowdHuman (Table 6), showing that association reliability can be dataset-dependent.\n- Sensitivity to specific training components: Ablations show performance drops without multi-scale handling or task-alignment learning (Table 4 and A.4), suggesting the method is sensitive to these design choices and may degrade if they are altered or omitted.\n- Incremental rather than universal detection gains: On COCO-HumanParts, subordinate APs are “on par” with BPJDet and improvements are not uniform across all categories (Table 2), reflecting limited or uneven gains over anchor-based baselines.\n\n2) Learning better with Dale’s Law (NeurIPS 2023; spectral behavior of EI recurrent nets)\n- Pathological spectra and poor learning in ColEI networks: The simple column EI partition (ColEI) yields multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra with large singular values, leading to deformed activations/gradients and impaired learning relative to standard RNNs and DANNs (Figures 3–4). ColEI requires gradient clipping and shows higher instability and variance across seeds.\n- Strong dependence on EI ratio and network size: ColEI performance degrades with fewer inhibitory units and in small networks; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) captures this pathology (Figures 5–7). Robust performance requires larger networks and balanced E/I ratios, limiting practical deployment under tight resource or architectural constraints.\n- Restricted theoretical assumptions: Analysis relies on orthogonal initializations and diagonal, simultaneously diagonalizable covariances (Assumption 3.1), which may not hold in typical settings. The authors note these constraints and the need for generalization beyond the simplified linear regime (Section 6).\n\n3) How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features (NeurIPS 2024; implicit bias of deep linear JEPA)\n- Limited scope of theory: Results are derived in deep linear models under simultaneously diagonalizable Σxx and Σxy, with special initializations; generalization to non-linear encoders and real-world settings is not established (Section 6 Limitations).\n- Depth dependence and potential vulnerability: JEPA’s bias toward features with high regression coefficients only appears with deep encoders; shallow encoders do not exhibit the benefit. The bias can invert learning order relative to MAE (Figure 1), potentially prioritizing “slow” or spurious features in some regimes (Section 7 Discussion), which may harm utility if those features are not semantically aligned.\n- Predictor reliance and collapse prevention tricks: The formulation depends on StopGrad to avoid collapse, and the observed advantages hinge on accurate conditions of the linearized setup. These constraints limit practical robustness outside the analyzed setting.\n\n4) Active, anytime-valid risk-controlling prediction sets (NeurIPS 2024)\n- i.i.d. data assumption and distribution shift: Guarantees are derived under i.i.d. streams; handling distribution shift is cited as future work (Section 6). Thus, safety control may not hold under common test-time shifts without additional mechanisms.\n- Label policy constraints: Some results require a lower bound on labeling probabilities (q_min) and assume the existence of optimal policies within [0,1] (Proposition 5, Assumption 2). These constraints may be difficult to satisfy or verify in practice.\n- Predictor quality impacts utility: While risk control remains valid, poor predictors increase variance and slow e-process growth (Proposition 3, Theorem 3), degrading label efficiency and practical utility.\n- Computational/implementation considerations: The framework uses e-processes and sequential updates with tuning of α, θ, and policy/predictor learning; although guarantees hold, practical deployments must manage label budgets and the overhead of adaptive policies and regret-minimizing updates.\n\n5) CleanDiffuser (NeurIPS 2024 Datasets & Benchmarks; diffusion library for decision making)\n- Slow sampling and real-time constraints: Iterative denoising leads to slow inference, limiting real-time control; e.g., DiffusionPolicy with Chi_UNet1d is accurate but slow and heavy (Table 5), forcing a performance–latency trade-off.\n- Instability of high-order guided solvers: The authors warn that higher-order DPM-Solver variants can be unstable under guidance; they restrict implementations (e.g., to DPM-Solver-1, DPM-Solver++ ≤ 2) to avoid instability (Appendix F).\n- Sampling degradation phenomenon: Increasing sampling steps can reduce performance in some tasks (Figures 6, 10–11), an unresolved anomaly that complicates design choices and ablations.\n- Sensitivity to EMA rates and steps: Performance and stability depend on EMA settings (Figure 7); excessively long training (gradient steps) may be unnecessary or harmful.\n- Limited action space support: Current version does not directly support discrete or hybrid action spaces; authors suggest possible workarounds (Appendix H), indicating a functional gap for broader decision-making tasks.\n- Heavy compute demand: The benchmark suite consumed ~30,000 GPU hours, and larger architectures (e.g., Chi_UNet1d) significantly increase training and inference costs (Sections 1, 5; Table 5), posing resource barriers for users.\n\nThese defects and limitations are drawn solely from the papers’ own results, analyses, and stated constraints.'}

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the document collection, the five requested papers are:
> 
> **(a) PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association** (doc 08b70bc3…) — anchor-free part-body association via a single part-to-body center offset, built on YOLOv5/YOLOv7 CNN backbones, trained with an SGD optimizer over 100 epochs with task-alignment classification/localization/DFL losses, benchmarked on COCO-based BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, and CrowdHuman.
> 
> **(b) "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (doc e63a94c4…) — spectral behavior and learning stability of excitatory–inhibitory recurrent nets obeying Dale's Law (ColEI vs. DANN vs. standard RNNs). Related: BSO/T-BSO (doc 4741ca1f…) covers stochastic (Adam-like) optimizers for spiking networks.
> 
> **(c) "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks"** (doc 40fde037…) — implicit bias of JEPA/self-distillation toward high-influence (informative) features in deep linear settings, vs. MAE.
> 
> **(d) "Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets"** (doc cda0aa75…) — anytime-valid, sequential RCPS with active labeling policies under label budgets and online updates, via e-processes/betting.
> 
> **(e) CleanDiffuser** (doc c122328b…) — easy-to-use modular library for diffusion models in decision-making, with CNN-UNet/DiT-Transformer architectures, guided sampling (CG/CFG), solvers (DDPM, DDIM, DPM-Solver++, EDM, RectifiedFlow), evaluation in 37 RL/IL environments, and self-fine-tuning pipelines (AdaptDiffuser).
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods
> 
> **(a) PBADet**: The anchor-free design still inherits anchor-free weaknesses—relying on dense per-pixel predictions, it demands careful task-alignment anchor selection (top-K per step), and the part-to-body offset only works under the assumption each part has a unique enclosing body (occlusions/one-to-many cases complicate it, as with BPJDet's invalid offsets). On the single-part CrowdHuman face-body task its advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced; evaluation against ED-Pose used ground-truth part boxes and favored PBADet's IoU criterion, limiting comparability. Ablations show performance depends critically on the association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task alignment—removing any degrades metrics.
> 
> **(b) Dale's Law RNNs**: ColEI networks learn markedly worse with higher variance across seeds and are highly unstable without gradient clipping, due to multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra (pathological large singular values causing exploding gradients). Sign constraints further impair learning; the method's findings are limited to the examined initializations, spectral radii, and EI ratios; inhibitory-inhibitory connections, cell-type time constants, and hybrid architectures were not explored; NSE is only an empirical diagnostic, with open questions about the origin of the multi-modal spectrum. The BSO optimizer's uniform gradient treatment across time steps discards temporal dynamics (T-BSO mitigates but incurs memory that scales linearly with timesteps).
> 
> **(c) JEPA deep-linear analysis**: Results are restricted to deep linear MLPs with a special initialization and the strong assumption of simultaneously diagonalizable covariances; generalization to non-linear models and general data distributions is unproven. The bias toward high-influence, low-variance "slow features" can also make JEPA vulnerable to spurious features, and representation collapse remains a risk. Note: the context does not support the CIFAR-100/MNIST/SVHN and AUROC/F1/Precision claims—the paper's experiments use Gaussian simulations and ImageNet CCA analysis instead.
> 
> **(d) Anytime-valid RCPS**: Guarantees rely on the i.i.d. data assumption and a bounded label-policy assumption; the existence assumption in Proposition 5 is not removed; risk control in an average sense (via empirical-Bernstein supermartingales) and extensions to covariate/label shift or adaptive conformal inference are left as future work. Label efficiency depends on the accuracy of learned/pretrained policies and predictors, whose estimation error degrades the wealth-process growth rate.
> 
> **(e) CleanDiffuser**: Does not directly support discrete or hybrid action spaces; exhibits unexplained "sampling degradation" (more sampling steps can hurt performance); SDE vs. ODE solvers differ consistently in performance and guidance sensitivity; iterative denoising makes sampling slow (diffusion policies are slower than transformer-based ACT and require many forward passes); diffusion planners are prone to OOD plans, sensitive to guidance, and lack safety constraints; algorithm choice dominates model size effects, and simply enlarging transformer-based DMs (e.g., DiT1d) can harm performance. The context does not substantiate guidance on LoRA/SFT fine-tuning, self-supervised learning, or vision-language models—those are only referenced indirectly, not part of the library's scope.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the context, here is the analysis. I found 5 papers that jointly cover your 5 topics, with a careful caveat about topic (c)'s dataset/metrics requirement.
> 
> ---
> 
> ## The 5 Matching Papers
> 
> **(a) PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association (ICLR 2024)**
> - Anchor-free one-stage detection for human body-part association via a single part-to-body center offset; CNN backbones (YOLOv5l6/YOLOv7), classification/DFL/IoU losses + dedicated association loss, SGD optimizer, COCOHumanParts (COCO 2017) benchmark.
> - **Development defects:** On CrowdHuman's single-part face-body task, advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced; poses rely on NMS/threshold tuning; compared to multi-person pose estimators like ED-Pose, association is box-based (less precise limbs); anchor-free detection relies on dense per-pixel prediction that can miss small/occluded parts.
> 
> **(b) Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective (NeurIPS 2023)**
> - Studies spectral behavior/learning stability of E/I recurrent nets under Dale's Law (ColEI vs DANN); shows the initial singular-value spectrum (multimodal, dispersed; NSE) matters more than sign constraints; ColEI is more variable and unstable without gradient clipping.
> - **Development defects / gaps vs. your query:** The paper does **not** discuss "training dynamics under stochastic optimizers" (SGD/Adam) — it uses projected gradient descent; no Adam experiments; no stochastic-optimizer comparison. It also uses only sequential MNIST/adding/PTB/object-recognition, not large vision benchmarks. So the "stochastic optimizer" aspect is **not covered**.
> 
> **(c) How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks (NeurIPS 2024)**
> - Exactly matches: implicit bias of JEPA self-distillation toward high-regression-coefficient ("influential") features in deep linear settings, with depth-dependent suppression of noisy features; critical-time analysis; ImageNet-1K CCA experiments confirm I-JEPA aligns faster with perceptual (low-variance) subspace than MAE.
> - **Development defects / gaps vs. your query:** It does **not** benchmark on CIFAR-100/MNIST/SVHN, and does **not** report AUROC/F1/Precision. Its ImageNet experiment measures CCA alignment of I-JEPA vs MAE features, not classification metrics. Its theory assumes deep linear networks, balanced orthogonal initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable data; the paper itself flags non-linearity and non-diagonalizable distributions as open limitations, and notes JEPA's bias may cause vulnerability to spurious or slow features.
> 
> **(d) Active, Anytime-Valid Risk-Controlling Prediction Sets (NeurIPS 2024)**
> - Extends RCPS to sequential/anytime-valid settings with active labeling under a label budget; uses e-processes/betting, IPW, control variates, regret bounds; optimal labeling policy ∝ conditional risk std; ImageNet experiments show learned/pretrained policies cut risk faster while keeping violations below α — directly relevant to safety gating of model outputs.
> - **Development defects:** i.i.d. assumption (no distribution shift during test time); bounded label policy assumption; relies on accurate pretrained/learned risk predictors; ImageNet experiments only run until 3000 labels queried.
> 
> **(e) CleanDiffuser: An Easy-to-Use Modularized Library for Diffusion Models in Decision Making (NeurIPS 2024)**
> - Modular library: diffusion models/solvers (DDPM, DDIM, DPM-Solver++, EDM, RectifiedFlow), network architectures (UNet1d, DiT1d/Transformers, CNN-based), guided sampling (CG/CFG), masking, Diffusion-X sampling, warm-starting, noise/data prediction switching; 9 algorithms benchmarked on D4RL and IL benchmarks (37 environments).
> - **Development defects:** Does **not** directly support discrete/hybrid action spaces; diffusion policies are slower than transformer ACT (sampling speed bottleneck); "sampling degradation" anomaly (performance drops as sampling steps increase) remains unexplained; SDE vs ODE solver impact in decision-making unexplored; diffusion planners sensitive to guidance and lack safety constraints, prone to OOD plans. **Regarding your "fine-tuning (LoRA, SFT), feature embeddings, self-supervised learning, and vision-language models" requirements — these are NOT part of CleanDiffuser.** (LoRA/SFT/VLM/self-supervised content appears only in *other* documents in the collection — e.g., RTB fine-tuning text-to-image diffusion models with LoRA, and various LLM fine-tuning papers — not in this library paper.)
> 
> ---
> 
> ## Verdict
> 
> - **Strong matches:** (a) PBADet ✓, (b) Dale's Law spectral paper ✓ (spectral/stability part), (c) JEPA implicit bias ✓ (deep-linear part), (d) anytime-valid RCPS ✓, (e) CleanDiffuser ✓ (modular library part).
> - **Gaps to flag:**
>   - (b) lacks stochastic-optimizer (SGD/Adam) training-dynamics analysis — not covered.
>   - (c) lacks CIFAR-100/MNIST/SVHN benchmarks and AUROC/F1/Precision metrics — not covered.
>   - (e) lacks LoRA/SFT fine-tuning, feature-embedding, self-supervised, and vision-language-model guidance — not covered by this paper.
> 
> If your intent is to find *one* paper per topic that satisfies every stated requirement, only (a) and (d) fully match; (b), (c), and (e) match their core topics but miss the specific extra requirements (stochastic optimizers; AUROC/F1/Precision on CIFAR-100/MNIST/SVHN; LoRA/SFT/VLM/SSL guidance). No additional papers in the collection bridge those gaps for (b), (c), or (e).

Are there works that collectively address detection/association, stability of recurrent training, robust SSL representations, anytime-valid risk control with active labeling, and modular diffusion frameworks for decision making?Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Development defects and limitations per method:
> 
> PBADet (one-stage, anchor-free part–body association detector)
> - Gains are task-dependent: On single-part association (CrowdHuman face–body), the advantages over BPJDet are “not as pronounced,” with performance only comparable to BPJDet (Table 5), which limits the benefit of the design in such settings.
> - Not universally superior across categories: On COCOHumanParts, the method is “on par” with BPJDet in overall AP. It leads in some metrics (e.g., APM/APL and certain categories) but not all; average mMR−2 is lowest only for some parts, while other parts show higher mismatch rates than competing methods (Tables 2–3).
> - Training sensitivity: Ablations show notable drops without multi-scale anchors and task-aligned learning (Table 4), indicating reliance on multi-scale supervision and specific task-alignment hyperparameters (K, α, β) and the center-offset scaling λ.
> - Dataset-specific tuning needed: Inference depends on hand-tuned NMS thresholds that differ per dataset (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman), implying non-trivial per-dataset calibration.
> 
> Learning with Dale’s Law (EI recurrent networks; spectral perspective)
> - ColEI (column-sign constrained) RNNs learn poorly due to spectral pathology: They exhibit multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra with large singular values, causing unstable training, exploding/vanishing dynamics, and higher variance across seeds.
> - Strong dependence on EI ratio and size: Performance and spectra degrade in small networks and when inhibitory units are few; learning improves only in larger networks with more balanced E/I, making small EI controllers fragile.
> - Requires gradient clipping and shows instability: ColEI networks benefit substantially more from gradient clipping and otherwise are highly unstable.
> - Open issues remain: The origin of the unusual multi-modal spectra and why large max singular values do not harm large ColEI networks are unresolved, complicating principled design.
> 
> JEPA self-distillation (deep linear analysis of implicit bias)
> - Depth-dependent bias: JEPA’s beneficial bias (towards high-influence features with large regression coefficients) manifests only when the encoder is deep; shallow encoders lose this advantage and can learn in a less favorable order.
> - Potential vulnerability to “slow”/spurious features: The paper notes JEPA may focus on slow features; in cases where slow or spurious signals dominate high-influence directions, this can be undesirable.
> - Restricted theory setting: Results rely on deep linear networks and simultaneously-diagonalizable covariances; generalization to non-linear models, non-diagonal settings, and practical data is not established.
> 
> Active, anytime-valid Risk Controlling Prediction Sets (RCPS)
> - Distributional assumptions: Guarantees are proven in the i.i.d. sequential setting; handling distribution shift is future work, limiting robustness in changing environments.
> - Label-policy constraints: Theory uses a lower bound on labeling probability (ε) and existence of an optimal policy; these bounded-propensity assumptions may be hard to satisfy or verify in practice.
> - Predictor quality affects efficiency: Poor conditional risk predictors (r̂) increase variance and slow e-process growth, making the method conservative and label-inefficient until better predictors are learned.
> - Conservativeness and parameter dependence: The anytime-valid guarantee hinges on α (Ville’s inequality); smaller α improves safety but can increase conservativeness and label usage.
> 
> CleanDiffuser (modular diffusion library for decision making)
> Library/engineering limitations surfaced by the authors and evaluations:
> - Steep learning curve: Despite modularity, diffusion methods remain complex; understanding and customizing modules requires substantial effort.
> - Action-space coverage: Current version does not directly support discrete or hybrid action spaces; workarounds (e.g., action representations or categorical diffusion) are needed.
> - Real-time constraints: Iterative denoising yields slow inference; extra steps like Diffusion-X further increase latency. In IL tasks, diffusion policies are notably slower than transformer/RNN baselines (e.g., ACT), constraining real-time deployment.
> 
> Algorithmic limitations highlighted by the library’s comprehensive benchmarks:
> - Diffusion planners are fragile: They often underperform diffusion policies in hard sparse-reward navigation (e.g., Antmaze), being sensitive to guidance and prone to generating out-of-distribution (OOD) trajectories; require additional safety/dynamics constraints to be reliable.
> - Sampling degradation: Increasing sampling steps can hurt performance in several tasks, contradicting expectations; this anomaly persists across backbones and is unresolved.
> - SDE vs ODE differences: SDE solvers can perform better in some policy settings but are more prone to sampling degradation; the choice affects robustness and remains underexplored for decision making.
> - EMA/training dynamics: Performance is sensitive to EMA rates and gradient steps; training can degrade with long schedules, necessitating careful tuning to avoid overfitting/instability.
> - Model size trade-offs: Larger networks (e.g., Chi_UNet1d) improve IL performance but raise training cost and inference latency; scaling transformer-based DMs does not consistently help, indicating non-trivial size–quality–speed trade-offs.
> 
> Overall, across this literature set, the main development defects are: reliance on dataset-specific tuning and hyperparameters (PBADet); instability and spectral pathologies in straightforward EI RNNs (Dale’s Law, ColEI); depth-limited and potentially spurious-feature bias in JEPA; i.i.d. and labeling-policy constraints for active RCPS; and diffusion decision-making systems facing slow inference, planner fragility, sampling anomalies, and under-characterized solver effects (CleanDiffuser).

**naive 最终答案**

> Yes — the collection contains works covering each component of your pipeline, and each has identifiable development defects.
> 
> **1. Detection/association — PBADet (one-stage anchor-free part–body association)**
> Fits your medical-scan-room use case (technician hands/face vs. patient), extending anchor-free detection with a single part-to-body center offset.
> - Defects: prior two-stage/heuristic methods (BodyHands, Zhou et al. 2018) add complexity and can compromise efficiency; BPJDet's body-to-part offsets make representations grow with the number of parts, degrading detection and becoming invalid when parts are occluded; anchor-based systems introduce many hyperparameters; multi-person pose estimators (ED-Pose) give no part bounding boxes and yield imprecise/speculative predictions; on the single-part face-body CrowdHuman task PBADet's advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced.
> 
> **2. Stability of recurrent training — "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (EI RNNs)**
> Shows initial spectral properties matter more than sign constraints for EI recurrent controllers.
> - Defects: ColEI networks have multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra from a rank-one nilpotent column-mean term, causing worse, more seed-variable learning and exploding gradients (gradient clipping helps substantially but is a patch); small networks and skewed E:I ratios further degrade spectra/performance; sign constraints alone also impair learning; open questions remain (origin of the spectra; why large ColEI nets learn well despite large max singular value); NSE is only a predictive diagnostic, not a cure.
> 
> **3. Robust SSL/JEPA — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"**
> Explains JEPA's latent-space prediction implicitly biases toward high-influence features and slows learning of noisy pixel features (unlike MAE).
> - Defects: the JEPA objective is collapse-prone, requiring stop-gradients/architectural tricks; it still learns noisy features, only with lower-amplitude weights; theory is limited to deep linear MLPs, special initialization, and simultaneous diagonalizability; JEPA prioritizes slow/low-variance features. Related LDReg work notes SSL suffers local dimensional collapse, LID estimation degrades in high dimensions, and forcing very low LID can trigger complete collapse; video SSL for RL fails when exogenous noise is too large and has an exponential identifiability barrier.
> 
> **4. Anytime-valid risk control with active labeling — "Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets"**
> Extends RCPS to sequential streams with e-processes/betting, active labeling under a fixed label budget (IPW), conditional-risk predictors, and regret bounds; explicitly covers gating classifier outputs (e.g., calibrating a safety-classifier cutoff).
> - Defects: assumes i.i.d. data and bounded label policies; guarantees are conservative (starts from the always-safe β=1), and label efficiency depends on accurate conditional-risk predictors/optimal labeling policies.
> 
> **5. Modular diffusion decision-making — CleanDiffuser**
> Modular library (diffusion models/solvers, network architectures, guided sampling) unifying planner, policy, and data-synthesizer roles for RL/IL.
> - Defects: no direct support for discrete/hybrid action spaces; module complexity still demands expertise; "sampling degradation" (more steps hurt performance, especially on narrow medium-expert MuJoCo/Kitchen distributions) is an open problem; SDE solvers suffer more degradation; higher-order solvers show no superiority; ~5 steps usually suffice; diffusion policies are slower than ACT; algorithm choice dominates model size.
> 
> **6. LoRA fine-tuning (your training stack)**
> The Hessian-spectrum paper finds LoRA fine-tuning does not induce the power-law Hessian structure that full fine-tuning produces, suggesting potential generalization differences; the power-law structure is also lost with small width/depth, limited data, noisy labels, and large-batch training. The 4-bit optimizer work notes optimal quantization may be task-dependent and was tested only on language/vision tasks.
> 
> In short, each requirement has a supporting work, but all remain at various stages of development maturity — detection suffers occlusion/representation-scalability issues, EI RNNs still need spectral-aware init/clipping, JEPA analysis is idealized and collapse-prone, risk control is conservative and i.i.d.-bounded, and diffusion decision frameworks have sampling-degradation and action-space gaps.

**community 最终答案**

> Yes — the collection contains works covering each of your five needs, though they are standalone building blocks, not one integrated system:
> 
> 1. **Detection/association (hands, face, COCO-style part–body): PBADet** (ICLR 2024, one-stage anchor-free part-to-body association).
> 2. **Stability of recurrent training (EI recurrent controllers, spectral): "Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023, on excitatory–inhibitory RNNs and their singular-value spectra).
> 3. **Robust SSL representations (JEPA vs. noisy pixel features): "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks"** (NeurIPS 2024).
> 4. **Anytime-valid risk control with active labeling: "Active, Anytime-Valid Risk-Controlling Prediction Sets"** (Xu, Karampatziakis, Mineiro).
> 5. **Modular diffusion frameworks for decision making: CleanDiffuser** (NeurIPS 2024), covering diffusion planners/policies/data synthesizers (incl. Diffusion Policy, IDQL, EDP).
> 
> ## Development defects (limitations) of these methods
> 
> **PBADet (part-body association):** head/face and hand accuracy is still the weak point — on COCOHumanParts, head/face/hand mMR-2 values (≈27.9–44.7) are clearly worse than feet (≈47.9–52.6). Its advantage over BPJDet largely vanishes on the single-part CrowdHuman face-body task, and it only outputs part/body bounding boxes plus one part-to-body center offset, so it cannot give per-keypoint hand/face detail. Occlusion/multi-person cases still rely on offset validity; the offset is always defined (one-to-one), but body–part association degrades when parts are hidden. Compared to pose estimators (ED-Pose), it improves precision but trades away keypoint-level localization.
> 
> **EI recurrent training stability (Dale's-Law RNNs):** simple E/I partitioning (ColEI) learns poorly and with high variance — the initial recurrent spectrum becomes multimodal/dispersed (rank-one nilpotent column-mean term), so constraining the eigenvalue radius does not constrain large singular values, causing exploding activations/gradients; without gradient clipping ColEI networks are highly unstable. Small networks with few inhibitory units are worst. The analysis is limited to initialization-time spectra (normalized SVD entropy as a pre-training diagnostic); the origin of the multi-modal spectrum and why large ColEI networks still learn remain open questions. DANN-style architectures fix this but add complexity.
> 
> **JEPA robust SSL:** the theory holds only for deep linear MLPs, special initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances — assumptions real data distributions violate; extension to nonlinear models is unproven. The implicit bias toward high-influence, low-variance "slow" features is double-edged: JEPA is vulnerable to spurious or slow features and still risks representation collapse, needing stop-gradient/architectural tricks. The analysis covers only self-distillation JEPA, not other joint-embedding designs.
> 
> **Anytime-valid risk control with active labeling:** assumes i.i.d. streaming data — distribution/covariate/label shift at test time is explicitly left unhandled. It requires monotone risk/utility, right-continuous ρ with ρ(1)=0, and lower-bounded label policies; guarantees hold only under these. Label-policy/predictor suboptimality (bounded by regret bounds) slows the wealth process and label efficiency; the framework controls risk of prediction *sets* via e-processes/betting, so applying it as a safety-gating classifier threshold in your pipeline needs careful adaptation, and it does not by itself bound harms like toxicity, only expected risk.
> 
> **CleanDiffuser (modular diffusion decision-making):** modular decoupling has a steep learning curve and may need tailored adjustments; it does not directly support discrete or hybrid action spaces. Its own analysis finds open defects: **sampling degradation** (performance *drops* as sampling steps increase, especially for SDE solvers and narrow data distributions), diffusion planners are **prone to OOD plans** due to sensitivity to guidance and a **lack of safety constraints**, and iterative denoising makes sampling too slow for real-time robot control. Diffusion policies are slower than non-diffusion baselines (e.g., ACT).
> 
> **Cross-cutting gap:** none of these works are integrated — e.g., CleanDiffuser has no built-in safety-gating classifier, the RCPS work is not coupled to the diffusion policy or the pose detector, and the LoRA/Hessian-analysis work (e.g., "Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure") shows LoRA fine-tuning does **not** induce the same power-law Hessian structure as full fine-tuning, suggesting LoRA-adapted backbones may generalize differently — a defect to consider when fine-tuning your CNN/Transformer detectors and policies.

<a id="case-paperscope-gap-427"></a>

### paperscope:gap:427 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively address efficient and reliable deep-network training and inference across vision, sequence modeling, and scientific computing, with the following elements: (a) use of MSE/CE objectives under Adam/AdamW/SGD optimizers; (b) analyses of joint‑embedding self‑supervised learning (JEPA) and its implicit bias (e.g., cosine‑style prediction in latent space); (c) an anchor‑free, one‑stage method for part–body association with results on COCO; (d) recurrent models obeying excitation/inhibition constraints (Dale’s law) studied via spectral properties on tasks like (sequential) MNIST; (e) memory‑saving optimizers using sub‑byte (≈4‑bit) states for fine‑tuning/LoRA on Transformers; and (f) interpretable tensor‑decomposition neural solvers for PDEs using finite‑element‑like interpolation. Prefer works reporting metrics such as AP/F1/AUROC on datasets like COCO, MNIST, CIFAR‑100, or SVHN.Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

**score：2→3（Δ+1）；rounds：3→4（Δ+1）。**
