> {'answer': "Below are the main development defects or stated constraints for each method, extracted only from the provided papers.\n\n1) PBADet (one-stage, anchor‑free part–body association on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman)\n- Limited advantage in single‑part association: On CrowdHuman (face–body association, a single‑part task), the advantage over BPJDet is “not as pronounced,” and PBADet’s mMR−2 is worse than BPJDet’s best (50.8 vs 50.1; lower is better). The paper explicitly notes that with just one part, PBADet’s benefits are small compared to multi‑part settings.\n- Dataset/task dependence of gains: On COCOHumanParts the gains are “on par” with BPJDet (some APs lead, others do not). Improvements are not uniform across categories, indicating dependence on dataset composition (multi‑part vs single‑part) and metrics.\n- Decoding assumption: Inference assigns a part to the nearest center among “bodies that are unassigned and also enclose the part.” This decoding requires the detected body box to enclose the part; mislocalized boxes or heavy occlusions can make association fail under this rule (the paper’s decoding step explicitly constrains assignments to enclosing bodies).\n\n2) Learning with Dale’s Law in RNNs (ColEI vs DANNs) – “Learning better with Dale’s Law: A Spectral Perspective”\n- ColEI (column‑constrained EI) spectral pathology: ColEI recurrent weights exhibit a multimodal, dispersed singular‑value spectrum with large singular values, leading to poor learning, instability, and need for gradient clipping. This is especially pronounced in small networks and when the inhibitory population is small (biologically realistic E:I). The paper shows high variance across seeds and strong dependence on E/I ratio and network width.\n- Performance sensitivity to size/EI ratio: Small ColEI networks and networks with few inhibitory units learn markedly worse; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) reveals more “pathological” spectra that correlate with high test error.\n- Sign constraints are not the main driver: Freezing signs explains only part of the performance gap; spectral properties dominate. This underscores a development defect of simple ColEI impositions: they degrade spectra and thus learning.\n- Biological fidelity gaps (for DANNs): Recurrent DANNs perform well but currently omit biologically relevant features (e.g., inhibitory‑to‑inhibitory connections, cell‑type–specific time constants). The paper flags these as directions needed to increase biological realism.\n\n3) JEPA implicit bias (deep linear self‑distillation) – “How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features”\n- Scope/assumption limits: The theoretical results rely on deep linear networks and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances (Σxx, Σxy). The authors state that generalization to nonlinear models and non‑simultaneously‑diagonalizable data remains open; thus conclusions may not hold in more general practical regimes.\n- Depth requirement for the bias: The beneficial JEPA bias toward “influential” (high‑regression‑coefficient) features emerges with deep encoders; it “diminishes substantially” for shallow encoders (L≈1), reducing the purported advantage.\n- Potential vulnerability: The paper notes that JEPA’s focus on predictive, low‑variance/slow features “may shed light on JEPA’s vulnerability to spurious or slow features,” i.e., an implicit bias that can prioritize slowly varying but potentially non‑causal signals.\n\n4) Memory‑efficient 4‑bit optimizers – “Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4‑bit States”\n- Zero‑point problem in second moment: Quantizing v to include a zero code causes many non‑zero v entries to map to zero, which catastrophically distorts the update direction (1/√v) and leads to instability and accuracy loss. This must be fixed (e.g., DE‑0/Linear mappings that exclude zero) for 4‑bit to work; without it, training is frequently unstable (as shown on GPT‑2 Medium E2E‑NLG).\n- Non‑trivial quantization design is required: Robust 4‑bit training needs small blocks (e.g., B128), rank‑1 normalization for v, and a zero‑free mapping. Block/mapping choices that work at 8‑bit can fail at 4‑bit, so the method is sensitive to scheme selection.\n- Potential speed regressions before kernel fusion: For smaller models (e.g., RoBERTa‑L, GPT‑2 Medium), their unfused 4‑bit implementation can be slower than 8‑bit Adam; only with fused operators does speed match/surpass 8‑bit.\n- Task coverage is limited: Authors explicitly note evaluation is limited to language and vision; the applicability to RL, audio, and graphs remains to be demonstrated. They also acknowledge that the “optimal quantization setting probably depends on task/dataset/training details.”\n\n5) INN‑TD (Interpolating Neural Network–Tensor Decomposition) for PDEs\n- Manual structural/hyperparameter design: Accuracy depends on user‑controlled mesh resolution (number and placement of elements per input dimension) and C‑HiDeNN hyperparameters (patch size s, dilation a, reproducing order p), as well as the number of TD modes M. The paper shows that “by controlling mesh density and hyperparameters s and p, INN‑TD can accurately predict,” implying performance is sensitive to these design choices.\n- Mode selection/tuning burden: The total number of modes (and whether to train via boosting or all‑at‑once) must be chosen a priori; the method’s efficiency hinges on capturing the problem’s low‑rank structure with few modes. Poor mode selection can degrade accuracy or efficiency.\n- Scalar‑to‑vector extension not central in main text: The framework in the main text focuses on scalar outputs (vector/tensor outputs are relegated to appendices). While extensions are provided, core exposition and many results center on scalar cases, which may require extra engineering for complex vector/tensor PDE systems.\n- FEM‑style formulation requirements: INN‑TD solves PDEs in a weighted‑residual (Galerkin) integral form and relies on Gaussian quadrature and integration by parts. While this brings accuracy and stability, it also imposes solver‑style setup (test/trial choice, quadrature grids) rather than a purely black‑box training loop.\n\nNotes\n- All points above are drawn directly from the papers’ own results, ablations, discussions, and stated limitations or constraints. No claims are added beyond what is stated or explicitly implied by the algorithmic steps described in the texts."}

**naive 最终答案**

> I have sufficient evidence from the context. Here is my analysis.
> 
> ## Papers matching each element
> 
> **(a) MSE/CE under Adam/AdamW/SGD (optimization)**
> - *Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure* (ICML 2025): SGD, VanillaSGD, Adam, AMSGrad, AdaBound, Yogi, RAdam, Adai, PNM, Lookahead, DiffGrad on LeNet/FCN/ResNet18/ViT over MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10/100; AdamW for GPT-2/TinyLlama (incl. LoRA fine-tuning). Reports test error/accuracy and KS-statistic power-law fits.
> - *4-bit Optimizers* (NeurIPS 2023): Adam/AdamW variants, reports accuracy, F1 (SQuAD), BLEU, SacreBleu.
> - *Automatic Differentiation & Clarke Subdifferentials* (ICLR 2024): SGD/Adam-style training of MNIST MLPs and CIFAR-10 VGG/ResNet, checking proxy-gradient correctness.
> 
> **(b) JEPA implicit bias**
> - *How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks* (NeurIPS 2024): deep-linear analysis of JEPA vs MAE, showing JEPA (latent-space prediction, cosine/regression-coefficient "influential features") prioritizes high-regression-coefficient, low-variance features and suppresses noisy features; ImageNet-1K CCA confirmations. (Cosine-style latent prediction is also analyzed in *On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning*.)
> 
> **(c) Anchor-free one-stage part–body association (COCO)**
> - *PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association* (ICLR 2024): single part-to-body center offset on YOLOv5/v7 backbones; results on COCOHumanParts (e.g., AP 42.7/41.5, AP.5 69.5/67.9) and BodyHands (HandAP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98), plus CrowdHuman face-body and AnimalPose.
> 
> **(d) Dale's-law RNNs via spectral properties (sequential MNIST)**
> - *Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective* (NeurIPS 2023): ColEI vs DANN vs standard RNNs; finds multimodal/dispersed singular-value spectra (rank-one nilpotent column-mean origin) explain poor learning, more than sign constraints; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) predicts performance; tasks include sequential MNIST, adding problem, PTB, object recognition.
> 
> **(e) Sub-byte (≈4-bit) memory-saving optimizers for fine-tuning/LoRA**
> - *4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States* (NeurIPS 2023): B128/DE first-moment, rank-1/linear second-moment quantization with zero-point exclusion; RoBERTa-L (GLUE), SQuAD, GPT-2 Medium E2E-NLG, Transformer WMT14, Swin-T ImageNet, LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning (incl. LoRA repo baselines); up to 57.7% memory saving; 4-bit matches/slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW.
> 
> **(f) Interpretable tensor-decomposition PDE solver with FE-like interpolation**
> - *INN-TD: Interpolating Neural Network-Tensor Decomposition* (ICML-revision): C-HiDeNN locally-supported FEM interpolation + tensor (CP) decomposition; MSE data-driven training, boosting/Galerkin data-free solving, inverse optimization; high-dim Poisson (relative L2 ~1e-8–1e-6), Helmholtz, space-time heat, elasticity.
> 
> ## Development defects / limitations of these methods
> 
> 1. **Hessian power-law (a)**: The KS test relies on approximation and batch sampling (SLQ); only ~top-1000 eigenvalues considered; power-law emerges only for sufficiently deep/wide, well-trained nets and can mislead generalization for pretrained/LoRA models (Hessian trace is a more reliable indicator there); SOTA LLMs excluded due to Hessian cost; no rigorous proof of the power-law, only maximum-entropy heuristics.
> 
> 2. **JEPA analysis (b)**: Restricted to deep *linear* MLPs with specific balanced orthogonal initialization and simultaneously diagonalizable Σ_yx, Σ_xx — real data deviate significantly; generalization to nonlinear networks and non-self-distillation JEPA variants is unexplored. The authors themselves note JEPA's bias toward predictive yet low-variance features may make it *vulnerable to spurious or slow features*, and the objective is susceptible to collapse without stop-gradient tricks.
> 
> 3. **PBADet (c)**: Depends heavily on auxiliary losses and task-alignment — ablations show removing association loss, multi-scale offsets, or task-align drops Cond. Accuracy/JointAP notably. On COCOHumanParts it still shows sub-category AP gaps (original/subordinate splits) and on single-part CrowdHuman its advantage over BPJDet is modest. Small/medium object AP (AP_M) is weaker (e.g., 31.4–31.5), and YOLOv5l6 variants trail YOLOv7 in mMR-2; reliability issues persist for limbs such as legs/arms.
> 
> 4. **Dale's-law RNNs (d)**: ColEI networks are fundamentally limited — they learn worse and with higher variance across all four tasks, benefit disproportionately from gradient clipping (unstable without it), and are pathological at small width or skewed E:I ratio. The work provides only empirical/interpretive (SVD/nilpotent) explanations, not a rigorous convergence theory; open questions remain (e.g., why large ColEI networks learn well despite large max singular value). No general design rule beyond NSE guidance.
> 
> 5. **4-bit optimizers (e)**: Optimal quantization is task/dataset-dependent — the proposed setting may not be globally optimal. Accuracy is "comparable" but with marginal drops on some tasks (e.g., ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2, MT SacreBleu 26.28 vs 26.61); without fused operators 4-bit can be *slower* than 8-bit (RoBERTa-L/GPT-2M). Only language and vision tasks were tested (no broader domains); convergence proof limited to quantized SGD(M), not full Adam analysis.
> 
> 6. **INN-TD (f)**: Hyperparameter sensitivity (mesh density, patch size s, polynomial order p must be tuned node-by-node for adaptivity). Data-free solving relies on bespoke boosting/subspace-iteration + sparse direct solvers (155s on RTX A6000 for one 101-point/100-mode case), which is not a general end-to-end deep method; only regression (MSE) tasks considered for data-driven training; inverse problems depend on the accuracy of the learned parametric surrogate; theoretical convergence shown only for certain PDEs, and FEM comparison made under specific (k, P, t) settings.
> 
> **Overall**: The six works collectively cover reliable training/inference (optimization spectra, 4-bit optimizers), robust representation learning (JEPA), efficient detection (PBADet), biologically-constrained sequence modeling (Dale's-law RNNs), and interpretable scientific computing (INN-TD). Their common weaknesses are: strong idealized assumptions or small-scale scope (JEPA, Hessian), task/hyperparameter sensitivity (4-bit optimizers, INN-TD, PBADet), limited generalization guarantees or empirical-only diagnostics (Dale's-law NSE, Hessian power-law), and lack of validation outside the specific benchmarks/metrics reported.

**community 最终答案**

> ## Papers matching each element
> 
> (a) **Efficient/reliable training & inference via loss-landscape/optimizer analysis** — *"Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure: From CNNs to LLMs"* (ICML 2025). Shows a power-law Hessian spectrum in well-trained networks trained with SGD/Adam/AdamW-family optimizers on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10/100 (LeNet, FCN, ResNet18, GPT-2, TinyLlama+LoRA), using it as a generalization predictor.
> 
> (b) **JEPA implicit bias** — *"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks"* (NeurIPS 2024). Proves JEPA's latent-space (cosine-style, non-contrastive) objective is biased toward high-influence, low-variance "slow" features, unlike MAE; validated on ImageNet-1K with I-JEPA vs MAE (CCA).
> 
> (c) **Anchor-free one-stage part-body association** — **PBADet** (ICLR 2024). Single part-to-body center offset on anchor-free YOLO heads; SOTA on BodyHands and COCO-HumanParts (e.g., AP 42.7–43.0 all-categories), strong F1 vs ED-Pose on COCO.
> 
> (d) **Dale's-law recurrent models, spectral study** — *"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"* (NeurIPS 2023). Compares ColEI/DANN/standard RNNs on adding, **sequential MNIST**, PTB, object recognition; links poor learning to multimodal/dispersed singular-value spectra and normalised SVD entropy.
> 
> (e) **Sub-byte (~4-bit) memory-saving optimizers** — *"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"* (NeurIPS 2023). 4-bit Adam/AdamW with rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion, factorization; up to 57.7% memory savings, matches 32-bit on RoBERTa-L (GLUE, F1), Swin-T (ImageNet), GPT-2 (E2E-NLG), LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning (Alpaca).
> 
> (f) **Interpretable tensor-decomposition neural PDE solver** — **INN-TD**. C-HiDeNN finite-element-like interpolation + tensor decomposition; data-free solver (boosting/PGD, Galerkin) and data-driven training; ~1e-8 relative L2 on high-dim Poisson, solves Helmholtz, S-P-T and inverse problems.
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods
> 
> **(a) Hessian power-law analysis**
> - The structure holds **only for well-trained, overparameterized networks**; it disappears for underparameterized models, limited training data, noisy labels, and large-batch training (abrupt phase transition around batch 640→768). So its diagnostic value is conditional on training already succeeding.
> - It "can sometimes predict" LLM generalization; conventional sharpness measures largely **fail for LLMs**, and power-law/KS metrics are **empirical and correlational** (Pearson correlations, not causal). LoRA-only fine-tuning **does not induce** the structure the way full fine-tuning does.
> - Computationally, computing Hessian spectra of SOTA LLMs is prohibitive (excluded), limiting practical scope; the analysis relies on a KS-test fit that admits ~10 outlier eigenvalues deviating from the fitted line.
> 
> **(b) JEPA implicit-bias theory**
> - Rigorous results are confined to **deep linear MLPs**, balanced orthogonal initialization, and **simultaneously diagonalizable** covariances (Σyx, Σxx)—an assumption the authors admit real data violates; generalization to nonlinear models and non-self-distillation JEPA architectures is unexplored.
> - The implicit bias to low-variance/slow features is a double-edged sword: JEPA can be **vulnerable to spurious or slow features**, and feature prioritization only diverges from MAE when the encoder is **deep**.
> - ImageNet evidence is qualitative (CCA alignment with low-variance PCA subspace) rather than downstream accuracy metrics.
> 
> **(c) PBADet**
> - The single-part-to-body offset is most advantageous for **multi-part** association; on single-part tasks (CrowdHuman face-body) its gain over BPJDet is **marginal** and mMR-2 is only comparable/competitive.
> - Body AP is "comparable" to DETR detectors, not clearly superior; results depend heavily on backbone (YOLOv7 vs YOLOv5l6) and hand-set NMS thresholds (τ_conf/τ_iou).
> - Its superiority over pose estimators (ED-Pose) relies on the fact that pose keypoint outputs are noisy/ambiguous for limbs—so the comparison favors box-based parts by construction; ablations show all three components (association loss, multi-scale offsets, task alignment) are needed to avoid degradation.
> 
> **(d) Dale's-law RNNs**
> - The motivating architecture (ColEI) **trains poorly, with high variance**, and is **unstable without gradient clipping**; performance degrades sharply for small networks with few inhibitory units (biologically realistic E:I ratios).
> - The spectrum pathology is only partially explained (rank-one nilpotent column-mean term), and the analysis is largely empirical; NSE is a **heuristic** diagnostic, not a proven bound.
> - Even with good spectra, **sign constraints still impair learning** (0.7–1% accuracy cost), so Dale's law is not free. DANN models lack biological fidelity (no I→I connections, no cell-type time constants), and I-to-I connectivity is left as future work.
> 
> **(e) 4-bit optimizers**
> - Optimal quantization settings are **task/dataset dependent**; the authors note settings outside their study might be needed for lossless performance. Only **language and vision** tasks were tested—RL, audio, and graph learning are unvalidated.
> - Pretraining (CLS/MT) only reaches **comparable**, not lossless, accuracy; there are small degradation trends. Without **fused operators**, 4-bit is **slower** than 8-bit AdamW (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2).
> - Reported memory savings **saturate at 57.7%** because totals include data/activations/fragmentation (not just optimizer states); factorization is hard to apply when FSDP packs parameters into 1-D arrays (only 4-bit AdamW used for LLaMA).
> 
> **(f) INN-TD**
> - Benchmarks are largely restricted to **smooth, analytically-solvable** problems (Poisson, Helmholtz, heat, elasticity) with known reference solutions; error is relative L2 to analytical/FEM solutions, so robustness to complex/chaotic PDEs is untested.
> - Accuracy is tied to user-chosen **mesh nodes, patch sizes (s), dilation (a), and reproducing orders (p)**—heavy hyperparameter/inductive-bias engineering; the data-free solver uses boosting + subspace iteration + sparse direct solvers rather than standard stochastic training, limiting generality.
> - The KAN comparison is potentially **unfair**: KAN used batch-size 256 for 30%/100% data but full-batch for 10% data (giving it artificially low error); inverse optimization only recovers a few parametric coefficients (k, P). Interpretability is limited to nodal TD values, and scaling/real-world industrial validation remains limited to single-GPU runs.
> 
> **Cross-cutting development concerns:** Most works validate on limited regimes (small/linear models, single datasets, specific optimizers); theoretical claims (b, d, and partly a) rest on simplifying assumptions; efficiency gains (a, e) can invert or disappear outside narrow settings; and perceptual/detection metrics (c) can be gamed by task formulation (part-box vs keypoint). None of the papers offers end-to-end reliable training+inference guarantees across vision, sequence, and scientific computing simultaneously.

</details>

### paperscope:gap:436 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building an end-to-end system that: (1) pretrains detectors from unlabeled videos to reliably link hands/face to the correct person; (2) uses those video embeddings to initialize an RL policy; and (3) gates model outputs with anytime-valid risk thresholds while labeling only the most useful points. We need guidance on avoiding spurious features in self-supervised pretraining (JEPA-style vs reconstruction), dealing with exogenous noise in time-series, anchoring detectors without anchors, and applying active, sequential risk control. Our stack mixes CNNs and Transformers trained with SGD/Adam, standard losses (MSE, cross-entropy), and we’ll evaluate with Precision/F1 on COCO-like data as well as MNIST/CIFAR-100. Please point to works that together cover part–body association, self-distillation biases, spectral constraints in deep nets, and active anytime-valid risk-controlled prediction sets—ideally with insights transferable to vision-language models and adapter-based fine-tuning.Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

**score：3→2（Δ-1）；rounds：4→3（Δ-1）。**

Gold 1：

> {'answer': 'Below are the development defects for each method, drawn only from the provided papers.\n\n1) PBADet (one-stage, anchor-free part–body association)\n- Sensitivity to design choices: Ablations show performance drops without multi-scale formulation (“w/o Multi-scale”) and without task-alignment learning (“w/o Task-align”), indicating the method depends critically on these design elements for accuracy and stability.\n- Limited gains in single-part association: On CrowdHuman (face–body only), advantages are “not as pronounced,” suggesting the approach yields smaller improvements when the task involves a single part rather than multiple parts.\n- Post-processing dependence: Inference requires NMS thresholds and Euclidean matching to nearest body center; these settings are dataset-specific and can affect robustness under occlusion or dense scenes.\n- Dataset-specific hyperparameters: Performance hinges on tuned λ (scaling), K (top-K anchors), and NMS parameters; suboptimal choices degrade metrics (reported declines in ablations).\n\n2) ColEI vs DANN EI recurrent networks (Dale’s Law)\n- ColEI (column-wise EI constraint) defects:\n  • Spectral pathology: Multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra (including large modes) cause exploding/vanishing gradients and poor learning; markedly worse than standard RNNs and DANNs.\n  • Instability and high variance: Training is more unstable and seed-sensitive; requires gradient clipping much more than other networks.\n  • Small-network fragility: Performance and spectra worsen for small nets and for biologically realistic E:I ratios with few inhibitory units; lower normalised SVD entropy correlates with poor learning.\n  • Sign constraints hurt but are not sole culprit: Freezing parameter signs degrades performance, and even without sign constraints, the spectrum remains the dominant issue.\n- DANN (recurrent Dale’s ANNs) caveats:\n  • Biological scope: Models fast feedforward inhibition (PV+), omits inhibitory–inhibitory connections and other interneuron subtypes; less faithful for some biological modeling tasks.\n  • Initialization dependence: Results rely on specific initializations and spectral properties; deviations may reduce benefits.\n\n3) JEPA vs MAE for self-supervised representation learning (deep linear analysis)\n- MAE defects:\n  • Bias toward highly covarying features: Prioritizes reconstruction of high-variance pixels, which can be unpredictable/uninformative for perception; risks learning noisy features.\n- JEPA defects:\n  • Depth-dependent bias: The favorable bias toward influential (high-regression-coefficient) features emerges only with deep encoders; shallow encoders lose this advantage.\n  • Vulnerability to spurious/slow features: Predicting in latent space can over-emphasize slow or spurious features, potentially harming downstream control.\n  • Strong theoretical assumptions: Analysis requires simultaneously diagonalizable covariances and deep linear models; practical generality is limited by these assumptions.\n\n4) Active, anytime-valid risk-controlling prediction sets (betting-based e-processes)\n- I.I.D. requirement: Guarantees are derived for i.i.d. streams; distribution shift and adaptive covariate changes are not handled (flagged as future work).\n- Label-policy constraints: Requires a lower bound q_min on querying probability to ensure nonnegativity and validity; extremely small q_min can invalidate the e-process or slow growth.\n- Predictor dependence: Utility and label efficiency hinge on accurate risk predictors; poor predictors increase variance and slow rejection of unsafe β.\n- Optimality assumptions: The optimal labeling policy and predictor derivations assume existence/regularity (e.g., exp-concavity, existence in Proposition 5); deviations incur regret and slower calibration.\n- Tuning sensitivity: Betting parameter λ must be chosen within bounded ranges; mis-tuning slows wealth growth and delays risk-certified thresholds.\n\n5) Video pretraining for RL (autoencoding, forward modeling, temporal contrastive)\n- Temporal contrastive learning defects:\n  • Failure under exogenous noise: Learns to rely on temporally correlated distractors (e.g., moving background) to solve contrastive tasks, leading to poor latent state recovery and downstream RL performance.\n  • Margin sensitivity: Requires positive margins separating latent states via temporal relationships; violated or small margins impair representation recovery.\n- Forward modeling defects:\n  • Degradation with exogenous noise: More robust than contrastive but still quickly degrades as exogenous noise grows; latent state recovery becomes unreliable.\n  • Dependence on k-selection and data coverage: Requires appropriate multi-step k sampling and good state coverage by the video dataset; weak coverage or fixed k choices can hurt learnability.\n- Autoencoder defects:\n  • Lack of finite-sample guarantees: The paper provides no theoretical guarantees; empirically, performance is unpredictable and domain-dependent (fails in gridworld, works in one VizDoom task).\n- Fundamental limitation with video-only pretraining:\n  • Exponential hardness with exogenous noise: Proven lower bound shows learning compact, frozen representations from video can be exponentially worse than using action-labeled trajectories when exogenous noise is present; highlights a statistical gap vs trajectory-based pretraining.\n  • Strong assumptions for positive results: Upper bounds require noise-free data policies, realizability of model classes, and positive margins; violations negate guarantees.\n'}

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the context, here are the works covering your requested areas, together with their development defects (limitations):
> 
> ## Recommended works
> 
> **Part–body association / anchor-free detectors**
> - **PBADet** (ICLR 2024): one-stage, anchor-free part-body association via a single part-to-body center offset; state-of-the-art on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman; extends to quadruped pose (AnimalPose, AP-10K).
> 
> **JEPA vs reconstruction / self-distillation biases / spurious features**
> - **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024): deep-linear analysis showing JEPA/self-distillation implicitly learns high-influence, low-variance (perceptually relevant) features, whereas MAE reconstruction prioritizes high-variance, uninformative subspaces; JEPA learns "slow features."
> - **LDReg** (ICLR 2024): counters local dimensional collapse via local intrinsic dimensionality regularization (Fisher-Rao metric), improving SSL transfer to COCO detection.
> 
> **Spectral constraints in deep nets**
> - **"Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023): spectral properties of weight matrices at initialization (normalized SVD entropy) matter more than sign constraints.
> - **"Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure"** (ICML 2025): power-law Hessian spectra in CNNs/LLMs; relevant to SGD/Adam training and LoRA-style adapter fine-tuning.
> 
> **Exogenous noise in time-series / video for RL**
> - **"Video-Based Representation Learning for RL in Exogenous Block MDPs"** (ICLR 2024): forward modeling is more robust than temporal contrastive learning to exogenous noise; trajectory-based methods (ACRO) are more robust than any video-only method.
> - **RaMP / "Random Features for Model-Free Planning"**: self-supervised RL pretraining (random-feature Q-bases) that transfers to new rewards via linear regression + MPC — relevant to initializing RL from pretrained embeddings.
> 
> **Active anytime-valid risk-controlled prediction sets**
> - **"Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets"** (Xu, Karampatziakis, Mineiro): extends RCPS to sequential/adaptive data via betting e-processes, with active labeling policies and a label budget; optimal predictor = conditional risk, optimal labeling ∝ risk std; regret bounds.
> 
> ## Development defects (limitations)
> 
> **JEPA/MAE analysis**: theory is restricted to deep *linear* MLPs, special initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances Σyx, Σxx; results may not hold for real data/architectures. JEPA is itself vulnerable to *spurious or slow features* (it can prioritize low-variance features that are irrelevant), and it is prone to representation collapse without stop-grad/spectral tricks. MAE, by contrast, learns features explaining bulk variance that are often uninformative for perception.
> 
> **Exogenous Block MDPs**: a worst-case lower bound shows video data cannot identify the endogenous state (exponential identifiability barrier) — no compact frozen video-pretrained representation can guarantee efficient RL under exogenous noise; temporal contrastive learning fails at *any* noise level (it can exploit noise to minimize the loss), and forward modeling degrades as noise grows; autoencoders have no theory and fail in GridWorld.
> 
> **PBADet**: advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced on the single-part CrowdHuman face-body task; ablations show it depends on association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and task-alignment learning; on COCOHumanParts it is only on par with BPJDet in some AP metrics.
> 
> **RaMP**: Monte-Carlo value estimation has high variance; on pixel observations it only matches (not beats) Dreamer and fails on Pixel Door Open; relies on shared dynamics and finite-horizon MPC approximation of infinite-horizon planning.
> 
> **Active anytime-valid RCPS**: assumes i.i.d. streamed data; requires bounded label policies (Assumption 2) and an existence assumption (Prop 5); risk control holds in expectation only — no guarantees under covariate/label shift (potential extension to ACI noted).
> 
> **LDReg**: LID estimation degrades in high dimensions and uses minibatch nearest neighbors; forcing very low LID can trigger complete collapse; global covariance/variance regularizers barely help.
> 
> **Dale's Law / spectral**: ColEI networks have multimodal, dispersed singular spectra, worse for small networks or few inhibitory units, high variance across runs, and instability without gradient clipping; sign constraints alone are not the cause of poor learning.
> 
> **Hessian power-law**: the power-law structure is lost with small width/depth, limited data, noisy labels, or large-batch training; LoRA-only fine-tuning does *not* induce the power-law Hessian structure that full fine-tuning does — a caveat if you plan adapter-based fine-tuning; SOTA LLMs were excluded due to Hessian computation cost.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the works that cover your pipeline, with their development defects (limitations as reported in the papers):
> 
> **1. Part–body association / anchor-free detection → PBADet** (08b70bc3)
> - Two-stage predecessors (BodyHands, BPJDet) introduce complexity; BPJDet's body-to-part offsets grow with #parts and become invalid when parts are occluded.
> - PBADet itself: a single part-to-body center offset; on CrowdHuman face-body its advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced for this single-part task; it still needs supervised COCO-like data, and its association/displacement branches rely on task-alignment learning (TOOD) for stability.
> 
> **2. Self-distillation biases / JEPA vs MAE → "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (40fde037)
> - Defects: theory is restricted to deep *linear* MLPs, special balanced-orthogonal initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable covariances; non-linear models unexplored. JEPA is susceptible to representation collapse (needs stop-grad), and the paper explicitly flags JEPA's **vulnerability to spurious or slow features** (it prioritizes low-variance "slow" features) — a risk for your spurious-feature concern. Its noise-suppression bias holds mainly for deep encoders and with finite training budgets (learning-order inversion).
> 
> **3. Dimensional collapse / spurious features in SSL → LDReg** (51526068)
> - Defects: LID estimation accuracy degrades in high dimensions and relies on minibatch nearest neighbors; global covariance/variance regularizers barely help; over-regularizing (forcing very low LID) can trigger complete collapse; gains depend on pretraining length.
> 
> **4. Spectral constraints in deep nets → Hessian power-law (582d138d) + Dale's-law RNN spectral study (e63a94c4)**
> - Hessian paper defects: power-law structure is lost with small width/depth, limited data, noisy labels, and large-batch training; sharpness-based measures largely fail as LLM generalization predictors; Hessian computation cost excludes SOTA LLMs; **LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the power-law structure that full fine-tuning does** — a direct caution for your adapter-based fine-tuning.
> - Dale's-law paper defects: naive sign constraints (ColEI) produce multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra, unstable training (needs gradient clipping), and worse, higher-variance learning; spectral properties at initialization matter more than sign constraints.
> 
> **5. Active, anytime-valid risk control → "Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets"** (cda0aa)
> - Defects: assumes i.i.d. streamed data (no covariate/label shift guarantees); label policies must be lower-bounded and an existence assumption (Prop. 5) is required; the risk control is for prediction sets, with bounded-label-policy assumptions that the authors say need relaxing.
> 
> **Exogenous noise in time-series**: the JEPA paper's temporal flickering-image generative model studies the noise/temporal-correlation trade-off — JEPA is slower to learn noisy features and converges to lower-weight amplitudes for them, but its "slow features" bias is also its spurious-feature risk.
> 
> **VLM / adapter transfer**: the Hessian paper's LoRA finding is the most directly transferable caution; LDReg (LID regularization) applies to SSL encoders generally and improves transfer/detection; the contrastive-embedding analysis (160e1407) adds that variance-reduction losses help small-batch training but can suppress meaningful semantic variance, at the cost of an extra hyperparameter.
> 
> In short, the recurring development defects are: (a) theory limited to linear/specialized settings (JEPA), (b) metric estimation instability in high dimensions (LDReg), (c) spectral-structure loss under small scale/noisy labels/LoRA-only tuning (Hessian), (d) i.i.d. and bounded-policy assumptions in the anytime-valid guarantees, and (e) anchor-free part-body association relying on supervised data and showing weaker gains in single-part regimes.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Here’s a concise list of the **development defects / limitations** of the methods described in the paper *“What Does Automatic Differentiation Compute for Neural Networks?”*, extracted directly from the text without fabrication:
> 
> 1. **Strong Assumptions on Bias Parameters and Minibatch Size for Guaranteed Correctness**  
>    - Theorem 1’s guarantee that AD always computes a Clarke subderivative holds **only** when all non‑differentiable neurons have *distinct bias parameters* **and** minibatch size = 1.
>    - Removing either condition (distinct biases or minibatch size = 1) breaks the guarantee, as shown by Lemmas 2 and 3.
> 
> 2. **Dependence on Carefully Chosen Proxy Derivatives**  
>    - For minibatch sizes > 1 (Theorem 4, Theorem 6), correctness requires *specific* proxy derivative choices (a fixed convex combination of left/right derivatives per layer).  
>    - Using default AD framework settings (e.g., PyTorch defaults) may violate these conditions and lead to incorrect outputs.
> 
> 3. **Architectural Restrictions in Some Theorems**  
>    - Theorem 5’s sufficient condition applies to *fully‑connected layers* only, limiting generality.
>    - Distinction between networks satisfying Condition 1 vs. Condition 2: convolutional and many modern architectures fall outside Condition 1 and require separate treatment.
> 
> 4. **Shared Bias Parameters and Maxpool Limitations**  
>    - Theorem 6’s “always correct” result for networks with shared bias parameters requires *no non‑trivial maxpools*.  
>    - Lemma 7 shows correctness can fail in presence of non‑trivial maxpools.
>    - Theorem 8 provides a sufficient condition in the presence of maxpools, but it is **not necessary**—there can still be cases where AD is correct that the condition cannot certify.
> 
> 5. **Sufficient Conditions May Be Conservative**  
>    - Theorem 5 and Theorem 8 offer *sufficient* but not *necessary* conditions for correctness, meaning they may fail to label AD correct in some cases where it actually is.
> 
> 6. **Empirical Verification Scope**  
>    - Experiments check the sufficient conditions in certain practical setups (MNIST FC nets, CIFAR‑10 CNNs), but do not establish universality across all architectures or training regimes.
>    - Real‑world settings outside tested cases might not satisfy the sufficient conditions.
> 
> 7. **Framework‑Dependent Behaviour**  
>    - Results assume AD’s proxy gradients for non‑differentiable functions are elements of their Clarke subdifferential and use a specific tie‑breaking rule in maxpool; differences in AD system implementation can change correctness outcomes.
> 
> 8. **Computational Overhead of Condition Checking**  
>    - Algorithm 1 / 2 to verify Theorem 8’s condition involve extra backward passes and LP solves; although reported overhead is moderate in experiments, it is non‑zero and scales with number of ties in maxpool outputs.
> 
> These limitations identify when the formal correctness results provably apply, where they may fail, and what practical or computational constraints exist.

**naive 最终答案**

> Here is the paper set matching the five topics, followed by the development defects of each method (all from the provided context only).
> 
> ## Matched papers
> 
> 1. **PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association** (ICLR 2024, doc `08b70bc3…`) — one-stage anchor-free part-body association via a single part-to-body center offset; evaluated on COCO-HumanParts (COCO 2017), BodyHands, CrowdHuman; reports AP, Precision/Recall/F1 (vs ED-Pose).
> 2. **What Does Automatic Differentiation Compute for Neural Networks?** (ICLR 2024, doc `c9b4b87f…`) — proves forward/reverse AD returns a Clarke subdifferential for ReLU/maxpool networks under conditions; empirically checked on MNIST MLPs and CIFAR-10 VGG/ResNet.
> 3. **Learning better with Dale’s Law: A Spectral Perspective** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `e63a94c4…`) — spectral/interpretability analysis of excitatory–inhibitory RNNs; ColEI singular values are multimodal/dispersed vs clustered for standard RNNs/DANNs; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with test error.
> 4. **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks** (doc `40fde037…`) — self-supervised joint-embedding (JEPA/self-distillation) biased toward high-influence features, unlike MAE reconstruction losses; analyzed with deep linear models, confirmed on ImageNet-1K.
> 5. **Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `8d5e1455…`) — 4-bit Adam/AdamW optimizer states (B128/dynamic-exponent for first moment; rank-1/linear zero-point-excluded quantizer for second moment); fine-tuning RoBERTa-L, GPT-2, Swin-T, LLaMA-7B/13B/33B, Transformer; up to 57.7% memory savings.
> 
> ## Development defects
> 
> 1. **PBADet**: On CrowdHuman face-body association its advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced; part-to-body offset requires every part to lie in the body box, and anchor-free positives are restricted to points inside boxes; gains come from ablations (association loss, multi-scale offsets, task-alignment), which individually degrade metrics when removed.
> 2. **Autodiff paper**: AD may return arbitrary values when non-differentiable functions/control flow exist; the Clarke-subdifferential guarantee fails for minibatches >1 or shared bias parameters, and shared bias is safe only for trivial maxpools — general maxpool networks can fail; correctness requires an LP-checkable sufficient condition, so it is a verification burden rather than a free guarantee.
> 3. **Dale’s Law paper**: Sign-constrained ColEI networks learn worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs/DANNs; the pathology is traced to initialization singular-value spectra (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure), so performance depends on network size and EI ratio; gradient clipping is needed; the analysis is limited to recurrent weights at initialization and benchmark tasks, not broader architectures.
> 4. **JEPA paper**: The high-influence-feature bias is proven only for deep *linear* networks with special (balanced orthogonal) initialization and simultaneous diagonalizability; generalization to real nonlinear self-distillation is qualitative; noise suppression trades off against temporal correlation, and MAE behavior differs.
> 5. **4-bit optimizer paper**: Optimal quantization settings are task/dataset/training dependent; quantizing both moments causes a marginal accuracy drop; without fused operators it is slower than 8-bit optimizers on small models; the zero-point problem for the second moment requires special quantizers; only language/vision tasks were tested.
> 
> ## Coverage gaps relative to your interests
> 
> - **End-to-end LoRA fine-tuning guidance**: not provided by any document; the 4-bit optimizer paper only cites LoRA as a delta-tuning alternative, the Hessian paper analyzes LoRA adapter spectra (TinyLlama/MathQA), and another work uses LoRA for diffusion fine-tuning — none gives practical End-to-end LoRA guidance.
> - **Metrics/datasets**: no AUROC or CE-vs-MSE comparisons; CIFAR-100 and SVHN are not used by these five papers (CIFAR-100 appears only in a related Hessian-spectrum paper); COCO appears in PBADet (AP/Precision/Recall/F1), and ImageNet in the JEPA and 4-bit-optimizer papers.

**community 最终答案**

> Based only on the provided context, here are the matching papers and an analysis of their development defects.
> 
> ## 1. One-stage anchor-free part–body association (COCO)
> **PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association** (ICLR 2024, doc `08b70bc3…`)
> - Extends anchor-free detection (YOLOv5/7) with a single part-to-body center offset; handles multiple parts without extra offsets. Evaluated on BodyHands, **COCO-HumanParts/COCO-WholeBody**, CrowdHuman; reports AP, JointAP, conditional accuracy, MR-2.
> - **Defects:** advantage over BPJDet is small on the single-part CrowdHuman face-body task; the one-to-one part-to-body mapping (unlike body-to-part offsets) can be invalid when parts are invisible; per-pixel dense inference and multi-scale heads add complexity; results depend heavily on task-alignment learning and multi-scale offsets (ablations show drops without them).
> 
> ## 2. Forward/reverse autodiff and generalized subgradients (MNIST/CIFAR)
> **"What Does Automatic Differentiation Compute for Neural Networks?"** (ICLR 2024, doc `c9b4b87f…`)
> - Proves forward/reverse AD returns a Clarke subderivative for ReLU/maxpool networks under conditions (distinct bias parameters, single minibatch, proper proxy gradients), with empirical checks on **MNIST MLPs and CIFAR-10 VGG/ResNet**.
> - **Defects:** correctness can fail for minibatches >1 or shared biases; general maxpool networks may fail (shared bias safe only for trivial maxpools); conditions are sufficient, not necessary; the practical check relies on an LP-checkable rank condition that doesn't cover all architectures.
> 
> ## 3. Spectral/interpretability analysis of E/I nets under Dale's principle
> **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `e63a94c4…`)
> - Shows column-constrained E/I RNNs (ColEI) have multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra; introduces **normalised SVD entropy (NSE)** as a spectrum-pathology measure anti-correlating with test error; benchmarks: adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition.
> - **Defects:** ColEI trains worse and with higher variance; small networks or few inhibitory units worsen spectra and performance; needs gradient clipping; NSE is a heuristic diagnostic (not the entropy of a probability distribution) and only weakly accounts for the rank-one nilpotent column-mean contribution; eigenvalue analysis is unreliable for non-symmetric (non-orthogonal) weight matrices.
> 
> ## 4. Self-supervised joint embedding biased to high-influence features vs reconstruction
> **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks"** (NeurIPS 2024, doc `40fde037…`)
> - Shows JEPA/self-distillation joint embeddings are implicitly biased toward **high-influence features (high regression coefficients)** compared with MAE-style reconstruction losses; validated via CCA on ImageNet.
> - **Defects:** analysis restricted to deep linear networks, balanced orthogonal initialization and simultaneous diagonalizability; the qualitative claim is only partially supported empirically; no SVHN/CIFAR-100 or CE-vs-MSE/AUROC results in the available context.
> 
> Related SSL work in context (less direct matches): **LDReg** (doc `51526068…`) regularizes local intrinsic dimensionality against dimensional collapse (ImageNet, COCO detection/segmentation), and **"On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning"** (doc `160e1407…`) reports CIFAR-100 top-1 accuracy with variance-reduction loss. Neither reports Precision/AUROC or SVHN.
> 
> ## 5. Memory-efficient 4-bit optimizer states for Adam/AdamW fine-tuning
> **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `8d5e1455…`)
> - 4-bit first/second moments for Adam/AdamW: smaller block size (B128) for the first moment; second moment uses zero-point-excluded linear quantization and rank-1 normalization, optionally factorized ("4-bit Factor"). Fine-tunes RoBERTa-L, Swin-T, GPT-2, Transformer, and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B with ≤57.7% memory savings and accuracy matching 32-bit.
> - **Defects/limits:** optimal quantization appears task-dependent; tested only on language/vision (no SVHN/CIFAR-100); slower than 8-bit without fused kernels; "4-bit Factor" only helps tensors with dimension >1; **no dedicated End-to-end LoRA fine-tuning guidance** — LoRA is only mentioned as related work (frozen weights, low-rank tuning). The Hessian paper (doc `582d138d…`) adds a caveat: LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the power-law Hessian structure that full fine-tuning does.
> 
> ## Coverage gaps
> - **Precision/AUROC:** only appears in an unrelated deepfake-detection paper (DiffusionFake, AUC 75.8→81.9 on FF++→other datasets), not in the five matched topics.
> - **CE vs MSE:** explicit comparisons appear only in unrelated work (e.g., GEEA entity alignment uses BCE vs MSE for different modalities).
> - **SVHN:** no paper in the retrieved context evaluates on SVHN.
> - **End-to-end LoRA fine-tuning practical guidance:** not covered by any paper in the collection; the 4-bit optimizer paper only touches LoRA tangentially.

### paperscope:gap:448 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building an HMI system that needs reliable hand/face–body association on COCO‑style data while also fine‑tuning a large Transformer with LoRA on limited GPUs. I need: a compact anchor‑free detector for part‑to‑body matching in crowded scenes; optimizer states compressed to very low precision (≈4‑bit) to run Adam/AdamW during instruction tuning; guidance on why my joint‑embedding self‑supervised pipeline outperforms masked reconstruction for downstream feedforward classifiers; and assurances that automatic differentiation returns meaningful gradients in deep nets with ReLU, BatchNorm, and maxpools. I also care about interpretability via spectral diagnostics under Dale’s Law, regularization choices (CE vs MSE), and robust metrics like Precision/AUROC on MNIST/CIFAR/ResNet‑50. Are there works that cover these needs end‑to‑end?Please analyze the development defects of these methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> The development defects or limitations mentioned in the paper *What Does Automatic Differentiation Compute for Neural Networks?* can be summarized as:
> 
> 1. **Limited Scope of Main Theorem (Theorem 1)** – The strongest guaranteed correctness result for AD with respect to the Clarke subdifferential for networks with pointwise, piecewise-analytic activations requires **both distinct bias parameters and a minibatch size of one**. This setup is restrictive and not always applicable in practice, especially since minibatch sizes >1 are standard.
> 
> 2. **Necessity of Conditions** – Lemmas 2 and 3 show that **removing either distinct bias parameters or the single-sample minibatch assumption can break correctness**. AD can return a value *not* in the Clarke subdifferential in these cases.
> 
> 3. **Dependence on Special Proxy Derivatives** – Theorem 4 and Theorem 6 require special choices of proxy derivatives (convex combinations of left- and right-hand derivatives, with equal weights within a layer). This requirement may not hold for default AD frameworks, where proxy choices are fixed (e.g., PyTorch’s `ReLU'(0)=0`). Incorrect proxy derivative selection can break theoretical guarantees.
> 
> 4. **Additional Sufficient Conditions May Be Nontrivial to Check** – The sufficiency conditions in Theorems 5 and 8 for general minibatch sizes (including linear independence of certain activation columns or non-empty constraint sets from LP formulations per layer) can be nontrivial to verify, especially in large-scale, complex architectures.
> 
> 5. **Failure in Presence of Non-Trivial Maxpools** – Lemma 7 shows that **non-trivial maxpools can cause AD to produce values outside the Clarke subdifferential**, even when using shared bias parameters and valid proxy derivatives, unless additional sufficient conditions (Theorem 8) are checked.
> 
> 6. **Computational Overhead for Verification** – Verifying Theorem 8’s sufficient condition via Algorithm 1/2 can add overhead during training (∼77% in the ResNet18 CIFAR-10 experiment). While tractable, it still impacts efficiency.
> 
> 7. **Scope Exclusions** – Results focus on Clarke subdifferential correctness; they **do not guarantee correctness for other generalized derivatives**, nor do they treat architectures with certain control-flow or non-analytic ops.
> 
> 8. **Empirical Observations Are Conditional** – While correctness was upheld in tested scenarios, this is contingent on training setups that happened to satisfy the sufficient conditions—**guarantees do not cover all possible inputs/parameters**, especially in adversarial or atypical configurations.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Are there end-to-end works?
> 
> **No.** The collection contains no single work covering all your needs end-to-end. Each need maps to a separate paper:
> 
> | Need | Work found |
> |---|---|
> | Anchor-free part-to-body detector (hand/face–body, COCO-style, crowded) | **PBADet** (ICLR 2024): one-stage anchor-free, single part-to-body center offset, evaluated on BodyHands, COCO-WholeBody, COCO-HumanParts, CrowdHuman |
> | ~4-bit optimizer states for Adam/AdamW during instruction tuning | **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023): 4-bit AdamW/4-bit Factor, LLaMA-7B/13B/33B on Alpaca, up to 57.7% memory saving; LoRA discussed as complementary |
> | Why joint-embedding SSL beats masked reconstruction for downstream classifiers | **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024): JEPA is biased to high-influence features and suppresses noise; MAE ordering depends mainly on eigenvalue λ; I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance perceptual PCA subspace (measured by CCA) |
> | AD gradients meaningful with ReLU/BatchNorm/maxpool | **"What Does Automatic Differentiation Compute for Neural Networks?"** (ICLR 2024): AD almost always returns a Clarke subdifferential element in practical setups (MNIST MLPs, CIFAR-10 VGG/ResNet) |
> | Spectral diagnostics under Dale's Law | **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023): normalized SVD entropy (NSE) as spectrum-pathology diagnostic; also **Hessian power-law paper** (ICML 2025) |
> | CE vs MSE regularization; Precision/AUROC benchmarks on MNIST/CIFAR/ResNet-50 | **Not covered** by any dedicated study here — only incidental mentions (CE in MLM/NAS code, MSE for regression, AUROC in Synthcity, Precision/Recall/F1 in GEEA) |
> 
> ## Development defects of these methods (from context)
> 
> **PBADet**
> - Its advantage over BPJDet is *less pronounced for the single-part face-body task* on CrowdHuman (it leads mainly in body MR-2, only competitive AP).
> - Performance degrades without each design component: removing the association loss, using non-multi-scale center offsets, or dropping task-alignment learning all reduce metrics (Hand AP, conditional accuracy, Joint AP).
> - Dense per-pixel prediction across multi-scale feature maps adds inference complexity; anchor-free recall can suffer vs anchor-based near-center points.
> 
> **4-bit optimizers**
> - *Slower than 8-bit AdamW* on small models (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2 Medium) because operators are not fused; speed parity only after fusion.
> - Optimal quantization settings are *task/dataset-dependent*; the paper admits settings outside its study may be needed for lossless performance.
> - Only language/vision tasks tested; reported memory savings (57.7%) saturate because total memory (activations, fragments) is counted.
> 
> **JEPA-vs-MAE analysis**
> - Theory is restricted to *deep linear MLPs, special balanced-orthogonal initialization, and simultaneously diagonalizable networks*; generalization to real nonlinear nets is only qualitative.
> - JEPA objectives are *susceptible to collapse* (need predictor/distillation tricks); MAE is shown to suffer dimensional collapse (LDReg paper).
> 
> **AD/Clarke-subdifferential paper**
> - AD can return values *outside the Clarke subdifferential* when minibatch size ≥ 2 or bias parameters are absent; shared biases are safe only for trivial maxpools — general maxpool networks can fail.
> - Correctness relies on *proper proxy-gradient choices* and an LP-checkable rank condition that must be verified per network; it is not guaranteed for arbitrary architectures.
> 
> **Dale's Law spectral paper**
> - Naïve EI partitioning (ColEI) *impairs learning*: multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra (from a rank-one nilpotent column-mean term) cause instability without gradient clipping, high variance, worse performance for small networks/fewer I units.
> - The defect is spectral, not the sign constraints — so the fix (DANN-style architecture) is an architectural redesign, and NSE only predicts performance *at initialization*, not during training.
> 
> **Hessian power-law (spectral diagnostics)**
> - The power-law structure *disappears* with small width/depth, limited data, noisy labels, or large-batch training; *LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce it* the way full fine-tuning does — limiting its use for your LoRA setup.
> - SOTA LLMs are excluded by Hessian computation cost; power-law goodness and sharpness capture *different* regimes, so it is not a universal generalization predictor.
> 
> **LDReg (SSL representation quality)**
> - LID estimation *degrades as dimensionality increases* and uses only minibatch nearest neighbors (less accurate than full-dataset).
> - Assumes higher dimensionality is always desirable and needs a tunable β; effective rank correlates inconsistently across different SSL methods (similar ranks, different accuracy).
> 
> **Bottom line:** use PBADet + the 4-bit optimizer paper + the JEPA analysis + the AD paper as the matching works; the Dale's Law and Hessian papers give interpretability diagnostics but with the caveats above; **CE-vs-MSE and Precision/AUROC benchmarking on MNIST/CIFAR/ResNet-50 are not addressed** by any work in this collection.

**community 最终答案**

> **Short answer:** No single work covers all your needs end-to-end. Each need maps to a **separate paper** in this collection, and one need (Precision/AUROC on MNIST/CIFAR/ResNet-50 with CE-vs-MSE regularization) is only **partially** supported.
> 
> **Where each need is covered:**
> 1. **Anchor-free part-to-body detection (crowded scenes)** — *PBADet* (one-stage, anchor-free, single part-to-body center offset, evaluated on COCO-WholeBody, COCO-HumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman). This directly fits your HMI hand/face-body association use case.
> 2. **4-bit optimizer states for Adam/AdamW during instruction tuning on limited GPUs** — *"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"* (NeurIPS 2023): 4-bit AdamW/4-bit Factor with B128 + rank-1 normalization and zero-point-excluding linear quantizer; tested on LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning on Alpaca, matches 32-bit AdamW, enables LLaMA-7B on a single 80GB GPU. LoRA is discussed as a compatible complementary technique.
> 3. **Why joint-embedding SSL beats masked reconstruction for downstream (linear) classifiers** — *"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"*: JEPA/self-distillation is biased toward high-influence features and suppresses noise, whereas MAE's feature ordering depends mainly on eigenvalue magnitude; I-JEPA features align faster to the perceptual PCA subspace. *LDReg* adds that MAE is prone to dimensional collapse and that local-dimensionality regularization improves linear-evaluation accuracy (ResNet-50 on ImageNet/CIFAR-10/100).
> 4. **AD gradients in nets with ReLU + BatchNorm + maxpool** — *"What Does Automatic Differentiation Compute for Neural Networks?"* (ICLR 2024): AD returns a Clarke subdifferential element for pointwise piecewise-analytic activations (ReLU) with distinct biases (batch=1), and with proper proxy gradients for arbitrary batch sizes; covers convolution + BatchNorm + maxpool + residual nets; empirically verified on MNIST MLPs and CIFAR-10 VGG/ResNet.
> 5. **Spectral diagnostics under Dale's Law** — *"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"*: singular-value spectrum and normalized SVD entropy (NSE) diagnose why Dale's-Law-constrained (ColEI) RNNs train poorly; spectral properties matter more than sign constraints.
> 6. **CE vs MSE regularization, Precision/AUROC on MNIST/CIFAR/ResNet-50** — only partial: the *shallow-ReLU implicit-bias* paper analyzes square (MSE) loss and implicit rank/norm minimization in ReLU nets; the *power-law Hessian* paper benchmarks LeNet/FCN/ResNet-18 on MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/CIFAR-10/100 and links spectral structure to generalization, but **no retrieved work reports Precision/AUROC** on these datasets. That specific evaluation need is **not covered**.
> 
> **Development defects / limitations of the methods:**
> 
> - **PBADet**: its advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced on the single-part face-body task (CrowdHuman); relies on YOLOv7/v5 backbones; part-body association can be challenged under heavy occlusion, and one-to-one correspondence is assumed rather than guaranteed in all crowded configurations.
> - **4-bit optimizers**: optimal quantization is task/dataset-dependent (task-specific settings could beat the fixed recipe); only language and vision tasks tested; without fused operators, 4-bit AdamW is *slower* than 8-bit on smaller models (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2); quantizing both first and second moments causes a marginal accuracy drop; the second-moment zero-point problem requires special handling.
> - **JEPA analysis**: proofs are for deep *linear* networks with special (balanced orthogonal, simultaneously diagonalizable) initializations; nonlinear networks are only qualitatively supported by ImageNet experiments. LDReg notes MAE/contrastive methods are susceptible to (local) dimensional collapse, and LDReg's LID estimation degrades in high dimensions and relies on minibatch neighbors.
> - **AD correctness**: AD is *not* guaranteed to return a Clarke subdifferential when the minibatch is ≥2 and bias parameters are absent/shared, or for general maxpool networks with shared biases; correctness rests on sufficient conditions (e.g., a rank condition) that are verified only empirically — failure cases exist even though practical training almost always satisfies them.
> - **Dale's-Law spectral work**: ColEI networks show higher variance and instability (gradient clipping is needed); spectra worsen for small networks with few inhibitory units; the origin of the multimodal spectrum and why large ColEI networks still learn are left as open theoretical questions.
> - **MSE/implicit-bias analysis**: restricted to a single hidden-layer ReLU network learning one teacher neuron, gradient flow from small initialization, and correlated inputs (angles < π/4); extensions to multi-layer/other activations are explicitly open.
> 
> So: the four technical pillars (detector, 4-bit optimizer, JEPA-vs-MAE explanation, AD correctness) plus Dale's-Law spectral diagnostics each have dedicated works with known limitations, but the CE-vs-MSE + Precision/AUROC validation on MNIST/CIFAR/ResNet-50 is not established by any of these works.

</details>
